```
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error getting request for apiKey: DESCRIBE_GROUPS,
apiVersion: 5, connectionId: …, listenerName: ListenerName(PLAINTEXT), principal: User:ANONYMOUS
Caused by: java.nio.BufferUnderflowException
	at org.apache.kafka.common.utils.ByteUtils.readUnsignedVarint(ByteUtils.java:146)
```

The last two are bodies, not versions: a JoinGroup **v1** frame carrying a **v0** body — the key and the version are
served, the bytes behind them are not — and a DescribeGroups **v5** frame whose compact array announces three groups
and carries none, or which forgets the tagged-field section at the end of its body. **A flexible frame is refused
exactly like any other malformed one**: there is no error code for a length the broker cannot follow, the
`readUnsignedVarint` in the stack trace is the only hint, and the connection is gone.

Note the first example: the version of the *error* moves with the release. On 1.1.1 the connection died for
OffsetCommit **v4**, which a 2.8.2 broker serves; the frame that dies here is v9. The same holds for every api this
line raises, which is exactly why the test that pins this behaviour derives its frames from the served api table
instead of hard-coding version numbers.

For a client this means:

* The answer to "why did my request never come back" is "the broker hung up", not "the broker dropped it". A
  read on that connection ends in the end of the stream, which this client reports as `NetworkException` (code 13),
  not in a request timeout.
* Only that one connection is lost. The broker itself is unaffected, and the next connection is answered normally.
* A client must never send a version it has not seen in an ApiVersions answer, and never a **flexible** frame to a
  version that is not flexible, or the other way round.

There is exactly **one** exception, and it is verified by the probe:

**ApiVersions answers an unknown version instead of closing.** `RequestContext.parseRequest()` @ 2.8.2 special-cases
key 18 before it parses anything: `isUnsupportedApiVersionsRequest()` rebuilds the request as an
`ApiVersionsRequest(new ApiVersionsRequestData(), (short) 0, header.apiVersion())` and never touches the body, so
that `KafkaApis.handleApiVersionsRequest` sees `hasUnsupportedRequestVersion` and answers
`getErrorResponse(Errors.UNSUPPORTED_VERSION)` — the error code **35**, written in the layout of **version 0** no
matter which version was asked for. The connection survives it, which is what makes the answer usable: a client that
guessed too high reads the 35 and retries with a version it knows. Two details of that answer changed in Kafka 2.4:

* the array is **not empty any more**. KIP-511 fills it with the one row of the ApiVersions api itself
  (`18 0 3` on this container), so that the client learns *which* version to ask for instead of only that it asked
  wrongly. A 1.1.1 broker answered `00 00 00 00` here.
* the **request header still has to be the one the requested version prescribes**. `RequestHeader.parse` @ 2.8.2
  reads the api key and the api version and asks `ApiKeys.forId(apiKey).requestHeaderVersion(apiVersion)` how to
  read the rest of the header, *before* anything validates the version — and for ApiVersions that answer is the
  header **v2** for every version above 2, served or not. A v4 frame with the plain header of the versions 0 to 2 is
  therefore a parse failure like any other:

```
ERROR Closing socket for … because of error (kafka.network.Processor)
org.apache.kafka.common.errors.InvalidRequestException: Error parsing request header. Our best guess of the
apiKey is: 18
Caused by: java.nio.BufferUnderflowException
	at org.apache.kafka.common.utils.ByteUtils.readUnsignedVarint(ByteUtils.java:146)
```

  while the same frame with an empty tag buffer behind the client id is answered with the 35. "Raise the version
  until the broker complains" is therefore not a strategy a client can use above Kafka 2.3 without also raising the
  header.

### Every api of the table validates its version

*Up to Kafka 0.11 this section described the opposite, and its heading was "The last Scala api does not check its
version".* Kafka 0.10 moved every api but one to the schemas of the Java client, which validate the version, and
0.11 did not finish the job either: the exception was **ControlledShutdown (key 7)**, whose frame `RequestChannel`
still handed to the Scala `ControlledShutdownRequest.readFrom(buffer)` before the request header was parsed at all,
and that parser only asked whether the version was above 0, to decide whether a client id followed. A 0.9 to 0.11
broker therefore answered key 7 with **any** version, although its ApiVersions answer reported the single version 1
for it.

**Kafka 1.0 removed the exception** — `ControlledShutdownRequest` became an ordinary request class, and the one
thing that really is special about its v0, a request header without a client id, became a schema of its own — and
Kafka 2.4 made that schema a specification like every other: `RequestHeader.json` @ 2.8.2 declares three header
versions, `"validVersions": "0-2"`, with the comment *"Version 0 of the RequestHeader is only used by v0 of
ControlledShutdownRequest"* and the `ClientId` field marked `"versions": "1+"`.

So on this line key 7 carries the whole history of the request header in one api, and the probe sends all four of
its versions: **v0** with the header v0 (no client id), **v1** and **v2** with the common header v1, and **v3** —
the flexible version of Kafka 2.4 — with the header v2 and a compact body. All four are answered with the code 8
(`BrokerNotAvailable`) for a broker id the controller does not know, and **v4** closes the connection like every
other version above the table.

Every other key of the table validates its version the same way, including the fourteen that Kafka 2.x added: a
2.8.2 broker closes the connection for Produce v10, Fetch v13, Metadata v12, ElectLeaders v3, DescribeCluster v1 and
every other "one above the table" frame alike, and for the api key **65** (`DescribeTransactions`, Kafka 3.0) as
well. Every one of those frames is *served* by a 3.9.2 node, and its "one above the table" — Produce v12, Fetch
v18, Metadata v13, ElectLeaders v3 still, DescribeCluster v2 and the key 88 — closes the connection the same way,
measured by the probe of the foundation (the log line is now `… which is not enabled` for every version above the
table, see the note above). ControlledShutdown, whose four versions the paragraph above measured on the 2.8.2
broker, is not served on a client listener of the KRaft node at all: all four frames (v0 with its header v0
included) close the connection with `Received request api key CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN with version N which is not
enabled`, and the code 8 of an unknown broker id can no longer be observed from a client.

### What is not in Kafka 4.3.1

Everything below is later than Kafka 4.3.1, or a deliberate omission of this line, and must not appear here:

* **The api keys above 92.** `ApiKeys.java` @ 4.3.1 ends at `DELETE_SHARE_GROUP_OFFSETS` (92); `ApiKeys` of this
  branch stops at **92**, and the api key 93 is what the probe sends to see what a node does with a key it cannot
  name.
* **The error codes above 133**: `Errors.java` @ 4.3.1 ends at `SHARE_SESSION_LIMIT_REACHED` (133).
  `KafkaException::fromCode()` answers an unknown code with `UnknownErrorException`, which is what a client should
  do with a code it has never heard of.
* **The versions a 4.4 release adds**, and the unstable versions of 4.3.1 — InitProducerId v6 (the two-phase
  commit of KIP-939) is `latestVersionUnstable` and not served by the node.
* **The versions Kafka 4.x adds that this line has not reached yet** are *in* this document — every row of the
  api-key table names them — but not on the wire of this branch: the client sends the 3.9.2 ceiling of every api
  until the milestone that raises it lands.
* **Streams groups (KIP-1071)**: the apis 88 and 89 and the codes 130 to 132 are declared and probed; nothing sends
  them. Out by decision of the owner.
* **Client metrics (71, 72, 74)**: wire only, by decision — classes and vectors of what a node without a
  client-metrics receiver answers, no client method, and no `metrics.reporter` plugin in the container.
* **The raft, controller and lifecycle apis 52 to 54, 56, 58, 59, 62, 63, 67, 70, 73 and 82**: probe only. The four
  controller apis a client listener serves are in: DescribeQuorum (55) is implemented, UnregisterBroker (64) is
  probed, and AddRaftVoter (80) and RemoveRaftVoter (81) get admin methods on this line.
* **The share-group state apis 83 to 87**: the share coordinator's own apis, **wire only** by decision — classes
  and vectors, no client method.
* **Tiered storage beyond the wire**: the offsets of ListOffsets v8, v9 and v11 and the code 109 of Fetch v14 are
  frames; no test of this repository configures a remote log.
* **SASL/SCRAM, SASL/OAUTHBEARER and SASL/GSSAPI.** The transport of this line speaks PLAIN over SASL_PLAINTEXT and
  SASL_SSL, in the framed exchange of KIP-152; a delegation token can be *issued* by the apis 38 to 41 but not
  *used*, and a SCRAM credential can be created and described through the apis 50 and 51 but not logged in with,
  because both mean SASL/SCRAM.
* **Cooperative rebalancing** (KIP-429) and the subscription v1/v2 of the embedded consumer protocol: a
  client-library feature on top of the wire; the assignors of the classic protocol of this package stay the range
  and round-robin ones. The **server-side** assignment of the KIP-848 protocol is a different thing, and it is in.

## ApiVersions API (key 18, v0 to v4)

Asks a broker which api keys and versions it serves. Kafka 0.10.0 added it, and it is the only request whose answer
tells a client what the peer on the other side speaks; on the two lowest lines of this repository there is no such
api, and the api-key table had to be probed frame by frame. Kafka 0.11 raised it to **version 1**, Kafka 2.0 to
**version 2**, Kafka 2.4 to **version 3** — the first flexible frame of the whole protocol — and Kafka 3.9 to
**version 4**, the version this client sends, which adds no field to the version 3 at all.

```
ApiVersionsRequest (Version: 0 … 2) =>

ApiVersionsRequest (Version: 3 … 4) => ClientSoftwareName ClientSoftwareVersion TAG_BUFFER
  ClientSoftwareName    => compact_string
  ClientSoftwareVersion => compact_string
```

The request has **no body at all** in the versions 0, 1 and 2 — *"Versions 0 through 2 of ApiVersionsRequest are the
same"*, `ApiVersionsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 — so the whole frame is 4 bytes of `Size` plus 8 bytes of header plus the
client id, and the only difference between them is the `ApiVersion` field of the header.

**Version 3 carries the two fields of KIP-511**, and they are not the client id: the client id names the
*application* and may be anything, these two name the client *library* and its version, so that a broker can count
`kafka.server:type=ClientMetrics` per library instead of guessing. The broker matches both against
`[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-.]*[a-zA-Z0-9])?` (`ApiVersionsRequest.isValid()`) and answers the error code **42**
(`InvalidRequest`) when either fails — measured on the container with an empty name, an empty version, a name that
contains a `/` and a name that starts with a `-`, and captured as the vector
`apiversions.response.v3.invalid-software-name`. This client sends `lisachenko-kafka-client` and the Kafka line it
speaks, `3.9`, as `ApiVersionsRequest::CLIENT_SOFTWARE_NAME` and `::CLIENT_SOFTWARE_VERSION`.

```
ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 0) => ErrorCode [ApiKey MinVersion MaxVersion]
  ErrorCode  => int16
  ApiKey     => int16
  MinVersion => int16
  MaxVersion => int16

ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 1) => ErrorCode [ApiKey MinVersion MaxVersion] ThrottleTimeMs
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32

ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 2) => the frame of version 1, byte for byte

ApiVersionsResponse (Version: 3 … 4) => ErrorCode compact_[ApiKey MinVersion MaxVersion TAG_BUFFER] ThrottleTimeMs TAG_BUFFER
  TAG_BUFFER of the body =>
    tag 0 => SupportedFeatures  compact_[Name MinVersion MaxVersion TAG_BUFFER]
    tag 1 => FinalizedFeaturesEpoch  int64, default -1
    tag 2 => FinalizedFeatures  compact_[Name MaxVersionLevel MinVersionLevel TAG_BUFFER]
```

* `ErrorCode` belongs to the whole answer and is `0` or **35** (`UnsupportedVersion`).
* One entry per api the broker serves **on the listener the request arrived on**, in ascending order of `ApiKey`,
  including the broker-to-broker keys 4, 5, 6, 27 and 56 that no client ever sends. Both version bounds are
  **inclusive**, and the entry itself has no version of its own: the versions 0, 1 and 2 use the same three int16
  fields for it.
* A 2.8.2 broker answers with the **56** keys of the api-key table above. A client must not assume that set — the
  whole point of the api is that a later broker reports more and an older one reports fewer, and a KRaft controller
  or a broker with another `inter.broker.protocol.version` reports something else again.

**`ThrottleTimeMs` closes this answer instead of opening it.** KIP-124 gave fifteen apis of Kafka 0.11 a throttle
time and put it in front of the body in every one of them, and every api Kafka 1.x and 2.x add leads with it as
well, with exactly one exception, this api, where the field is appended. The reason is the paragraph below: the
answer to a version the broker cannot parse is written in the version 0 layout, so the `ErrorCode` has to sit at the
same offset in both versions or a client that guessed too high could not read it. Without a `request_percentage`
quota the field is 0, and an ApiVersions request is the last request a quota would ever throttle.

**What version 2 changes is not the frame but the moment it arrives.** KIP-219 (Kafka 2.0) bumped this api together
with almost every other one: a broker that has to throttle a request of the bumped version answers **first** and
mutes the channel for the throttle window afterwards, where a broker that has to throttle an older version mutes the
channel first and answers at the end of it. A client that sends a bumped version therefore promises to honour
`throttle_time_ms` itself. `ApiVersionsResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 writes it down as *"Starting in version 2, on quota
violation, brokers send out responses before throttling"*, and the schema of v2 is the schema of v1.

**What version 3 changes is the encoding, and one thing about it is unique in the protocol.** The body is flexible —
the api array counts `56 + 1` in a single byte, every entry ends in a tag buffer of its own, and the body ends in
one that carries the three features of KIP-584 — but the **response header stays v0**: no tag buffer behind the
correlation id, so that the error code sits where a client of any version can read it. `ApiVersionsResponse.json`
says so in as many words (*"Tagged fields are only supported in the body but not in the header. The length of the
header must not change in order to guarantee the backward compatibility"*), and it is the only api of Kafka 2.8.2
whose two headers disagree that way: the *request* v3 uses the header v2.

The three tagged fields are the feature mechanism of **KIP-584**, which was meant to replace
`inter.broker.protocol.version` in a KRaft cluster: `supported_features` (tag 0) is what the broker can do,
`finalized_features` (tag 2) what the cluster agreed on, and `finalized_features_epoch` (tag 1) the version of that
agreement. **A ZooKeeper-backed 2.8.2 broker answers exactly one of them**, tag 1 with the value `0`: it supports no
feature, has finalized none, and the epoch is on the wire only because its default is `-1` — a tagged field whose
value is the default is left out, so the `0` of the feature ZooKeeper node has to be written. That is the whole
tagged-field section of the answer, `01 01 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00`, and it is the shortest demonstration of the
rule that governs every tagged field of the protocol.

**What version 4 changes is neither the frame nor the encoding but one filter.** Kafka 3.9 bumped this api for
KAFKA-17011, and the comment above its `validVersions` @ 3.9.2 is the whole specification of the bump: *"Version 4
fixes KAFKA-17011, which blocked SupportedFeatures.MinVersion in the response from being 0"*. A **supported
feature** whose `min_version` is 0 could not be reported before, because the clients of Kafka 3.0 to 3.8 read a 0
minimum as "there is no such feature" and would have refused the cluster; so a broker simply leaves such a feature
out of the tagged field 0 of every answer below the version 4
(`ApiVersionsResponse.maybeFilterSupportedFeatureKeys` @ 3.9.2), and a client that asks for the version 4 declares
that it can read it.

On the node of this line the feature in question is **`kraft.version`** (KIP-853), supported 0 to 1 — 0 being the
static `controller.quorum.voters` of KIP-595 and 1 the reconfigurable voter set the raft-voter apis 80 and 81
change. The two answers were captured seconds apart, and the whole difference between them is that one entry:

| | v3 (`apiversions.response.v3.kraft-node`) | v4 (`apiversions.response.v4`) |
|---|---|---|
| Size | **499** bytes | **518** bytes |
| Api rows | the same 61 | the same 61 |
| `supported_features` (tag 0) | `metadata.version` 1…21 | `kraft.version` **0**…1, `metadata.version` 1…21 |
| `finalized_features_epoch` (tag 1) | the offset of the metadata log | the same |
| `finalized_features` (tag 2) | `metadata.version` 21/21 | the same — a feature finalized at the level **0** is not in the map at all |

Nineteen bytes, and they are the reason the version exists. The **request** of the two is one frame with one byte
changed, and a version 5 is answered with the 35 in the version 0 layout like any other unknown version.

`Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\Request\ApiVersionsResponse` indexes the array by `ApiKey`, so a caller asks for one api
directly (`supports(ApiKeys::FETCH, 12)`, `maxVersionOf(ApiKeys::METADATA)`) and reads the features of KIP-584 from
`$supportedFeatures`, `$finalizedFeaturesEpoch` and `$finalizedFeatures`; `ApiVersionsResponseV3`,
`ApiVersionsResponseV2`, `ApiVersionsResponseV1` and `ApiVersionsResponseV0` are the same class with the version
constant lowered, and `ApiVersionsRequestV3`, `ApiVersionsRequestV2`, `ApiVersionsRequestV1` and
`ApiVersionsRequestV0` the same request with the lower version in its header — the v3 with the body of v3, the
three below it without a body at all.
`Client::apiVersions(Node $node)` returns the whole response and `Admin\AdminClient::getApiVersions(Node $node)`
the indexed array; every broker answers for itself, so a rolling upgrade shows up as brokers with different ranges.

**This client does not negotiate with the answer.** Like the lines below it, it sends the fixed versions a broker of
its own Kafka release serves — the "Implemented here" column of the api-key table — and the api is there to report
what the peer is, not to choose a version at runtime.

Three properties make the request usable as the *first* frame on a connection, and all three are verified against
the container:

1. **An unknown version is answered, not punished.** Every other key or version a 2.8.2 broker cannot parse costs
   the connection; ApiVersions is special-cased in `RequestContext.parseRequest()`, so a version it does not serve
   comes back as the error code 35 in the layout of **version 0**, and the connection stays open. Since Kafka 2.4
   (KIP-511) the array of that answer carries the single row of ApiVersions itself instead of being empty, and since
   the same release the frame has to carry the **request header v2** as soon as the version asked for is above 2 —
   both are described under "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection" above, and both are what the
   vector `apiversions.response.v0.unsupported-version` shows.
2. **It is answered before authentication.** On a SASL listener the broker answers ApiVersions while the connection
   is still unauthenticated (`KafkaApis.handleApiVersionsRequest` says so in a comment), so a client can learn the
   surface of a broker before it knows whether it may talk to it at all. On an SSL listener the TLS handshake still
   comes first.
3. **It is cheap.** The request carries no state, changes nothing, and the answer of a 2.8.2 broker is 350 bytes in
   the versions 1 and 2 (346 in version 0) with a 23-character client id. The **v3** answer is 414 bytes: the
   compact array saves three bytes on its count and the 56 entries cost one tag buffer each, so the flexible
   encoding is *longer* here — it pays off where a frame carries strings, not fixed-width triples. On the 3.9.2
   node, with five more keys and the features of a KRaft cluster in the tagged section, the same answer is **499**
   bytes at the version 3 and **518** at the version 4.

A broker of a lower line answers fewer keys, and one older than 0.10 has no key 18 at all: a **0.9.0.1** broker
drops the frame and never answers it, a **0.8.2.2** broker closes the socket. "No answer at all" is therefore how a
client recognises a pre-0.10 peer — there is no error code for it. A peer below Kafka 3.9 answers the
version 4 request of this line with the error code 35 in the version 0 layout, and has to be asked again with
`ApiVersionsRequestV3`, `ApiVersionsRequestV2`, `ApiVersionsRequestV1` or `ApiVersionsRequestV0` — which is exactly
the negotiation KIP-511 had in mind when it put the version range of this api into that error answer. On this line
that answer is what a 2.8.2 broker of the line below sends: it serves v0 to v3 and refuses the v4.

## MessageSet and Message

The message set format is shared by the Produce and Fetch APIs and by the on-disk log. Note that a `MessageSet` is
**not** preceded by an `int32` element count like a regular array — it is a raw byte region whose length is given by
the surrounding `MessageSetSize` field.

Kafka 0.10.0 added **message format v1** (KIP-31 and KIP-32) next to the format v0 of 0.8 and 0.9. A 0.10.2.2 broker
reads and writes both, and the `MagicByte` of a message says which one it is in — it is the discriminator that has to
be read before the rest of the message:

```
MessageSet => [Offset MessageSize Message]
  Offset      => int64
  MessageSize => int32

Message (MagicByte = 0) => Crc MagicByte Attributes Key Value
  Crc        => int32
  MagicByte  => int8
  Attributes => int8
  Key        => bytes
  Value      => bytes

Message (MagicByte = 1) => Crc MagicByte Attributes Timestamp Key Value
  Crc        => int32
  MagicByte  => int8
  Attributes => int8
  Timestamp  => int64
  Key        => bytes
  Value      => bytes
```

* `Crc` — CRC-32 (IEEE, the same polynomial as `crc32()` in PHP) of the message bytes that follow the CRC field,
  i.e. of `MagicByte Attributes [Timestamp] Key Value`. The `Timestamp` of a v1 message is part of the checksum.
* `Attributes`:

  | Bits | Meaning | Values |
  |------|---------|--------|
  | 0–2  | compression codec | 0 none, 1 gzip, 2 snappy, **3 lz4** |
  | 3    | timestamp type (v1 only) | 0 `CreateTime`, 1 `LogAppendTime` |
  | 4–7  | reserved, always 0 | |

  All four codecs are implemented by this client. In a message of format v0 bit 3 is reserved and stays 0.
* `Timestamp` — milliseconds since the epoch, or **-1** (`Message.NoTimestamp`) for a message that carries none. The
  broker accepts -1 and stores it as it is; `message.timestamp.difference.max.ms` (unlimited by default) is what
  bounds a `CreateTime` that is far away from the clock of the broker, and a violation is answered with
  **32 `InvalidTimestamp`**.
* The timestamp type is a property of the **topic** (`message.timestamp.type`, `CreateTime` by default): with
  `LogAppendTime` the broker overwrites the timestamp of every message it appends with its own clock and sets bit 3
  of the attributes.
* A compressed message is a regular message whose `Value` is a complete, compressed `MessageSet`.
* The server is allowed to return a **partial message at the end of a message set**; clients must silently drop a
  trailing message that is shorter than its announced size. The size of the smallest possible message —
  `MinMessageOverhead`, 14 bytes — is the one of a format v0 message without key and value, and a `MessageSize`
  below it means a corrupt set (a format v1 message without key and value is 22 bytes).

### Offsets inside a compressed message set

The `Offset` of the entries of a *produced* set is ignored: the broker assigns the real offsets when it appends the
set, so a producer numbers its messages 0, 1, 2 … Inside a **compressed** set the two message formats differ:

* **v0** — the broker rewrites the offset of every inner message with the absolute offset of the log.
* **v1** — the inner offsets stay **relative** (0, 1, 2 …) and only the offset of the **wrapper** message is
  rewritten, with the absolute offset of the *last* inner message. A reader has to decompress the whole set to see
  the last relative offset before it can translate the others:

      absolute = wrapperOffset - lastInnerOffset + innerOffset

  (`ByteBufferMessageSet.scala` and `RecordsIterator.DeepRecordsIterator` @ 0.10.2.2). The reason is streaming
  compression: the relative offset of an inner message is known while it is written, its absolute one is not.
  The vectors `messageformat.v1.createtime.gzip` and `messageformat.v0.lz4.broken-checksum` below are the same three
  records at the offsets 3, 4 and 5 in both formats: relative `0, 1, 2` under a wrapper at offset 5 in v1, absolute
  `3, 4, 5` under the very same wrapper offset in v0.

### Timestamps inside a compressed message set

The wrapper message of a v1 set carries the timestamp of the whole batch, and it is the only message whose
attributes are meaningful:

* the timestamp type of the wrapper applies to **every** message of the set;
* with `CreateTime` the wrapper carries the **largest** timestamp of its inner messages, and every inner message
  keeps its own;
* with `LogAppendTime` the wrapper carries the append time of the batch and the timestamps of the inner messages are
  **ignored** — the broker does not even rewrite them, as `messageformat.v1.logappendtime.gzip` below shows: the
  wrapper announces `0x09` (gzip + LogAppendTime) and the append time, while the compressed inner messages still
  hold the `CreateTime` values of the producer;
* a producer must write `CreateTime` in the attributes of every inner message, otherwise the broker rejects the set.

### The lz4 codec and the KAFKA-3160 checksum

The `Value` of an lz4 message is an **LZ4 frame** (the v1.5.1 frame format), as `KafkaLZ4BlockOutputStream` writes
it: the magic number `04 22 4d 18`, the `FLG` byte `0x60` (version 1, independent blocks, no checksums), the `BD`
byte `0x40` (64 KiB blocks), the header checksum `HC`, then `int32` little-endian block lengths with their blocks,
and a block length of `0` as the end mark. The highest bit of a block length marks a block that is stored
uncompressed because compressing it made it bigger.

`HC` is the second byte of the xxHash32 of the frame descriptor, `(xxh32(FLG BD) >> 8) & 0xff` = `0x82`. Until
Kafka 0.10.0 the clients hashed the magic number **together with** the descriptor, which gives `0x1a`
([KAFKA-3160](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-3160)). The fix could not be applied to the messages that
older clients still have to read, so the broken checksum became part of the format of **message format v0** and the
correct one is used from format v1 on (`MemoryRecordsBuilder.wrapForOutput()`:
`useBrokenFlagDescriptorChecksum = magic == 0`). A reader has to accept both, which is what this client does — the
0.10.2.2 broker itself writes `04 22 4d 18 60 40 1a` in every answer it down-converts to format v0.

### What the broker converts, and when

The message format of the **log** is the `message.format.version` of the topic (`log.message.format.version` of the
broker by default, **`2.8-IV1`** on the container of this line, which is still the magic byte 2), and the broker
converts whatever it is given on the way in and on the way out. Re-measured on the 2.8.2 container with three
topics — one on the default format, one with `message.format.version=0.10.0` and one with `0.9.0` — each written
once and then fetched with every version of the Fetch api this client has a class for:

| Topic format | Stored as | Fetch v0/v1 answers | Fetch v2/v3 answers | Fetch v4 and above answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `2.8-IV1` (the default) | magic **2**, record batch | magic **0**, no timestamps, **no headers**, absolute inner offsets | magic **1**, timestamps kept, **no headers** | magic **2**, as it lies in the log |
| `0.10.0` | magic **1**, timestamps kept | magic **0**, timestamps dropped | magic **1**, as stored | magic **1**, as stored |
| `0.9.0` | magic **0** | magic **0** | magic **0** | magic **0** |

The conversion is what `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` @ 2.8.2 decides on two things at once, the magic of the log
and the version of the request: `magic > V0 && versionId <= 1` asks for `MAGIC_VALUE_V0`, `magic > V1 && versionId
<= 3` for `MAGIC_VALUE_V1`, and everything else is answered with the region as it lies. A *higher* fetch version
than the log needs is never a conversion: a magic 1 log is answered as magic 1 to a Fetch v8.

**The record headers of the message format v2 are dropped by that conversion, silently.** The answer of a Fetch v2
or v3 for a batch whose records carry headers is the error code **0** and every record, without its headers —
"Ignore headers when down-converting to V0 and V1 since they are not supported",
`AbstractRecords.convertRecordBatch` @ 2.8.2. A **0.11.0.3** broker answered such a partition with the error code
-1 (`UnknownServerError`) and an empty record set instead, because the very same call threw
`IllegalArgumentException: Magic v1 does not support record headers`; that changed with Kafka 1.0 and is unchanged
on 2.8.2. The measurement is in "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)" below.

A client of this line therefore sees timestamps only through a Fetch request of version 2 or above, which is what
`Client::fetch()` sends (v12); `Record::$timestamp` is `null` and `Record::$timestampType` is `NO_TIMESTAMP_TYPE`
for everything that arrives in format v0 — a topic of the older `message.format.version`, or any partition read
with an explicitly built `FetchRequestV1`/`FetchRequestV0`.

**A node of Kafka 4.0 or later converts nothing, in either direction (KIP-896).** The versions that needed a
conversion are gone - Produce v0 to v2, the only ones that carry a message set, and Fetch v0 to v3, the only ones
that read one - and a frame of them closes the connection. The topic configuration went with them: `TopicConfig` @
4.0.0 has no `message.format.version` any more (KIP-724 had made it a no-op in Kafka 3.0), and the node refuses it
in a CreateTopics or an IncrementalAlterConfigs with the **40** `InvalidConfiguration`, "Unknown topic config name:
message.format.version". Re-measured on `kafka-4-3-1`:

| | Answer of `kafka-4-3-1` |
|---|---|
| a topic created with `message.format.version=0.10.0` or `0.9.0` | **40**, "Unknown topic config name: message.format.version" - the topic is not created (`MessageFormatV1Test`) |
| a message set of the magic 0 or 1 in a Produce v2 | **connection closed** |
| the same message set in a Produce v3 … v12 | **87** `INVALID_RECORD` for the partition |
| a record batch v2 in a Produce v3 and above | appended as it is |
| Fetch v0 … v3 of any log | **connection closed** |
| Fetch v4 and above | the record batch v2 as it lies in the log, headers and timestamps included |

Every log of a 4.x node is a log of record batches v2, and every fetch it serves answers it unconverted. The message
sets of the formats v0 and v1 stay a format of this package - their classes, the vectors the lines below captured on
real brokers, and the unit tests of the codecs - for a peer of Kafka 3.x.

#### KIP-283 (Kafka 2.0): lazy down-conversion, and the switch that refuses it

Down-conversion is the most expensive thing a broker does for a client: before Kafka 2.0 the whole converted region
was built in the heap before the answer was written, which is how a single old consumer could drive a broker into
an out-of-memory death. **KIP-283** changed two things:

* the conversion became **lazy and chunked** — `LazyDownConversionRecords` converts a batch at a time while the
  answer is written to the socket, and guarantees only that at least one batch is converted, so the answer of a
  down-converting fetch may be **shorter** than `max_bytes` would allow;
* the conversion can be **switched off**, per topic with `message.downconversion.enable` and cluster-wide with the
  broker option `log.message.downconversion.enable` (`true` by default, which is what the container of this line
  answers for the broker resource 0).

With the option off, a fetch that would need a conversion is not served at all. Measured on a topic created with
`--config message.downconversion.enable=false`, written with one magic 2 batch:

| Request | Answer of the 2.8.2 container |
|---|---|
| Fetch **v3** (needs magic 1) | error code **35** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` for the partition, `high_watermark = -1`, an **empty** record set (`fetch.response.v3.downconversion-disabled`) |
| Fetch **v8** (needs nothing) | error code 0 and the record batch as it lies |

**The code is 35, not 43.** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` is what `KafkaApis` puts into the partition entry — "if
down-conversion is disabled for the particular partition … sending unsupported version response" — and **43**
`UNSUPPORTED_FOR_MESSAGE_FORMAT`, which is the code of a *timestamp lookup* on a log below magic 1, never appears
here. The error is per partition, not per request: the other partitions of the same fetch are served normally, and
the connection stays open.

A follower is exempt (`!fetchRequest.isFromFollower`), so replication is never refused by this option — it only
ever stops a *client* from paying for the conversion.

**Kafka 4.0 removed both halves of KIP-283 with the conversion itself** (KIP-896). `TopicConfig` @ 4.0.0 keeps the
constant `MESSAGE_DOWNCONVERSION_ENABLE_CONFIG`, deprecated, but the node no longer knows the configuration: a
CreateTopics with `message.downconversion.enable=false` is answered **40** `InvalidConfiguration`, "Unknown topic
config name: message.downconversion.enable", and the topic is not created. The per-partition 35 is gone with it: the
Fetch v3 that asked for a conversion is refused by the request parser, which **closes the connection** instead of
answering a partition - and the convertible partitions of the same request with it. `DownConversionTest` measures
that on `kafka-4-3-1`; the vector pair `fetch.request.v3.downconversion-disabled` / `fetch.response.v3.downconversion-disabled`
is the answer of the 2.8.2 container and stays a replay.

## RecordBatch (message format v2)

Kafka 0.11 replaced the message set with the **record batch** (KIP-98 for the format, KIP-82 for the headers). It
is the third message format of the protocol, the `MagicByte` 2, and it is what the log of a topic with the default
`message.format.version=0.11.0` holds and what a Produce v3 and a Fetch v4/v5 carry. A byte region of a partition is
still not a protocol array — it has no element count, only the `MessageSetSize`/`RecordSetSize` of the field around
it — but the entries of that region are now batches instead of messages:

```
RecordBatch =>
  BaseOffset           => int64
  BatchLength          => int32
  PartitionLeaderEpoch => int32
  Magic                => int8 (2)
  Crc                  => int32 (CRC-32C, unsigned)
  Attributes           => int16
  LastOffsetDelta      => int32
  FirstTimestamp       => int64
  MaxTimestamp         => int64
  ProducerId           => int64
  ProducerEpoch        => int16
  BaseSequence         => int32
  RecordCount          => int32
  Records              => the RecordCount records, compressed as one block when a codec is announced

Record =>
  Length         => varint
  Attributes     => int8
  TimestampDelta => varlong
  OffsetDelta    => varint
  Key            => varint-prefixed bytes
  Value          => varint-prefixed bytes
  Headers        => varint-counted [Header]

Header =>
  HeaderKeyLength   => varint
  HeaderKey         => string
  HeaderValueLength => varint
  HeaderValue       => bytes
```

Every length and both deltas are **zigzag varints** (`TYPE_VARINT_ZIGZAG`, `TYPE_VARLONG_ZIGZAG`,
`TYPE_VARCHAR_ZIGZAG` of the engine, see "Protocol primitive types"), a length of -1 (`01`) is `null` and a length
of 0 (`00`) is the empty byte array. The `Attributes` of a *record* are unused in 0.11 and always 0; the count of the
headers is a varint too, and a header key is a UTF-8 string that is never null, while a header value may be.

The fixed part of a batch is exactly **61 bytes** (`RECORD_BATCH_OVERHEAD`), from `BaseOffset` through
`RecordCount`; `BatchLength` counts everything after itself, so a batch occupies `12 + BatchLength` bytes, the same
`Offset`/`MessageSize` shape a message set entry has. That is not an accident: the `MagicByte` sits at **offset 16**
of an entry in all three formats — after the 8-byte offset, the 4-byte length and either the CRC of a message or the
`PartitionLeaderEpoch` of a batch — which is what lets a reader look at the format of a region before it decides how
to parse it. `MemoryRecords` of this client does exactly that, entry by entry, and hands each entry to `MessageSet`
or to `RecordBatch`.

### Attributes

| Bits | Meaning | Values |
|------|---------|--------|
| 0–2  | compression codec | 0 none, 1 gzip, 2 snappy, 3 lz4, **4 zstd** (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110) |
| 3    | timestamp type | 0 `CreateTime`, 1 `LogAppendTime` |
| 4    | transactional | 1 when the batch belongs to a transaction (KIP-98) |
| 5    | control batch | 1 when the records are markers of the transaction protocol |
| 6–15 | reserved, always 0 | |

The field is an `int16` now, and only its low byte is used — `DefaultRecordBatch.attributes()` reads the `int16` and
casts it to a `byte`. A batch of the format v2 always announces a timestamp type: unlike a message of the format v0,
it has no "no timestamp type" state.

### The checksum is a CRC-32C, and it does not cover the whole batch

`Crc` is the **CRC-32C** (Castagnoli, RFC 3720 section B.4 — `hash('crc32c')` of PHP, `Crc32C.java` of the broker),
not the CRC-32 (IEEE) of a message, and it covers the batch from the `Attributes` field to its end, i.e. everything
that follows the checksum itself. Three fields are therefore *outside* of it:

* `BaseOffset` — the broker assigns the real offsets when it appends the batch;
* `BatchLength` — it does not change;
* `PartitionLeaderEpoch` — assigned by the leader on append (KIP-101), and the whole point of leaving it out of the
  checksum is that a broker must not have to recompute the checksum of every batch it receives.

The checksum is also *behind* the magic byte, which is what makes reading the magic first mandatory: in the message
formats v0 and v1 the CRC comes first and the magic second.

### Offsets, timestamps and sequence numbers are deltas

A record stores none of its three numbers in full, only the difference to the header of its batch:

    offset    = BaseOffset     + OffsetDelta
    timestamp = FirstTimestamp + TimestampDelta
    sequence  = BaseSequence   + OffsetDelta

`LastOffsetDelta` is the delta of the last record, so `BaseOffset + LastOffsetDelta` is the last offset of the batch
and `BaseSequence + LastOffsetDelta` its last sequence number (wrapping at the largest int32, as
`DefaultRecordBatch.incrementSequence()` does). Both survive log compaction even when the records they describe are
removed, because the broker rebuilds the state of a producer from them; that is why a batch may hold **zero**
records and still exist, and why `RecordCount` is a plain `int32` outside the compressed block.

`FirstTimestamp` is always the `CreateTime` of the first record, *even in a `LogAppendTime` batch*: with
`LogAppendTime` the broker only overwrites `MaxTimestamp` with the time of the append and sets bit 3, and every
record of the batch reads that `MaxTimestamp` as its timestamp while the deltas of the producer stay in the log
untouched. The vector `messageformat.v2.none.logappendtime` shows it: `FirstTimestamp` and `MaxTimestamp` are 19
milliseconds apart, the records still carry the deltas 0, 8 and 8, and `DumpLogSegments` prints the same
`LogAppendTime` for all three of them. With `CreateTime` `MaxTimestamp` is simply the largest timestamp of the
batch. An empty batch has `FirstTimestamp` -1 (`NO_TIMESTAMP`).

### Compression compresses the records, not a wrapper

There is no wrapper message any more. The 61 header bytes are always plain and the bytes after them are the
compressed block of the `RecordCount` records, so a reader knows how many records a batch holds, what their offsets
and timestamps are and whether the batch is transactional without decompressing anything. The codecs and their
framings are the ones of the message set — gzip, xerial-framed snappy, an LZ4 frame — with one difference:

* an **lz4** batch of the magic 2 always carries the *correct* frame descriptor checksum `0x82`. The KAFKA-3160
  breakage is bound to the message format v0 (`useBrokenFlagDescriptorChecksum = magic == 0`), so it can never
  appear in a record batch; `messageformat.v2.lz4.createtime` starts with `04 22 4d 18 60 40 82`.

Re-compressing a block with another implementation gives different — equally valid — bytes, which is why
`RecordBatch` keeps the records part exactly as it read it and `toBuffer()` reproduces a captured batch byte for
byte.

### The zstd codec (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110)

**Kafka 2.1 added a fourth codec, the compression type `4`, zstd**, and it belongs to the message format v2 alone.
`CompressionType.ZSTD` @ 2.8.2 is `new CompressionType(4, "zstd", …)`, a produce of a zstd batch needs **Produce
v7** and a fetch of a zstd *topic* needs **Fetch v10**; both of the lower versions are refused with the error code
**76** `UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE`, see "Version 10 and the zstd codec (KIP-110)" under the Fetch api for the
two measurements. Nothing else about the batch changes: the three attribute bits hold the codec as they always
did, the 61 header bytes stay plain, and the records block is a zstd stream instead of a gzip, snappy or lz4 one.

**This client compresses and decompresses zstd through `ext-zstd`** (`zstd_compress()` and `zstd_uncompress()`), a
**suggested** dependency of `composer.json` and the only codec of the four that needs an extension which is not in
a default PHP build — gzip is `ext-zlib`, snappy and lz4 are implemented in PHP in this package. Writing a
pure-PHP zstd codec is not the business of a protocol client, so the extension is where the line is drawn, and the
absence of it is handled instead of hidden:

* `CompressionCodec::isSupported(CompressionCodec::ZSTD)` is `false` without the extension, and
  `CompressionCodec::isZstdAvailable()` says so directly;
* `ProducerConfig` refuses `compression.type = zstd` at construction time with the list of the codecs that are
  really available, so a producer fails where the mistake is, not inside a broker answer;
* a zstd batch that a **fetch** brings in raises `UnsupportedCompressionTypeException` — the client-side half of
  the code 76 — instead of handing half-decoded bytes to the application. It is raised where the answer is
  *decoded*, not where the records are used: `MemoryRecords::fromBuffer()` decodes every batch of a fetched
  region, so a partition of a zstd topic is an exception for the whole answer it arrived in. The header of a
  batch is readable either way — `RecordBatch::fromBuffer()` reads the 61 plain bytes, and with them the codec,
  the record count and the offsets, without touching the compressed block.

With the extension installed all four codecs round trip, and a batch this client compressed is read back by the
Java client and the other way round: zstd has one frame format (RFC 8478) and no Kafka-specific framing, unlike
the xerial framing of snappy or the KAFKA-3160 lz4 checksum.

### Control batches

A batch whose attributes have bit 5 set carries **markers of the transaction protocol** instead of data. A client
never hands its records to an application: `MemoryRecords::getRecords()` drops them, and a `read_committed` consumer
uses them to decide which of the batches around them belong to a committed transaction. The only markers of Kafka
0.11 are the two ends of a transaction, written by the transaction coordinator itself:

```
Key => Version Type
  Version => int16 (0)
  Type    => int16 (0 ABORT, 1 COMMIT)

Value => Version CoordinatorEpoch
  Version          => int16 (0)
  CoordinatorEpoch => int32
```

Such a batch holds exactly one record, is never compressed, is always transactional, carries the `ProducerId` and
the `ProducerEpoch` of the transaction it ends and has `BaseSequence` -1 — the marker is not part of the sequence of
the producer. `messageformat.v2.none.control` is the marker that the coordinator of this container wrote when the
transaction of `messageformat.v2.none.transactional` was committed.

### What the broker stores, and what it answers

The message format of the **log** is the `message.format.version` of the topic (`log.message.format.version` of the
broker by default, `0.11.0` on the container of this branch). The broker converts a produced batch **down on write**
and converts the log **down on read** for every client that asks with a Fetch version that does not know the format
it holds. All of the following was measured against the 0.11.0.3 container by producing the very same record batch
v2 with a raw Produce v3 frame into three topics and reading each of them back with a raw Fetch v4, v3 and v1:

| `message.format.version` | Log stores | Fetch v0/v1 answers | Fetch v2/v3 answers | Fetch v4/v5 answers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0.9.0` | **v0**, timestamps dropped | v0 | v0 | v0 |
| `0.10.x` | **v1**, timestamps kept | **v0** | v1 | v1 |
| `0.11.0` (default) | v2, as produced | **v0** | **v1** | v2 |

A batch converted down becomes one *message per record* — the batch is unwrapped, not re-wrapped into a compressed
message — and a v0 answer loses every timestamp. A **`LogAppendTime`** batch is rebuilt with a magic 1 builder
(`AbstractRecords.convertRecordBatch()`), which stamps the append time and bit 3 of the attributes on **every** one
of those messages, where a 0.10.2.2 broker set the bit on the wrapper of a compressed set alone; measured on the
topic `t2-rb-lat`, whose three messages come back from a Fetch v3 with the attributes `0x08` and the very same
timestamp. `messageformat.v2.downconverted.v1` and
`messageformat.v2.downconverted.v0` are the two conversions of the log of `messageformat.v2.none.createtime`; the
raw frames that produced them are

```
00 01 00 03 00 00 00 0c 00 0a 74 32 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73 ff ff ff ff 00 00 03 e8 00 00 00 00 00 10 00 00
00 00 00 01 00 0a 74 32 2d 72 62 2d 6e 6f 6e 65 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 10 00 00
```

for the Fetch **v3** and

```
00 01 00 01 00 00 00 0d 00 0a 74 32 2d 76 65 63 74 6f 72 73 ff ff ff ff 00 00 03 e8 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01
00 0a 74 32 2d 72 62 2d 6e 6f 6e 65 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 10 00 00
```

for the Fetch **v1** (the client id is `t2-vectors`, the topic `t2-rb-none`, `max_bytes` 1 MiB, `max_wait_time` 1000
ms). Both are the request frames without their `Size` field, i.e. what `RawRecordBatchProbe` sends.

A client of this line therefore sees a record batch — and with it the headers, the producer id and the transaction
flags — only through a Fetch request of version 4 or above; everything below it is answered in a format that has no
place for any of them.

## Metadata API (key 3, v0 to v13)

This is the only request that may be addressed to any broker of the cluster. This line implements **every version
a 4.3.1 node serves, v0 to v13** - KIP-896 removed none of them; the request has seven shapes and the answer
eleven - the flexible encoding of version 9, the topic ids of version 10, the version 11 that dropped the
cluster-wide authorized operations (KIP-700) and the top-level error code of version 13 (KIP-1102) are the last
four.

```
Metadata Request (Version: 0) => [TopicName]
  TopicName => string

Metadata Request (Version: 1, 2 and 3) => [TopicName]     # the array is NULLABLE
  TopicName => string

Metadata Request (Version: 4, 5, 6 and 7) => [TopicName] AllowAutoTopicCreation
  TopicName              => string           # the array is NULLABLE
  AllowAutoTopicCreation => boolean          # since version 4

Metadata Request (Version: 8 and 9) => [TopicName] AllowAutoTopicCreation
                                       IncludeClusterAuthorizedOperations IncludeTopicAuthorizedOperations
  IncludeClusterAuthorizedOperations => boolean    # versions 8 to 10 only
  IncludeTopicAuthorizedOperations   => boolean    # since version 8

Metadata Request (Version: 10) => [TopicId TopicName TAG_BUFFER] AllowAutoTopicCreation
                                  IncludeClusterAuthorizedOperations IncludeTopicAuthorizedOperations TAG_BUFFER
  TopicId   => uuid                          # since version 10, 16 raw bytes, IN FRONT of the name
  TopicName => compact nullable string        # nullable since version 10

Metadata Request (Version: 11) => [TopicId TopicName TAG_BUFFER] AllowAutoTopicCreation
                                  IncludeTopicAuthorizedOperations TAG_BUFFER
  # version 11 (KIP-700) dropped IncludeClusterAuthorizedOperations
```

Version 1 (Kafka 0.10.0) made the topic array **nullable**, and the versions 2 (Kafka 0.10.1) and 3 (Kafka 0.11)
send the very same frame — `METADATA_REQUEST_V2 = METADATA_REQUEST_V1` and `METADATA_REQUEST_V3 =
METADATA_REQUEST_V2` in `MetadataRequest.schemaVersions()` @ 1.1.1, only the answer grew each time; the versions 5
(Kafka 1.0) and 6 (Kafka 2.0) repeat the version 4 frame for the same reason — `MetadataRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 has
no field between version 4 and version 8. The nullable array is the whole point of version 1: it separates two
intentions that version 0 has to express with the same empty array.

| Version | `topics`         | Frame         | The broker answers                                                |
|---------|------------------|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0       | `[]`             | `00 00 00 00` | every topic of the cluster                                        |
| 0       | `["a"]`          | one string    | topic `a`, creating it when `auto.create.topics.enable` is on     |
| 1 … 7   | `null`           | `ff ff ff ff` | every topic of the cluster, the internal ones included            |
| 1 … 7   | `[]`             | `00 00 00 00` | **no topic at all** — the brokers, the ids and an empty topic array |
| 1 … 3   | `["a"]`          | one string    | topic `a`, creating it when `auto.create.topics.enable` is on     |
| 4 … 7   | `["a"]`          | one string    | topic `a`; whether it is created is now the client's decision, see below |

`KafkaApis.handleTopicMetadataRequest` @ 0.11.0.3 spells the difference out — *"Handle old metadata request logic.
Version 0 has no way to specify 'no topics'"* — and the empty array of version 1 creates nothing either, because
only the topics a request NAMES are auto-created. An empty array is therefore the cheapest way of asking a broker
who the members of the cluster are (`metadata.request.v2.no-topics`), and it is what
[`AdminClient::findAllBrokers()`](../../src/Kafka/Admin/AdminClient.php) sends.

### `AllowAutoTopicCreation` (v4, Kafka 0.11, KIP-4): asking without creating

Until version 4 a metadata request for a topic that does not exist **created** it whenever the broker ran with the
default `auto.create.topics.enable=true` — with the broker's default partition count and replication factor, and
answered with the topic error code 5 (`LeaderNotAvailable`) and an empty partition list, because the controller had
not elected the leaders yet. There was no way for a client to say "just tell me whether it is there". Version 4
adds the trailing `allow_auto_topic_creation` BOOLEAN, and `KafkaApis.handleTopicMetadataRequest` @ 0.11.0.3
auto-creates a named topic only when

```scala
allowAutoCreation = config.autoCreateTopicsEnable && metadataRequest.allowAutoTopicCreation
```

holds. A request below version 4 has no such field, and `MetadataRequest.allowAutoTopicCreation()` answers `true`
for it, so nothing about the older versions changed.

This client makes the decision per caller, and the split is deliberate:

* **`Common\Cluster`** — the metadata path of a producer and a consumer — sends **`true`**. A named topic that does
  not exist yet has always been created for them, and version 4 must not silently change that behaviour.
* **`Admin\AdminClient`** — `describeTopics()`, `listTopics()` and `findAllBrokers()` — sends **`false`**. An
  administrator must be able to look at a topic without bringing it into being.

Verified on the container: a version 4 request naming an absent topic with the flag `false` is answered with the
topic error code **3** (`UnknownTopicOrPartition`) and an empty partition list, and `kafka-topics.sh --list`
afterwards does not show the topic (`metadata.request.v4.no-auto-creation` / `metadata.response.v4.unknown-topic`).

```
Metadata Response (Version: 0) => [Broker][TopicMetadata]
  Broker => NodeId Host Port
    NodeId => int32
    Host   => string
    Port   => int32
  TopicMetadata => TopicErrorCode TopicName [PartitionMetadata]
    TopicErrorCode => int16
    TopicName      => string
  PartitionMetadata => PartitionErrorCode PartitionId Leader Replicas Isr
    PartitionErrorCode => int16
    PartitionId        => int32
    Leader             => int32
    Replicas           => [int32]
    Isr                => [int32]

Metadata Response (Version: 1) => [Broker] ControllerId [TopicMetadata]
  Broker => NodeId Host Port Rack
    Rack => nullable string
  ControllerId => int32
  TopicMetadata => TopicErrorCode TopicName IsInternal [PartitionMetadata]
    IsInternal => boolean

Metadata Response (Version: 2) => [Broker] ClusterId ControllerId [TopicMetadata]
  ClusterId => nullable string

Metadata Response (Version: 3 and 4) => ThrottleTimeMs [Broker] ClusterId ControllerId [TopicMetadata]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32          # since version 3

Metadata Response (Version: 5 and 6) => ThrottleTimeMs [Broker] ClusterId ControllerId [TopicMetadata]
  PartitionMetadata => PartitionErrorCode PartitionId Leader Replicas Isr OfflineReplicas
    OfflineReplicas => [int32]     # since version 5

Metadata Response (Version: 7) => ThrottleTimeMs [Broker] ClusterId ControllerId [TopicMetadata]
  PartitionMetadata => PartitionErrorCode PartitionId Leader LeaderEpoch Replicas Isr OfflineReplicas
    LeaderEpoch => int32           # since version 7, BETWEEN the leader id and the replicas

Metadata Response (Version: 8) => ThrottleTimeMs [Broker] ClusterId ControllerId [TopicMetadata]
                                  ClusterAuthorizedOperations
  TopicMetadata => TopicErrorCode TopicName IsInternal [PartitionMetadata] TopicAuthorizedOperations
    TopicAuthorizedOperations   => int32     # since version 8, at the END of a topic entry
  ClusterAuthorizedOperations   => int32     # since version 8, at the END of the frame

Metadata Request and Response (Version: 9) => the fields of version 8 in the FLEXIBLE encoding (KIP-482):
  every string and array is compact, every structure ends in a tagged-field section, the request carries
  the request header v2 and the answer the response header v1
```

Version 3 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) put the `ThrottleTimeMs` in front of everything and changed nothing else, and
version 4 answers the very same frame — `METADATA_RESPONSE_V4 = METADATA_RESPONSE_V3` in
`MetadataResponse.schemaVersions()` @ 1.1.1, because what version 4 added lives in the request.
`MetadataResponseV4` and `MetadataResponseV3` therefore decode the same bytes; the class of the answer still has to
match the version of the request, because a v2 answer read with the v3 class would take the broker count for a
throttle time.

**Version 5 (Kafka 1.0, KIP-112/113) appends `OfflineReplicas` to every partition entry**, an int32 array of the
replicas of that partition that are not available. `PARTITION_METADATA_V2` is the first change the partition entry
ever saw — `PARTITION_METADATA_V1` **is** `PARTITION_METADATA_V0` — which is why the classes of this client are
`PartitionMetadata` (v5) and `PartitionMetadataV0` (v0 to v4), and `TopicMetadata` (v5), `TopicMetadataV1` (v1 to
v4) and `TopicMetadataV0`. A replica is offline when the broker that holds it is down or when the **log directory**
that holds it has failed: with JBOD (more than one `log.dirs` entry) a broker survives the loss of one directory by
taking the replicas it held offline instead of shutting down, and those replicas stay in `Replicas`, leave `Isr`
and appear here.

**On the one-broker container the array is always empty**, and that is not a defect of the capture: the only
broker of the cluster holds every replica and is up, so no replica of any topic can be offline. Every partition of
`metadata.response.v5` below therefore ends with `00 00 00 00`. An answer below version 5 does not carry the field
at all, and `PartitionMetadata::$offlineReplicas` is then `[]` — "the answer did not say", not "every replica is
online". `AdminClient::describeTopics()` hands the whole `TopicMetadata` over, so a caller reads the offline
replicas of a partition from `$partition->offlineReplicas`.

**Version 6 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) changes neither side.** `MetadataRequest.json` has no field of it and
`MetadataResponse.json` says "Starting in version 6, on quota violation, brokers send out responses before
throttling", so `metadata.request.v6` and `metadata.response.v6` below are the version 5 frames with another number
in the header; what version 6 states is that the **client** waits out the `throttle_time_ms` itself, see "KIP-219"
under "Quotas and throttle time". `MetadataRequestV5`/`MetadataResponseV5` keep the version the 1.x line sent, and
`Client`'s cluster metadata goes out as **version 6**.

**Version 7 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-320) inserts `LeaderEpoch` behind the leader id of every partition**, and leaves the
request alone — `MetadataRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 has no field between version 4 and version 8, so `metadata.request.v7`
below is the version 4 frame with another number in its header. The field is the epoch of the leadership the answer
describes: it starts at 0 for a partition whose leader was elected once, and every election raises it by one.
Note the position — **between** `Leader` and `Replicas` — which is why the partition entry needs a class of its own
again (`PartitionMetadata` for v7, `PartitionMetadataV5` for v5 and v6, `PartitionMetadataV0` for v0 to v4), and
why a v7 answer read with the v5 class walks off into the replica array.

This is the field a consumer tracks: it is the `current_leader_epoch` of its next fetch and the trigger of the
position validation when it **moves**, see "The leader epoch (KIP-320)" and "KIP-320 in the consumer: leader epochs
and truncation detection" under the Fetch api. `Cluster` stores it per partition and refuses an answer that moves
it backwards, and `PartitionMetadata::$leaderEpoch` is `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` (`-1`) for every answer below version
7, which does not carry the field at all. `Client`'s cluster metadata goes out as **version 7**, and
`MetadataRequestV6`/`MetadataResponseV6` keep the version the Kafka 2.0 part of this line sent.

**Version 8 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-430) asks and answers what the caller may do**, with two booleans in the request and
two bitfields in the answer, see "The authorized operations (v8, KIP-430)" below. `MetadataRequestV7` and
`MetadataResponseV7` keep the version the Kafka 2.1 part of this line sent, and `TopicMetadataV7` its topic entry;
`Client`'s metadata goes out as **version 8** with both booleans off, which is the same question version 7 asked
and two more fields in the answer.

**Version 9 (Kafka 2.4) is the same question and the same answer in the other encoding.** It is the first
**flexible** version of this api — `MetadataRequest.json` and `MetadataResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 both declare
`"flexibleVersions": "9+"` — and not one field is added, removed or moved. What changes is how the fields are
written, and the engine does all of it from two constants (`VERSION = 9`, `FLEXIBLE_VERSION = 9`), see "Flexible
versions in the engine (KIP-482)":

* the **request header v2**: the client id stays an `int16`-prefixed string (`"flexibleVersions": "none"` in
  `RequestHeader.json`) and gains a tag buffer behind it; the answer carries the **response header v1**, i.e. a
  tag buffer behind the correlation id;
* every **string** and every **array** announces its length as an unsigned varint of `length + 1`, so the single
  topic of `metadata.request.v9` below is `02` (one item) and its name `0b` plus ten bytes, where version 8
  needed four and two;
* every **structure** ends in a tagged-field section — the body, every broker, every topic, every partition —
  which is `00` while nothing is tagged.

**One thing in this client had to change for it, and it is the trap of KIP-482**: the topics of the request were
a plain array of *strings* here, because that is what the frame looks like up to version 8; the specification has
always declared them as a `[]MetadataRequestTopic` **structure** with a single `Name`. In a flexible version that
structure ends in a tagged-field section, so a frame of bare compact strings is **one byte short per topic** and
the broker closes the connection on it — measured. `Protocol\Data\MetadataRequestTopic` is that structure, and
`MetadataRequest::getTopics()` still answers the list of names.

`MetadataRequestV8`/`MetadataResponseV8` keep the plain encoding, and `MetadataRequestV9`/`MetadataResponseV9`
the flexible frame whose topic entries are the name alone.

### Topic ids (v10, KIP-516)

**Version 10 (Kafka 2.8, KIP-516) gives every topic an id**, and it is one field on each side:

* the request gains a `TopicId` **in front of** the name of every topic entry, and the name itself becomes
  nullable, so that a client could name a topic by its id alone;
* every topic entry of the answer gains the same `TopicId`, **between** the name and `is_internal` — the field
  order of `MetadataResponse.json` @ 2.8.2, which is the wire order.

A `uuid` is **16 raw bytes** with no length prefix, which is why the compact encoding of a flexible version does
not touch it (`BinarySchema::TYPE_UUID`). The text form is *not* the `8-4-4-4-12` hex of RFC 4122: `Uuid.toString()`
@ 2.8.2 prints a url-safe base64 without padding, 22 characters, which is what `kafka-topics.sh --describe` shows
and what `Protocol\Kafka\Common\Uuid::toString()` answers here. `Uuid::ZERO` (16 zero bytes,
`AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA`) is the "no topic id" of the protocol.

**The id is a property of the topic, not of its name**: it is created with the topic and a topic that is deleted
and created again under the same name gets a **new** one. That is what the KIP is for — a broker that missed the
deletion can tell the two apart, while the name alone cannot.

**The request half of it does not work on a 2.8.2 broker**, and the specification says so itself:
"Version 10 adds topicId and allows name field to be null. However, this functionality was not implemented on the
server. Versions 10 and 11 should not use the topicId field or set topic name to null." This client therefore
writes `Uuid::ZERO` and the real name in every entry, exactly as the Java client does, and reads the id out of the
answer (`TopicMetadata::$topicId`).

**Version 11 (Kafka 2.8, KIP-700) takes a field away instead of adding one**:
`include_cluster_authorized_operations` is gone from the request and `cluster_authorized_operations` from the end
of the answer — both are declared `"8-10"` in the json, a closed range. The cluster-wide question is the new
**DescribeCluster** api (key 60); the per-topic bitfield is untouched. `MetadataRequestV10`/`MetadataResponseV10`
are the version to ask with when a caller wants the cluster bitfield from this api, and `Client`'s cluster
metadata goes out as **version 11**.

`Leader` is `-1` while a leader election is in progress. The three fields that Kafka 0.10 added are:

* **`Rack`** (v1) — the `broker.rack` of that broker, a `NULLABLE_STRING`. The container of `docker-compose.yml`
  declares none, so it answers `ff ff` for its single broker, as does every cluster that is not rack aware.
* **`IsInternal`** (v1) — a `BOOLEAN` (one byte, `00` or `01`) for every topic. `Topic.isInternal` @ 1.1.1 knows
  two internal topics, `__consumer_offsets`, the log the group coordinator keeps the committed offsets in, and
  `__transaction_state`;
  the vector `metadata.response.v2.internal-topic` is its metadata, with the five partitions of
  `offsets.topic.num.partitions=5`.
* **`ControllerId`** (v1) and **`ClusterId`** (v2) — see below. Note the ORDER: version 2 inserts the cluster id
  **before** the controller id, so a v1 answer and a v2 answer only differ in those bytes, and reading one with the
  class of the other silently walks off into the topic array.

Version 0 differs in one more thing that the grammar does not show. `errorUnavailableEndpoints = requestVersion == 0`
in `KafkaApis` @ 0.10.2.2: a version 0 answer reports the error code 9 (`ReplicaNotAvailable`) for a partition whose
replica set contains a broker that is currently down, while version 1 and above simply leave that broker out of the
`Replicas` and `Isr` lists. A client of v1+ therefore sees fewer errors and shorter replica lists for the same
cluster.

### Metadata by topic id (v12, KIP-516)

**Version 12 (Kafka 3.1) adds not a single field.** `MetadataRequest.json` @ 3.1.2 ends its comment block with the
one line "Version 12 supports topic Id", and `MetadataResponse.json` with "Version 12 supports topicId"; the only
declaration that moves is `"nullableVersions": "12+"` on the `Name` of a topic entry of the **answer**. What the
version really is, is the server finally honouring the two fields version 10 put on the wire and then told
everybody not to use ("Versions 10 and 11 should not use the topicId field or set topic name to null").

So from version 12 a topic entry of the request may carry a **real id and a `null` name**, which is the
`describeTopics(TopicCollection.ofTopicIds(...))` of the Java admin client and
`MetadataRequest::byTopicIds()` / `AdminClient::describeTopicsByIds()` here. The **answer** of such a request is
the ordinary one: a topic the node could resolve is reported with its name *and* its id, so
`metadata.response.v12.by-topic-id` is byte for byte the answer of the same question asked by name. The nullable
name exists for the entry the node could **not** resolve: the error code **100** `UnknownTopicId`, the id that was
asked for, a `null` name and no partition at all (`metadata.response.v12.unknown-topic-id`). Such an entry has no
name to index it by, so it is appended to `MetadataResponse::$topics` with an integer key.

**Two things the node does that the specification does not say** (both measured on `kafka-3-9-2`, both in
`KafkaApis.handleTopicMetadataRequest` @ 3.9.2):

* **A request that mixes the two shapes loses the named half, silently.** `useTopicId` is `topicIds.nonEmpty`
  — *one* entry with a non-zero id is enough — and the topics of the answer are then `knownTopicNames`, the names
  the ids resolved to. The entries that named their topic by name are not reported, not even with an error;
  `metadata.response.v12.mixed` is the answer to a request that named one topic by id and another by name, and it
  holds the first one alone. A client asks by id **or** by name.
* **A version below 12 that is asked by id is refused with a whole error response, not with a per-topic error.**
  The same method throws `InvalidRequestException` for every entry whose name is null or whose id is not the zero
  uuid while the version is below 12, and the answer that reaches the client
  (`metadata.response.v11.by-topic-id`) has **zero brokers**, a `null` cluster id, the controller id -1 and one
  topic entry per request entry, each with the error code **42** `InvalidRequest`, an empty name and the id that
  was asked for. An empty broker array is what `Cluster::reload()` reads as "the metadata cache of that broker is
  not filled yet" and answers with `AllBrokersNotAvailableException`, so a version below 12 must never be asked by
  id — which is why `MetadataRequest::byTopicIds()` builds a version 12 or higher request and `MetadataRequestV11`
  keeps the version that names its topics.

A version 12 entry that carries the zero id *and* a null name — neither a name nor an id — is answered by the node
with the topic error code **-1** (`UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR`) and an empty name, which is the one shape of this api
that has no sensible answer.

### The top-level error code of KIP-1102 (v13)

**Version 13 (Kafka 4.0) adds one field to the answer and none to the request.** `MetadataRequest.json` and
`MetadataResponse.json` @ 4.0.0 both comment "Version 13 supports top-level error code in the response", and the
answer declares

```
{ "name": "ErrorCode", "type": "int16", "versions": "13+", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The top-level error code, or 0 if there was no error." }
```

behind `cluster_authorized_operations` (versions 8 to 10 only) - so on the wire it is the **last field of the body**,
behind the topic array and in front of the tagged-field section: a version 13 answer is the version 12 answer and
two bytes. `MetadataRequestV12`/`MetadataResponseV12` keep the version under it; `MetadataRequest` sends 13, and the
code is `MetadataResponse::$errorCode`.

```
MetadataResponse v13 => ThrottleTimeMs [Broker] ClusterId ControllerId [TopicMetadata] ErrorCode TAG_BUFFER
  ErrorCode => int16          # since version 13 (KIP-1102): 0, or 129 REBOOTSTRAP_REQUIRED
```

The code it was added for is the **129** `REBOOTSTRAP_REQUIRED` of KIP-1102 (Kafka 4.0, `Errors.java` @ 4.0.0: "Client
metadata is stale. The client should rebootstrap to obtain new metadata"): the brokers a client knows are not the
cluster any more, so it has to start over from its `bootstrap.servers`. **No broker of Kafka 4.0 to 4.3.1 writes it.**
Every reference to `REBOOTSTRAP_REQUIRED` at the tag 4.3.1 outside the tests is a client one - `NetworkClient`
(`metadataRecoveryStrategy == REBOOTSTRAP && response.topLevelError() == Errors.REBOOTSTRAP_REQUIRED`) and
`KafkaAdminClient` - and `MetadataRequest.getErrorResponse` @ 4.3.1, which builds the answer of a failed request,
puts the code into every **topic** entry and leaves the top level at 0. Measured on the node:

| Request | Answer of `kafka-4-3-1` |
|---|---|
| one existing topic at v13 (`metadata.request.v13`) | the version 12 answer and `00 00` in front of the tag buffer of the body (`metadata.response.v13`) |
| a topic that does not exist, without auto creation (`metadata.request.v13.unknown-topic`) | **3** in the topic entry, the zero topic id, no partition - and the top-level code **0** (`metadata.response.v13.unknown-topic`) |

**What this client does with it.** `Cluster::reload()` always asks the `bootstrap.servers` and never a broker it
learned from an earlier answer, so a rebootstrap is what it does anyway: an answer whose top-level code is not 0 is
dropped, the next bootstrap server is asked, and when none of them answers without a code, the code of the last
answer is thrown - `RebootstrapRequiredException` for the 129 - and the metadata the cluster already had is kept.
The unit tests script both halves; the node can produce neither.

### The authorized operations (v8, KIP-430)

**Version 8 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-430) answers what the caller is allowed to do**, so that a tool does not have to try
an operation to find out. It is two booleans in the request — `include_cluster_authorized_operations` and
`include_topic_authorized_operations`, in that order, behind the `allow_auto_topic_creation` of version 4 — and
two `int32` **bitfields** in the answer: one at the end of every topic entry, behind its partitions, and one at
the very end of the frame.

A bit is the **code of an operation** of `AclOperation` @ 2.8.2, and `Utils.to32BitField` sets the bit with that
number:

| Code | Operation | Code | Operation |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 0 | `UNKNOWN` | 7 | `ALTER` |
| 1 | `ANY` (a filter value, never answered) | 8 | `DESCRIBE` |
| 2 | `ALL` | 9 | `CLUSTER_ACTION` |
| 3 | `READ` | 10 | `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` |
| 4 | `WRITE` | 11 | `ALTER_CONFIGS` |
| 5 | `CREATE` | 12 | `IDEMPOTENT_WRITE` |
| 6 | `DELETE` | | |

`Common\AclOperation` of this client is both halves — the codes, `fromBitField()`, `toBitField()` and
`describe()` — and `TopicMetadata::$authorizedOperations` and `MetadataResponse::$clusterAuthorizedOperations`
carry the two fields.

**`Integer.MIN_VALUE` is "you did not ask", and it is not the empty set.** A broker writes `80 00 00 00` into a
bitfield whose boolean was `false`, which is what `metadata.response.v8.not-requested` below shows: the fields are
part of the *version*, not of the question, so they are on the wire either way.
`AclOperation::NOT_REQUESTED` is that value and `AclOperation::wasRequested()` the test, because the bitfield `0`
is a real answer — "this principal may do nothing here".

**What a broker without an authorizer answers**, measured on the container with both booleans on:

| Resource | Bitfield | Operations |
|---|---:|---|
| the cluster | `8096` (`00 00 1f a0`) | `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DESCRIBE`, `CLUSTER_ACTION`, `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS`, `ALTER_CONFIGS`, `IDEMPOTENT_WRITE` |
| a topic | `3576` (`00 00 0d f8`) | `READ`, `WRITE`, `CREATE`, `DELETE`, `ALTER`, `DESCRIBE`, `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS`, `ALTER_CONFIGS` |

Neither is "everything": it is **the set of operations the resource type has**
(`AclEntry.supportedOperations(ResourceType)` @ 2.8.2), with `ALL` and `ANY` left out, because an unsecured broker
authorizes whatever is asked of it. A secured cluster answers the subset its ACLs allow, and the same bitfield is
what DescribeGroups v3 gained in the same release for a group.

`Client`'s metadata request sends **version 11** with `IncludeTopicAuthorizedOperations` **off** — the client needs
the field for none of its own work, and asking costs the broker an authorizer round trip per topic — so the answers
it reads carry `NOT_REQUESTED`. A caller that wants the per-topic bitfield asks for it:
`new MetadataRequest($topics, $allowAutoTopicCreation, $clientId, $correlationId, includeTopicAuthorizedOperations: true)`.
The **cluster-wide** bitfield is not on the wire of a version 11 request at all — KIP-700 declared the field `"8-10"`,
see "Version 11" above — so `includeClusterAuthorizedOperations: true` is silently without effect there. The version
to ask this api the cluster-wide question with is `MetadataRequestV10`/`MetadataResponseV10`; the api KIP-700 moved
it to is **DescribeCluster** (key 60).

### `ControllerId`: which broker is the controller

`ControllerId` is the broker id of the active controller as the ANSWERING broker knows it, taken from its metadata
cache (`metadataCache.getControllerId.getOrElse(MetadataResponse.NO_CONTROLLER_ID)`); it is `-1` while the cluster
has no controller, i.e. while it is electing one. It is what the topic administration apis need, because
CreateTopics and DeleteTopics are served by the controller alone and answer 41 (`NotController`) on every other
broker.

On the container the field answers `0`, which is the `brokerid` of the `/controller` znode in ZooKeeper:

```
$ docker exec kafka-0-10-2-2 /opt/kafka/bin/zookeeper-shell.sh localhost:2181 get /controller
{"version":1,"brokerid":0,"timestamp":"1788928975914"}
```

Before Kafka 0.10.0 there was no way to ask this over the protocol at all: a client had to send a request that only
the controller serves and watch for the 41. [`AdminClient::findController()`](../../src/Kafka/Admin/AdminClient.php)
now reads the field instead, and asks for the metadata once more when it comes back `-1` or names a broker that is
not among the alive brokers of the same answer.

### `ClusterId`: the identity of the cluster

`ClusterId` arrived with version 2 (Kafka 0.10.1). The first broker of a cluster generates it —
`KafkaServer.getOrGenerateClusterId` @ 0.10.2.2, a 22 character URL-safe base64 encoding of a random UUID — and
stores it in ZooKeeper under `/cluster/id`, from where every other broker reads it, so every broker of one cluster
answers the same string. The container answers a real one, which is the content of that znode:

```
$ docker exec kafka-0-10-2-2 /opt/kafka/bin/zookeeper-shell.sh localhost:2181 get /cluster/id
{"version":"1","id":"_w793L5LQk2vaX_a6Lm3lw"}
```

The field is a `NULLABLE_STRING` because a broker may have none — a 0.10.1 broker that was upgraded from an older
release before it wrote the znode — so `null` is a legal answer and not an error.

## Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)

```
ProduceRequest v0, v1 and v2 => RequiredAcks Timeout [TopicName [Partition MessageSetSize MessageSet]]
  RequiredAcks   => int16
  Timeout        => int32
  TopicName      => string
  Partition      => int32
  MessageSetSize => int32
```

```
ProduceRequest v3 to v6 => TransactionalId RequiredAcks Timeout [TopicName [Partition RecordSetSize RecordSet]]
  TransactionalId => nullable string
```

```
ProduceResponse v0 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode Offset]]
  TopicName => string
  Partition => int32
  ErrorCode => int16
  Offset    => int64
```

```
ProduceResponse v1 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode Offset]] ThrottleTime
  ThrottleTime => int32
```

```
ProduceResponse v2, v3 and v4 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode Offset LogAppendTime]] ThrottleTime
  LogAppendTime => int64
```

```
ProduceResponse v5 and v6 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode Offset LogAppendTime LogStartOffset]] ThrottleTime
  LogStartOffset => int64
```

```
ProduceRequest v9 => TransactionalId RequiredAcks Timeout
                     [TopicName [Partition RecordSet TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER
  TransactionalId => compact nullable string   # the single byte 00 for the null of a plain producer
  TopicName       => compact string
  RecordSet       => compact bytes             # an unsigned varint of length + 1, not an int32

ProduceResponse v9 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode Offset LogAppendTime LogStartOffset
                                  [RecordErrors] ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER] ThrottleTime TAG_BUFFER
  RecordErrors => compact array of [BatchIndex int32, BatchIndexErrorMessage compact nullable string, TAG_BUFFER]
  ErrorMessage => compact nullable string
```

`RequiredAcks`: `0` — do not wait and **send no response at all**; `1` — wait for the leader's local log; `-1` — wait
for all in-sync replicas.

**The request did not change between the versions 0 and 2.** `PRODUCE_REQUEST_V2` is `PRODUCE_REQUEST_V1` is
`PRODUCE_REQUEST_V0` in `clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/protocol/Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3, so up to
version 2 a version only selects the layout of the answer — and, from 0.10.0 on, states which message format the
client speaks. Version 1 (Kafka 0.9) appended `ThrottleTime` to the **end** of the response, the milliseconds the
