broker delayed this request because the client exceeded its `producer_byte_rate` quota (see "Quotas and throttle
time" below). Version 2 (Kafka 0.10.0) added `LogAppendTime` to every partition entry, **between** `Offset` and that
throttle time.

**Version 3 (Kafka 0.11.0, KIP-98) is the first version that changed the request.** It prefixes the body with the
nullable `TransactionalId` of the producer, and the record set of every partition is a **record batch of the message
format v2** (see "RecordBatch (message format v2)" above) instead of a message set. That batch is what carries the
record headers, the producer id, the producer epoch and the sequence numbers of an idempotent or transactional
producer, so **none of them can travel below version 3**: a client that writes a message set of the format v0 or v1
sends it as a Produce v2 request, which is what `ProducerConfig::MESSAGE_FORMAT_VERSION` selects here.

**The answer of version 3 is the answer of version 2, byte for byte, and so is the answer of version 4.**
`PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V4` **is** `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V3` **is** `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V2` in
`clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/requests/ProduceResponse.java` @ 1.1.1, and the 1.1.1 container
really answers a version 3 and a version 4 request with that frame — the vectors `produce.response.v3` and
`produce.response.v4` below are 50 and 50 bytes and end with the `ThrottleTime` right behind the `LogAppendTime`.

**Version 4 (Kafka 1.0) sends and receives the very same bytes as version 3 and states one thing about the
client**: that it understands the error code **56 `KAFKA_STORAGE_ERROR`**, the answer of a broker whose log
directory for that partition has failed. A client that asks with version 3 or lower is answered **6
`NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION`** for the same condition instead (`ProduceRequest.java` @ 1.1.1: "The
KafkaStorageException will be translated to NotLeaderForPartitionException in the response if version <= 3"). A
one-broker container with healthy log directories can not be made to answer 56, so the translation is documented
from the sources and from the api version alone; see "Broker quirks and observations".

**Version 5 (Kafka 1.0) appends `LogStartOffset` to every partition entry of the answer**, behind the
`LogAppendTime`: the offset the log of that partition begins at, i.e. the first offset that has not been removed by
the retention of the topic or by a DeleteRecords request. It is what lets an idempotent producer tell a *spurious*
`OutOfOrderSequenceException` — the broker forgot its producer state because the producer's records fell below that
offset, which arrives as **59 `UNKNOWN_PRODUCER_ID`** — from a real gap in its own sequence numbers. The vector
`produce.response.v5` below was captured right after a DeleteRecords request had removed the first two records of
the partition, and reports `LogStartOffset = 2`; a log nothing was deleted from reports 0, never -1.

**Version 6 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) changes neither the request nor the answer.** `ProduceRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 has
no field above version 3 and `ProduceResponse.json` none above version 5, so a version 6 frame is a version 5 frame
with another number in its header — the vectors `produce.request.v6` and `produce.response.v6` below are exactly
that. What version 6 states is that the **client** honours the `ThrottleTime` of the answer itself, because a
throttled request is answered *first* and the channel is muted afterwards; see "KIP-219" under "Quotas and throttle
time". A 2.8.2 broker throttles a version 5 request in exactly the same way, so the version is a promise of the
client and not a switch of the broker.

The fourteen response classes are therefore `ProduceResponse` (v13, the topics named by id of KIP-516),
`ProduceResponseV12` (the transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 part 2),
`ProduceResponseV11` (the abortable transaction error of KIP-890), `ProduceResponseV10` (the leader discovery of
KIP-951),
`ProduceResponseV9` (the flexible frame of KIP-482), `ProduceResponseV8`,
`ProduceResponseV7`, `ProduceResponseV6`, `ProduceResponseV5`, `ProduceResponseV4`, `ProduceResponseV3`,
`ProduceResponseV2`, `ProduceResponseV1` and `ProduceResponseV0` — several of which read the same bytes and differ
only in the version of the request they belong to — with `ProduceResponsePartition` (v10 to v13, the only entry
with a tagged field), `ProduceResponsePartitionV8` (the record errors of KIP-467),
`ProduceResponsePartitionV5`, `ProduceResponsePartitionV2` and
`ProduceResponsePartitionV0` for their partition entries, and `ProduceResponseTopic` (v13, by id) and
`ProduceResponseTopicV10` (v10 to v12, by name) for the topic entries of the flexible versions. `ProduceRequestV12`
down to `ProduceRequestV3` send one and the same body, and `ProduceRequest` (v13) the same body with the id of every
topic in place of its name (`ProduceRequestTopic`, `ProduceRequestTopicV12` below it). The version is chosen in one
place, `Client::produceVersion()`: **version 13** for the message format v2 outside a transaction and inside one of
the protocol v2, the cap `ProduceRequestV11` for a transactional producer of the protocol v1 (`Client::produce()` hands it over, see "The transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 part 2
(v12)" below), and version 2 for a message set of the legacy formats - refused before it is sent to a node that no
longer serves it.

`LogAppendTime` is the timestamp the broker stamped the whole appended batch with, in milliseconds since the epoch,
or **-1** when it stamped nothing. It is not -1 only for a topic configured with
`message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime`: the broker then overwrites the timestamp of every record of the batch with
its own clock and reports that one value here (`Log.append` @ 0.11.0.3). In the message format v2 that overwriting
is a single field — the `MaxTimestamp` of the batch header plus bit 3 of its attributes, the records keep their
deltas — see "Offsets, timestamps and sequence numbers are deltas" above. `RecordMetadata::$timestamp` of this
client carries whichever of the two applies, exactly as the Java `RecordMetadata` does; the vectors
`produce.response.v3` and `produce.response.v3.log-append-time` below are the two answers. The Java
`RecordMetadata` of 1.1.1 does **not** carry the `LogStartOffset` of version 5, and neither does this client's:
the field belongs to the producer's own bookkeeping, not to the metadata of an appended record.

**A Produce request of version 3 and above accepts the message format v2 and nothing else — and on a 2.8.2 broker
that is an error code, not a closed connection.** `ProduceRequest.validateRecords` @ 2.8.2 walks the record set of
every partition and throws `InvalidRecordException: Produce requests with version 3 or higher are only allowed to
contain record batches with magic version 2`; a 1.1.1 broker turned that into an `InvalidRequestException` and
**closed the socket**, a 2.8.2 broker answers the offending **partition** with **87 `INVALID_RECORD`** and leaves
the connection open. (87 is the code KIP-467 gave to record validation in Kafka 2.4; from version 8 of the api on
the same answer also carries the `record_errors` array and an `error_message`, see below.)
The check runs one way only; re-measured on the 2.8.2 container with the very same single record in each of the
three formats:

| Request | magic 0 | magic 1 | magic 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Produce v0, v1, v2 | accepted | accepted | accepted |
| Produce v3, v4, v5, v6 | **87 `INVALID_RECORD`** | **87 `INVALID_RECORD`** | accepted |

A client that writes a message set of the format v0 or v1 therefore had to send a **Produce v2** request, which is
what `message.format.version` selects here. Below version 3 the 3.x broker still did not care: it stored whatever it
was given in the `message.format.version` of the topic and converted it on append (see "What the broker stores, and
what it answers" above), so a magic 0 batch sent with a Produce v2 landed in the log as a record batch v2 without a
timestamp, and a magic 2 batch sent with a Produce v0 landed there unchanged.

**Kafka 4.0 removed the versions 0 to 2 (KIP-896), and with them every way a message set reaches a log.**
`ProduceRequest.json` @ 4.0.0: "Versions 0-2 were removed in Apache Kafka 4.0, version 3 is the new baseline. Due to
a bug in librdkafka, these versions have to be included in the api versions response (see KAFKA-18659), but are
rejected otherwise" - the ApiVersions answer of the node lists Produce **0 to 13** (`ApiKeys.PRODUCE_API_VERSIONS_RESPONSE_MIN_VERSION`
@ 4.0.0 is 0), and a frame of version 0, 1 or 2 closes the connection. Re-measured on the 4.3.1 node with the same
single record in each format:

| Request | magic 0 | magic 1 | magic 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Produce v0, v1, v2 | **connection closed** | **connection closed** | **connection closed** |
| Produce v3 … v12 | **87 `INVALID_RECORD`** | **87 `INVALID_RECORD`** | accepted |

`docker logs kafka-4-3-1` names the refusal: `ERROR Closing socket for … because of error
(kafka.network.Processor)` with `UnsupportedVersionException: Received request for api with key 0 (Produce) and
unsupported version 2` behind it. So a `message.format.version` below `0.11.0` can not write to a 4.x node at all,
and **`Client::produceRecords()` refuses it before anything is sent**: it asks the leader of every partition of the
batch for its ApiVersions once per client and throws `InvalidConfigurationException` ("… serves Produce from version
3 only: Kafka 4.0 removed the versions 0 to 2 (KIP-896) …") when the node does not serve version 2. Because the row
of a 4.x node starts at 0 anyway, the node is recognised by the **top** of its row: `"validVersions": "3-12"` came in
the very commit that added version 12, so a Produce row that reaches `ProduceRequest::BASELINE_RAISED_WITH_VERSION`
(12) serves nothing below `ProduceRequest::BASELINE_VERSION` (3), and a row that starts above 2 says so itself. A node
of Kafka 3.x - its row is `0-11` - still gets the Produce v2 it serves. The record batch v2 never asks: the version
choice of `Client::produceVersion()` needs no ApiVersions round trip for it.

**A transactional id needs the message format v2.** It travels in a version 3 or higher request alone, so a
transaction can only ever be written in the message format v2; `Client::produceRecords()` refuses a transactional id together with a
`message.format.version` below `0.11.0` before anything is sent.

**Version 9 (Kafka 2.8) is the flexible version of KIP-482 and nothing else.** `ProduceRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 says
"Version 9 enables flexible versions" and declares `"flexibleVersions": "9+"` on both halves: the same fields as
version 8 with the request header **v2**, compact strings and arrays, a tagged-field section behind the body,
every topic entry and every partition entry, and - the one that matters for the size of a produce frame - a
**compact record set**, i.e. an unsigned varint of `length + 1` in front of the batches instead of an int32. The
vector pair `produce.request.v9`/`produce.response.v9` below is the same exchange as the version 8 pair in 124
and 60 bytes instead of 140 and 67. `ProduceRequestV8`/`ProduceResponseV8` keep the plain frame.

**Version 10 (Kafka 3.7, KIP-951) sends that body once more and gives the answer its first two tagged fields**:
the `current_leader` of a partition entry and the `node_endpoints` of the body, which together say where a
partition that was refused **6** `NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER` went. See "The
leader discovery of KIP-951 (v10)" below, and `ProduceRequestV9`/`ProduceResponseV9` keep the version under it.

**Version 11 (Kafka 3.8, KIP-890) sends that body an eighth time and changes one error code.** What it promises is
that a transactional producer understands the **120** `TransactionAbortable` in a partition of the answer, where
every version below it is answered the **48** `InvalidTxnState` for the same condition. See "The abortable
transaction error of KIP-890 (v11)" below; `ProduceRequestV10`/`ProduceResponseV10` keep the version under it.

**Version 12 (Kafka 4.0, KIP-890 part 2) sends that body a ninth time and changes what a transactional batch
means.** `ProduceRequestV12`/`ProduceResponseV12` keep it, and `ProduceRequestV11`/`ProduceResponseV11` the version
under it. See "The transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 part 2 (v12)" below.

**Version 13 (Kafka 4.1, KIP-516) names every topic by its id**, in the request and in the answer, and changes
nothing else. See "The topic ids of the produce path (v13, KIP-516)" below.

### The record errors of a refused batch (v8, KIP-467)

**Version 8 (Kafka 2.4, KIP-467) tells a producer which of its records the broker refused.** Every partition
entry of the answer gains a `record_errors` array of `[batch_index, batch_index_error_message]` pairs and an
`error_message`, both behind the `log_start_offset`; the request is the version 3 body once more.

The gap it closes is small and sharp. A batch is validated as a whole (`LogValidator` @ 2.8.2), and one bad
record refuses **all** of it: the partition is answered **87** `INVALID_RECORD`, the base offset `-1`, and — up to
version 7 — nothing else. A producer that batches a hundred records then knows only that the hundred were
rejected, and has no way to drop the offender and re-send the rest; the Java producer had to fail the whole
batch. From version 8 the answer names the records **by their position in the batch that was sent** — a *batch
index*, counted from 0, not an offset and not a position in the log, which those records never reached.

**Measured on the container**, with a topic created `cleanup.policy=compact` and a batch of three records of
which the second and the third have **no key** (`produce.request.v8.invalid-record` and its answer below):

| field | value |
|---|---|
| `error_code` | **87** `INVALID_RECORD` |
| `base_offset`, `log_append_time` | `-1` — nothing was appended |
| `record_errors` | two entries, `batch_index` **1** and **2** |
| `batch_index_error_message` | `Compacted topic cannot accept message without key in topic partition t2-24-compacted-0.` (both) |
| `error_message` | `One or more records have been rejected` |

The first record, the one **with** a key, is not named: the array holds the offenders, not the batch. And the
same request sent as a **version 7** one (`produce.response.v7.invalid-record`) comes back with the 87 and the
two `-1`s alone — the frame has no room for the rest, which is exactly the difference the version buys.

A compacted topic is the easiest way to produce the condition; an invalid timestamp
(`message.timestamp.difference.max.ms`) and a broken record checksum are the other two a client can trigger.

`ProduceResponsePartition::$recordErrors` is the array — keyed by the batch index, holding
`ProduceResponseRecordError` objects — and `$errorMessage` the summary. `Client::produce()` puts both into the
context of the exception it raises for the partition, so an application that catches the
`InvalidRecordException` of a produce reads `recordErrors` (batch index ⇒ message) and `errorMessage` from it
instead of guessing. An answer below version 8 leaves the array empty and the message `null`, which is "the
broker did not say", not "nothing was refused".

### The leader discovery of KIP-951 (v10)

**Version 10 (Kafka 3.7, KIP-951) is the first version of this api that declares a tagged field, and it declares
two of them.** `ProduceRequest.json` @ 3.7.2 has no field of the version — "Version 10 is the same as version 9
(KIP-951)", so `produce.request.v10` below is `produce.request.v9` with another number in its header — and
`ProduceResponse.json` says "Version 10 adds 'CurrentLeader' and 'NodeEndpoints' as tagged fields (KIP-951)":

```
ProduceResponse v10 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode Offset LogAppendTime LogStartOffset
                                   [RecordErrors] ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                       ThrottleTime TAG_BUFFER
  CurrentLeader => tag 0 of a PARTITION entry, [LeaderId int32 LeaderEpoch int32 TAG_BUFFER]
                   # both default -1, so an entry that names no leader does not carry the structure
  NodeEndpoints => tag 0 of the BODY, [NodeId int32 Host compact string Port int32
                                       Rack compact nullable string TAG_BUFFER]
                   # default [], so a body that names no leader does not carry the array
```

**What the two fields buy is a round trip.** A producer whose partition was moved to another broker is answered
**6** `NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER`, and until this version that was all it learned: it had to throw its metadata away,
ask Metadata for the topic, wait for the answer and only then re-send the batch — and a client that does this for
every partition of a rolling restart asks the same question again and again. The `current_leader` names the node
and the epoch the partition really has, and the `node_endpoints` of the body says where that node can be reached,
so the producer can send the batch to the right broker at once and correct its own metadata on the way.

**A broker fills them in for the error code 6 and for no other.** The callback of
`KafkaApis.handleProduceRequest` @ 3.9.2 walks the partitions of the answer and asks `getCurrentLeader` only
inside `if (request.header.apiVersion >= 10) { status.error match { case Errors.NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER => … } }`,
collecting the nodes it found in a `HashMap[Int, Node]` that becomes the `node_endpoints` — each node once,
whatever the number of partitions that point at it — and the endpoint it names is the one of the **listener the
request arrived on**, so a client may connect to it as it stands.

**On the node of this line the hint cannot be produced at all** (measured). Its one broker is the leader of every
partition it hosts, so no produce of a client of this repository is ever answered 6:

| Version 10 produce | Answer of `kafka-3-9-2` |
|---|---|
| an accepted batch | the version 9 answer, byte for byte: three **empty** tagged sections and 60 bytes of body (`produce.response.v10`) |
| the partition 99 of a topic with one partition | the per-partition **3** `UnknownTopicOrPartition`, and again not a tagged field (`produce.response.v10.unknown-partition`) |
| a partition this broker does not lead | not reachable on one broker — `produce.response.v10.current-leader` below is **constructed** from the specification and from the very structures the same node writes into a Fetch v16 answer of that condition |

The version is therefore in the client with its fields decoded and exposed and its answer measured, and the one
frame that carries the hint is the constructed one. `ProduceResponsePartition::$currentLeader` is the structure of
a partition entry, `ProduceResponse::$nodeEndpoints` the array of the body, indexed by the node id;
`ProduceRequestV9`/`ProduceResponseV9` keep the version below, whose partition entry is
`ProduceResponsePartitionV8` — the same bytes, without the place for the tag.

**This client reads the hint and does not re-route the batch yet.** `Client::produce()` puts the leader of a
refused partition into the context of the exception it raises for it - `currentLeaderId`,
`currentLeaderEpoch`, and `currentLeaderHost` / `currentLeaderPort` when the answer named the address as well
(`Client::leaderHintOf()`, which the fetch path of version 16 shares) - but the retry of a 6 still goes through
a metadata refresh, as it did before the KIP. Following the endpoint without one is a change of the producer's
send path and not of the protocol, and it waits for a wave of its own.

### The abortable transaction error of KIP-890 (v11)

**Version 11 (Kafka 3.8, KIP-890) adds no field to either half of the api.** `ProduceRequest.json` @ 3.8.1 and
`ProduceResponse.json` @ 3.8.1 carry the same one-line comment — "Version 11 adds support for new error code
TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE (KIP-890)" — and declare nothing, so a version 11 frame is a version 10 frame with another
number in its header, on both sides. What the version states is what the **client** understands:

| | Version 10 and below | Version 11 |
|---|---|---|
| a transactional batch for a partition the coordinator has not verified | **48** `InvalidTxnState`, `error_message` "Partition was not added to the transaction" | **120** `TransactionAbortable`, no `error_message` |

**The api version alone decides it.** `KafkaApis.handleProduceRequest` @ 3.9.2 turns the header into the
`TransactionSupportedOperation` of the append in one line —

```scala
val transactionSupportedOperation = if (request.header.apiVersion > 10) genericError else defaultError
```

— and `AddPartitionsToTxnManager` @ 3.9.2, the piece of the broker that asks the transaction coordinator whether
the partitions of a transactional produce really belong to the open transaction (`verify_only`, see
"AddPartitionsToTxn API (key 24, v0 to v4)"), maps the answer back for everybody else:

```scala
else if (partitionResult.partitionErrorCode() == Errors.TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE.code
         && transactionDataAndCallbacks.transactionSupportedOperation != genericError) // For backward compatibility with clients.
  Errors.INVALID_TXN_STATE.code
```

So the 120 is not a new condition: it is the condition the 48 always named, under a code that says what a producer
should do about it. `Errors.java` @ 3.9.2 spells the difference out — "The server encountered an error with the
transaction. The client can abort the transaction to continue using this transactional ID." — where the 48 reads
like the end of the producer, and `TransactionManager` @ 1.1.1 (and this package, in
`TransactionManager::transactionalRequest()`) really does treat a 48 of the *transaction protocol* as fatal.

**Measured on the node**, with the topic `t2-38-vectors` of two partitions, the partition 0 added to the open
transaction of `t2-38-vectors-tx` and the batch sent to the partition **1**:

| Request | Answer of `kafka-3-9-2` |
|---|---|
| the transactional batch at **v11** (`produce.request.v11.unverified-partition`) | **120** `TransactionAbortable`, `base_offset` / `log_append_time` / `log_start_offset` all -1, `error_message` **null**, 60 bytes of body |
| the very same frame at **v10** (`produce.request.v10.unverified-partition`) | **48** `InvalidTxnState` with the `error_message` "Partition was not added to the transaction", 102 bytes of body |
| an ordinary, accepted batch at **v11** (`produce.request.v11`) | the version 10 answer byte for byte — three empty tagged sections, 60 bytes |

The two requests differ in the **two bytes of the api version and the correlation id** and in nothing else: the
same transactional id, the same producer id and epoch, the same record batch, sent inside the same transaction.
The `error_message` is not part of the bargain either way — `ReplicaManager.handleProduceAppend` @ 3.9.2 writes a
custom message for the 48 alone (`case Errors.INVALID_TXN_STATE => Some(error.exception("Partition was not added
to the transaction"))`), so the 120 travels with the null of its own exception class.

**`transaction.version` is not a feature of a 3.9.2 node.** KIP-890 has a second part — the epoch bump of the
transaction protocol v2, which replaces the `verify_only` round trip altogether — and it rides on a cluster
feature of that name. The node of this line finalizes exactly two features, and neither is it: `metadata.version`
at 21 (`3.9-IV0`) and `kraft.version` at 0, both in the ApiVersions v3 answer and in
`kafka-features.sh --describe`. So the 120 of this line is the one the *verification* produces, not the one TV2
would, and every produce of this client goes through the `AddPartitionsToTxn` of KIP-98 as it always did.

**What this client does with it.** `Client::produce()` reports the code as
`TransactionAbortableException` for that topic-partition, with the `logStartOffset` of the answer in its context
like every other produce error, and `TransactionManager::batchFailed()` takes it down the path every non-fencing
error of a transactional batch takes: the producer moves into `ABORTABLE_ERROR`, `commitTransaction()` refuses,
and `abortTransaction()` rolls the transaction back and leaves the producer usable with the same transactional id
— which is precisely what the code asks for. No branch of its own is needed for that, and none was added; the
exception class is what tells an application the difference. A well-behaved producer of this package never
provokes it, because `TransactionManager::maybeAddPartitionsToTransaction()` adds every partition of a batch to
the transaction before the batch is sent; the frames above are the wire-level proof that the promise of the
version holds.

### The transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 part 2 (v12)

**Version 12 (Kafka 4.0) adds no field to either half of the api**, like the four versions before it.
`ProduceRequest.json` @ 4.0.0 says "Version 12 is the same as version 11 (KIP-890). Note when produce requests are
used in transaction, if transaction V2 (KIP_890 part 2) is enabled, the produce request will also include the
function for a AddPartitionsToTxn call. If V2 is disabled, the client can't use produce request version higher than
11 within a transaction", and `ProduceResponse.json` @ 4.0.0 "Version 12 is the same as version 10 (KIP-890)". The
same commit removed the versions 0 to 2 ("validVersions": "3-12", see above).

**What the version changes is decided on the broker, by the version alone.**
`AddPartitionsToTxnManager.produceRequestVersionToTransactionSupportedOperation` @ 4.0.0:

```scala
if (version > 11) addPartition
else if (version > 10) genericErrorSupported
else defaultError
```

A transactional batch of version 12 for a partition the coordinator has not been told about is therefore **added to
the transaction by the broker** and appended - the `AddPartitionsToTxn` round trip of the protocol v1 is part of the
produce - where version 11 is refused with the 120 of the verification and version 10 with the 48. The node of this
line finalizes `transaction.version` **2**, the feature the protocol v2 rides on. Measured with the topic
`t2-40-vectors` and two transactional ids that were handed a producer id by InitProducerId and nothing else:

| Request | Answer of `kafka-4-3-1` |
|---|---|
| a plain batch at **v12** (`produce.request.v12`) | appended at the offset 0, the version 10 answer byte for byte (`produce.response.v12`) |
| a transactional batch for an unannounced partition at **v12** (`produce.request.v12.transactional`) | **0**, appended at the offset 2: the broker added the partition (`produce.response.v12.transactional`) |
| the same question at **v11** (`produce.request.v11.transactional`) | **120** `TransactionAbortable`, nothing appended (`produce.response.v11.transactional`) - as on 3.9.2 |

**The version choice.** `Client::produceVersion(int $messageFormatMagic, ?int $maxVersion = null)` is the one
place the version is chosen: `ProduceRequest::VERSION` (12 in Kafka 4.0, 13 since the next section) for a record
batch, lowered to `$maxVersion` when the caller caps it, and version 2 for a message set. `Client::produce()` hands the cap over from the private
`Client::produceVersionCapOf(TransactionManager)`: a **transactional** producer whose transaction manager speaks
the protocol v1 (`TransactionManager::isTransactionV2Enabled()` is false - its coordinator does not finalize
`transaction.version` 2, or the manager was not initialized) is capped at
`TransactionManager::LAST_PRODUCE_VERSION_BEFORE_TRANSACTION_V2` (11, `ProduceRequestV11`): it sends
`AddPartitionsToTxn` before the batch and `EndTxn` v4 after it, and "the client can't use produce request version
higher than 11 within a transaction" of that protocol - the `useTransactionV1Version` cap of `ProduceRequest.Builder`
@ 4.0.0. A producer on the protocol v2 sends version 12, which enrols its partitions, and so do an idempotent
producer, which writes outside every transaction, and a plain one. Both paths are measured on `kafka-4-3-1` in
`TransactionAbortableProduceApiTest`: a manager held on the protocol v1 is answered the 120 for its unannounced
partition, the manager of the node's protocol v2 has the same batch appended and commits it.

### The topic ids of the produce path (v13, KIP-516)

**Version 13 (Kafka 4.1) replaces the name of every topic with its id**, in both halves of the api and in nothing
else. `ProduceRequest.json` @ 4.1.0 declares the `Name` of a topic entry for the versions "0-12" and a `TopicId`
uuid for "13+" - "Version 13 replaces topic names with topic IDs (KIP-516). May return UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID error
code." - and `ProduceResponse.json` @ 4.1.0 does the same to the topic entry of the answer, "Version 13 replaces
topic names with topic IDs (KIP-516)":

```
ProduceRequest v13 => TransactionalId Acks TimeoutMs [TopicId [Index Records TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER
  TopicId => uuid          # NEW in v13, in place of the compact string Name of v9 to v12

ProduceResponse v13 => [TopicId [Index ErrorCode BaseOffset LogAppendTimeMs LogStartOffset
                                 [BatchIndex BatchIndexErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER] ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER]
                        TAG_BUFFER] ThrottleTimeMs TAG_BUFFER
  TopicId => uuid          # NEW in v13, in place of Name
```

So a version 13 frame is the version 12 frame with the compact string of every name exchanged for the 16 bytes of
the id - `produce.request.v13` is 142 bytes where the same batch for the 13-character name `t2-41-vectors` would
be 140 - and the Metadata of KIP-516 (Kafka 2.8) is where the client learns the id. The broker resolves the id
through its metadata cache before anything else is looked at. Measured on `kafka-4-3-1` with the topic
`t2-41-vectors`:

| Version 13 request | Answer of `kafka-4-3-1` |
|---|---|
| a batch for the id of the topic, acks = 1 (`produce.request.v13`) | appended at the offset 0, the version 12 answer with the id in place of the name (`produce.response.v13`) |
| the same batch for an id the node does not have (`produce.request.v13.unknown-topic-id`) | the per-partition **100** `UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID` under the id of the request, base offset -1, nothing appended (`produce.response.v13.unknown-topic-id`) |
| the same at acks = -1, or for the zero uuid | the same **100** |
| the id of the topic with a partition it does not have | the per-partition **3** `UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION`, as by name |
| a batch for the id of the topic at **acks = 0** | no answer, and the batch is appended - the next fetch reads it |
| an unknown id at **acks = 0** | the node **closes the connection**, as for every refused batch of a request it would not answer |

**The Java client sends version 13 whether it knows the id or not**: `Sender.topicIdsForBatches` @ 4.1.0 puts
`Uuid.ZERO_UUID` into the frame for a topic its metadata has no id of, the node answers the 100 and the retry after
the metadata update carries the id. **This client does not put a frame on the wire without the id.**
`ProduceRequest::__construct()` takes the ids as its last argument (`$topicIds`, topic name => the 16 raw bytes of
its uuid, `ProduceRequest::getTopicIds()`) and refuses a topic whose id is missing or zero with the retriable
`UnknownTopicIdException` (100) before anything is written. `Client::produce()` resolves the ids of the topics of
every node request through `Cluster::topicIdsOf()`, which reloads the metadata once for a topic it does not know;
a topic still without an id fails with that 100, and the retry of `Client::produce()` reloads the cluster and asks
again - which is also what a **recreated** topic goes through: the node answers the 100 for the id of the deleted
topic, the reload brings the new id and the retry appends. `Network\RetryPolicy` counts the 100 among the codes a
metadata refresh can fix, as the Java client makes `UnknownTopicIdException` an `InvalidMetadataException`; nothing
was appended, so sending the batch again duplicates nothing. With no retry left - `retries` 0 is the default of the
producer - the batch is reported with the 100 and the metadata is reloaded all the same, so that the next call
names the topic by its current id instead of failing until `metadata.max.age.ms` runs out. The answer names its topics by id alone and is read
back through the map of the request, so `Client::produce()` reports every partition under its name exactly as for
version 12.

The version choice does not change: version 13 goes out wherever version 12 went - outside a transaction, for an
idempotent producer and inside a transaction of the protocol v2 - and a transactional producer of the protocol v1
stays capped at `TransactionManager::LAST_PRODUCE_VERSION_BEFORE_TRANSACTION_V2` (11, `ProduceRequestV11`), whose
topics travel by name. `ProduceRequestV12`/`ProduceResponseV12` keep the version below this one, and
`ProduceRequestTopicV12`/`ProduceResponseTopicV10` its topic entries. `ProduceTopicIdsApiTest` measures all of the
table above against the node and `Client::produce()` through a freshly created and a recreated topic.

## The idempotent producer

Kafka 0.11 gave the producer a delivery guarantee that no release before it had: **exactly once, in order, within
one producer session** (KIP-98). It costs three fields of the record batch v2 and one new api, and the whole of it
happens between the producer and the *leader* of a partition — no coordinator is involved, and a producer that only
wants idempotence never touches `__transaction_state`.

**What the producer sends.** Every batch of an idempotent producer carries

* the **producer id** that `InitProducerId` handed out (`ProducerId`, int64),
* the **epoch** of that id (`ProducerEpoch`, int16, always 0 without a transactional id),
* the **base sequence** of its first record (`BaseSequence`, int32), the last one being
  `BaseSequence + LastOffsetDelta`,

and the sequence numbers are **per topic-partition**, counted from 0, gapless, and *re-used unchanged* when a batch
has to be sent again. A batch that carries `-1` as its producer id is not deduplicated at all, which is what a
plain producer writes.

**What the broker keeps.** `ProducerStateManager` @ 1.1.1 holds, per **log** (i.e. per topic-partition) and per
producer id, one `ProducerStateEntry`: the epoch and — this is the 1.x change — the **last five** batches that
producer appended, each of them with its first and last sequence number, its offset and its timestamp
(`ProducerStateEntry.NumBatchesToRetain = 5`; the `ProducerIdEntry` of 0.11.0.3 kept a single batch). Five is also
why the Java producer of 1.x may keep up to five requests in flight per connection with idempotence on, where the
0.11 producer was forced down to one: a reordering of at most five batches is still recognised. This client is
synchronous — one produce request is written and its answer read before the next one — so it satisfies either
requirement by construction.

**What the broker checks**, in this order (`ProducerAppendInfo.checkSequence` in `ProducerStateManager.scala`, `Log.analyzeAndValidateProducerState`):

1. the batch is *exactly* one of the five the entry holds — same epoch, same first and last sequence: the request
   is a **duplicate**, and the broker answers it with the error code **0 and the base offset, the timestamp and the
   `LogAppendTime` of the original append**, without writing anything;
2. the epoch of the batch is **below** the one of the entry: **47** `InvalidProducerEpoch` — another producer took
   this producer id over;
3. the entry does not exist at all and the first sequence of the batch is not 0: **59** `UnknownProducerId` (Kafka
   1.0) — the broker never had, or no longer has, any state of this producer id for this partition. A 0.11.0.3
   broker, which had no such error code, answered **45** here;
4. the epoch is **above** the one of the entry: the entry is reset, and the first sequence of the batch has to be
   **0**, otherwise **45**;
5. the first sequence is not `lastSeq + 1` (with a wrap-around from `Int.MaxValue` to 0): **45**
   `OutOfOrderSequenceNumber`.

Verified against the container, one partition, one producer id, sequences as the table says:

| Batch sent                                       | Answer                                        |
|--------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| sequences 0-1, first time                        | 0, `baseOffset = 0`, `LogAppendTime = -1`     |
| the very same bytes again                        | **0**, `baseOffset = 0`, `LogAppendTime = 1789060474393` |
| sequence 2                                       | 0, `baseOffset = 2`                           |
| sequences 0-1 again, now that 2 was appended     | **0**, `baseOffset = 0` — the batch is still one of the last five, where 0.11.0.3 answered 45 |
| five batches, then a duplicate of each of the five | **0** and the base offset of its own original append, five times |
| a sixth batch, then a duplicate of the first     | **45** — the first one fell out of the window |
| sequence 9 (a gap)                               | **45**                                        |
| sequence 3, after the 45                         | 0, `baseOffset = 3` — a rejected batch changes nothing |
| sequence 0 of another *partition*, same producer | 0 — the sequence space is per partition       |
| sequence 5 as the *first* batch of a new producer id | **59** — 0.11.0.3 answered 45 here        |
| a DeleteRecords of every record, then the next sequence | **59**, `logStartOffset` = the new start of the log |
| epoch 1, sequences 0-1, then epoch 0             | 0, 0, then **47** for every batch of epoch 0  |
| epoch 2 with a first sequence of 5, then 0       | **45**, then 0 — an epoch bump on an entry that exists has to start at 0 |

**The error code 46 (`DuplicateSequenceNumber`) never reaches a client of a 1.1.1 broker either.** Its own
duplicate check (step 1 above) runs in `Log.analyzeAndValidateProducerState`, guarded by `isFromClient`, and
returns the original offset *before* `ProducerAppendInfo.maybeValidateAppend` is ever reached; the
`DuplicateSequenceNumberException` that the validation can throw is therefore only reachable on the replication
path. A client sees the *success* answer for a duplicate. The `LogAppendTime` of that success answer is the
giveaway: a `CreateTime` topic answers `-1` for a real append and the stored timestamp of the batch for a
duplicate.

**59 `UnknownProducerId`, and what `log_start_offset` is for.** The producer state of a log lives in the log: when
`Log.maybeIncrementLogStartOffset()` moves the low watermark — a `DeleteRecords` request, or a retention run —
`ProducerStateManager.truncateHead()` drops the entry of every producer whose last record fell below the new start.
The next batch of such a producer then meets a broker that has never heard of it, and since it does not start at
the sequence 0, the answer is 59. Nothing is wrong with that producer, and this is exactly why version **5** of the
Produce answer (Kafka 1.0) carries the `log_start_offset` of every partition: it is what tells the two cases apart.

| The answer carries              | What it means                                       | What the producer does |
|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|------------------------|
| 59, `log_start_offset = -1`     | The partition moved away from this broker between the error and the answer, so it could not name the offset | Sends the very same batch again, unchanged, until an answer names it |
| 59, `log_start_offset` **above** the last offset the producer had acknowledged for the partition | Every record this producer wrote there was deleted, and the state went with it | Numbers **that partition** from the sequence 0 again and sends the batch once more, keeping its producer id and every other partition |
| 59, `log_start_offset` at or below it | The records are still in the log and the state was lost for another reason | Reports the error; it is an `OutOfOrderSequence` like any other |

That decision is `TransactionManager.canRetry()` / `startSequencesAtBeginning()` @ 1.1.1, and this client
implements it in `Producer\Internals\TransactionManager::canRetryBatch()`, with `Client::produce()` sending the
repaired batch again. It holds for a **transactional** producer as well: the Java method does not exclude one, the
1.1.1 coordinator accepts the batch that starts the partition over under the epoch of the open transaction, and
only a 59 that can not be repaired makes the transaction abortable.

**What this client does** (`TransactionManager`, `Producer\Internals`): it holds the producer id, its epoch, the
next sequence of every topic-partition and the offset of the last record the broker acknowledged for it, asks for
the producer id lazily with the first flush, stamps every batch, and moves the sequence of a partition on by the
number of records the broker acknowledged. On a **47** the producer is finished: the state is fatal and every
further send reports the same `ProducerFencedException`. On a **45** — and on a **59** that the log start offset
does not explain — an idempotent producer throws its producer id away and asks for a new one with the next batch;
the batch that hit the error is reported to the caller, and the deduplication starts over, which is what
`Sender.failBatch()` @ 1.1.1 does. A *transactional* producer must not, because that would bump the epoch behind
the back of an open transaction: it reports the error and goes into an abortable state. A **46**, should a broker
ever send one, counts as an append: the sequence numbers are consumed and the partition is reported as accepted
with an unknown offset.

`enable.idempotence = true` also constrains two options, and this client refuses the configuration exactly as the
Java producer does: `acks` has to be `all` (`-1`) and `retries` must not be 0. Both are overridden when the caller
did not set them; `retries` becomes 3 here rather than the `Integer.MAX_VALUE` of the Java producer
(`KafkaProducer.configureRetries()` @ 1.1.1, unchanged since 0.11), which has a background sender to bound a batch
by time instead of by a number of attempts. The `acks` rule is enforced one layer lower as well: `Client::produce()`
refuses producer state next to anything but `acks = all`, because a request the broker does not answer leaves the
sequence numbers of this client where they were and would send every following batch with the very same ones. The
`retries` budget is what the repair of a 59 is spent from, and a `Client` that was handed producer state without
going through the producer configuration is still given one attempt — the repaired batch starts at the sequence 0,
which is never a 59 again.

**The guarantee ends with the producer.** A new producer asks for a new producer id, so it cannot deduplicate
against anything the previous one wrote, and an application that re-sends a record itself builds a *new* batch,
which the broker has no way of recognising. Deduplication across sessions is what a `transactional.id` is for.

**The error code 59 (`UnknownProducerId`) is gone from the produce path of a 2.8.2 broker.**
`ProducerAppendInfo.checkSequence` @ 2.8.2 no longer raises it anywhere: "If there is no current producer epoch
(possibly because all producer records have been deleted due to retention or the DeleteRecords API) accept writes
with any sequence number". Two of the cases that a 1.1.1 broker refused are therefore appended without a word:

* the next batch of a producer whose records were **all deleted** - by a DeleteRecords or by the retention - is
  taken with the sequence it carries, so the producer keeps counting where it stood instead of numbering the
  partition from 0 again. The repair path of this client (the `logStartOffset` of the answer, see below) is still
  in place for the brokers of the lines below and is never entered on a 2.8.2 one;
* the **first batch of a producer id the broker knows nothing about** is appended whatever sequence it starts at.

What is left of the guarantee is the **45** (`OutOfOrderSequence`) of a producer whose state the broker does hold,
the five-batch deduplication window, and the **47** of a fenced epoch.

## Transactions

The second half of KIP-98, and the one the whole api block 24-28 exists for: several partitions - and the
committed offsets of a consumer group - are written **atomically**, so that a reader either sees all of it or none
of it. The idempotent producer above is the foundation (the producer id, the epoch and the sequence numbers stay
exactly what they were); a transaction adds a **coordinator**, a **flag on the record batch**, a **control batch**
per partition and one option on the reading side.

### The pieces

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| `transactional.id` | The name the *application* gives its producer. It is what makes the guarantee survive a restart, and only one producer may use it at a time. |
| Transaction coordinator | The broker that leads the partition of the internal topic `__transaction_state` the id hashes to; found with the GroupCoordinator api and `CoordinatorType = 1`. It serves InitProducerId, AddPartitionsToTxn, AddOffsetsToTxn and EndTxn. |
| `__transaction_state` | The log of the coordinator: producer id, epoch, timeout, state (`Empty`, `Ongoing`, `PrepareCommit`, `PrepareAbort`, `CompleteCommit`, `CompleteAbort`, `Dead`) and the list of partitions of the open transaction. It is created by the **first** coordinator lookup of any transactional id. |
| The transactional bit | Bit 4 (0x10) of the record batch attributes. A batch that carries it belongs to a transaction; the `transactional_id` of the Produce v3 request names which. |
| The control batch | Bits 4 and 5 (0x30) and one record whose key is `(version, type)` and whose value is `(version, coordinatorEpoch)`: **COMMIT** (type 1) or **ABORT** (type 0). It is written by the coordinator, not by the producer, and no client ever hands it to an application. |
| Last stable offset (LSO) | The first offset of the oldest transaction that is still open, or the high watermark when none is. It is the bound of a `read_committed` fetch and what version 2 of the Offsets api answers such a reader for `LATEST`. |

### The flow of one transaction

```
producer                        transaction coordinator          partition leaders        group coordinator
   |  GroupCoordinator(type=1)  |                                       |                        |
   |--------------------------->|  (creates __transaction_state)        |                        |
   |  InitProducerId(txn id)    |                                       |                        |
   |--------------------------->|  producer id + epoch+1, aborts        |                        |
   |                            |  whatever the last incarnation left   |                        |
   |  ---- beginTransaction() is a client-side state change, no frame ----                       |
   |  AddPartitionsToTxn        |                                       |                        |
   |--------------------------->|  state Ongoing, timeout starts        |                        |
   |  Produce v3 (txn id, batch attributes 0x10)  ------------------->  |                        |
   |  AddOffsetsToTxn(group)    |                                       |                        |
   |--------------------------->|  adds __consumer_offsets-N            |                        |
   |  TxnOffsetCommit(group)  ------------------------------------------------------------------>|
   |  EndTxn(commit|abort)      |                                       |                        |
   |--------------------------->|  PrepareCommit / PrepareAbort         |                        |
   |             <--------------|  WriteTxnMarkers ------------------>  |  control batch         |
   |                            |  CompleteCommit / CompleteAbort       |                        |
```

Two things about that picture are easy to get wrong and were verified against the container:

* **`EndTxn` is answered before the markers exist.** The coordinator answers as soon as it has written its decision
  into `__transaction_state`; the control batches follow, one `WriteTxnMarkers` per partition leader. A
  `read_committed` consumer therefore sees the records of a committed transaction a moment *after* `EndTxn`
  returned, which is why the integration tests of this line poll for them.
* **A transaction is started by `AddPartitionsToTxn`, not by anything the client calls "begin".** The protocol has
  no BeginTransaction request at all.
* **On the 3.9.2 KRaft node the AddPartitionsToTxn is no longer optional** (it never was for the coordinator, but
  the log used to take the batch anyway). `transaction.partition.verification.enable` is true by default from
  Kafka 3.6 (KIP-890), so the leader asks the coordinator with a broker-side AddPartitionsToTxn **v4** whether the
  partition belongs to the transaction and refuses the batch with **48** and `Partition was not added to the
  transaction` when it does not — where the 2.8.2 ZooKeeper broker appended it and left a transaction hanging in
  the partition. → "Broker quirks and observations".

### What a reader sees

`isolation.level` is one byte in the Fetch (v4+) and the Offsets (v2) request, and it changes three things at once:

| | `read_uncommitted` (0) | `read_committed` (1) |
|---|---|---|
| The answer ends at | the high watermark | the **last stable offset** |
| `last_stable_offset` of the answer | **-1** | the real LSO |
| `aborted_transactions` of the answer | **null** | an array, possibly empty |
| Offsets v2 `LATEST` answers | the high watermark | the last stable offset |

**The broker does not filter anything.** A `read_committed` answer of a partition that holds an aborted
transaction carries the aborted records *and* the ABORT control batch, and only names the transaction in
`aborted_transactions` as a `(producer_id, first_offset)` pair. Verified on the container: a partition with one
aborted transaction of two records answers `hw = 3`, `lso = 3`, one aborted transaction, two record batches and
two records - both of which a client has to drop. The filtering algorithm is
`Fetcher.PartitionRecords.nextFetchedRecord()` @ 0.11.0.3 and this client implements it in
`Consumer\Internals\AbortedTransactionFilter`:

1. walk the **batches** of the answer in log order;
2. every aborted transaction whose `first_offset` is at or below the last offset of the current batch is taken off
   the list and its producer id is remembered as aborted;
3. a control batch never reaches an application, and an **ABORT** marker makes its producer id "not aborted" again;
4. every other batch of an aborted producer id is skipped whole.

A control batch is dropped in **both** isolation levels - `read_uncommitted` shows the aborted records but never
the marker.

The level travels in the **Offsets** request as well, and this client sends it there for the same reason the Java
consumer does: a `read_committed` consumer whose `endOffsets()` answered the high watermark would wait for records
it is never going to be shown. `Client::fetchPartitions()` and `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()` -
and with them `KafkaConsumer::endOffsets()`, `position()` and `seekToEnd()` - therefore all read
`ConsumerConfig::ISOLATION_LEVEL`. **`Admin\AdminClient::listOffsets()` deliberately stays at
`read_uncommitted`**: an administrator asks what is in the log, not what a particular reader may see, and the
admin client has no consumer configuration to take a level from.

### Where this client stands

`Producer\Internals\TransactionManager` keeps the state of the producer - `UNINITIALIZED`, `INITIALIZING`,
`READY`, `IN_TRANSACTION`, `COMMITTING_TRANSACTION`, `ABORTING_TRANSACTION`, `ABORTABLE_ERROR`, `FATAL_ERROR`,
with the transitions of `TransactionManager.State` @ 1.1.1 - the coordinators it talks to and the partitions of
the open transaction, and `Producer\KafkaProducer` exposes it under the names of the Java producer:
`initTransactions()`, `beginTransaction()`, `sendOffsetsToTransaction()`, `commitTransaction()`,
`abortTransaction()`. A `send()` outside a transaction is refused, `commitTransaction()` flushes what is buffered
first and `abortTransaction()` throws it away. On a cluster that finalizes `transaction.version` 2 the same calls
run the transaction protocol **v2** of Kafka 4.0 - see "The transaction protocol v2 on a node that finalizes it
(Kafka 4.0)" below.

Which error ends what:

| Code | Name | The producer then |
|---|---|---|
| 47 | InvalidProducerEpoch | **fatal** - another incarnation of the transactional id took over, nothing this producer sends is ever accepted again |
| 48 | InvalidTxnState | **fatal** - the coordinator and the producer disagree about what is open |
| 49 | InvalidProducerIdMapping | **fatal** - the producer id is not the one `__transaction_state` holds for the id |
| 51 | ConcurrentTransactions | **retried** after `retry.backoff.ms`; the coordinator is still completing the transaction before this one |
| 14, 15, 16 | GroupLoadInProgress, GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable, NotCoordinatorForGroup | **looks the coordinator up again** and repeats the request |
| anything else while a transaction is open | | **abortable** - `abortTransaction()` is the only way on |

`transactional.id` implies `enable.idempotence`, and with it `acks = all` and a non-zero `retries`; the empty
string is not an id (a broker answers it with 42) and this client refuses it as a configuration error.

### What Kafka 1.1 changed here: nothing on the wire, one thing in the producer

The api block 24-28 is still at version 0, `TransactionCoordinator` and `TransactionStateManager` @ 1.1.1 carry
the same state table and the same defaults as 0.11.0.3 (`transactional.id.expiration.ms` 604800000,
`transaction.abort.timed.out.transaction.cleanup.interval.ms` 60000,
`transaction.remove.expired.transaction.cleanup.interval.ms` 3600000, `transaction.max.timeout.ms` 900000), and
every observation of the two sections above was re-measured against the 1.1.1 container: the epoch that a fencing
`InitProducerId` bumps by more than one while it answers 51, the 48 of an abort that follows a commit and the 0 of
a second commit, the per-partition error codes of AddPartitionsToTxn, the COMMIT and ABORT control batches, the
last stable offset of an open transaction, and the coordinator rolling a transaction back after
`transaction.timeout.ms`. All of them answer exactly as they did on 0.11.0.3.

The one difference a transactional producer sees is the **59** of the section above: when a `DeleteRecords` (or a
retention run) removes every record a producer wrote into a partition of its transaction, the next batch is
answered with `UnknownProducerId` and a `log_start_offset` above what the producer had acknowledged. That is not
the end of the transaction - the partition is numbered from the sequence 0 again, the batch is sent once more under
the epoch of the open transaction, and the commit goes through. Only a 59 the log start offset does not explain is
an abortable error, and `KafkaProducer::commitTransaction()` then reports the stored error instead of committing,
exactly as the Java `KafkaProducer` throws the `KafkaException` of `maybeFailWithError()`.

### Bumping the epoch (KIP-360)

Until Kafka 2.5 an abortable error was the end of a transactional producer: it could abort the open transaction,
but the sequence state the coordinator held for its producer id was no longer the one the producer had, so the
next transaction was answered **47** `InvalidProducerEpoch` (or the 45 of an out-of-order sequence) and nothing
could be done but build a new producer with a new `transactional.id`. KIP-360 gave the producer a way out with the
**version 3 of InitProducerId**: the request carries the `producer_id` and the `producer_epoch` the producer holds,
and the coordinator answers **the same id with `epoch + 1`** instead of a fresh one.

```
InitProducerIdRequest (Version: 3) => transactional_id transaction_timeout_ms producer_id producer_epoch
  producer_id    => int64   -- -1 to ask for a NEW id, as every version below did
  producer_epoch => int16   -- -1 with it
```

`TransactionCoordinator.handleInitProducerId` @ 2.8.2 is where the two meanings part: with the -1/-1 it hands out
the next id (or the stored one with a bumped epoch, which is what fences the previous producer of that
transactional id), and with a real pair it calls `prepareInitProducerIdTransit` for **that** id and bumps its
epoch, after aborting whatever transaction was still open. Everything that still writes under the old epoch is
fenced from that moment on, which is the point: the producer keeps its identity and loses only the transaction it
had to abort.

What a producer does with it (`TransactionManager.bumpIdempotentEpochAndResetIdIfNeeded()` /
`initializeTransactions(boolean keepPreparedTxn)` @ 2.8.2, and
{@see \Protocol\Kafka\Producer\Internals\TransactionManager} here): after an abortable error it aborts the
transaction and, **if it is transactional**, asks for the bump with its own id and epoch; an **idempotent**
producer has no coordinator that remembers it and simply asks for a new id with the -1/-1. The five-batch window
and the 59 `UnknownProducerId` of the 1.x line are untouched by it - they are the cure for a partition whose
records were deleted, not for a fenced producer.

Here it is one flag and one request: `transitionToAbortableError()` sets `epochBumpRequired`, and
`abortTransaction()` sends the `InitProducerId` v3 of the bump **after** the `EndTxn(ABORT)` went through, then
throws the sequence numbers of every partition away. Measured on the container: a producer that aborts under an
abortable error keeps its producer id and comes back with `epoch + 1`, writes its next transaction under that
epoch and has it committed, while the records of the aborted one stay in the log with an ABORT marker behind them
(`TransactionalProducerTest::testAnAbortableErrorBumpsTheEpochAndTheProducerGoesOn`). An abort that no error
caused sends no `InitProducerId` at all - there is no sequence state to fence.

### The consumer group metadata of a transactional commit (KIP-447)

The consume-transform-produce loop commits the offsets of its consumer **inside** the producer's transaction, with
TxnOffsetCommit. Until Kafka 2.5 that request named the consumer group and nothing else, and the group coordinator
had no way of telling a commit of the current generation from one of a consumer that had already been rebalanced
away: the loop could write offsets for partitions that another member owned by then. The **version 3** of the api
carries who the consumer is:

```
TxnOffsetCommitRequest (Version: 3) => transactional_id group_id producer_id producer_epoch
                                       generation_id member_id group_instance_id [topics]
  generation_id     => int32                     -- -1 for a producer that is not a member
  member_id         => COMPACT_STRING            -- the empty string with it
  group_instance_id => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING   -- the `group.instance.id` of a static member (KIP-345)
```

`GroupCoordinator.handleTxnCommitOffsets` @ 2.8.2 checks the three against the group it holds and answers, **per
partition**:

| Code | Name | When |
|------|------|------|
| 22 | `IllegalGeneration` | the generation of the request is not the current one |
| 25 | `UnknownMemberId` | the member id is not a member of the group |
| 82 | `FencedInstanceId` | the `group.instance.id` belongs to another member id now (KIP-345) |

and the generation **-1** with an empty member id skips the check entirely - `validateOffsetCommit` treats it as
the "not a member" commit that every version below 3 was, which is what keeps a producer that commits for a group
it does not belong to working. `Consumer\ConsumerGroupMetadata` carries the four values and
`KafkaProducer::sendOffsetsToTransaction()` takes it in place of the bare group id, exactly as the Java
`Producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(Map, ConsumerGroupMetadata)` does; the 1.x form with a `string $groupId` still
works and means `ConsumerGroupMetadata::forGroup()`. On the consumer side
`Consumer\KafkaConsumer::groupMetadata()` answers that object - the `KafkaConsumer.groupMetadata()` of the Java
client - with the generation and the member id its coordinator holds, or the -1 and the empty member id of a
consumer that never joined a group (one that picked its partitions with `assign()`), so that the
consume-transform-produce loop is:

```php
$producer->sendOffsetsToTransaction($consumer->position(...), $consumer->groupMetadata());
```

Measured on the container with a real member of a real group: the commit of the current generation is answered
**0**, the same commit with the generation before it **22**, a member id the group does not have **25**, and the
-1 with the empty member id **0** - the commit every version below 3 sent.

### The transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 (Kafka 3.8), and what a client reaches on this node

KIP-890 came in two parts. The **first** is the verification that closed the hanging-transaction hole: the leader
of a partition asks the transaction coordinator whether a partition really belongs to the transaction of the batch
it is about to append, with the **AddPartitionsToTxn v4** Kafka 3.5 added for brokers (see the section of key 24
and "A transactional batch for a partition the transaction does not hold is refused" under "Broker quirks and
observations"). The **second** is the transaction protocol **v2**: the producer epoch is bumped once per
transaction, the partitions of a transaction are enrolled implicitly by the Produce request itself instead of by
an AddPartitionsToTxn of the client, and a coordinator that hits an error the producer can recover from answers
the new error code **120** `TransactionAbortable` instead of ending the producer.

Kafka 3.8 put the **wire half** of that second part in place and nothing else: nine client-facing versions whose
whole content is the promise that the sender understands the 120 - Produce **v11**, FindCoordinator **v5**,
InitProducerId **v5**, AddPartitionsToTxn **v5**, AddOffsetsToTxn **v4**, EndTxn **v4** and TxnOffsetCommit
**v4**, each of them declared with the same sentence in its JSON and with not one new field. This client sends the
five of the transaction apis; the two of the producer belong to the Produce and FindCoordinator sections.

**The behaviour half is gated on a feature this node does not have.** The switch is the `transaction.version` of
KIP-1022, `TransactionVersion` in `server-common` @ 3.9.2: `TV_0` is the coordinator as it always was, `TV_1`
("flexible transactional state records") and `TV_2` ("epoch bump per transaction and optimizations") are the two
levels KIP-890 part 2 needs - and **both of them declare `bootstrapMetadataVersion = IBP_4_0_IV0`**, the metadata
version of Kafka 4.0. Measured on the node:

* The **ApiVersions answer names one feature**: `metadata.version`, supported 1 to 21 and finalized at 21
  (`3.9-IV0`), with the finalized-features epoch of the metadata log. There is **no `transaction.version` entry at
  all**, neither supported nor finalized, because `BrokerFeatures.defaultSupportedFeatures` @ 3.9.2 only puts a
  production feature into the map `if (maxVersion > 0)` and `TransactionVersion.latestProduction` at the metadata
  version `3.9-IV0` is `TV_0`, the level **0**. A missing feature is read as the level 0
  (`finalizedFeatures.getOrDefault(TransactionVersion.FEATURE_NAME, 0)`), so this node runs at **TV_0** and
  `kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 describe` lists `kraft.version` and `metadata.version` and
  nothing else.
* An **ApiVersions v4** answer names two supported features, `kraft.version` 0 to 1 next to `metadata.version`.
  The v3 this client sends leaves the first one out on purpose: `ApiVersionsResponse.maybeFilterSupportedFeatureKeys`
  @ 3.9.2 drops every feature whose *minimum* supported level is 0 below the version 4, "some older clients will
  have deserialization problems if a feature's minimum supported level is 0" (KAFKA-17492). It is a filter of the
  answer, not of the cluster, and it never hides `transaction.version`, which is not in the map to begin with.
* The one thing `transaction.version` gates in 3.9.2 is `TransactionStateManager.usesFlexibleRecords()`, the
  record format of `__transaction_state` - **TV_2 is not implemented at that tag at all**. There is no epoch bump
  per transaction and no implicit AddPartitionsToTxn of a Produce to reach: a client of this line opens every
  transaction with an AddPartitionsToTxn of its own, exactly as on the lines below.
* The **120 is reachable, and one of the five version bumps really earns it.**
  `Errors.TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE` is written by exactly one line of the broker at 3.9.2,
  `TransactionCoordinator.handleVerifyPartitionsInTransaction` - the `verify_only` AddPartitionsToTxn of the
  **partition verification** of KIP-890 part 1, which a broker sends before it appends a transactional record.
  It reaches a client in two ways. **Directly**, when the client sends that broker frame itself: the
  AddPartitionsToTxn **v4 and v5**, measured since the 3.5 wave and again at the version 5. And **through the
  verification**, when the broker asks the question on the client's behalf: `AddPartitionsToTxnManager` @ 3.9.2
  maps the 120 back to the 48 "for backward compatibility with clients" unless the request version says the
  client understands it, and that gate is a version comparison per api -
  `if (apiVersion >= 4) genericError else defaultError` in `GroupCoordinator.handleTxnCommitOffsets` for
  **TxnOffsetCommit**, `if (request.header.apiVersion > 10)` in `KafkaApis.handleProduceRequest` for **Produce**.
  So a TxnOffsetCommit **v4** whose `__consumer_offsets` partition the open transaction does not hold - a commit
  that no AddOffsetsToTxn preceded - is answered the **120**, where the same commit at the version 3 is answered
  the **48**: measured, and the pair of frames is in the vectors of this wave.
* The other three bumps are promises and nothing more, because **the apis they belong to verify no partition**:
  InitProducerId hands out an id, AddOffsetsToTxn *adds* the offsets partition to the transaction, EndTxn ends
  it. Measured at the new versions: a fenced producer is the **90**, a producer id the coordinator does not hold
  the **49** (or the 90 at InitProducerId), a commit of a member the group does not hold the **25**, an abort of
  a committed transaction the **48** - at the version below just as at the new one.

`TransactionManager` here needs no new branch for it: `TransactionAbortableException` is not one of the five
exceptions `transactionalRequest()` treats as fatal, so a 120 from any of these apis puts the producer into
`ABORTABLE_ERROR`, out of which `abortTransaction()` leads with the epoch bump of KIP-360 - which is what the Java
`TransactionManager` @ 3.9.2 does with `Errors.TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE` in all six of its handlers.

### The transaction protocol v2 on a node that finalizes it (Kafka 4.0)

The section above measured the 3.9.2 node of the 3.x line, which knew no `transaction.version`. **Kafka 4.0
implements the behaviour half of KIP-890 part 2**, and a 4.x cluster formatted with the defaults of its release
finalizes it: the 4.3.1 node of this line reports `transaction.version` **2** (supported 0 to 2) in the finalized
features of its ApiVersions answer. Two version bumps of Kafka 4.0 carry the protocol, and one of Kafka 4.0 that
belongs to the Produce section:

| Api | Version | What the version switches on (`TransactionSupportedOperation` / `TransactionVersion` @ 4.0.0) |
|---|---|---|
| Produce | **v12** | `addPartition`: the leader enrols the partition of a transactional batch into the transaction instead of verifying it |
| TxnOffsetCommit | **v5** | `addPartition`: the group coordinator enrols the `__consumer_offsets` partition of the group |
| EndTxn | **v5** | `TV_2`: the coordinator bumps the epoch with every end of a transaction and answers the new producer id and epoch |

So a transaction of the protocol v2 sends **no AddPartitionsToTxn and no AddOffsetsToTxn** at all, and its producer
runs every transaction under a new epoch. The Java client guards every one of the three: `ProduceRequest`,
`TxnOffsetCommitRequest` and `EndTxnRequest` @ 4.0.0 each cap the version at their
`LAST_STABLE_VERSION_BEFORE_TRANSACTION_V2` (11, 4 and 4) unless `TransactionManager.isTransactionV2Enabled()`,
which reads the finalized `transaction.version >= 2` off the ApiVersions answers of the cluster.

**What the node answers** (the vectors `txnoffsetcommit.*.v4.not-enrolled`, `txnoffsetcommit.*.v5` and the five
`endtxn.*.v5*` pairs, and `TransactionProtocolV2Test`):

* A TxnOffsetCommit **v4** without an AddOffsetsToTxn in front of it is still the **120** `TransactionAbortable` -
  the partition verification of KIP-890 part 1, on a node that has the feature exactly as on the one that had not.
  That is where the 120 reaches a client of this line: the v4 frames of the protocol v1, TxnOffsetCommit and the
  Produce v11 of the Produce section; `TransactionCoordinator.handleVerifyPartitionsInTransaction` @ 4.3.1 is still
  the one line of the broker that writes it.
* The same commit at the version **5** is **0**: the offsets partition is enrolled and the transaction started.
* An EndTxn **v5** COMMIT is answered **0 with the producer id and the epoch one higher**; a retry of it with the
  epoch it was sent with is answered the same once the markers are written (the **51** while they are not), a commit
  under the new epoch of a transaction that enrolled nothing is the **48**, an abort of such a transaction is **0**
  and bumps the epoch once more, and an epoch two behind is the **90**. An expired transaction is rolled back with
  an epoch bump as well, so the producer that abandoned it is answered the **48** by its commit - one epoch below
  the current one reads as a retry of the abort - where the protocol v1 answered the 90.

**Where this client stands.** `Producer\Internals\TransactionManager` does what the Java one does:

* `initTransactions()` asks the transaction coordinator for its ApiVersions and reads the finalized
  `transaction.version` (a 3.x node has none, the level 0); `isTransactionV2Enabled()` answers `true` from the level
  2 on - `TransactionManager::TRANSACTION_VERSION_2` - provided the Produce request of the client can enrol a
  partition, `ProduceRequest::VERSION` above `TransactionManager::LAST_PRODUCE_VERSION_BEFORE_TRANSACTION_V2` (11).
* In the protocol v2 `maybeAddPartitionsToTransaction()` sends nothing and only notes the partitions,
  `sendOffsetsToTransaction()` sends one `Client::txnOffsetCommit(…, $transactionV2 = true)` - the version 5 - and
  no AddOffsetsToTxn, and `commitTransaction()`/`abortTransaction()` send `Client::endTxnBumpingEpoch()` - the
  EndTxn v5 - and take the producer id and epoch of its answer over, every sequence from 0 again.
* An abortable error needs no InitProducerId of KIP-360 any more: the abort is an EndTxn v5, which bumps the epoch
  itself (`needToTriggerEpochBumpFromClient()` @ 4.0.0 is `false` in the protocol v2).
* A transaction that enrolled nothing - no partition, no offsets - is not ended at the coordinator at all, which
  would answer the commit of it the 48 (`transactionStarted` @ 4.0.0); this holds for the protocol v1 as well,
  where the coordinator answers an EndTxn of an `Empty` transactional id the same 48.
* The feature is read again before every end of a transaction, which ends with the protocol it began with; a
  cluster that moved up to the level 2 in the meantime makes the producer bump its epoch once with an InitProducerId
  after the EndTxn v4, "to fence the old V1 transaction epoch", and one that moved down sends the next transaction
  with the protocol v1 again.
* The protocol **v1** stays for a node below the level 2 and for every 3.x node: AddPartitionsToTxn v3,
  AddOffsetsToTxn v4, TxnOffsetCommit **v4** (`TxnOffsetCommitRequestV4`) and EndTxn **v4** (`EndTxnRequestV4`,
  `Client::endTxn()`), with a Produce of at most the version 11 inside the transaction.

The Produce version is the one piece the manager does not send itself: `Client::produce()` writes the batch, and
`TransactionManager::isTransactionV2Enabled()` is what it chooses the version by - 12 and above inside a
transaction of the protocol v2, at most 11 inside one of the protocol v1. `KafkaProducer`'s public api does not
change.

## Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)

```
FetchRequest v0, v1 and v2 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes [TopicName [Partition FetchOffset MaxBytes]]
  ReplicaId   => int32
  MaxWaitTime => int32
  MinBytes    => int32
  TopicName   => string
  Partition   => int32
  FetchOffset => int64
  MaxBytes    => int32
```

```
FetchRequest v3 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes [TopicName [Partition FetchOffset MaxBytes]]
  MaxBytes => int32
```

```
FetchRequest v4 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel
                   [TopicName [Partition FetchOffset MaxBytes]]
  IsolationLevel => int8
```

```
FetchRequest v5 and v6 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel
                          [TopicName [Partition FetchOffset LogStartOffset MaxBytes]]
  LogStartOffset => int64
```

```
FetchRequest v7 and v8 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel SessionId Epoch
                          [TopicName [Partition FetchOffset LogStartOffset MaxBytes]]
                          [TopicName [Partition]]
  SessionId => int32
  Epoch     => int32
```

```
FetchResponse v0 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset MessageSetSize MessageSet]]
  TopicName           => string
  Partition           => int32
  ErrorCode           => int16
  HighwaterMarkOffset => int64
  MessageSetSize      => int32
```

```
FetchResponse v1, v2 and v3 => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset
                                                          MessageSetSize MessageSet]]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
```

```
FetchResponse v4 => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset LastStableOffset
                                               [AbortedTransactions] RecordSetSize RecordSet]]
  LastStableOffset    => int64
  AbortedTransactions => nullable [ProducerId FirstOffset]
    ProducerId  => int64
    FirstOffset => int64
```

```
FetchResponse v5 and v6 => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset LastStableOffset
                                                      LogStartOffset [AbortedTransactions] RecordSetSize RecordSet]]
  LogStartOffset => int64
```

```
FetchResponse v7 and v8 => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode SessionId
                           [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset LastStableOffset
                                       LogStartOffset [AbortedTransactions] RecordSetSize RecordSet]]
  ErrorCode => int16
  SessionId => int32
```

```
FetchRequest v9 and v10 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel SessionId Epoch
                           [TopicName [Partition CurrentLeaderEpoch FetchOffset LogStartOffset MaxBytes]]
                           [TopicName [Partition]]
  CurrentLeaderEpoch => int32       # since version 9, BETWEEN the partition id and the fetch offset
```

```
FetchResponse v9 and v10 => the frame of v7 and v8, field for field
```

```
FetchRequest v11 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel SessionId Epoch
                    [TopicName [Partition CurrentLeaderEpoch FetchOffset LogStartOffset MaxBytes]]
                    [TopicName [Partition]] RackId
  RackId => string                  # since version 11, the LAST field of the frame
```

```
FetchResponse v11 => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode SessionId
                     [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset LastStableOffset
                                 LogStartOffset [AbortedTransactions] PreferredReadReplica
                                 RecordSetSize RecordSet]]
  PreferredReadReplica => int32     # since version 11, BETWEEN the aborted transactions and the records
```

```
FetchRequest v12 => ReplicaId MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel SessionId Epoch
                    [TopicName [Partition CurrentLeaderEpoch FetchOffset LastFetchedEpoch
                                LogStartOffset MaxBytes TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                    [TopicName [Partition] TAG_BUFFER] RackId TAG_BUFFER
  LastFetchedEpoch => int32         # since version 12, BETWEEN the fetch offset and the log start offset
  TopicName        => compact string        # every string of a flexible frame
  RackId           => compact string
  ClusterId        => tag 0, compact nullable string, default null
```

```
FetchResponse v12 => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode SessionId
                     [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset LastStableOffset
                                 LogStartOffset [AbortedTransactions] PreferredReadReplica
                                 RecordSetSize RecordSet TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER
  RecordSet      => compact bytes           # the record set of a flexible frame is a COMPACT byte array
  DivergingEpoch => tag 0, [Epoch int32 EndOffset int64]
  CurrentLeader  => tag 1, [LeaderId int32 LeaderEpoch int32]
  SnapshotId     => tag 2, [EndOffset int64 Epoch int32]
```

Ordinary consumers always send `ReplicaId = -1`. Version 1, added by Kafka 0.9, leaves the request untouched and
prefixes the response with `ThrottleTimeMs` — the **opposite end** of the frame from where the Produce API put its
`ThrottleTime`. `FetchResponse.readFrom` reads the field only when the request version is greater than 0, so reading
a v0 answer with the v1 layout takes the size of the topics array for the throttle time and desynchronizes the whole
frame; the two layouts therefore live in `FetchResponse` and `FetchResponseV0`. Without quotas — the default
`consumer_byte_rate` is unlimited — the field is always `00 00 00 00`, see "Quotas and throttle time" below for what
a broker with a quota answers instead.

**Version 2 (Kafka 0.10.0) is one bit of information and no field at all.** `FETCH_REQUEST_V2` is `FETCH_REQUEST_V1`
and `FETCH_RESPONSE_V2` is `FETCH_RESPONSE_V1`, so the two frames are byte-identical; what changes is what the broker
does with the log before it answers, see "What the broker stores, and what it answers" above for the whole
conversion table of a 0.11 broker.

**Version 3 (Kafka 0.10.1, KIP-74) adds the request-level `MaxBytes`** after `MinBytes` and changes nothing in the
response. It bounds the **whole answer**, while the `MaxBytes` of a partition entry keeps its per-partition meaning
(`fetch.max.bytes` and `max.partition.fetch.bytes` of a consumer). Two things follow from
`ReplicaManager.readFromLocalLog`, and both were verified on the broker:

* **The order of the partitions in the request is the order in which the answer is filled.** The broker walks the
  partitions as they arrive, subtracts what it read from the remaining budget (`limitBytes`) and stops filling once
  it is used up; the partitions behind that point come back with an empty record set although their high water mark
  shows that there is something to read. A fetch of two partitions with `MaxBytes = 40` — less than a single message
  of either — returns the message of the *first* one and nothing for the second (`fetch.response.v3.max-bytes`
