  below), and the very same fetch with the two partitions in the other order returns the message of the other one. A
  consumer therefore has to **rotate the order of its partitions** between fetches, otherwise the ones at the end of
  its assignment would starve; this client rotates a partition that returned records behind the ones that did not,
  which is what `Fetcher.parseCompletedFetch` ⇒ `SubscriptionState.movePartitionToEnd` does in the Java consumer.
* **The first non-empty partition always makes progress.** As long as nothing has been read yet the broker ignores
  both `MaxBytes` limits (`minOneMessage = !hardMaxBytesLimit`, and `hardMaxBytesLimit` is `versionId <= 2`), so a
  message that is larger than either of them is returned in full; an answer may therefore be *bigger* than the
  `MaxBytes` that were asked for. A 4 KiB message came back complete from a v3 request with a partition `MaxBytes` of
  64 and a request `MaxBytes` of 64, and even with a request `MaxBytes` of **0**, while the same fetch with a v1
  request returned 64 bytes without a single complete message. Once a partition has been read the guarantee is over
  for the rest of the answer, and an incomplete record set is replaced with an empty one
  (`!hardMaxBytesLimit && fetch.firstEntryIncomplete`), so a v3 answer never carries a partial-only partition.

The second point retires the `RecordTooLargeException` of the lower versions for a client that fetches with v3 or
above: a partition can no longer be stuck on a message that does not fit into `max.partition.fetch.bytes`. It also
means that an empty partition below the high water mark says nothing about the size of its next message — it usually
means that the budget of the answer was used up by the partitions in front of it — so
`FetchResponsePartition::isSingleMessageTooLarge()` is only asked about an answer of the versions 0 to 2.

**Version 4 (Kafka 0.11.0, KIP-98) is the version of the transactional protocol.** It adds a single `IsolationLevel`
byte behind the request-level `MaxBytes` and two fields to every partition entry of the answer, and it is the first
version that is answered with **the log as it lies**: a record batch of the message format v2, with the headers, the
producer ids and the transaction flags that no lower version has a place for. Its partition *request* entry is
unchanged.

* `IsolationLevel = 0` is `read_uncommitted`: every record up to the high water mark is visible, transactional ones
  included and whether or not their transaction was ever committed. `= 1` is `read_committed`: the answer stops at
  the **last stable offset** and the broker reports which transactions it aborted in the range it covers.
  `FetchRequest::READ_UNCOMMITTED` / `READ_COMMITTED` of this client, `ConsumerConfig::ISOLATION_LEVEL` in the
  configuration.
* `LastStableOffset` (LSO) is the offset below which the state of every transactional record has been decided. A
  partition that no transaction ever touched has an LSO equal to its high water mark.
* `AbortedTransactions` is a **nullable** array of `[ProducerId, FirstOffset]` pairs: the id of a producer whose
  transaction was aborted and the first offset it wrote in that transaction, read out of the `.txnindex` file of the
  segment (`TransactionIndex` @ 0.11.0.3).

**What a 2.8.2 broker really answers**, re-measured on the container for the versions 4, 5 and 8 and pinned by
`FetchApiTest::testTheLastStableOffsetAndTheAbortedTransactionsAreTheAnswerOfAReadCommittedFetchAlone()`:

| Fetch | `isolation_level` | `LastStableOffset` | `AbortedTransactions` | `LogStartOffset` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v4 | `read_uncommitted` | **the real LSO** | **null** (count -1) | — |
| v4 | `read_committed` | the real LSO | array, empty without an abort | — |
| v5 and v8 | `read_uncommitted` | **the real LSO** | **null** (count -1) | the real one, e.g. 0 |
| v5 and v8 | `read_committed` | the real LSO | array, empty without an abort | the real one |

**The first column is the one that changed with this line.** A **0.11.0.3** and a **1.1.1** broker answered
`LastStableOffset = -1` to a `read_uncommitted` fetch — "you did not ask, so I did not compute it" — and the
vectors of those lines (`fetch.response.v5`, `fetch.response.v4` below) still carry that -1. A 2.8.2 broker fills
the field in **for both isolation levels**: `Partition.readRecords` @ 2.8.2 always puts the last stable offset into
its `LogReadInfo`, and `KafkaApis` copies it into every partition entry whatever the isolation level was. The
constant `FetchResponsePartition::INVALID_LAST_STABLE_OFFSET` (-1) therefore only ever appears in an answer below
version 4 now, which does not carry the field at all.

`AbortedTransactions` did **not** change, and its two states are still not the same thing: `null` means "the broker
was not asked to track transactions", the **empty array** means "asked, and nothing was aborted here"
(`fetch.response.v5` and `fetch.response.v5.read-committed` below are the two answers of the very same partition).
`LogStartOffset`, like the LSO, is filled in for both isolation levels: it is a property of the partition, not of
the transaction protocol.

**The broker filters nothing.** A `read_committed` answer carries the records of an aborted transaction *and* the
control batch with its `ABORT` marker; dropping them is the job of the consumer, which walks the batches and skips
the ones of a producer that is named in `AbortedTransactions` until it sees that producer's marker.
`fetch.response.v5.aborted` below is such an answer, with both batches in its record set.

**A record with headers is converted down by dropping the headers — a 1.x broker fixed what 0.11 refused.** A
partition whose log holds a record with headers is answered to a Fetch request **below version 4** with the error
code **0** and the full record set, converted to the message format the version understands and **without** the
headers; key, value and timestamp survive, not a single record is skipped and no offset is left out.
`AbstractRecords.convertRecordBatch` @ 1.1.1 says so in one line — "Down-convert this record. Ignore headers when
down-converting to V0 and V1 since they are not supported" — and appends the record with the four-argument
`appendWithOffset(offset, timestamp, key, value)` instead of `append`, which is exactly the call that threw
`IllegalArgumentException: Magic v1 does not support record headers` on 0.11.0.3 and made that broker answer the
partition with the error code **-1** (`UnknownServerError`) and an empty record set (KAFKA-5760).

**This is a behaviour a client has to know about.** On 0.11 headers made a partition *unreadable* below Fetch v4
and the reader knew it; on this line the reader gets records that quietly lost a part of themselves, and the only
trace is the broker's own `Down-converting records with headers` warning. Measured on the container with a batch of
three records, the middle one carrying the header `trace-id: abc` (`DumpLogSegments --print-data-log` shows
`headerKeys: [trace-id]` on that record in the log, so nothing about the stored batch changes):

| Fetch | error code | magic of the answer | records | headers | timestamps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v5 | 0 | 2 | all three | `trace-id: abc` on the middle one | the `CreateTime` of the producer |
| v3 | 0 | 1 | all three | **dropped** | the `CreateTime` of the producer |
| v1 | 0 | 0 | all three | **dropped** | none — magic 0 has no timestamp |

`FetchApiTest::testAPartitionWhoseRecordsCarryHeadersIsDownConvertedWithoutThemBelowVersionFour()` pins both
halves — the values that survive and the headers that do not. Re-measured on the 2.8.2 container: unchanged since
the 1.x line, and a `message.downconversion.enable=false` topic refuses the whole conversion with **35** instead,
see "KIP-283" above.

**Version 5 (KIP-107) adds `LogStartOffset` twice**: to a partition entry of the *request*, where only a follower
replica fills it in (an ordinary consumer sends -1, `FetchRequest.PartitionData` of the Java consumer), and to every
partition of the *answer*, where it is the earliest offset the log still holds. A consumer learns from it that the
front of the log moved — by the retention of the broker or by a `DeleteRecords` call — without asking the Offsets
api for the earliest offset.

**Version 6 (Kafka 1.0) is the version 5 frame in both directions and one bit of information.** `FETCH_REQUEST_V6`
is `FETCH_REQUEST_V5` and `FETCH_RESPONSE_V6` is `FETCH_RESPONSE_V5` in
`clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/requests/FetchRequest.java` @ 1.1.1, and what the version states is
that the client understands the error code **56 `KAFKA_STORAGE_ERROR`**; a client that asks with version 5 or lower
is answered **6 `NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION`** for the same condition. `fetch.request.v6` and `fetch.response.v6`
below are the pair, and they differ from the version 5 vectors in the api version of the header alone.

### Fetch sessions (v7, KIP-227)

**Version 7 (Kafka 1.1, KIP-227) turns the Fetch api into an incremental protocol.** A consumer with many
partitions repeats the whole partition list in every fetch, and the broker answers with an entry for every one of
them even when nothing changed; a *fetch session* lets the broker remember that list, so that the request carries
only the partitions whose parameters changed and the answer only the partitions that have news.

Three fields carry it:

* the request gains **`SessionId`** and **`Epoch`** (two int32) between the `IsolationLevel` and the topics array,
  and a trailing **`forgotten_topics_data`** array of `[TopicName [Partition]]` behind it — the partitions the
  session should drop. `FetchRequest.java` @ 1.1.1 spells the field `forgetten_topics_data`, a typo that never
  reached the wire because a Kafka request carries no field names;
* the answer gains a top-level **`ErrorCode`** (int16) and **`SessionId`** (int32) between the `ThrottleTimeMs` and
  the topics array. This is the only top-level error code the Fetch api has, and it is about the session alone.

`FetchMetadata` of this client is the Java `org.apache.kafka.common.requests.FetchMetadata`, field for field, and
the pair of int32 is a small state machine:

| what the client wants | `SessionId` | `Epoch` | what the broker does |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| no session at all (`FetchMetadata::legacy()`, the `LEGACY` of the Java client) | 0 | -1 | serves the request like a version 6 one and answers `SessionId = 0` |
| open a session (`FetchMetadata::initial()`, `INITIAL`) | 0 | 0 | serves the whole request and answers with the id of a new session |
| the next incremental fetch (`newIncremental()`, then `nextIncremental()`) | the id | 1, 2, 3 … | answers only the partitions that changed |
| drop the session (`nextCloseExisting()`) | the id | 0 | removes the session, opens a **new** one and answers its id |
| close the session for good | the id | -1 | removes the session and answers `SessionId = 0` |

A request whose epoch is 0 or -1 is a **full fetch** (`FetchMetadata::isFull()`): it carries every partition the
client wants to read, and the broker answers all of them. Anything above 0 is an **incremental fetch**: its topics
array carries only the partitions whose fetch offset or `MaxBytes` changed — an empty array is perfectly legal and
means "the partitions you already know, with the parameters you already know" — and the broker answers only the
partitions that have something new (`FetchSession.scala` @ 1.1.1: a partition is included when its record set is
non-empty, when its high water mark or its log start offset moved, or when it has an error code).

**Measured on the container** — every row of this table is a real exchange, and
`FetchSessionApiTest` replays it:

| request | answer |
|---|---|
| `SessionId = 0`, `Epoch = -1` (session-less), two partitions | `ErrorCode = 0`, `SessionId = **0**`, both partitions |
| `SessionId = 0`, `Epoch = 0`, two partitions | `ErrorCode = 0`, `SessionId = **a random non-zero int32**`, both partitions |
| that id, `Epoch = 1`, an **empty** topics array | both partitions again — the session still holds their old fetch offsets, so the broker re-reads the same records |
| that id, `Epoch = 2`, the two partitions with their **new** fetch offsets (the end of both logs) | `ErrorCode = 0`, the session id, and **no topic at all** |
| that id, `Epoch = 3`, an empty topics array, after a record was appended to one of the two | only **that** partition |
| that id, next epoch, an empty topics array, one partition in `forgotten_topics_data` | that partition is gone from the answer, and stays gone in every following one — even after records are appended to it |
| that id, a **wrong** epoch | `ErrorCode = **71** INVALID_FETCH_SESSION_EPOCH`, `SessionId = **0**`, an **empty** topics array. The session itself survives: the next request with the right epoch is served normally |
| a session id the broker does not know | `ErrorCode = **70** FETCH_SESSION_ID_NOT_FOUND`, `SessionId = **0**`, an empty topics array |
| that id, `Epoch = -1` | the session is removed; the answer carries `SessionId = 0` and the partitions of the *request*, like a session-less fetch. A later request with that id is answered with 70 |
| an incremental fetch that forgets **every** partition of its session | the session is removed as well (`session.isEmpty` ⇒ `SessionlessFetchContext`), the answer carries `SessionId = 0` |
| `Epoch = 0` **with** an existing session id | the old session is removed and a **new id** is handed out; the old id is then answered with 70 |

Two of those are worth spelling out, because a client can not derive them from the KIP:

* **the session id of an error answer is 0, not the id that was asked for.** `SessionErrorContext` @ 1.1.1 builds
  the answer with `INVALID_SESSION_ID`, so a client that keeps the session id from the answer would forget its own
  session on the first 70 or 71;
* **70 and 71 do not destroy the session** — they only refuse the request. Both are retriable, and the way back is
  a full fetch: `FetchMetadata::nextCloseExisting()` (the same id with the epoch 0) closes whatever is left and
  opens a new session in one request.

`Client::fetchPartitions()` sends version **12** with `FetchMetadata::legacy()`, i.e. the session-less full fetch,
which a 2.8.2 broker serves exactly as it serves a version 6 request. That is the bare client, and it is unchanged;
the consumer speaks the session half of the frame, see below.

**Version 8 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) is version 7 with another number in its header.** `FetchRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 says
"Version 8 is the same as version 7" and `FetchResponse.json` "Starting in version 8, on quota violation, brokers
send out responses before throttling", so the frames of `fetch.request.v8` and `fetch.response.v8` below are the
frames of version 7 — fetch sessions, isolation level, last stable offset and all. What version 8 states is that
the **client** waits out `throttle_time_ms` itself; see "KIP-219" under "Quotas and throttle time", and note that a
throttled fetch is answered with an **empty topics array** (`fetch.response.v8.throttled`), so a consumer that
ignores the field reads nothing and asks again into a muted channel.

### The leader epoch (KIP-320)

**Version 9 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-320) puts a `current_leader_epoch` into every partition entry of the request**, and
leaves the answer alone — `FetchResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 has no field between version 7 and version 11.

A **leader epoch** is a counter the controller keeps per partition and raises by one with every leader election.
It is not new: KIP-101 gave it to the message format v2 in Kafka 0.11, where every record batch carries the
`PartitionLeaderEpoch` of the leader that appended it, and KIP-101 and KIP-279 made the *brokers* speak it, through
the OffsetForLeaderEpoch api. What KIP-320 adds is that a **consumer** speaks it too, so that the two questions a
reader could never answer before become answerable:

* *"is the broker I am asking still the leader I think it is?"* — the epoch travels **into** the request, and a
  leader that is on another epoch refuses it instead of serving records from a leadership the client does not know
  about;
* *"did the log I am reading diverge under me?"* — the epoch travels **out** of the Metadata, the ListOffsets and
  the Fetch answers, so a consumer can tell a leader change from a quiet continuation and check its position
  against the new leader, see "KIP-320 in the consumer: leader epochs and truncation detection" below.

**The field sits between the partition id and the fetch offset**, not behind the fetch offset as the KIP reads:
`FetchRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 declares `"name": "Partition"`, `"name": "CurrentLeaderEpoch"`, `"name": "FetchOffset"`
in that order, and the order of the fields in the json **is** the order on the wire. `fetch.request.v9` below is the
frame, with the epoch `00 00 00 00` between `00 00 00 00` and the eight bytes of the offset. `-1` is
"I do not know", the value `FetchRequestTopicPartition::UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` of this client and the value every
version below 9 is read back with.

**What a 2.8.2 broker answers**, measured on the container with the same partition and three different epochs:

| `current_leader_epoch` | what it means | the answer |
|---|---|---|
| `-1` | the client does not track epochs | the records, error code 0 — the check is skipped entirely |
| `0` | the epoch the partition really is led with | the records, error code 0 |
| `1` | an epoch **above** the current one | **75** `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH`, `high_water_mark = -1`, an empty record set |

The fourth case, an epoch **below** the current one, is **74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH`, and a one-broker container
cannot produce it: nothing ever re-elects the single leader, so the epoch of every partition stays 0.
`Partition.checkCurrentLeaderEpoch` @ 2.8.2 is the whole rule — smaller than the leader's epoch is 74, larger is
75, equal or `-1` passes — and both codes are **retriable**: they say that the client's picture of the leadership
is stale in one direction or the other, and the cure is a metadata refresh, never a move of the position.
`Client::fetchPartitions()` and `fetchPartitionsWithSessions()` already do that for every retriable partition
error, so a 74 or a 75 costs one metadata round trip and the records arrive in the same call.

**Where else the epoch travels in Kafka 2.1**, all of it added by the same KIP and all of it in this line:

| api | version | field | direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Metadata | v7 | `leader_epoch` of every partition, behind the leader id | out |
| Fetch | v9 | `current_leader_epoch` of every partition entry | in |
| ListOffsets | v4 | `current_leader_epoch` in, `leader_epoch` of every partition entry out | both |
| OffsetForLeaderEpoch | v2 | `current_leader_epoch` in front of the epoch that is asked about | in |
| OffsetCommit | v6 | `committed_leader_epoch` of every partition | in |
| OffsetFetch | v5 | `committed_leader_epoch` of every partition | out |

The last two are the reason a committed offset survives a leader change with its epoch: a consumer that starts on
a partition reads the offset **and** the epoch it was taken at, and can validate that position before it reads a
single record. `OffsetAndMetadata::$leaderEpoch` of this client carries it, `null` when the answer did not say.

### Version 10 and the zstd codec (KIP-110)

**Version 10 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110) is the version 9 frame in both directions and one bit of information**: that the
client understands a record batch compressed with **zstd**, the compression type `4` of the message format v2.
`FetchRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 has no field of version 10, and `fetch.request.v10` below is `fetch.request.v9` with
another number in its header. Version 10 is where a client's promise to understand zstd begins;
`Client::fetchPartitions()` and the consumer send **version 12** on this line, which carries it.

**What the broker refuses is not a batch, it is a topic.** Measured on the container with a topic created with
`compression.type=zstd`:

| Fetch | the partition of a `compression.type=zstd` topic | a default topic whose log holds a zstd batch |
|---|---|---|
| v9 and below | **76** `UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE`, `high_water_mark = -1`, empty record set | the batch, as it lies |
| v10 and above | the batch, as it lies | the batch, as it lies |

`KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` @ 2.8.2 asks the **configuration** of the partition's topic
(`versionId < 10 && logConfig.compressionType == ZStdCompressionCodec`) and refuses the partition before it reads
anything, whatever the records of that partition really are; a zstd batch that lies in a topic which is *not*
configured that way — produced by a client that compressed it itself — is served to a Fetch v9 unchecked. The
second column is therefore not an oversight of the broker but the documented hole: the codec of a batch is only
guaranteed to be one the version understands through the *down-conversion* path, which refuses with **35**
`UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` when `message.downconversion.enable` is off, see "KIP-283" above. `fetch.request.v9.zstd-topic`
and `fetch.response.v9.zstd-topic` are the 76, `fetch.response.v10.zstd` the same partition read with version 10.

**A node of Kafka 4.0 or later dropped the fetch half of the rule.** The check of the 76 belonged to the
down-conversion path of `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` (`logConfig.compressionType == ZSTD && versionId < 10` @
3.9.2) and is gone @ 4.0.0 with the conversion (KIP-896). Measured on `kafka-4-3-1` with a topic created
`compression.type=zstd` and one uncompressed record the broker recompressed on append: a **Fetch v9 and a Fetch v4**
of that partition are answered the error code **0**, the high watermark 1 and the zstd batch as it lies, with the
compression type `4` in its attributes (`ZstdCodecTest`). The version 10 promise of KIP-110 is therefore no longer
enforced on the fetch side; a client that sends a version below 10 and can not decompress zstd has to refuse the
batch itself, as this package does without `ext-zstd` (`UnsupportedCompressionTypeException`).

**A Produce request has the same rule, one version lower, and a 4.x node keeps it.**
`ProduceRequest.validateRecords` @ 2.8.2 refuses a record set whose compression type is zstd below **Produce v7** — the broker parses the request with that very class
— and answers the partition with **76** rather than closing the connection (`produce.response.v6.zstd`). That is
why `ProduceRequest` never sends below version 7 on this line — it sends version 9; see "The zstd codec
(Kafka 2.1, KIP-110)" under "RecordBatch (message format v2)" for what the codec costs a PHP client.

### Reading from a follower (v11, KIP-392)

**Version 11 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-392) lets a consumer read from a replica that is not the leader**, and it is two
fields: a `rack_id` at the **very end** of the request — behind `forgotten_topics_data`, which is where
`FetchRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 declares it — and a `preferred_read_replica` in every partition entry of the answer,
**between** the aborted transactions and the record set.

The problem it solves is money, not correctness. A cluster that spreads the replicas of a partition over racks or
availability zones has exactly one broker per partition that a consumer may read from — the leader — so a reader
in another zone pays for the traffic to cross it, however many replicas sit next to it. KIP-392 keeps the read
inside the zone:

* the consumer states its own rack in every fetch (`client.rack`, `ConsumerConfig::CLIENT_RACK`, the empty string
  by default);
* the **leader** decides, not the consumer: its `replica.selector.class` maps the rack (and the position of the
  consumer in the log) to a replica and names it in `preferred_read_replica`;
* the consumer fetches that partition from **that broker** until an answer names another one — the field travels
  in every answer, so the leader can take the reader back at any time, and a follower that falls behind or leaves
  the ISR is answered with the leader's own id again.

A follower serves such a fetch only up to **its own** high watermark, which is why the two leader-epoch codes of
KIP-320 matter here: a consumer that reads from a follower validates its position against that follower, and
**74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH` or **75** `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` send it back to the metadata, see "The leader epoch
(KIP-320)" above. That is also why OffsetForLeaderEpoch v3 gained a `replica_id` in the same release, see its
section.

**On the container the field is always `-1`.** `replica.selector.class` is unset by default — and in
the `docker/kafka-2.8.2/` image of the 2.x line, as in `docker/kafka-3.9.2/` — so `ReplicaManager` has no selector to ask and every partition of every answer carries
`NO_PREFERRED_READ_REPLICA`, whatever rack the request names. Measured with an empty rack and with `eu-1a`, which
no broker of the container declares: the same `ff ff ff ff` and the same records, no error either way
(`fetch.request.v11` and `fetch.response.v11` below). A single-broker cluster could not hand a reader to a
follower in any case — there is none.

`FetchRequest::NO_RACK` is the empty string of "I am in no rack",
`FetchResponsePartition::NO_PREFERRED_READ_REPLICA` the `-1` of "read from me", and
`FetchedPartition::$preferredReadReplica` is where a caller of `Client::fetchPartitions()` reads the answer. A
client that acts on it has to hold a connection to the named broker and to re-resolve it on every answer; this
client reports the field and keeps fetching from the leader, which is what a consumer without a `client.rack`
does in the Java client as well.


### Epoch validation in the fetch itself (v12, KIP-595)

**Version 12 (Kafka 2.7) is the first flexible version of the Fetch api** — compact strings, compact arrays, a
**compact record set**, a tagged-field section at the end of every structure, the request header v2 and the
response header v1, see "Flexible versions in the engine (KIP-482)" above — and it adds the pieces of **KIP-595**
that let a fetcher and a leader find a divergence of their logs **inside the fetch**, without the extra
OffsetForLeaderEpoch round trip of KIP-320:

* the request gains `last_fetched_epoch` in every partition entry, **between the fetch offset and the log start
  offset** (`FetchRequest.json` @ 2.8.2, `"versions": "12+"`, default -1) — the epoch of the last record the
  fetcher really read, not the epoch it believes the partition is led with, which is the separate
  `current_leader_epoch` of version 9 and still travels in front of the fetch offset;
* the answer gains three **tagged** fields in every partition entry: `diverging_epoch` (tag 0,
  `[epoch int32, end_offset int64]`), `current_leader` (tag 1, `[leader_id int32, leader_epoch int32]`) and
  `snapshot_id` (tag 2, `[end_offset int64, epoch int32]`, KIP-630, the raft snapshot of a KRaft quorum);
* the request gains the tagged `cluster_id` (tag 0 of the body, a nullable compact string), which a broker that
  has not registered yet sends to make sure it is talking to the cluster it thinks it is. A wrong one is answered
  **100** `INCONSISTENT_CLUSTER_ID`; a consumer leaves it out, and so does this client
  (`FetchRequest::$clusterId`).

**What the broker does with it** (`Partition.readRecords` @ 2.8.2) applies to *every* fetcher, a plain consumer
included, as soon as the field is not -1: the leader asks its own epoch cache where the stated epoch ends, and

* if the epoch is not in the cache at all — an epoch the log never had — it throws `OffsetOutOfRangeException`,
  i.e. the partition comes back with **1** and a high water mark of **-1**, *not* with a diverging epoch;
* otherwise, if the end offset of that epoch is **below the fetch offset**, or the cache answers a *smaller*
  epoch than the one that was stated, the answer is the tagged `diverging_epoch` — the largest epoch from which
  the two logs are known to differ and the offset it ends at — with an **empty record set** and the error code
  **0**. The fetcher truncates to that offset and carries on;
* otherwise the fetch is served as usual and no tagged field is written at all.

Measured on the container against a fresh one-partition topic with a single record (so the log is at epoch 0 and
ends at offset 1), each row a real v12 exchange:

| `fetch_offset` | `last_fetched_epoch` | error | `high_watermark` | records | `diverging_epoch` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | -1 (nothing read yet) | 0 | 1 | the record | — |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | the record | — |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | none (the log end) | — |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 | none | `[epoch 0, end_offset 1]` |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | 1 | none | `[epoch 0, end_offset 1]` |
| 0 | 5 (an epoch the log never had) | **1** | **-1** | none | — |

`fetch.request.v12.last-fetched-epoch` and `fetch.response.v12.diverging-epoch` below are the fourth-to-last row
of that table, and they are **the only frames of this api in which a ZooKeeper-backed broker fills a tagged field
in**: `current_leader` and `snapshot_id` belong to the raft replication of a KRaft quorum and stayed empty in
every answer measured here, whatever was asked.

**What a client sends.** The Java consumer @ 2.8.2 does *not* use the field: `Fetcher.sendFetches` builds every
`FetchRequest.PartitionData` with `Optional.empty()` for it, so an ordinary consumer sends -1 and keeps detecting
a truncation the KIP-320 way — an OffsetForLeaderEpoch after the metadata changed, see "KIP-320 in the consumer"
below. This client does the same: `FetchRequestTopicPartition::UNKNOWN_LAST_FETCHED_EPOCH` is what
`Client::fetchPartitions()` puts on the wire. A caller that *wants* the validation states it as the **triple**
`[offset, currentLeaderEpoch, lastFetchedEpoch]` in the `$topicPartitions` map of `FetchRequest`, next to the
plain offset and the `[offset, currentLeaderEpoch]` pair that version 9 introduced
(`FetchRequest::lastFetchedEpochOf()`), and reads the answer from
`FetchResponsePartition::$divergingEpoch`, `$currentLeader` and `$snapshotId`.


### The topic ids of the fetch path (v13, KIP-516)

**Version 13 (Kafka 3.1) takes the topic NAME out of the Fetch api.** `FetchRequest.json` @ 3.1.2 declares the
`Topic` of a topic entry and of a `forgotten_topics_data` entry as `versions 0-12` and their `TopicId` as `13+`,
and `FetchResponse.json` does the same for the topic entry of the answer ("Version 13 replaces the topic name
field with topic ID"). Nothing else of the frame changes: a version 13 fetch is the flexible version 12 body with
16 raw bytes of `uuid` where the compact name used to be, four bytes more for a topic whose name is twelve
characters long and fewer for a long one.

The id has been in the *answer* of the Metadata api since Kafka 2.8 (`TopicMetadata::$topicId`, see "Topic ids
(v10, KIP-516)"), so a client that reads its metadata already knows it. What version 13 changes is that it must:

* `Cluster::topicIdOf()` is the name → id map this client keeps, filled from every Metadata answer, and
  `Cluster::topicNameById()` is the way back;
* `Client::fetchPartitions()` and `Client::fetchPartitionsWithSessions()` resolve the names of the request against
  that map **before every round**, so that a topic which was deleted and re-created travels under its new id after
  the metadata refresh that the error of the old one triggers;
* `FetchRequest` refuses to build a version 13 frame for a topic whose id it was not given
  (`UnknownTopicIdException`) — there is no "fall back to the name", which is the whole point of the KIP;
* the answer is read back through the same map, and the **session** keeps one of its own
  (`FetchSessionHandler::rememberTopicIds()`, the `sessionTopicNames` of the Java `FetchSessionHandler`), because
  the verification of an incremental answer is keyed by topic-partition and a version 13 answer names no topic.

Because the entries of a version 13 frame carry no name, there is no field to index their array by: the
`topicPartitions` of a `FetchRequest` and the `topics` of a `FetchResponse` are a plain **list** from that version
on, where every version below keys them by the topic name.

**What the node answers (measured).**

| Question | Answer of `kafka-3-9-2` |
|---|---|
| v13 of a topic id the node hosts | the records, and the answer names that id and nothing else (`fetch.response.v13`) |
| v13 of an id the node does not host | **100** `UnknownTopicId` **per partition**, top-level error 0, every offset -1 and a null record set (`fetch.response.v13.unknown-topic-id`) |
| v13 of the **zero** uuid | the same per-partition **100** — no topic ever carries the zero id |
| v12 of a topic that does not exist | **3** `UnknownTopicOrPartition` per partition, as on every line below |
| a session opened by **id** at v13, continued by **name** at v12 | top-level **106** `FetchSessionTopicIdError`, session id 0, empty topics array |
| a session opened by **name** at v12, continued by **id** at v13 | the same **106**, in the other direction |
| a session opened by id and continued by id | served as any incremental fetch, `forgotten_topics_data` included — a partition is forgotten under the id of its topic |

**106 `FETCH_SESSION_TOPIC_ID_ERROR` is the one error code Kafka 3.1 adds**, and this is what produces it: a fetch
session (KIP-227) is keyed by topic **id** from version 13 on, and `FetchSession` @ 3.9.2 remembers whether the
session was opened with ids. A request that names its topics the other way round is refused with the code, which
is *top-level* like the 70 and the 71 of KIP-227, is answered with an empty topics array and the session id 0, and
is retriable: the client throws the session away and starts over with a full fetch, which is exactly what
`FetchSessionHandler::handleResponse()` does for the codes 70 and 71 already.

A consumer of this client never mixes the two, because every request it sends is a version 13 one; the mix is
reachable for a caller that builds a `FetchRequestV12` by hand for a session this client opened, and for a client
that falls back to a lower version between two requests.

### The tiered-storage error of KIP-405 (v14)

**Version 14 (Kafka 3.5) adds not a field and one error code.** `FetchRequest.json` @ 3.5.2 says "Version 14 is
the same as version 13 but it also receives a new error called OffsetMovedToTieredStorageException (KIP-405)" and
`FetchResponse.json` says the same, so `fetch.request.v14` and `fetch.response.v14` below are the version 13
frames with another number in the header — the third version of this api in a row whose whole content is a promise
of the client.

The promise is **109** `OFFSET_MOVED_TO_TIERED_STORAGE`. With tiered storage on
(`remote.log.storage.system.enable`) the front of a partition lives in an object store and only the newest
segments are on the broker's own disk; a fetch of an offset that is below the **local** log start offset can
therefore not be served from the log at all, and the broker answers it with that code so that the consumer knows
to read the record through the remote-storage path instead of treating the offset as lost.
`ReplicaManager.handleOffsetMovedToTieredStorage` @ 3.9.2 is the branch, and it turns the code into **1**
`OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE` for a request below version 14, which is exactly the answer that made the situation
indistinguishable from a real out-of-range offset before the KIP.

**The node of this line has no remote storage**, so the code cannot be produced on it and this version is
documented on the wire alone. What was measured instead is the condition itself: a version 14 fetch of the offset
99 of a log that ends at 3 is answered the ordinary **1** with the high water mark -1 and an empty record set
(`fetch.response.v14.offset-out-of-range` below), and a version 13 and a version 15 fetch of that very offset are
answered exactly the same way. `OffsetMovedToTieredStorageException` is declared with the other error codes of
this line and is the class a client of a tiered cluster gets; the rest of tiered storage — the api keys 74 and 75,
`remote.log.metadata` and the `LATEST_TIERED_TIMESTAMP` of ListOffsets v9 — is out of this line by decision.

### The replica state of KIP-903 (v15)

**Version 15 (Kafka 3.5) is the first version of this api that takes a field OUT of the frame.**
`FetchRequest.json` @ 3.5.2 declares the top-level `ReplicaId` as `"versions": "0-14"` and puts a `ReplicaState`
in its place — `"taggedVersions": "15+", "tag": 1`, with a `ReplicaId` int32 and a `ReplicaEpoch` int64 that both
default to `-1`. `FetchResponse.json` adds nothing at all ("Version 15 is the same as version 14 (KIP-903)").

```
FetchRequest v15 => MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel SessionId Epoch
                    [TopicId [Partition CurrentLeaderEpoch FetchOffset LastFetchedEpoch
                              LogStartOffset MaxBytes TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                    [TopicId [Partition] TAG_BUFFER] RackId TAG_BUFFER
  ReplicaId    => int32                     # versions 0 to 14 only: GONE from the body of v15
  ReplicaState => tag 1, [ReplicaId int32 ReplicaEpoch int64 TAG_BUFFER], default -1 / -1
```

**What the epoch is for.** A follower that is fenced — one whose broker epoch is stale because it was restarted,
or because the partition was moved away from it — used to be able to talk its way back into the in-sync replica
set by simply fetching: the leader recorded the fetch position of "the replica 3" without any way of telling the
current incarnation of that broker from an older one, and an `AlterPartition` built on that state could add a
replica that is not really caught up. With the broker epoch on the wire the leader compares it against the epoch
the controller published and ignores the fetch of a stale incarnation
(`Partition.updateFollowerFetchState` @ 3.9.2, `ReplicaState`).

**A consumer has nothing to say here.** Its state is the pair `-1` / `-1`, which is the default of the
specification, and the Java generator writes a tagged field only when its value differs from its default — so the
structure is simply absent from a consumer's frame. A version 15 consumer fetch is therefore the version 14 frame
**minus the four bytes** of the old field: 105 bytes where the version 14 request of the same question is 109
(`fetch.request.v15` next to `fetch.request.v14` below). This client builds the structure from the `$replicaId`
and the new `$replicaEpoch` of `FetchRequest` and leaves it off the wire for `-1` / `-1`, which keeps the frame
byte-identical to the one the Java client sends; `FetchRequest::getReplicaId()` reads the value back out of
whichever of the two places the version has.

**What the node answers a client that claims to be a replica** (measured, the topic `t2-35-vectors` of one
partition on the one broker of the node, which is its **leader**):

| Version 15 fetch | Answer of `kafka-3-9-2` |
|---|---|
| no `replica_state` at all (a consumer) | the records, exactly as at v13 and v14 |
| `replica_state` `-1` / `7` | the records — `FetchRequest.isFromFollower` is `replicaId >= 0`, so an epoch alone changes nothing |
| `replica_state` `-2` / `-1` | the records — the debugging replica id of the lower versions still works, now inside the structure |
| `replica_state` `1` / `0` (the node's own broker id) | per-partition **6** `NotLeaderForPartition`, high water mark, LSO and log start offset `-1`, no records |
| `replica_state` `1` / `-1` and `1` / `100000` | the same **6** — the epoch is never even reached |
| `replica_state` `42` / `5` (a broker that does not exist) | the same **6** |
| `replica_state` `1` / `0` **and** `current_leader_epoch = 0` in the partition entry | per-partition **75** `UnknownLeaderEpoch` |

Three things follow from it:

* **A follower fetch is authorized on this node.** `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` @ 3.9.2 demands `CLUSTER_ACTION`
  on the cluster resource for a request whose replica id is not negative, and the `super.users` of the container
  contain `User:ANONYMOUS`, so a PLAINTEXT client passes that check. On a cluster whose ordinary clients are not
  super users the same frame is answered **29** `TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` per partition instead.
* **The refusal comes from the replica set, not from the epoch.** The broker 1 is the *leader* of the partition
  and not one of its followers, so `Partition.followerReplicaOrThrow` finds no replica to record a position for
  and answers before the epoch is looked at. Which code it answers depends on the request: **75** when the
  partition entry named a `current_leader_epoch` — "the tuple (replicaId, leaderEpoch) is not yet recognized as
  valid", which is what a KRaft reassignment looks like to a follower that fetches too early — and **6** when it
  did not, because a request without an epoch cannot be told apart from an old one.
* **A one-broker cluster cannot show the fencing itself.** The epoch is compared only once the fetch belongs to a
  real follower of the partition, which needs a second broker; what this line documents is the wire shape of the
  structure and the two refusals above.

**Raising the version inside a fetch session is not an error.** A session opened by a version 13 full fetch and
continued by a version 15 incremental request is served normally — the same session id, the top-level 0 and an
empty topics array (`fetch.request.v15.session` / `fetch.response.v15.session` below). What the **106**
`FetchSessionTopicIdError` of Kafka 3.1 fences is a session that changes the *kind of name* its topics travel
under, and the versions 13, 14 and 15 all name them by id.

### The leader discovery of KIP-951 (v16)

**Version 16 (Kafka 3.7, KIP-951) adds the address of the leader the answer already named.** `FetchRequest.json`
@ 3.7.2 declares no field of the version — "Version 16 is the same as version 15 (KIP-951)", so `fetch.request.v16`
below is `fetch.request.v15` with another number in its header — and `FetchResponse.json` adds one tagged field to
the **body**:

```
FetchResponse v16 => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode SessionId
                     [TopicId [Partition ErrorCode HighwaterMarkOffset LastStableOffset LogStartOffset
                               [AbortedTransactions] PreferredReadReplica RecordSetSize RecordSet
                               TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER
  CurrentLeader => tag 1 of a PARTITION entry, [LeaderId int32 LeaderEpoch int32 TAG_BUFFER]  # since v12
  NodeEndpoints => tag 0 of the BODY, [NodeId int32 Host compact string Port int32
                                       Rack compact nullable string TAG_BUFFER]               # NEW in v16
                   # default [], so a body that names no leader does not carry the array at all
```

The `current_leader` of a partition entry is four versions older than this one — version 12 (KIP-595, KIP-630)
declared it as the tag 1 — and it names the node id and the leader epoch, which is half of what a consumer that
was sent away needs: the other half is where that node listens. The `node_endpoints` is that half, and with it a
consumer that is refused **6** `NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER` or **74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH` can go to the new leader
at once instead of asking Metadata and waiting for the answer. `FetchResponse.json` @ 3.7.2 says it in the `about`
of the field: "Endpoints for all current-leaders enumerated in PartitionData, with errors NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER &
FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH".

**`KafkaApis` writes both fields behind one version gate**, and that gate is the surprise of this version:

```scala
if (versionId >= 16) {
  data.error match {
    case Errors.NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER | Errors.FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH =>
      val leaderNode = getCurrentLeader(tp.topicPartition(), request.context.listenerName)
      leaderNode.node.foreach { node => nodeEndpoints.put(node.id(), node) }
      partitionData.currentLeader().setLeaderId(leaderNode.leaderId).setLeaderEpoch(leaderNode.leaderEpoch)
    case _ =>
  }
}
```

The `current_leader` is on the wire from version 12 on, but a 3.9.2 node fills it in **from version 16 on** —
below that version a fetch is refused with the bare error code, as every version before the KIP was.
Measured on `kafka-3-9-2`, against the topic `t2-37-vectors` of one partition whose only broker is its leader:

| Version 16 fetch | Answer of `kafka-3-9-2` |
|---|---|
| an ordinary consumer fetch | the records, and an **empty** tagged section at the end of the body (`fetch.response.v16`) — 170 bytes, the version 15 answer of the same question |
| `current_leader_epoch = 0`, the epoch the partition really has | the records, and again nothing |
| `current_leader_epoch = 5`, an epoch from the future | the per-partition **75** `UnknownLeaderEpoch` and **no hint at all**: the 75 is not one of the two codes the KIP names (`fetch.response.v16.unknown-leader-epoch`) |
| `replica_state` `1` / `0` — a follower the partition does not have | the per-partition **6**, the tagged `current_leader` **1 / 0** and the tagged `node_endpoints` **1 ⇒ 127.0.0.1:9092**, rack `null` (`fetch.response.v16.replica-state`) |
| the same frame at **version 15** | the same 6 in **76** bytes instead of 110, with neither field (`fetch.response.v15.replica-state` above) |
| an incremental fetch of a session a version 15 fetch opened | served, the same session id, the top-level 0 (`fetch.response.v16.session`) |

**A one-broker cluster can show the hint after all** — not through a consumer, but through the follower fetch of
KIP-903. The one broker is the *leader* of the partition and not one of its followers, so
`Partition.followerReplicaOrThrow` @ 3.9.2 refuses a fetch that claims to be the replica 1 with **6**
`NotLeaderForPartition`, and that code is the one the KIP writes the hint for: the node names **itself** as the
current leader and its own PLAINTEXT endpoint as the address, `127.0.0.1:9092`, with the `rack` of a broker that
has none. It is a truthful answer to a wrong question, and it is the shape a consumer of a real cluster is
answered with when its partition has moved.

**A node of Kafka 4.0 or later leaves the endpoint out of that answer.** `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` @ 4.0.0 (and
@ 4.3.1) still collects the endpoints of every refused partition, but answers a request with
`fetchRequest.isFromFollower` through `fetchContext.updateAndGenerateResponseData(partitions, Seq.empty.asJava)` - a
follower knows the endpoints of its cluster already - where 3.9.2 put them into every answer. Re-measured on
`kafka-4-3-1`, the follower claim of the row above is answered the **6** and the `current_leader` **1 / 0**, and an
**empty** `node_endpoints` (`LeaderDiscoveryApiTest`); a consumer fetch refused 6 or 74 still carries them, and a
one-broker node has none to refuse. The vector pair `fetch.request.v16.replica-state` /
`fetch.response.v16.replica-state` is the answer of the 3.9.2 node and stays a replay.

**The 74 `FencedLeaderEpoch` is not reachable here.** It needs a request whose `current_leader_epoch` is *below*
the one of the partition, and the log of a one-broker KRaft node that was never re-elected stays in the epoch **0**
(`FetchEpochValidationTest` measures the whole epoch table); an epoch above it is the 75 of the row above, which
the KIP deliberately leaves without a hint — a client whose metadata is *ahead* of the broker has nowhere better
to go.

**In this client** the fields are decoded and handed to the caller.
`FetchResponse::$nodeEndpoints` is the array of the body, indexed by the node id
(`FetchResponseNodeEndpoint`), `FetchResponsePartition::$currentLeader` the structure of the partition entry, and
`Client::leaderHintOf()` puts both into the context of the exception of a refused partition, as
`currentLeaderId`, `currentLeaderEpoch`, `currentLeaderHost` and `currentLeaderPort`. The consumer still corrects
its picture of the cluster with a metadata refresh when it is sent away; following the endpoint without one is a
change of the fetch path and not of the protocol, and it waits for a wave of its own.
`FetchRequestV15`/`FetchResponseV15` keep the version below, which is the same frame in both directions.

### The replica directory id of KIP-853 (v17)

**Version 17 (Kafka 3.9, KIP-853) adds one tagged field to the request and nothing at all to the answer.**
`FetchRequest.json` @ 3.9.2 comments "Version 17 adds directory id support from KIP-853" and declares the field
inside the **partition** entry, where no version had ever put a tagged field before; `FetchResponse.json` says
"Version 17 no changes to the response (KIP-853)" and declares none:

```
FetchRequest v17 => MaxWaitTime MinBytes MaxBytes IsolationLevel SessionId Epoch
                    [TopicId [Partition CurrentLeaderEpoch FetchOffset LastFetchedEpoch
                              LogStartOffset MaxBytes TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                    [TopicId [Partition] TAG_BUFFER] RackId TAG_BUFFER
  ReplicaDirectoryId => tag 0 of a PARTITION entry, uuid          # NEW in v17
                        # default the zero uuid, so a consumer does not carry the field at all
  ClusterId          => tag 0 of the BODY, compact nullable string  # since v12
  ReplicaState       => tag 1 of the BODY, [ReplicaId int32 ReplicaEpoch int64 TAG_BUFFER]  # since v15
```

```
FetchResponse v17 => the frame of v16, field for field and tag for tag
```

KIP-853 is "KRaft controller membership changes": it lets voters be added to and removed from the metadata quorum
while it runs, and to do that a replica has to be identified by more than its node id. A broker that was wiped and
came back with the same id is not the replica the quorum knew, and a replica that keeps its log in one of several
`log.dirs` has to say **which** directory it is fetching for. The `directory.id` of `meta.properties` is that
name — the node of this line writes one per log directory:

```
$ docker exec kafka-3-9-2 cat /tmp/kafka-logs/meta.properties
#
#Fri Sep 18 18:59:10 UTC 2026
node.id=1
directory.id=UZcrwW8KpJUY7I9lFtsjSA
version=1
cluster.id=AjizYhBLRFap7yVFPQ4OPQ

$ docker exec kafka-3-9-2 grep directory.id /tmp/kafka-logs-2/meta.properties
directory.id=aDcofX1g2lu5P3K6WfQ62g
```

**The field is read by the raft client, not by the data plane.** `KafkaRaftClient.handleFetchRequest` @ 3.9.2
builds the identity of the fetching replica out of both halves —

```java
ReplicaKey replicaKey = ReplicaKey.of(
    FetchRequest.replicaId(request),
    fetchPartition.replicaDirectoryId()
);
```

— and that handler serves the fetch of `__cluster_metadata` on the **CONTROLLER** listener. `ReplicaManager.fetchMessages`
@ 3.9.2, which serves every fetch of an ordinary topic, never looks at the field: it is on the wire of the api as a
whole, and it means something only where the api is the replication of the metadata log. Measured on
`kafka-3-9-2`, against the topic `t2-39-vectors` of one partition and two records:

| Version 17 fetch of an ordinary topic | Answer of `kafka-3-9-2` |
|---|---|
| a plain consumer fetch | the records — **109** request bytes and **170** answer bytes, the version 16 exchange with another number in the header (`fetch.request.v17`, `fetch.response.v17`) |
| a consumer fetch naming the real `directory.id` of `/tmp/kafka-logs` | the same records in the same 170 bytes; the tag costs the **request** 18 bytes and buys nothing (`fetch.response.v17.replica-directory-id`) |
| a consumer fetch naming a directory id that exists nowhere | the same answer again, byte for byte |
| `replica_state` `1` / `0` **and** a directory id | the per-partition **6** `NotLeaderForPartition` with the leader hint of KIP-951, exactly as at v15 and v16 (`fetch.response.v17.follower-directory-id`) |
| the same with `current_leader_epoch = 0` | the per-partition **75** `UnknownLeaderEpoch`, again as at v15 and v16 |
| the same without any directory id | byte for byte the answers of the two rows above |
| the debugging replica id `-2` with a directory id | served as an ordinary consumer fetch, records and all |
| an incremental fetch of a session a version 16 full fetch opened | served, the same session id, the top-level 0 (`fetch.response.v17.session`) |

The reason the directory never matters here is the one the 3.5 wave measured for the replica epoch:
`Partition.followerReplicaOrThrow` @ 3.9.2 refuses a fetch that claims to be the replica 1 before anything else is
read, because the one broker of this node is the **leader** of the partition and not one of its followers. The
epoch of KIP-903 is never reached, and neither is the directory of KIP-853.

**A consumer writes no directory id, so a version 17 frame of this client is the version 16 frame.** The zero uuid
is the default of the field, a tagged field whose value is its default is not written at all, and the partition
entry therefore still ends in the empty tag buffer `00`: `fetch.request.v17` and `fetch.request.v16` differ in the
single byte of their api version. That is the whole cost of the version for a consumer, and the whole gain is that
the node may answer it with anything a version 17 answer is allowed to carry.

**In this client** the field is `FetchRequestTopicPartition::$replicaDirectoryId`, the last argument of
`FetchRequest::__construct()` (`$replicaDirectoryId`, the 16 raw bytes of a uuid or `null` for none) and is read
back with `FetchRequest::getReplicaDirectoryId()`; one request writes one directory into every partition entry it
carries, which is what a follower that fetches for one of its log directories means.
`FetchRequestV16`/`FetchResponseV16` keep the version below, which is the same frame in both directions, and
`FetchRequestTopicPartitionV12`/`FetchRequestTopicV13` the partition and topic entries that have no place for the
tag.

### The high watermark of a follower, KIP-1166 (v18)

**Version 18 (Kafka 4.1, KIP-1166) adds a second tagged field to the partition entry of the request and nothing to
the answer.** `FetchRequest.json` @ 4.1.0 comments "Version 18 adds high-watermark from KIP-1166" and declares

```
{ "name": "HighWatermark", "type": "int64", "versions": "18+", "default": "9223372036854775807",
  "taggedVersions": "18+", "tag": 1, "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The high-watermark known by the replica. -1 if the high-watermark is not known and 9223372036854775807 if the feature is not supported." }
```

and `FetchResponse.json` @ 4.1.0 "Version 18 no changes to the response (KIP-1166)":

```
FetchRequest v18 => the frame of v17
  HighWatermark => tag 1 of a PARTITION entry, int64               # NEW in v18
                   # default Long.MAX_VALUE, "the feature is not supported", so a consumer does not carry it

FetchResponse v18 => the frame of v17, field for field and tag for tag
```

KIP-1166 lets a follower of a **KRaft quorum** tell the leader which high watermark it already knows, so that a
leader whose high watermark moved on answers the parked fetch at once instead of after its `max_wait_ms`
(`KafkaRaftClient.isHighWatermarkUpdated` @ 4.1.0 compares the two). Like the directory id of KIP-853 it is read by
the raft client of the metadata log on the **CONTROLLER** listener; `ReplicaManager.fetchMessages` @ 4.1.0, which
serves every fetch of an ordinary topic, never reads it. Measured on `kafka-4-3-1` against the topic
`t2-41-vectors` of one partition:

| Version 18 fetch of an ordinary topic | Answer of `kafka-4-3-1` |
|---|---|
| a plain consumer fetch (`fetch.request.v18`) | the records, the version 17 answer with another correlation id (`fetch.response.v18`); the request is the version 17 frame with the 18 in its header |
| a consumer fetch with the tag, the high watermark 1 or -1 | the same answer, records and all |
| `replica_state` `1` / `0` with the tag (`fetch.request.v18.follower-high-watermark`) | the per-partition **6** with the `current_leader` **1 / 0** and an empty `node_endpoints` (`fetch.response.v18.follower-high-watermark`), the answer of the same claim without the tag |
| the same with `current_leader_epoch = 0` | the per-partition **75**, again with or without the tag |

**In this client** the field is `FetchRequestTopicPartition::$highWatermark` with the constants
`FetchRequestTopicPartition::HIGH_WATERMARK_NOT_SUPPORTED` (`PHP_INT_MAX`, the default, left off the wire) and
`FetchRequestTopicPartition::UNKNOWN_HIGH_WATERMARK` (-1). A caller states it as the fourth element of a partition
value of `FetchRequest::__construct()`, `[offset, currentLeaderEpoch, lastFetchedEpoch, highWatermark]`, read with
`FetchRequest::highWatermarkOf()`; the tag is written behind the directory id of KIP-853 when both are set, as the
tags of one section go in ascending order. The consumer states none, so **a version 18 frame of a consumer is the
version 17 frame** with another number in its header, and `Client::fetchPartitions()` and the fetch sessions of the
consumer send it. `FetchRequestV17`/`FetchResponseV17` keep the version below, and
`FetchRequestTopicPartitionV17`/`FetchRequestTopicV17` the partition and topic entries that have no place for the
tag. `FetchHighWatermarkTest` measures the table above.

### The consumer side of a fetch session

`KafkaConsumer` fetches through `Client::fetchPartitionsWithSessions()`, which keeps **one session per broker** in a
`Consumer\Internals\FetchSessionHandler` - the `org.apache.kafka.clients.FetchSessionHandler` of the Java client,
whose counterpart on the broker is `kafka.server.FetchManager`. One round of a poll is:

```php
$builder = $handler->newBuilder();
foreach ($positions as $topic => $partitionOffsets) {          // what the consumer wants to read now
    foreach ($partitionOffsets as $partition => $offset) {
        $builder->add(new TopicPartition($topic, $partition), $offset);
    }
}
$data = $builder->build();      // ->toSend, ->toForget, ->sessionPartitions, ->metadata
new FetchRequest($data->toSend, …, $data->metadata, $data->toForget)->writeTo($stream);
…
if ($handler->handleResponse($response)) { /* the answer may be read */ }
```

and the rules the handler follows are the ones of the Java client:

* the **first** request to a broker is `FetchMetadata::initial()`, a full fetch that carries every partition and
  asks for a session; its answer names the session, and from then on the requests are incremental;
* an **incremental** request states the partitions whose fetch offset *moved since the request before it* - the
  broker knows the others and would answer them again anyway, which is the quirk above - and nothing else. A
  partition that has left the wanted set (a rebalance took it, `pause()` suspended it, its topic is gone) travels
  in `forgotten_topics_data` and is dropped from the session in the same request. The order is kept: an altered
  partition moves behind the others of its topic, because the broker fills a bounded answer in the order it is
  asked;
* the **answer** carries only the partitions with news, so `fetchPartitionsWithSessions()` returns exactly those.
  Everything the consumer knows about a partition the answer does not mention - its position, its high water mark,
  its last stable offset - is still valid, and `poll()` simply returns nothing for it;
* a **session error** never reaches the caller. `handleResponse()` answers **70** with `FetchMetadata::initial()`
  (the id is gone, there is nothing left to close) and **71** with `nextCloseExisting()` - the *own* session id
  with the epoch 0, never the `session_id = 0` of the error answer - and the client sends that full fetch **right
  away**, in the same call, so that a poll returns the records instead of an empty array. The same happens when a
  broker does not answer at all: `handleError()` puts the handler back to `nextCloseExisting()`, and the retry of
  the fetch opens a new session. The two frames of that recovery are the vectors `fetch.request.v7.close-existing`
  and `fetch.response.v7.close-existing`;
* an answer whose `session_id` is **0** although the request carried one means that the broker closed the session -
  the last partition was forgotten, or the cache had no slot for it - and the handler falls back to full fetches
  until one of them is answered with an id again. A consumer therefore works against a broker that hands out no
  session at all, which is exactly what a broker below Kafka 1.1 does.

`Client::fetchPartitions()` keeps its session-less behaviour for callers that want one request and one answer;
`Client::getFetchSessionHandlers()` is what a caller (and the integration suite) reads the state of the sessions
out of. The retry of a partition that a broker answered with a retriable error is the one place where the session
changes the shape of a request: the whole set is asked for again after the metadata refresh, because an incremental
request that carried the failed partitions alone would tell the broker to forget every other partition of the
session.

### KIP-320 in the consumer: leader epochs and truncation detection

The wire fields above are only half of KIP-320. The other half is what a consumer *does* with them, and it is the
first time this client keeps something next to a position: not the offset alone, but the **offset and the leader
epoch it was taken at** — the `FetchPosition` of the Java consumer, `SubscriptionState` of this one, which holds
three values per assigned partition:

| what | where it comes from | what it is for |
|---|---|---|
| `positionEpoch` | the `partition_leader_epoch` of the **last record batch** the partition answered | the epoch the position belongs to, the `leader_epoch` of the validation question |
| `currentLeaderEpoch` | the `leader_epoch` of the Metadata answer (the field of **v7**) | what the consumer believes the partition is led with; goes out as the `current_leader_epoch` of every fetch |
| `needsValidation` | set when `currentLeaderEpoch` **moves** | one validation per leader change, not one per poll |

`Cluster` keeps the metadata epochs and **only ever moves them forward**: `updateLastSeenEpochIfNewer()` ignores a
partition whose answer carries an epoch **below** the one already known, and `reload()` then drops that stale
partition out of the new metadata instead of storing it. A broker that has not caught up with the controller yet —
a perfectly ordinary state, since any broker may answer a Metadata request — would otherwise walk a consumer's
belief *backwards* and make every fetch look like a leader change.

One `poll()` therefore runs three steps before it fetches:

1. **stamp** every fetchable position with the epoch the metadata reports (`refreshLeaderEpochs()`); a partition
   whose epoch changed is marked for validation;
2. **validate** the marked partitions in one **OffsetForLeaderEpoch v4** request per leader, whose question is
   the one version 2 added (`validatePositionsIfNeeded()` — `Fetcher.validateOffsetsIfNeeded` of the Java client),
   which asks *"you are on
   the epoch `current_leader_epoch`; where did the epoch `leader_epoch` of my position end?"*;
3. **fetch** the partitions that are validated, with the `current_leader_epoch` of step 1 in every partition entry.

What the answer of step 2 means:

* `end_offset` **at or above** the position — the position is inside a part of the log the new leader really has,
  and the partition is fetched from as if nothing had happened;
* `end_offset` **below** the position — the log diverged there: the records the consumer was about to read never
  made it into this leadership, an unclean election or a leader elected out of a replica that had not caught up.
  This is the truncation KIP-320 detects and older consumers read past silently, reporting offsets whose records
  had quietly become other records;
* `end_offset = -1` with the code 0 — the leader has no entry for that epoch, which is an answer, not a failure,
  and nothing moves;
* **74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH` or **75** `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` — the belief about the leadership is stale, so the
  cluster metadata is reloaded and the partition stays unvalidated and unfetched for **this** poll. It is never a
  reason to move a position.

A detected truncation is `auto.offset.reset`, exactly as in the Java client: `earliest` and `latest` reset the
position to the bound of the log and the poll goes on, and **`none`** raises `LogTruncationException`, a
client-side exception with no error code behind it, whose context carries the topic, the partition, the position
the consumer stood at and the `truncationOffset` the leader answered, so that an application can report the gap it
lost.

Three properties of this are worth stating, because they are what makes the feature affordable:

* **a partition is validated once per leader change**, not once per poll: the flag is raised by a *change* of the
  metadata epoch and cleared by the answer;
* **a consumer that has never read a record batch of a partition has nothing to validate.** There is no
  `positionEpoch` then — a committed offset without an epoch (`OffsetAndMetadata::$leaderEpoch === null`, anything
  committed below OffsetCommit v6) is exactly this case — and the partition is simply marked validated;
* **nothing of this reaches a broker below Kafka 2.1.** The epochs are `-1` there, a `-1` skips the check on the
  broker, and a Metadata answer below v7 carries no epoch at all, so `currentLeaderEpoch` never moves and no
  validation is ever triggered.

## Quotas and throttle time

Kafka 0.9 introduced client quotas (KIP-13), and the `ThrottleTime` of Produce v1 and the `ThrottleTimeMs` of Fetch
v1 are the only place where a client sees them. A quota is a byte rate per `client.id`, stored in ZooKeeper under
`/config/clients/<client id>` and changed on a running broker with

```console
$ kafka-configs.sh --zookeeper localhost:2181 --alter \
    --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=1024,consumer_byte_rate=1024' \
    --entity-type clients --entity-name my-application
$ kafka-configs.sh --zookeeper localhost:2181 --alter \
    --delete-config producer_byte_rate,consumer_byte_rate \
    --entity-type clients --entity-name my-application
```

The broker watches that path and applies the change within milliseconds, no restart is needed
(`kafka/server/ConfigHandler.scala` @ 0.10.2.2, where the two keys are `producer_byte_rate` and `consumer_byte_rate`).
Without an override the broker defaults `quota.producer.default` and `quota.consumer.default` apply, and those are
`Long.MaxValue`, i.e. unlimited — which is why every vector captured on the test broker carries a throttle time of
zero.

**A quota never rejects anything.** There is no error code for it in 0.9: the broker appends the records, or reads
them, and then *delays the answer*. `ClientQuotaManager.recordAndMaybeThrottle` records the size of the request
against a rate over `quota.window.num` samples of `quota.window.size.seconds` each — 11 samples of one second by
default, so the rate is measured over a window of about ten seconds — and when that rate exceeds the bound it puts
the response into a delay queue for

```
throttleTimeMs = (observedRate - quotaBound) / quotaBound * windowSizeMs
```

milliseconds before it is written to the socket (`kafka/server/ClientQuotaManager.scala` @ 0.10.2.2). The answer then
carries that very number, so a client that measures the round trip of a throttled request finds the same value
again; the field is informational, the waiting has already happened by the time it is read.

What is counted differs between the two apis (`KafkaApis.handleProducerRequest` and `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest`
@ 0.9.0.1):

* **Produce** records `produceRequest.sizeInBytes`, the size of the whole request frame the client sent.
* **Fetch** records the size of the *response*, and never throttles a fetch of a replica
  (`fetchRequest.isFromFollower`), so replication traffic is unaffected by consumer quotas.

A fire-and-forget batch (`RequiredAcks = 0`) is throttled as well, and the client never learns about it: the
throttle callback of the broker runs after the delay and then does nothing, because such a request has no response.
This is why `RecordMetadata::$throttleTimeMs` is 0 for `acks = 0` — like the offset of such a batch, it is
simply unknown.

Observed on the 0.9.0.1 broker the two throttled vectors below were captured on (`docker/kafka-0.9.0.1`), with
`producer_byte_rate=1024` and a client id of its own - `tests/Integration/QuotaThrottleTest.php` re-verifies the
same behaviour against the 0.10.2.2 container, whose Produce v2 and Fetch v3 answers carry the field unchanged: ten
produce requests of 1113 bytes each were acknowledged without a delay, and the tenth answer came back after 793 ms
with `ThrottleTime = 793`. With `consumer_byte_rate=1024`, the second fetch of 8242 bytes was delayed by 6089 ms and
answered with `ThrottleTimeMs = 6089`; a following fetch at the high watermark, which returned no records at all,
still waited 5943 ms, because the rate of the window is what is over the bound, not the single request. Both
answers are the vectors `produce.response.v1.throttled` and `fetch.response.v1.throttled` below.

### KIP-124: Kafka 0.11 gave the throttle time to almost every api

Until Kafka 0.11 a client could only see a quota on the two apis that move data. KIP-124 ("Request rate quotas")
added a third quota - `request_percentage`, the share of the broker's request handler threads one client may use -
and, so that a client can see it wherever it applies, **a `throttle_time_ms` INT32 was added to the answer of every
remaining request-response api**. That is what raised the version of eleven apis of this line by exactly one, and
of Metadata and Offsets by more:

| Api                       | Version that gained the field | Position                               |
|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Metadata (3)              | v3                            | first field of the answer               |
| Offsets (2)               | v2                            | first field of the answer               |
| OffsetCommit (8)          | v3                            | first field of the answer               |
| OffsetFetch (9)           | v3                            | first field of the answer               |
| GroupCoordinator (10)     | v1                            | first field of the answer               |
| JoinGroup (11)            | v2                            | first field of the answer               |
| Heartbeat (12)            | v1                            | first field of the answer               |
| LeaveGroup (13)           | v1                            | first field of the answer               |
| SyncGroup (14)            | v1                            | first field of the answer               |
| DescribeGroups (15)       | v1                            | first field of the answer               |
| ListGroups (16)           | v1                            | first field of the answer               |
| ApiVersions (18)          | v1                            | **last** field of the answer            |
| CreateTopics (19)         | v2                            | first field of the answer               |
| DeleteTopics (20)         | v1                            | first field of the answer               |

`ApiVersions` is the one exception, and for a reason: a client that guessed the version wrong has to be able to read
the leading `error_code` of the version 0 layout out of the answer, so the field was appended instead of prepended
(see the ApiVersions section). Everywhere else the field opens the body, right behind the correlation id of the
response header, which is why a version 0 answer can never be read with the class of the version that has it.

Four apis of 0.11 were left out of KIP-124 altogether and have no throttle time at all: **SaslHandshake (17)**,
**ControlledShutdown (7)**, **OffsetForLeaderEpoch (23)** and **WriteTxnMarkers (27)** — the last two because they
are broker-to-broker requests, which a client quota does not apply to, and the first two because they are not
client traffic either. **SaslAuthenticate (36)**, added by Kafka 1.0, is the fifth: it is answered by the
authenticator before the connection has a principal a quota could be attached to, so its v0 response ends with
`sasl_auth_bytes` and nothing else. The apis that Kafka 0.11 introduced for the transactional producer carry the
field from their version 0 on.

Nothing else about a quota changed in 0.11: the field was still informational and the delay had already happened
when the answer arrived. On this repository's container - which sets no quota at all - **every one of the fourteen
fields is 0 in every vector captured below Kafka 2.0**. `tests/Integration/QuotaThrottleTest.php` is what shows a
non-zero one, by setting `producer_byte_rate` for a client id of its own.

### KIP-219: Kafka 2.0 turned the throttle around, and the client has to wait

**This is the one change of the 2.x protocol that is not a field.** Up to Kafka 1.1 a throttled request was
answered *late*: the broker did its work, put the response into a delay queue and wrote it to the socket when the
throttle had passed, so a client that read the answer had already paid for the delay and `throttle_time_ms` only
told it why the round trip had been slow. That is comfortable for the client and bad for the broker - the delayed
response sits in the broker's memory, the client cannot tell a throttle from a hanging leader, and a client that
keeps pipelining requests keeps filling the queue.

**KIP-219 turned it around.** From the api versions Kafka 2.0 introduced, a broker

1. answers the request **immediately**, with the delay it is about to impose in `throttle_time_ms`, and
2. **mutes the channel** for exactly that long: `KafkaChannel.mute()` stops reading anything from the connection
   until the throttle has passed (`ClientQuotaManager.throttle` and `SocketServer`'s `muteChannel` @ 2.8.2).

Nothing is *rejected*; a request written into a muted channel is simply not looked at until the mute ends. A
client that keeps writing therefore gains nothing at all - it only loses the ability to say what is happening.

**Which versions promise it.** Kafka 2.0 bumped the api of every request-response api by exactly one, with a
byte-identical schema, so that a client can *state* that it understands the new behaviour:

| Api | Version that promises KIP-219 | The version below it |
|---|---|---|
| Produce (0) | **v6** | v5 (Kafka 1.0) |
| Fetch (1) | **v8** | v7 (Kafka 1.1) |
| ListOffsets (2) | **v3** | v2 (Kafka 0.11) |
| Metadata (3) | **v6** | v5 (Kafka 1.0) |

The group, transaction and admin apis of Kafka 2.0 were bumped for the same reason, one version each; their rows
are in their own sections.

**But a 2.8.2 broker does not branch on the version at all** — measured, and confirmed in the sources. The same
burst under the same `producer_byte_rate=1024` was answered identically as **Produce v5** and as **Produce v6**:
`throttle_time_ms = 2370` in both, the answer back after **0.7 ms** in both. `KafkaApis.handleProduceRequest`
@ 2.8.2 records the quota, calls `quotas.produce.throttle(...)` — which mutes the channel — and then says, in its
own comment, "**Send the response immediately. In case of throttling, the channel has already been muted**", with
no api version anywhere near the decision; `RequestHandlerHelper.sendResponseMaybeThrottle` does the same for every
other api. The version is therefore a **statement of the client**, not a switch of the broker: an old client that
sends v5 to a 2.8.2 broker gets the new behaviour whether it understands it or not, and simply stalls on the muted
channel the next time it writes.

**What the mute really costs, measured.** With the throttle ignored — the client writing its next batch straight
after a throttled answer, which is what `THROTTLE_WAIT = false` does — the debt compounds:

| Round | `throttle_time_ms` of the answer | The answer arrived after |
|---|---|---|
| 3rd batch of ~4 KB | 2376 | 0.8 ms |
| 4th, written at once | 6125 | **2377 ms** — the mute of the previous throttle, to the millisecond |
| 5th, written at once | 10125 | **6126 ms** |

The request written into the muted channel is not read until the mute ends, and the bytes it then adds push the
rate further over the bound, so the *next* throttle is longer again. Waiting the reported time out instead keeps
the rate at the bound and every answer at about a millisecond.

**What this client does.** `Client` remembers, per broker, the **moment** the throttle of the last answer ends, and
sleeps whatever is left of it before it writes its next request to that broker, which is what the Java
`NetworkClient` does. The deadline is remembered rather than the value, so a caller that spent the throttle time
elsewhere does not wait for it twice, and the entry is spent by the request that waited it out.
`ClientConfig::THROTTLE_WAIT` (`throttle.wait`, `true` by default) switches the waiting off: the field is still
read and still reported to the caller, and the stall happens on the broker side instead, exactly as it did on the
lines below this one. There is no such option in the Java client.

**Measured on the container** with `producer_byte_rate=1024` and `consumer_byte_rate=1024` on a client id of its
own (`tests/Fixture/ClientQuota`, `tests/Integration/QuotaThrottleTest.php`):

| What was sent | `throttle_time_ms` of the answer | The answer arrived after |
|---|---|---|
| Produce v6, third batch of ~4 KB | **2381** | **~1 ms** |
| Fetch v8 right after it | **70** | **~1 ms** |

Both are vectors below: `produce.response.v6.throttled` and `fetch.response.v8.throttled`. A throttled **Fetch** is
additionally answered with an **empty topics array** - no partition, no records - so a consumer that ignores the
throttle time reads nothing and asks again immediately, into a muted channel.

**The `acks = 0` producer is the one case that cannot see any of this**: its request is never answered, so it never
learns of a throttle at all; the broker mutes the channel just the same, and this client waits out a throttle that
an *earlier* answer of that broker reported before it writes the next fire-and-forget batch.

## Offsets API (key 2, v0 to v11), a.k.a. ListOffset

```
OffsetRequest v0 => ReplicaId [TopicName [Partition Time MaxNumberOfOffsets]]
  ReplicaId          => int32
  TopicName          => string
  Partition          => int32
  Time               => int64
  MaxNumberOfOffsets => int32
```

```
OffsetResponse v0 => [TopicName [PartitionOffsets]]
  PartitionOffsets => Partition ErrorCode [Offset]
    Partition => int32
    ErrorCode => int16
    Offset    => int64
```

```
ListOffsets Request (Version: 1) => replica_id [topics]
  replica_id => INT32
  topics     => topic [partitions]
    topic      => STRING
    partitions => partition timestamp
      partition => INT32
      timestamp => INT64
```

```
ListOffsets Response (Version: 1) => [responses]
  responses => topic [partition_responses]
    topic               => STRING
    partition_responses => partition error_code timestamp offset
      partition  => INT32
      error_code => INT16
      timestamp  => INT64
      offset     => INT64
```

```
ListOffsets Request (Version: 2 and 3) => replica_id isolation_level [topics]
  replica_id      => INT32
  isolation_level => INT8       -- since version 2
  topics          => topic [partitions]
    topic      => STRING
    partitions => partition timestamp
      partition => INT32
      timestamp => INT64
```

```
ListOffsets Response (Version: 2 and 3) => throttle_time_ms [responses]
  throttle_time_ms => INT32     -- since version 2
  responses => topic [partition_responses]
    topic               => STRING
    partition_responses => partition error_code timestamp offset
```

