```
ListOffsets Request (Version: 4) => replica_id isolation_level [topics]
  topics => topic [partitions]
    partitions => partition current_leader_epoch timestamp
      current_leader_epoch => INT32    -- since version 4, BETWEEN the partition id and the timestamp
```

```
ListOffsets Response (Version: 4) => throttle_time_ms [responses]
  responses => topic [partition_responses]
    partition_responses => partition error_code timestamp offset leader_epoch
      leader_epoch => INT32            -- since version 4, BEHIND the offset
```

```
ListOffsets Request and Response (Version: 5) => the version 4 frames, field for field
```

```
ListOffsets Request (Version: 6) => replica_id isolation_level
                                    [topic [partition current_leader_epoch timestamp TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                                    TAG_BUFFER
  topic => compact string          # every string and every array of a flexible version is compact

ListOffsets Response (Version: 6) => throttle_time_ms
                                     [topic [partition error_code timestamp offset leader_epoch TAG_BUFFER]
                                      TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER
```

```
ListOffsets Request and Response (Version: 7) => the version 6 frames, byte for byte
                                                 # what changes is the set of target times the broker accepts:
                                                 # -3 (MAX_TIMESTAMP, KIP-734) needs version 7 and is refused below it
```

```
ListOffsets Request and Response (Version: 8) => the version 6 frames once more, byte for byte
                                                 # -4 (EARLIEST_LOCAL_TIMESTAMP, KIP-405) needs version 8
                                                 # -5 (LATEST_TIERED_TIMESTAMP, KIP-1005) needs version 9
                                                 # -6 (EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP, KIP-1023) needs version 11
```

**Version 6 (Kafka 2.8) is the flexible version of KIP-482 and adds no field**: `ListOffsetsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2
comments "Version 6 enables flexible versions" and declares `"flexibleVersions": "6+"` on both halves. The same
question as version 5 - the replica id, the isolation level, the `current_leader_epoch` of KIP-320 and the target
timestamp - travels with the request header **v2**, compact strings and arrays and a tagged-field section behind
the body, every topic entry and every partition entry, and the answer comes back in a response header **v1**. The
vector pair `offsets.request.v6`/`offsets.response.v6` below is the same exchange as the version 5 pair in 53 and
54 bytes instead of 56 and 57; `OffsetsRequestV5`/`OffsetsResponseV5` keep the plain frame.

`Time` / `timestamp` is a value in milliseconds with two special values in **all** versions: `-1`
(`ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff`) asks for the latest offset, `-2` for the earliest available one; a third one, `-3`
(`ff ff ff ff ff ff ff fd`), was added by **version 7** and asks for the offset of the record with the largest
timestamp. `ReplicaId` is `-1` for an ordinary consumer, `-2` for a debugging client that wants to read like a
follower, and the node id of a broker for replication traffic.

**Version 1 (Kafka 0.10.1, KIP-79) is a different question with the same api key.** Message format v1 gave every
message a timestamp and every log segment a time index next to its offset index, so the broker can now answer *"the
offset of the first message whose own timestamp is `>= t`"*. One partition gets exactly one offset, which is why the
`MaxNumberOfOffsets` of the request is gone, and the answer names the timestamp of the message that was found —
which is `>= t` and usually not equal to it. Version 0 knew nothing about message timestamps: an ordinary `Time`
there asks for the start offsets of the log segments that were last modified before it, of which the broker returns
up to `MaxNumberOfOffsets`, newest first.

The two versions therefore need different classes for their request and response entries, which is what
`OffsetsRequestV0`, `OffsetsResponseV0` and the `Data/Offsets*V0` DTOs are; `OffsetsRequestV1` and
`OffsetsResponseV1` are the version 1 pair, `OffsetsRequestV2` and `OffsetsResponseV2` the version 2 pair, and the
plain names are the version 6 the client sends.

**Version 2 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-98) adds the `isolation_level` to the request and the throttle time to the answer.**
The isolation level is the same INT8 as in Fetch v4 — `0` is `read_uncommitted`, `1` is `read_committed` — and it
changes what "the latest offset" means: with `read_uncommitted` the answer to the target time `-1` is the **log end
offset**, with `read_committed` it is the **last stable offset**, i.e. the offset of the first record that belongs
to a transaction which has neither committed nor aborted yet. `KafkaApis.fetchOffsetForTimestamp` @ 0.11.0.3 passes
the level into `Log.fetchOffsetsByTimestamp`, so a consumer that reads committed data has to list its end offsets
with the same isolation level it fetches with, or it will wait for records it is never going to be shown. Without
an open transaction the two offsets are the same, which is what the vectors `offsets.response.v2.latest` and
`offsets.response.v2.read-committed` show. A request below version 2 has no such field and is served as
`read_uncommitted`.

**Version 3 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) changes neither side.** `ListOffsetsRequest.json` and `ListOffsetsResponse.json`
@ 2.8.2 both say "Version 3 is the same as version 2" — the vectors `offsets.request.v3.latest` and
`offsets.response.v3.latest` below are the version 2 frames with another number in the header — and what version 3
states is that the **client** waits out the `throttle_time_ms` of the answer itself, see "KIP-219" under "Quotas
and throttle time". `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()` and everything else that lists offsets sends
version 3.

**Version 4 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-320) puts a leader epoch on both sides.** The request gains a `current_leader_epoch`
between the partition id and the target timestamp — the same field, in the same relative position, that Fetch v9
gained, and with the same rule: `-1` skips the check, an epoch below the leader's is **74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH`
and one above it **75** `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH`. The answer gains a `leader_epoch` **behind** the offset, the epoch
the leader was on when it resolved the question.

That second field is what makes a listed offset a *position*: a consumer that seeks to the end of a partition, or
resets after a truncation, now learns the epoch of the offset it jumped to and can hand it straight to the next
fetch as the `current_leader_epoch`, and to the next commit as the `committed_leader_epoch` of OffsetCommit v6 —
instead of starting again with "I do not know" every time it moves. `OffsetsResponsePartition::$leaderEpoch` and
`OffsetAndTimestamp::$leaderEpoch` of this client carry it, `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` (`-1`) when the leader did not
resolve one; `offsets.request.v4.latest` and `offsets.response.v4.latest` below are the pair, with the epoch 0 of a
partition that has never changed leader. Everything that lists offsets — `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsets()`,
`Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()` and `Admin\AdminClient::listOffsets()` — sends the plain classes,
version 6 today, and `OffsetsRequestV3` keeps the version the Kafka 2.0 part of this line sent.

**Version 5 (Kafka 2.2, KIP-207) adds no field and one error code: 78 `OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE`.**
`ListOffsetsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 says "Version 5 is the same as version 4" and `ListOffsetsResponse.json`
"Version 5 adds a new error code, OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE", so `offsets.request.v5.latest` and
`offsets.response.v5.latest` below are the version 4 frames with another number in the header.

The state the code describes is a **leader that has just been elected and whose high watermark has not caught up
with the start offset of its own epoch**. `Partition.fetchOffsetForTimestamp` @ 2.8.2 raises it for a **client**
request — `isolationLevel.isDefined`, so a follower is exempt — that asks for the latest offset, and for a
timestamp lookup whose answer would lie at or beyond the last fetchable offset:

```scala
val maybeOffsetsError: Option[ApiException] = leaderEpochStartOffsetOpt
  .filter(epochStart => isolationLevel.isDefined && epochStart > localLog.highWatermark)
  .map(epochStart => Errors.OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE.exception(…))
```

and `KafkaApis.handleListOffsetRequest` splits on the version — "Only V5 and newer ListOffset calls should get
OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE": below version 5 the very same condition is answered **5** `LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE`.

That substitution is the whole of KIP-207. Both codes are retriable, but they describe different worlds: 5 means
"this partition has no leader, go and ask the metadata again", while 78 means "the leader is right here and will
know in a moment, ask it again". A client that sends version 5 therefore retries the **same** broker without a
metadata refresh, and one that sends version 4 walks the cluster for a leader that was never missing. Nothing in
the frame says which of the two you get: the version of the request does.

**It cannot be produced on the container of this line.** A one-broker cluster never re-elects a leader, so no
partition is ever in the lagging-high-watermark state; the code is documented from `Partition.scala` and
`KafkaApis.scala` @ 2.8.2, and `OffsetNotAvailableException` (the code 78, a plain `RetriableException` as in
`Errors.java`) is what this client raises for it. Everything that lists offsets —
`Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsets()`, `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()` and
`Admin\AdminClient::listOffsets()` — sends the plain classes, version 6 today, and `OffsetsRequestV4` keeps the
version the Kafka 2.1 part of this line sent.

**Version 7 (Kafka 3.0, KIP-734) adds no field and one target time: `-3`, the max timestamp.**
`ListOffsetsRequest.json` @ 3.0.2 comments "Version 7 enables listing offsets by max timestamp (KIP-734)" and
`ListOffsetsResponse.json` "Version 7 is the same as version 6 (KIP-734)" — neither declares a field of it, so
`offsets.request.v7.latest` and `offsets.response.v7.latest` below are the version 6 frames with another number in
the header, and so are the `-2` pair and the `-3` pair.

What the version buys is the question `MAX_TIMESTAMP` (`-3`): **"which offset holds the record with the largest
timestamp of this partition?"**. That is not the same question as `-1`. The latest offset is the *end of the log*;
the max timestamp is the *largest value in the time index*, and the two only coincide while the timestamps of the
records rise with their offsets. A producer that stamps its records itself (`CreateTime` is the default
`message.timestamp.type`), a batch that was assembled out of order, or two producers whose clocks differ put the
largest timestamp anywhere in the log. The vectors below show exactly that: `t2-30-vectors` holds three records
stamped `t0`, `t0 + 5000`, `t0 + 2000`, so the log ends at offset **3** while `-3` answers the offset **1** with
the timestamp `t0 + 5000`.

The broker reads no record for it either: every log segment carries `maxTimestampSoFar` and
`offsetOfMaxTimestampSoFar` in its metadata, and `UnifiedLog.fetchOffsetByTimestamp` @ 3.9.2 walks the segments and
takes the largest. Unlike `-1` and `-2`, though, the answer carries a **real timestamp** next to the offset — it is
the one lookup of this api that answers both without touching a record.

**The version is enforced per partition, and the refusal is the code 35.**
`KafkaApis.handleListOffsetRequestV1AndAbove` @ 3.9.2 holds a map of every negative target time to the api version
that introduced it:

```scala
val timestampMinSupportedVersion = immutable.Map[Long, Short](
  ListOffsetsRequest.EARLIEST_TIMESTAMP -> 1.toShort,
  ListOffsetsRequest.LATEST_TIMESTAMP -> 1.toShort,
  ListOffsetsRequest.MAX_TIMESTAMP -> 7.toShort,
  ListOffsetsRequest.EARLIEST_LOCAL_TIMESTAMP -> 8.toShort,
  ListOffsetsRequest.LATEST_TIERED_TIMESTAMP -> 9.toShort
)
…
} else if (partition.timestamp() < 0 &&
  (!timestampMinSupportedVersion.contains(partition.timestamp()) || version < timestampMinSupportedVersion(partition.timestamp()))) {
  buildErrorResponse(Errors.UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, partition)
```

A `-3` asked with version 6 or below is therefore answered **35** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` **for that partition** —
with the timestamp, the offset and the leader epoch `-1`, the connection untouched and every other partition of the
same request served as usual (`offsets.request.v6.max-timestamp` / `offsets.response.v6.max-timestamp-unsupported`
below). A **3.0 broker did not check this at all**: the map and the branch were added later (they are not in
`KafkaApis.scala` @ 3.0.2, which passes every negative value straight into `fetchOffsetForTimestamp`), so `35` is
what the **3.9.2 node of this line** answers and what a client of a 3.x cluster has to expect. The same branch
answers 35 for any other negative value this cluster does not know — a `-6` was refused that way at **every** version
by the 3.9.2 node, including the version 9 Kafka 3.9 added (`OffsetsRequestV9`), and on the 4.3.1 node a `-7` is, up
to the version 11 — and it is the branch the target times of the later minors are gated by as well: `-4`
`EARLIEST_LOCAL_TIMESTAMP` needs v8 (KIP-405), `-5` `LATEST_TIERED_TIMESTAMP` v9 (KIP-1005) and `-6`
`EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP` v11 (KIP-1023, Kafka 4.2; see "The earliest pending upload offset of KIP-1023
(v11)").

**Version 8 (Kafka 3.5, KIP-405) adds no field and a fourth target time: `-4`, the local log start offset.**
`ListOffsetsRequest.json` @ 3.5.2 comments "Version 8 enables listing offsets by local log start offset (KIP-405)"
and `ListOffsetsResponse.json` says the same; neither declares a field of it, so `offsets.request.v8.latest` and
`offsets.response.v8.latest` below are the version 6 frames with another number in the header, and so is the `-4`
pair.

`EARLIEST_LOCAL_TIMESTAMP` (`-4`, `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff fc`) asks **"which offset does the part of this partition
that is still on the broker's own disk begin at?"**. With tiered storage on, the front of a log lives in an object
store: `-2` answers where the *log* starts, `-4` answers where the *local* log starts, and everything between the
two can only be read through the remote-storage path. It is the `OffsetSpec.earliestLocal()` of the Java admin
client, which has no consumer counterpart at all — `KafkaConsumer` never sends it, and neither does this client's
consumer; `AdminClient::listEarliestLocalOffsets()` is where it is named here.

**Without remote storage the answer is the one of `-2`.** `UnifiedLog.localLogStartOffset` @ 3.9.2 is the log
start offset itself as long as no segment was ever moved, which is how the node of this line runs
(`remote.log.storage.system.enable` is off, as it is by default). The pair below therefore answers the offset **0**
with the timestamp `-1` — this lookup reads no record either — on a three-record log and on an **empty** one
alike, where the max timestamp `-3` of KIP-734 answers `-1` / `-1` because an empty log has no largest timestamp
to report.

The version gate is the same one KIP-734 is behind: `timestampMinSupportedVersion` demands version **8** for `-4`,
so a version 7 request that asks for it is answered **35** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` for that partition, with the
timestamp, the offset and the leader epoch `-1` and the connection untouched
(`offsets.request.v7.earliest-local` / `offsets.response.v7.earliest-local-unsupported` below).

**Version 9 (Kafka 3.9, KIP-1005) adds no field either, and a fifth target time: `-5`, the last tiered offset.**
`ListOffsetsRequest.json` @ 3.9.2 comments "Version 9 enables listing offsets by last tiered offset (KIP-1005)"
and `ListOffsetsResponse.json` says the same; neither declares a field of it, so `offsets.request.v9.latest` and
`offsets.response.v9.latest` below are the version 6 frames a fourth time, with another number in the header.

`LATEST_TIERED_TIMESTAMP` (`-5`, `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff fb`) asks **"which offset does the part of this partition
that has been moved to remote storage end at?"**. It is the upper end of the range whose lower end `-4` names:
everything below the local log start offset can only be read through the remote-storage path, everything up to
this offset is in the object store, and the segments between the two lie on both. It is the
`OffsetSpec.latestTiered()` of the Java admin client, which — like `earliestLocal()` — has no consumer
counterpart; `AdminClient::listLatestTieredOffsets()` is where it is named here.

**Without remote storage the answer is the offset `-1`, and it is not an error.**
`UnifiedLog.fetchOffsetByTimestamp` @ 3.9.2 answers `highestOffsetInRemoteStorage()` only inside an
`if (remoteLogEnabled())` and writes the literal `TimestampAndOffset(NO_TIMESTAMP, -1L, Optional.of(-1))` when it
is off, which is how the node of this line runs. The pair below therefore answers the error code **0** with the
timestamp `-1`, the offset `-1` and the leader epoch `-1` — on a log of two records and on an **empty** one alike,
because the answer does not depend on the log at all. It is the one lookup of this api that answers `-1` for a
partition that has records, and a caller has to read it as "nothing of this partition is tiered" rather than as a
failure; `-4`, next to it, answers the offset **0** of both those logs.

The version gate is the same one again: `timestampMinSupportedVersion` demands version **9** for `-5`, so a
version 8 request that asks for it is answered **35** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` for that partition, with the
timestamp, the offset and the leader epoch `-1` and the connection untouched
(`offsets.request.v8.latest-tiered` / `offsets.response.v8.latest-tiered-unsupported` below).

Everything that lists offsets — `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsets()`,
`Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()`, `Consumer\KafkaConsumer::beginningOffsets()`/`endOffsets()`/
`offsetsForTimes()`/`maxTimestampOffsets()` and `Admin\AdminClient::listOffsets()`/`listMaxTimestampOffsets()`/
`listEarliestLocalOffsets()`/`listLatestTieredOffsets()` — sent the plain classes, **version 9**, on the 3.x line;
`OffsetsRequestV9`/`OffsetsResponseV9` keep that version now, `OffsetsRequestV8`/`OffsetsResponseV8` the version of
the local log start offset,
`OffsetsRequestV7`/`OffsetsResponseV7` the version of the max timestamp and
`OffsetsRequestV6`/`OffsetsResponseV6` the version the Kafka 2.8 part of the line below sent.

### The timeout of KIP-1075 (v10)

**Version 10 (Kafka 4.0) appends one field to the request and none to the answer.** `ListOffsetsRequest.json` @
4.0.0: "Version 10 enables async remote list offsets support (KIP-1075)",

```
{ "name": "TimeoutMs", "type": "int32", "versions": "10+", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The timeout to await a response in milliseconds for requests that require reading from remote storage for topics enabled with tiered storage." }
```

behind the topic array - the last field of the body, in front of its tagged-field section - and
`ListOffsetsResponse.json` @ 4.0.0 declares nothing of the version. The same commit removed version 0 ("Version 0 was
removed in Apache Kafka 4.0, Version 1 is the new baseline", KIP-896): the offset list of version 0 closes the
connection on a 4.x node.

```
ListOffsets Request (Version: 10) => replica_id isolation_level [topics] timeout_ms TAG_BUFFER
  timeout_ms => int32         # since version 10 (KIP-1075)
```

A broker of Kafka 4.0 looks a timestamp that lies in the **remote** part of a tiered log up asynchronously, and
answers the partition when the lookup is done or the timeout is over - with **7** `REQUEST_TIMED_OUT` then
(`DelayedRemoteListOffsets` @ 4.0.0). A timeout that is not above 0 - the default of the field, and what a version 9
request carries implicitly - is replaced with the broker's own `remote.list.offsets.request.timeout.ms`, 30000 by
default (`ReplicaManager.fetchOffset` @ 4.0.0). The Java consumer sends its `request.timeout.ms`
(`OffsetFetcher.sendListOffsetRequest` @ 4.0.0) and so does `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()`
(`OffsetsRequest::DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` = 30000 when nothing is configured); `OffsetsRequestV9`/`OffsetsResponseV9`
keep the version under it. A topic without remote storage - every topic of the node of this line - is answered at
once, whatever the value:

| Request | Answer of `kafka-4-3-1` |
|---|---|
| `-1` LATEST at v10 with `timeout_ms` = 30000 (`offsets.request.v10.latest`) | the offset 3, the timestamp -1, the leader epoch 0 (`offsets.response.v10.latest`) |
| a timestamp at v10 with `timeout_ms` = 0 (`offsets.request.v10.timestamp`) | the offset 1 of the first record at or after it, with its timestamp (`offsets.response.v10.timestamp`) |

### The earliest pending upload offset of KIP-1023 (v11)

**Version 11 (Kafka 4.2) adds no field and a sixth target time: `-6`, the earliest pending upload offset.**
`ListOffsetsRequest.json` @ 4.2.0 comments "Version 11 enables listing offsets by earliest pending upload offset
(KIP-1023)" and `ListOffsetsResponse.json` @ 4.2.0 says the same; neither declares a field of it, so
`offsets.request.v11.latest` and `offsets.response.v11.latest` below are the version 10 frames - the `timeout_ms` of
KIP-1075 included - with another number in the header. Neither file changed again up to `4.3.1`.

```
ListOffsets Request and Response (Version: 11) => the version 10 frames once more, byte for byte
                                                  # -6 (EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP, KIP-1023) needs version 11
```

`EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP` (`-6`, `ff ff ff ff ff ff ff fa`, `ListOffsetsRequest.java` @ 4.2.0) asks
**"which offset of this partition is the first that has not been copied to remote storage yet?"** - the offset
behind the end of the tiered part that `-5` names. `UnifiedLog.fetchEarliestPendingUploadOffset` @ 4.2.0:

```java
if (remoteLogEnabled()) {
    long curHighestRemoteOffset = highestOffsetInRemoteStorage();
    if (curHighestRemoteOffset == -1L) {
        if (localLogStartOffset() == logStartOffset()) {
            // No segments have been uploaded yet
            return fetchOffsetByTimestamp(ListOffsetsRequest.EARLIEST_TIMESTAMP, remoteOffsetReader);
        } else {
            // Leader currently does not know about the already uploaded segments
            return new OffsetResultHolder(Optional.of(new FileRecords.TimestampAndOffset(RecordBatch.NO_TIMESTAMP, -1L, Optional.of(-1))));
        }
    } else {
        long earliestPendingUploadOffset = Math.max(curHighestRemoteOffset + 1, logStartOffset());
        …
    }
} else {
    return new OffsetResultHolder(new FileRecords.TimestampAndOffset(RecordBatch.NO_TIMESTAMP, -1L, Optional.of(-1)));
}
```

On a tiered topic the answer is therefore the log start offset while nothing has been uploaded, the offset behind
the highest uploaded one afterwards, and `-1` while a new leader does not know yet what its predecessor uploaded. It
is the `OffsetSpec.earliestPendingUpload()` of the Java admin client @ 4.2.0 (`KafkaAdminClient.getOffsetFromSpec`
maps it to `-6`, and `ListOffsetsRequest.Builder.forConsumer` demands the version 11 as soon as one partition asks
for it), which - like `earliestLocal()` and `latestTiered()` - has no consumer counterpart;
`AdminClient::listEarliestPendingUploadOffsets()` is where it is named here, and
`OffsetsRequest::EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP` holds the value.

**Without remote storage the answer is the offset `-1`, and it is not an error** - the very answer of `-5`. The node
of this line runs with `remote.log.storage.system.enable=false` (its default), and it refuses to create a topic with
`remote.storage.enable=true` ("Tiered Storage functionality is disabled in the broker. Topic cannot be configured
with remote log storage.", an `InvalidConfigurationException`), so every partition takes the `else` branch above.
The version gate is the map of the four target times before it, which `KafkaApis` held on 3.9.2 and `ReplicaManager`
holds since 4.0.0, `timestampMinSupportedVersion`, with the new row `EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP -> 11` @ 4.2.0.
Measured on `kafka-4-3-1` against a partition of three records and an empty one, every frame with the isolation
level 0 and `timeout_ms` = 30000:

| Version | Target `timestamp` | three records: `error_code` / `timestamp` / `offset` / `leader_epoch` | empty log: the same four |
|---------|--------------------|------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 11 | `-6` | 0 / -1 / **-1** / -1 (`offsets.response.v11.earliest-pending-upload`) | 0 / -1 / **-1** / -1 (`offsets.response.v11.earliest-pending-upload-empty`) |
| 10 | `-6` | **35** / -1 / -1 / -1 (`offsets.response.v10.earliest-pending-upload-unsupported`) | **35** / -1 / -1 / -1 |
| 9 | `-6` | **35** / -1 / -1 / -1 | **35** / -1 / -1 / -1 |
| 11 | `-7` | **35** / -1 / -1 / -1 | **35** / -1 / -1 / -1 |
| 11 | `-5` | 0 / -1 / -1 / -1 | 0 / -1 / -1 / -1 |
| 11 | `-4` / `-2` | 0 / -1 / 0 / 0 | 0 / -1 / 0 / 0 |
| 11 | `-3` | 0 / the largest `CreateTime` / the offset that carries it / 0 | 0 / -1 / -1 / -1 |
| 11 | `-1` | 0 / -1 / 3 / 0 | 0 / -1 / 0 / 0 |

Four things follow from it:

* **The `-6` of a node without tiered storage does not depend on the log at all.** Three records or none, the
  partition is answered the code 0 with `-1` / `-1` / `-1`, exactly like the `-5` of KIP-1005 and unlike the `-4`
  of KIP-405, which answers the log start offset 0. A caller reads the `-1` as "nothing of this partition is
  pending upload" - `AdminClient::listEarliestPendingUploadOffsets()` hands it out as `-1`, and a timestamp lookup
  through `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()` as `null` - and never as a failure.
* **Version 10 and below refuse the `-6` per partition with the 35**, the timestamp, the offset and the leader
  epoch `-1`, and the connection untouched (`offsets.request.v10.earliest-pending-upload` /
  `offsets.response.v10.earliest-pending-upload-unsupported` below) - the shape of every target time gated by the
  version since KIP-734. A node of Kafka 4.0 or 4.1 does not know the value at all and answers the same 35 at every
  version, as the 3.9.2 node of the line below did.
* **`-7` is the first negative value no release knows**: the 35 at every version, 11 included.
* **Neither the isolation level nor the timeout changes the answer**: a `read_committed` request with `timeout_ms`
  = 0 is answered the same `-1`, because the lookup reads neither the log nor remote storage.

Everything that lists offsets - `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsets()`, `Client::fetchTopicPartitionOffsetsForTimes()`,
the consumer's `beginningOffsets()`/`endOffsets()`/`offsetsForTimes()`/`maxTimestampOffsets()` and
`Admin\AdminClient::listOffsets()`/`listMaxTimestampOffsets()`/`listEarliestLocalOffsets()`/
`listLatestTieredOffsets()`/`listEarliestPendingUploadOffsets()` - sends the plain classes, the version Kafka 4.2
added; `OffsetsRequestV10`/`OffsetsResponseV10` keep the version of the timeout of KIP-1075, and `OffsetsRequestV9`/
`OffsetsResponseV9` the one below it.

**ListOffsets v11 is the only version Kafka 4.2 and 4.3 gave the record surface.** `ProduceRequest.json`,
`FetchRequest.json` and `MetadataRequest.json` and their answers are the same at `4.1.0`, `4.2.0`, `4.2.1`, `4.3.0`
and `4.3.1` but for one spelling fix in a comment of `FetchRequest.json` ("reqestor") in 4.2.0, and the node lists
Produce 0-13, Fetch 4-18 and Metadata 0-13 - the versions of Kafka 4.1.

### What the broker answers (verified against the container)

`KafkaApis.handleListOffsetRequestV1AndAbove` and `Log.fetchOffsetsByTimestamp` @ 0.11.0.3 - unchanged against
0.10.2.2 but for the isolation level of version 2 - confirmed on the broker of
`docker/kafka-0.11.0.3` with a partition holding five messages one second apart, `t0` to `t0 + 4000` (the
integration suite stamps them relative to its own clock, because the retention of the broker deletes a segment by
the largest timestamp it holds):

| Target `timestamp`                    | `error_code` | answered `timestamp` | `offset` |
|---------------------------------------|--------------|----------------------|----------|
| `-1` (latest)                         | 0            | `-1`                 | 5 (the log end offset) |
| `-2` (earliest)                       | 0            | `-1`                 | 0        |
| below the first message               | 0            | `t0`                 | 0        |
| exactly a message's timestamp         | 0            | that timestamp       | that message |
| between two messages                  | 0            | the **later** one    | the later message |
| above the last message                | **0**        | `-1`                 | **`-1`** |
| any timestamp, empty log              | **0**        | `-1`                 | **`-1`** |
| any timestamp, `message.format.version=0.9.0` | **43** | `-1`           | `-1`     |

Five things are worth keeping in mind:

* **"Nothing matches" is not an error.** A timestamp above the last message of the log, and any timestamp on an
  empty partition, come back with the error code 0 and the pair `-1` / `-1`
  (`ListOffsetResponse.UNKNOWN_TIMESTAMP` and `UNKNOWN_OFFSET`). The Java consumer reports that as a `null` entry of
  `offsetsForTimes()`, and so does this client.
* **`-1` and `-2` never read a message**, so their answer carries the timestamp `-1` even on a topic full of
  timestamps: `KafkaApis` takes the high watermark for the latest offset of a consumer and `Log.fetchOffsetsByTimestamp`
  short-circuits both values before it looks at any segment.
* **A message format v0 log answers 43, `UnsupportedForMessageFormat`, but only for a real timestamp.** A topic
  created with `--config message.format.version=0.9.0` answers `-1` and `-2` normally — they need no timestamps —
  and refuses every other value, because `Log.fetchOffsetsByTimestamp` throws
  `UnsupportedForMessageFormatException` when `config.messageFormatVersion < KAFKA_0_10_0_IV0`. The same lookup
  through **version 0** of the api succeeds there and answers an empty offset array, since it only compares segment
  modification times.
* **A compressed batch is resolved to the inner message.** A gzip batch of the same five records answers a lookup
  for `t0 + 1500` with the offset 2 and the timestamp `t0 + 2000`, exactly like the uncompressed log: the
  broker searches the wrapper by its largest timestamp and then walks the decompressed inner messages
  (`LogSegment.findOffsetByTimestamp` → `FileMessageSet.searchForTimestamp`), so the answer is the offset of the
  single inner message, not the base offset of the wrapper.
* **`message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime` replaces what is searched.** On such a topic the timestamps the producer
  sent are ignored by the index — a lookup for the `CreateTime` the producer stamped finds the first message,
  because its append time is far above it — and every message of one batch carries the same append time, so a
  lookup at or below it answers offset 0 and a lookup above it answers `-1` / `-1`.

Two failures are answered per partition like everywhere else: the code 3 (`UnknownTopicOrPartition`) for a
partition the cluster does not host, with `-1` / `-1`, and the code 6 (`NotLeaderForPartition`) when the request
did not reach the leader. Naming the **same partition twice in one request** is answered with the code 42
(`InvalidRequest`) for that partition — `ListOffsetRequest.duplicatePartitions()` — which a client that indexes its
partitions by id, as this one does, cannot produce.

**And what the `kafka-3-9-2` node of this line answers the target time `-3`** (KIP-734, version 7), measured on the
topic `t2-30-vectors`: one partition, three records whose `CreateTime` is **not** monotonic — `t0`, `t0 + 5000`,
`t0 + 2000` at the offsets 0, 1 and 2 — and an empty partition next to it:

| Version | Target `timestamp`       | `error_code` | answered `timestamp` | `offset` | `leader_epoch` |
|---------|--------------------------|--------------|----------------------|----------|----------------|
| 7       | `-3`, three records      | 0            | `t0 + 5000`          | **1**    | 0              |
| 7       | `-1`, the same partition | 0            | `-1`                 | 3        | 0              |
| 7       | `-2`, the same partition | 0            | `-1`                 | 0        | 0              |
| 7       | `-3`, **empty** log      | **0**        | `-1`                 | **`-1`** | **`-1`**       |
| 6       | `-3`                     | **35**       | `-1`                 | `-1`     | `-1`           |
| 7       | `-4`                     | **35**       | `-1`                 | `-1`     | `-1`           |
| 8       | `-4`, three records      | 0            | `-1`                 | **0**    | 0              |
| 8       | `-4`, **empty** log      | 0            | `-1`                 | **0**    | 0              |
| 8       | `-1` / `-2`, three records | 0          | `-1`                 | 3 / 0    | 0              |
| 8       | `-5`                     | **35**       | `-1`                 | `-1`     | `-1`           |

Four things follow from it:

* **The max timestamp is not the last offset.** The log ends at 3 and `-3` answers 1, because the largest
  timestamp of the partition sits in the middle of it. A client that uses `-3` to find "the newest record" is
  asking a different question than `-1`, and on a log whose timestamps do not rise with its offsets the two
  answers differ.
* **`-3` is the one special target time whose answer carries a real timestamp.** `-1` and `-2` are answered `-1`,
  because the broker does not read what the offset points at; `-3` comes from `maxTimestampSoFar` /
  `offsetOfMaxTimestampSoFar`, which every log segment keeps, so the broker answers both halves without reading a
  record either.
* **An empty log has no largest timestamp, and that is not an error.** The partition is answered the code 0 with
  `-1` / `-1`, exactly like a timestamp that no record matches, and this client reports it as a `null` entry.
* **The local log start offset of KIP-405 is the log start offset here.** The target time `-4`, which version 8
  of Kafka 3.5 added, answers the offset **0** with the timestamp `-1` on a three-record log and on an empty one
  alike, because nothing of this node's logs lives in remote storage — `-2` and `-4` are two questions with one
  answer as long as `remote.log.storage.system.enable` is off. The same request sent as a **version 7** is the
  per-partition 35 above, and the `-5` of KIP-1005 is the 35 of a version 8 client.
* **The refusal of a version that is too low is a per-partition 35, not a closed connection.** The rest of the
  request is served as usual, and `-1` and `-2` of the same frame are answered normally. The one api that used to
  answer a version it lists as served with 35 on this node was OffsetCommit/OffsetFetch v0 (see their sections);
  this is a second shape of the same idea — here it is the *target time* that the version does not cover, not the
  version itself.

## The flexible versions of the group apis (Kafka 2.4)

Kafka 2.4 raised **every** api of the group protocol by one version and, with one exception, added not a single
field: what the new version changes is the *encoding* of the frame, the flexible one of KIP-482 that
"Flexible versions in the engine (KIP-482)" above describes. The one exception is DescribeGroups, which gained a
field one version earlier than its flexible version.

| Api | Flexible version | What else the version changed |
|---|---|---|
| OffsetCommit (8) | **v8** | nothing |
| OffsetFetch (9) | **v6** | nothing |
| FindCoordinator (10) | **v3** | nothing |
| JoinGroup (11) | **v6** | nothing |
| Heartbeat (12) | **v4** | nothing |
| LeaveGroup (13) | **v4** | nothing — the batch of KIP-345 is the **v3** of the same release |
| SyncGroup (14) | **v4** | nothing |
| DescribeGroups (15) | **v5** | **v4** (plain) gave every member entry the `group_instance_id` of KIP-345 |
| ListGroups (16) | **v3** | nothing |
| DeleteGroups (42) | **v2** | nothing |

Every one of them was the version this client sent when Kafka 2.4 landed, and the version below each is kept as
its own class (`OffsetCommitRequestV7`, `JoinGroupRequestV5`, `DescribeGroupsRequestV4` …), because a broker below
Kafka 2.4 closes the connection on a version above its table. Four of the ten have moved on since: OffsetFetch
**v7**, JoinGroup **v7** and SyncGroup **v5** with Kafka 2.5 (KIP-447, KIP-559) and ListGroups **v4** with Kafka
2.6 (KIP-518); the other six are still the versions of this table.

What the frames look like is in the vectors of this section — the pairs `groupcoordinator.request/response.v3`,
`joingroup.request/response.v6`, `syncgroup.request/response.v4`, `heartbeat.request/response.v4`,
`offsetcommit.request/response.v8`, `offsetfetch.request/response.v6`, `describegroups.request/response.v5` and
`.v4`, `listgroups.request/response.v3`, `leavegroup.request/response.v4` and `deletegroups.request/response.v2`,
all captured from the container with the client id `kafka-client-t3-24b`. Three things are worth seeing there:

* **the header travels with the body.** A flexible request carries the request header **v2** — the client id is
  still an `int16`-prefixed string (`"flexibleVersions": "none"`), but a tag buffer closes the header — and its
  answer the response header **v1**, whose tag buffer follows the correlation id;
* **an api without fields still has a body.** The ListGroups v3 request is the header plus a single `00`, the
  empty tagged-field section that every flexible structure ends in, where the version 2 request has no body at
  all;
* **an inline group of fields is not a structure.** The `node_id`, `host` and `port` of a FindCoordinator answer
  are three fields of that answer in `FindCoordinatorResponse.json` @ 2.8.2, not a nested structure, so the v3
  answer carries exactly one tag buffer behind them. The DTO that groups them in this client is marked
  {@see \Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\InlineStruct} for exactly that reason.

Nothing else changes for a caller: the classes, the fields and the values are the ones of the version below, and
a `Subscription` or a `MemberAssignment` stays the opaque byte array it always was — a `compact_bytes` in a
flexible frame and a `bytes` in a plain one, with the very same content.

## GroupCoordinator API (key 10, v0 to v6)

Called `ConsumerMetadataRequest` in the 0.8.2 sources; the client uses the `main` name, `GroupCoordinatorRequest`.

```
GroupCoordinatorRequest => ConsumerGroup
  ConsumerGroup => string
```

```
GroupCoordinatorResponse => ErrorCode CoordinatorId CoordinatorHost CoordinatorPort
  ErrorCode       => int16
  CoordinatorId   => int32
  CoordinatorHost => string
  CoordinatorPort => int32
```

```
FindCoordinator Request (Version: 1) => coordinator_key coordinator_type
  coordinator_key  => STRING
  coordinator_type => INT8       -- since version 1
```

```
FindCoordinator Response (Version: 1) => throttle_time_ms error_code error_message coordinator
  throttle_time_ms => INT32           -- since version 1
  error_code       => INT16
  error_message    => NULLABLE_STRING -- since version 1
  coordinator      => node_id host port
```

The coordinator is the broker that holds the committed offsets of the group; OffsetCommit and OffsetFetch requests
have to be sent to it. From 0.9 on it does more than that: the same broker runs the group membership protocol
(JoinGroup, SyncGroup, Heartbeat, LeaveGroup), so every request of a group member goes to the node this api names.
The wire format did not change with the rename from `ConsumerMetadataRequest`.

**Kafka 0.11 renamed the api once more, to `FindCoordinator`, and version 1 (KIP-98) is what made it serve two
kinds of coordinator.** The string that version 0 called `group_id` is now `coordinator_key`, and the trailing
`coordinator_type` says what to look it up as:

| `coordinator_type` | Constant                                             | Key is                | Internal topic        |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| `0`                | `GroupCoordinatorRequest::COORDINATOR_TYPE_GROUP`      | a consumer group id   | `__consumer_offsets`  |
| `1`                | `GroupCoordinatorRequest::COORDINATOR_TYPE_TRANSACTION`| a `transactional.id`  | `__transaction_state` |

The class names and the property that carries the key stay the ones of the `main` branch — `GroupCoordinatorRequest`
and `$consumerGroup` — as rule 2 of `CLAUDE.md` prescribes; with the transaction type that property holds a
transactional id. `Client::getGroupCoordinator()` sends the type 0, `Client::getTransactionCoordinator()` the type 1,
and both go through `Common\CoordinatorLookup::findCoordinator($key, $coordinatorType)`.

The first request for a key whose internal topic does not exist yet makes the broker **create that topic** and is
answered with the error code 15 (`GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable`) while that happens; the code 14
(`GroupLoadInProgress`) means the coordinator is still reading the state out of it. Both are retriable, and
`Common\CoordinatorLookup` retries them. That holds for both types: on this repository's container the very first
type 1 lookup logs *"Auto creation of topic `__transaction_state` with 50 partitions and replication factor 1 is
successful"* and answers 15, and the next one answers 0 with the broker 0 as the coordinator. **A transactional id
is not registered by the lookup** — the broker only hashes the key onto a partition of `__transaction_state` — so
asking for an id that was never used is a legal question with a normal answer, and it is the request a transactional
producer has to send before it does anything else.

**Version 2 (KIP-219, Kafka 2.0) is the version 1 frame with a higher version field** — `FindCoordinatorRequest.json`
@ 2.8.2 gives `Key` the versions `0+` and `KeyType` the versions `1+` and adds nothing else below the flexible
version 3 — and `GroupCoordinatorRequestV2` is the class that sends it, while this client speaks the flexible
**v3** of Kafka 2.4. What the number buys is the throttling contract of KIP-219: a
throttled broker answers first and mutes the channel afterwards, so the client has to wait out `throttle_time_ms`
itself. Both frames are captured, `groupcoordinator.request.v2` and `groupcoordinator.response.v2`.

Two things about the answer that a 2.x broker does **differently** from the lines below, both measured on the
container and recorded under "Broker quirks and observations": `error_message` is no longer null for a successful
lookup — it is the string `"NONE"`, the *name* of the error code 0, because `KafkaApis.handleFindCoordinatorRequest`
@ 2.8.2 builds every answer with `Errors.message()` — and an **unknown `coordinator_type` is answered with the
error code 42** (`InvalidRequest`) and the coordinator `-1:"":-1`, where a 0.11 or 1.1 broker closed the connection.
A client still acts on `error_code` alone: the message is a description of the code and never a second source of
truth.

### The batched lookup of v4 (KIP-699, Kafka 3.0)

**Version 4 is the first version that looks several coordinators up at once.** `FindCoordinatorRequest.json`
@ 3.0.2 — *"Version 4 adds support for batching via CoordinatorKeys (KIP-699)"* — ends the single `Key` at the
version 3 and puts the array `CoordinatorKeys` in its place, and `FindCoordinatorResponse.json` ends `ErrorCode`,
`ErrorMessage`, `NodeId`, `Host` and `Port` there and answers a `Coordinators` array instead, one entry per key:

```
FindCoordinator Request (Version: 4 to 6) => coordinator_type [coordinator_keys]
  coordinator_type => INT8
  coordinator_keys => COMPACT_STRING

FindCoordinator Response (Version: 4 to 6) => throttle_time_ms [coordinators]
  throttle_time_ms => INT32
  coordinators     => key node_id host port error_code error_message
    key           => COMPACT_STRING
    node_id       => INT32
    host          => COMPACT_STRING
    port          => INT32
    error_code    => INT16
    error_message => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING
```

Three things follow from that layout, and all three were measured on the node:

* **The coordinator type stays a single field** in front of the array, so a batch is always one type: a request
  can ask for the coordinators of ten groups or of ten transactional ids, never for a mixture of the two. The
  vectors `groupcoordinator.request.v4.batch` (two groups) and `groupcoordinator.request.v4.transaction` (the
  type 1) are the two shapes.
* **Every entry names the key it answers and carries an error code of its own**, so one key of a batch can be
  answered 15 while another one is answered its coordinator. The answer is read by key.
* **An empty batch is a legal request.** `coordinator_keys = []` — the compact count `01` — is answered with an
  empty `coordinators` array and nothing else, 11 bytes (`groupcoordinator.*.v4.no-keys`). That is the opposite of
  the empty `groups` array of an OffsetFetch v8, which the same node does not answer at all.

The client sends version 4 for **every** lookup: `Common\CoordinatorLookup` puts a single key into a one-element
batch, exactly as `FindCoordinatorRequest.Builder.build()` @ 3.9.2 does (and it turns a one-element batch back into
the single `key` for the versions below 4, where `GroupCoordinatorRequestV3` sends it).
`Client::getGroupCoordinators()` and `Client::getTransactionCoordinators()` are the batched half, and
`GroupCoordinatorResponse::coordinatorOf($key)` reads one key out of either shape — for a version below 4 it builds
the entry from the single top-level coordinator, so a caller never branches on the version.

**What the 3.9.2 node does differently from the 2.8.2 broker, measured:**

| Question | 2.8.2 (v2/v3) | 3.9.2 (v4) |
|---|---|---|
| `error_message` of a successful lookup | `"NONE"`, the *name* of the code 0 | the **empty string** |
| `error_message` of a failed lookup | the message of the code | the **empty string**, except on the error path |
| an unknown `coordinator_type` | 42, coordinator `-1:"":-1` | 42 per key, coordinator `-1:"":-1` |
| an empty batch | not expressible | an empty `coordinators` array |

The empty message is not an accident of the batch: `KafkaApis.handleFindCoordinatorRequestV4AndAbove` @ 3.9.2 sets
the key, the error code, the host, the node id and the port of every entry and **never** the message, so the field
keeps the empty-string default of the generated data class. The one version 4 answer that does carry a message is
the one the *error path* builds — `FindCoordinatorRequest.getErrorResponse()` fills it from `Errors.message()` —
which is what `groupcoordinator.response.v4.unknown-type` shows. The versions **below** 4 still answer `"NONE"` on
this node (`handleFindCoordinatorRequestLessThanV4` still uses `Errors.message()`), verified with a v3 lookup.

**The coordinator type 2 exists at 3.9.2 and is refused below version 6.** `CoordinatorType` @ 3.9.2 is
`GROUP(0)`, `TRANSACTION(1)`, `SHARE(2)` — the share coordinator of KIP-932, which is out of this line by decision
— and `KafkaApis.getCoordinator` answers the type 2 with **42** (`InvalidRequest`) while `apiVersion < 6`. A type
the enum does not know at all (99 in the vector) is answered 42 as well, but through the error path, with the
generic message of the code. Both keep the connection open, where a 1.1.1 broker closed it. What the node does
with the type 2 **at** the version 6 is the subject of the last subsection of this api.

### The promise of the code 120 (v5, KIP-890, Kafka 3.8)

Kafka 3.8 raised the api to **version 5** and changed not one byte of either half: *"Version 5 adds support for
new error code TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE (KIP-890)"* stands over the request and over the answer
(`FindCoordinatorRequest.json` / `FindCoordinatorResponse.json` @ 3.8.1), and the field lists below it are the
ones of version 4. It is the same kind of version as the KIP-219 bumps of Kafka 2.0: a number that says what the
*client* understands, not what the frame carries.

What it promises is the error code **120** `TransactionAbortable`, the code KIP-890 gave the transaction
verification of the producer apis: a producer that gets it has to abort its transaction instead of retrying the
request. FindCoordinator was raised with the rest of the transaction path so that a producer can speak one version
family across it.

**The node never answers a FindCoordinator with 120.** `KafkaApis.handleFindCoordinatorRequest` @ 3.9.2 has no
path that writes it — the codes a lookup produces are 0, 15 (`CoordinatorNotAvailable`), 14
(`CoordinatorLoadInProgress`), 42 (`InvalidRequest`) for a coordinator type it will not serve, and the
authorization codes — and every version 5 frame measured on the node is the version 4 frame of the same question
with the number 5 in its header: `groupcoordinator.request.v5` (one group key), `…v5.batch` (two keys) and
`…v5.transaction` (a transactional id, the type 1). The 120 of this line is observed at AddPartitionsToTxn, where
KIP-890 produces it.

`GroupCoordinatorRequestV5`/`GroupCoordinatorResponseV5` speak that version for a broker under Kafka 3.9, and
they declare the very same body as the version 4 pair — the classes differ in their `VERSION` constant and in
nothing else.

### The third coordinator type (v6, KIP-932, Kafka 3.9)

Kafka 3.9 raised the api to **version 6** and changed no byte of either half once more: *"Version 6 adds support
for share groups (KIP-932)"* stands over the request and over the answer (`FindCoordinatorRequest.json` /
`FindCoordinatorResponse.json` @ 3.9.2), and the field lists below it are the ones of version 4. It is the third
bump of this api in a row that adds nothing to the wire — and the first one that changes what a field on that wire
is allowed to **say**.

`CoordinatorType` @ 3.9.2 is `GROUP(0)`, `TRANSACTION(1)`, `SHARE(2)`, and the version gate of
`KafkaApis.getCoordinator` @ 3.9.2 is one line:

```
else if (keyType == CoordinatorType.SHARE.id && request.context.apiVersion < 6)
  (Errors.INVALID_REQUEST, Node.noNode)
```

So the whole of what version 6 buys is the right to ask `coordinator_type = 2`. Measured on the node, the gate
sits exactly there and nowhere else:

| Frame | `coordinator_type` | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `groupcoordinator.*.v4.share-type` | 2 | **42** `InvalidRequest`, coordinator `-1:"":-1`, empty message |
| `groupcoordinator.*.v5.share-type` | 2 | **42**, the very same bytes one version up |
| `groupcoordinator.*.v6.share-type` | 2 | **15** `CoordinatorNotAvailable`, coordinator `-1:"":-1`, empty message |
| `groupcoordinator.*.v6.unknown-type` | 99 | **42**, through the error path, *with* the generic message |

**The 15 is what a node without a share coordinator answers a legal share lookup.** Past the version gate and the
authorization check, the `CoordinatorType.SHARE` branch of the match in `getCoordinator` is a bare `return`:

```
case CoordinatorType.SHARE =>
  // When share coordinator support is implemented in KIP-932, a proper check will go here
  return (Errors.COORDINATOR_NOT_AVAILABLE, Node.noNode)
```

There is no `__share_group_state` topic to hash the key onto and no partition to name, on this node or on any
other 3.9.2 node: the share coordinator arrives with Kafka 4. Every key of a batch is answered that way
separately, so a two-key share lookup is two entries of 15.

That answer is a trap for a client that reads only the code, and the reason this client has **no** share lookup:
15 is a *retriable* code — the one a broker sends while it is still creating `__consumer_offsets` — so
`Common\CoordinatorLookup` would repeat a share lookup until `metadata.fetch.timeout.ms` ran out and then throw
the exception of a coordinator that never became available. `GroupCoordinatorRequest::COORDINATOR_TYPE_SHARE` is
therefore a constant and a measurement and nothing else; share groups are out of this line by the owner's
decision, and their apis 76–79 and 83–87 are not even announced by this node.

**A share lookup is authorized as `CLUSTER_ACTION` on the cluster**, which is the other half of "not for clients".
The three types are checked against three different resources, measured on the SASL_PLAINTEXT listener with
`acltest`, the one SASL user of the image that `super.users` does not name:

| `coordinator_type` | Authorized as | `acltest` is answered |
|---|---|---|
| `0` group | `DESCRIBE` on the **group** | **30** `GroupAuthorizationFailed` |
| `1` transaction | `DESCRIBE` on the **transactional id** | **53** `TransactionalIdAuthorizationFailed` |
| `2` share | `CLUSTER_ACTION` on the **cluster** | **31** `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` |

An ordinary client principal may not even ask where the share coordinator is. The version gate is checked
**before** that authorization, so the same frame sent by `acltest` at version 5 is the 42 and not the 31, measured
as well.

`GroupCoordinatorRequest`/`GroupCoordinatorResponse` are the version 6 now and every lookup of this client sends
it — with the type 0 or the type 1, which is all `Client::getGroupCoordinator()`,
`Client::getTransactionCoordinator()` and their batched halves ever ask for.

**A 4.x node has the share coordinator** (`share.version` 1 on the node of this line), and the 15 above is the
record of the 3.9.2 node. `KafkaApis.getCoordinator` @ 4.3.1 validates the key of a share lookup with
`SharePartitionKey.validate`, because a share coordinator is the coordinator of one **share partition**, not of a
group: the key is `<group id>:<topic id>:<partition>`, the topic id in the base64 of Kafka's `Uuid`. Measured on
the 4.3.1 node (`ShareCoordinatorTypeApiTest`):

| Key of a v6 share lookup | Answer |
|---|---|
| a plain group id, `t3-40-share-3bc1df` | **42** `InvalidRequest`, coordinator `-1:"":-1`, empty message |
| `…:not-a-uuid:0`, `…:<topic id>:x` | the same **42** |
| `t3-40-share-3bc1df:O8MEhkpLdGPCFKRazcf2Vw:0`, before `__share_group_state` existed | **15**: the lookup made the node create the internal topic, 50 partitions |
| the same key a moment later | **0**, node 1 at `127.0.0.1:9092` |
| a batch of two such keys and a plain group id | 0, 0 and the 42, each on its own |

The authorization is unchanged - `CLUSTER_ACTION` on the cluster, the 31 of `acltest` - and so is the version gate in
front of it. The 15 is a retriable code again, and `Common\CoordinatorLookup` waits it out and finds the share
coordinator of a share-partition key; the share groups themselves are the 4.1 wave of this line.

## OffsetCommit API (key 8, v0 to v9)

**Kafka 4.0 removed the versions 0 and 1** (KIP-896: `"validVersions": "2-9"` in `OffsetCommitRequest.json`
@ 4.0.0): a 4.3.1 node closes the connection on either of them, measured
(`OffsetsCoordinatorTest::testTheVersionsKafkaFourRemovedCloseTheConnection`), and answers the version 2 as it
always did. What this section says about the two versions is the record of the lines below; their classes and
vectors stay.

Version 0 stores the offsets in ZooKeeper, versions 1 and 2 store them in the `__consumer_offsets` topic of the
broker. `kafka/api/OffsetCommitRequest.scala` @ 0.10.2.2 asserts that the version is 0, 1 or 2 - it is one of the two
apis that check their version at all - and a frame above that is **silently dropped**, see "An api the broker does
not serve is dropped, not refused" above: the socket stays open and the request is simply never answered. Verified
against the broker.

```
OffsetCommitRequest v0 => ConsumerGroupId [TopicName [Partition Offset Metadata]]
  ConsumerGroupId => string
  TopicName       => string
  Partition       => int32
  Offset          => int64
  Metadata        => string
```

```
OffsetCommitRequest v1 => ConsumerGroupId ConsumerGroupGenerationId ConsumerId
                          [TopicName [Partition Offset TimeStamp Metadata]]
  ConsumerGroupId           => string
  ConsumerGroupGenerationId => int32
  ConsumerId                => string
  TopicName                 => string
  Partition                 => int32
  Offset                    => int64
  TimeStamp                 => int64
  Metadata                  => string
```

```
OffsetCommitRequest v2 => ConsumerGroupId ConsumerGroupGenerationId ConsumerId RetentionTime
                          [TopicName [Partition Offset Metadata]]
  ConsumerGroupId           => string
  ConsumerGroupGenerationId => int32
  ConsumerId                => string
  RetentionTime             => int64
  TopicName                 => string
  Partition                 => int32
  Offset                    => int64
  Metadata                  => string
```

```
OffsetCommitRequest v3 => (the frame of v2, with the version field 3)
OffsetCommitRequest v4 => (the frame of v2, with the version field 4)

OffsetCommitRequest v5 => ConsumerGroupId ConsumerGroupGenerationId ConsumerId
                          [TopicName [Partition Offset Metadata]]
  -- RetentionTime is GONE from the frame (KIP-211), not sent as -1

OffsetCommitRequest v6 => ConsumerGroupId ConsumerGroupGenerationId ConsumerId
                          [TopicName [Partition Offset CommittedLeaderEpoch Metadata]]
  CommittedLeaderEpoch => int32        # since version 6, -1 when the client does not know it

OffsetCommitRequest v7 => ConsumerGroupId ConsumerGroupGenerationId ConsumerId GroupInstanceId
                          [TopicName [Partition Offset CommittedLeaderEpoch Metadata]]
  GroupInstanceId      => nullable_string   # since version 7 (KIP-345), right after ConsumerId

OffsetCommitRequest v8 => (the frame of v7 in the flexible encoding of KIP-482: compact strings, compact
                           arrays, a tag buffer per structure and the request header v2)
OffsetCommitRequest v9 => (the frame of v8, with the version field 9 -- KIP-848, Kafka 3.6)
```

```
OffsetCommitResponse v0, v1 and v2 => [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode]]
  TopicName => string
  Partition => int32
  ErrorCode => int16

OffsetCommitResponse v3 to v7 => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicName [Partition ErrorCode]]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32          # since version 3

OffsetCommitResponse v8 => (the same answer in the flexible encoding of KIP-482)
OffsetCommitResponse v9 => (the same bytes as v8; what is new is the codes 69 and 113 they may carry)
```

Version 3 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) is the throttle time and nothing else: `OFFSET_COMMIT_REQUEST_V3 =
OFFSET_COMMIT_REQUEST_V2` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3, so `OffsetCommitRequestV2` and `OffsetCommitRequestV3` put
byte-identical bodies on the wire and only their version fields differ, while the answer needs a class per version
(`OffsetCommitResponseV0`, `…V1`, `…V2` all decode the same layout and exist so that the class of an answer names
the version of the request that asked for it).

**Version 4 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) repeats the exercise**: every field of the frame keeps the `versions` it had in
`OffsetCommitRequest.json` @ 2.8.2, and only the throttling contract changes — from this version on a throttled
broker sends the answer **first** and mutes the channel for the delay afterwards. It is the last version that
carries `retention_time`.

**Version 5 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-211) removes `retention_time`** — the field has the versions `2-4` in the JSON, it is
not sent as -1 — because the committed offsets of a group expire `offsets.retention.minutes` after the **group**
became empty from that release on, and a per-commit retention has no place in that model. Measured on the
container: a v5 commit is stored with the `__consumer_offsets` value schema **v3**, which has no `expire_timestamp`
field at all, exactly like a v4 commit that left the field at -1; there is no way to make a v5 commit expire by a
clock of its own. `OffsetCommitRequestV5` sends that frame and ignores the `$retentionTime` its constructor takes,
`OffsetCommitRequestV4` is the last one that writes it.

**Version 6 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-320) gives every partition a `committed_leader_epoch`**, see below.
`OffsetCommitRequestV6` is that frame, with `OffsetCommitRequestV5`, `…V4` and `…V3` below it; the next change
of the frame is the `group_instance_id` of version 7 (KIP-345, Kafka 2.3), and the last one is the flexible
encoding of version 8 (KIP-482, Kafka 2.4). **The version this client sends is the v9 of Kafka 3.6**, whose body
is the version 8 body byte for byte, see "The member epoch of KIP-848 (v9)" below;
`OffsetCommitRequestV8`/`OffsetCommitResponseV8` keep the version under it.

### The leader epoch of a committed offset (KIP-320)

Kafka 2.1 gave a client a way to notice that the log it committed an offset into was **truncated** behind its back
after a leader change: every record batch carries the epoch of the leader that appended it, a fetch answers the
epoch of the partition's current leader, and the offset a consumer commits carries the epoch it was read from.
Three apis of this document take part in it, and two of them are this section's:

* **OffsetCommit v6** puts `committed_leader_epoch` into every partition entry, between `Offset` and `Metadata`;
* **OffsetFetch v5** hands the same field back, in the same place of the answer's partition entry;
* Fetch v9, ListOffsets v4 and OffsetsForLeaderEpoch v2 carry the `current_leader_epoch` of the *request*, which
  is what the codes **74** `FencedLeaderEpoch` and **75** `UnknownLeaderEpoch` answer — they are the producer and
  consumer side of the same KIP and are documented with those apis.

The value is an `int32`, and **-1 means "not known"** (`RecordBatch.NO_PARTITION_LEADER_EPOCH`): that is what a
client sends when it never fetched the partition itself, and what the broker hands back for every offset that was
committed before Kafka 2.1 or by a client that sends a version below 6. In this client the epoch lives on
`Consumer\OffsetAndMetadata::$leaderEpoch` as a **nullable** int — `null` is the empty `Optional` of the Java
`OffsetAndMetadata.leaderEpoch()` and is written as -1 — and `Client::commitGroupOffsets()` passes it through;
`Protocol\Data\OffsetFetchResponsePartition::toOffsetAndMetadata()` is the way back.

Measured on the container with a fresh one-partition topic: the **current leader epoch of a partition whose leader
was elected once is 0**, a v6 commit of `(offset 21, epoch 0)` is answered with the error code 0, and an
OffsetFetch v5 of it answers `committed_leader_epoch = 0`; the same offset committed with a v4 frame comes back
as `-1`. The broker does **not** validate the epoch of a commit — it stores whatever it is given, including an
epoch far in the future — because the check belongs to the *fetch* side of KIP-320.

A client that is not a member of a group commits with generation id `-1` and an empty (not null) consumer id. If the
`TimeStamp` of v1 is left at `-1`, the broker uses its receive time.

Version 2, added by Kafka 0.9, replaced the per-partition `TimeStamp` with one `RetentionTime` for the whole request,
so **the partition entry of v2 has the layout of the v0 one again** and v1 is the odd version out. The retention is
handled in `KafkaApis.handleOffsetCommitRequest` @ 0.10.2.2:

* `RetentionTime = -1` (`OffsetCommitRequest.DEFAULT_RETENTION_TIME`) means "use the broker's own retention", i.e.
  `offsets.retention.minutes`, which defaults to 1440 (24 hours);
* any other value replaces that retention for this commit alone;
* the commit timestamp of the stored entry is always the receive time of the broker, and the expiry timestamp is
  `commitTimestamp + retention`. A v1 commit with an explicit `TimeStamp` counts its retention from that timestamp
  instead — that is the only thing the removed field could do.

Both were verified against the 0.9.0.1 broker of this branch by committing an offset and decoding the entry that
reached `__consumer_offsets` (value schema v1: offset, metadata, commit timestamp, expire timestamp):

```
retention_time = -1     -> commit = 1788893878450, expire = 1788980278450   (+86400000 ms, the broker default)
retention_time = 60000  -> commit = 1788893878452, expire = 1788893938452   (+60000 ms, as requested)
```

**A 2.8.2 broker no longer stores an expiry for the default case at all.** KIP-211 (Kafka 2.1) moved the expiry of
the committed offsets of a group from "a fixed time after each commit" to "`offsets.retention.minutes` after the
group itself became empty", and the field that carries it disappeared from the value schema with it:
`GroupMetadataManager.offsetCommitValue` @ 2.8.2 writes the `__consumer_offsets` value schema **v3** —
`offset leaderEpoch metadata commitTimestamp`, no expiry — for a commit that left `retention_time` at -1, and falls
back to the schema **v1**, the only one that has an `expire_timestamp`, as soon as a commit brought a retention of
its own. Both halves were measured on the 2.8.2 container by decoding the entries that reached
`__consumer_offsets` (`OffsetsCoordinatorTest::testRetentionTimeOfVersion2DecidesTheValueSchemaOfTheStoredOffset`):

```
retention_time = -1     -> value schema 3, leaderEpoch = -1, no expire timestamp at all
retention_time = 60000  -> value schema 1, expire = commit + 60000 (the field is still honoured at v2 to v4)
```

**A 4.3.1 node writes the value schema v4** for the default case. `OffsetCommitValue.json` @ 4.3.1 has the versions
0 to 4, and the version 4 is its first **flexible** one: the metadata is a compact string and the record ends in a
tagged-field section whose tag 0 is the `topicId` of the committed partition. The group coordinator of Kafka 4.0
still wrote the v3 (`GroupCoordinatorRecordHelpers.offsetCommitValueVersion` @ 4.0.0: *"Serialize with the highest
supported non-flexible version until a tagged field is introduced"*), the one of 4.1 and later writes the v4
(`@ 4.1.0`, `@ 4.3.1`: `return 4`), and a commit with a retention of its own still falls back to the v1. Measured on
the node by decoding the entries of `__consumer_offsets`:

```
retention_time = -1     -> value schema 4, leaderEpoch = -1, no expire timestamp at all
retention_time = 60000  -> value schema 1, expire = commit + 60000
```

The offsets of an expired entry are removed by the coordinator's cleanup, which runs every
`offsets.retention.check.interval.ms` (600000 by default), not at the instant of the expiry timestamp.

Because the versions have different fields, the request is described by a class per version: `OffsetCommitRequest`
is v9, `OffsetCommitRequestV8`, `…V7`, `…V6`, `…V5`, `…V4`, `OffsetCommitRequestV3`, `…V2`, `…V1` and `…V0` only lower its `VERSION` constant, which the version-aware
`getScheme()` of the request and of its `OffsetCommitRequestTopic`/`OffsetCommitRequestPartition` DTOs follows. A
scheme is a static property of a class, so a version that changes the layout needs a class of its own — and so does
a version that does not, because the api version in the header is what the broker branches on.

`Client::commitGroupOffsets()` sends **v9**; the `retention_time` a caller names has not reached the wire since
KIP-211 removed the field at version 5, and `offsets.storage = zookeeper` (the version 0) is gone from this line
altogether - a 3.9.2 KRaft node answered that version with the code 35, and a 4.x node closes the connection on it
as on the version 1.

Metadata longer than `offset.metadata.max.bytes` (4096 by default) is answered with the error code 12,
`OffsetMetadataTooLarge`, by every version - v0 checks it before writing to ZooKeeper, v1 and v2 filter the entry out
of the append to `__consumer_offsets`. **This behaves differently from 0.8.2.2**: there the rejected entry still
reached the in-memory cache of the coordinator and an immediate OffsetFetch read it back, while
`GroupMetadataManager.prepareStoreOffsets` @ 0.10.2.2 filters it out before both the append and the `putOffset` of
the cache. Verified on the broker of this branch with a 5000 character metadata: the commit answers 12 and the
OffsetFetch right after it answers the offset -1 with the error code 0, i.e. "never committed".

### The member epoch of KIP-848 (v9)

Kafka 3.6 raised this api to **version 9** without touching a single byte of either half: "Version 9 is the first
version that can be used with the new consumer group protocol (KIP-848). The request is the same as version 8"
(`OffsetCommitRequest.json` @ 3.6.2), and "the response is the same as version 8 but can return
STALE_MEMBER_EPOCH when the new consumer group protocol is used and GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND when the group does not
exist for both protocols" (`OffsetCommitResponse.json` @ 3.6.2). The version is a **promise about the answer**:
a client that sends it says that it understands two error codes the versions below it never carry.

The same release renamed the second field of the request, `generation_id` to `generation_id_or_member_epoch` —
"the generation of the group if using the generic group protocol or the member epoch if using the consumer
protocol". The four bytes are the same four bytes; what stands in them depends on which kind of group the member
belongs to. A published identifier is never renamed for a rename in the Java client, so the field is
`OffsetCommitRequest::$generationId` here, and a classic member goes on writing its generation into it.

At the tag 3.6.2 the version was still marked `"latestVersionUnstable": true`, so a 3.6 broker served it only
with `unstable.api.versions.enable`; the flag is gone at 3.9.2 and the node of this line announces the key 8 as
`0-9` on every client listener.

**Which code which kind of group answers**, measured on the node with one classic group (`t3-36-vectors-group`,
joined with JoinGroup/SyncGroup) and one KIP-848 group (`t3-36-vectors-modern`, created with a hand-built
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat of key 68 — the api of the last wave of this line):

| The commit | v8 | v9 |
|---|---|---|
| a classic member, its own generation and member id | **0** | **0** |
| a classic member, a generation the group does not have | **22** `IllegalGeneration` | **22**, the very same code |
| a classic member id the group does not have | **25** `UnknownMemberId` | **25** |
| a `group_instance_id` the group does not have | **25** | **25** |
| a group the coordinator does not know, generation ≥ 0 | **22** | **69** `GroupIdNotFound` |
| a group the coordinator does not know, generation -1 and an empty member id | **0** | **0**, a simple group is created for it |
| a member of a **KIP-848** group with its current member epoch | **35** `UnsupportedVersion` | **0** |
| the same member with an epoch **below** the one the coordinator holds | **35** | **113** `StaleMemberEpoch` |
| the same member with an epoch **above** it | **35** | **113**, the same code |

Three of those rows are the whole of KIP-848 on this api, and every one of them is a per-partition code, never a
top-level one — the answer has no top-level field to put it in:

* **The 69 of a group that does not exist** is decided by the api version alone.
  `OffsetMetadataManager::validateOffsetCommit` @ 3.9.2 catches the `GroupIdNotFoundException` of the lookup and
  answers it as itself `if (context.header.apiVersion() >= 9)` — "this error works for both the old and the new
  protocol for clients using this version of the API" — and as the **22** below that, "to preserve the backward
  compatibility". The two vectors `offsetcommit.*.v9.group-id-not-found` and `offsetcommit.*.v8.unknown-group`
  are the same body with two different numbers in the header and two different codes in the answer.
* **The generation -1 never reaches that branch.** The check above it accepts a commit whose
  `generation_id_or_member_epoch` is negative by creating a *simple* group for the name — the commit of an admin
  client or of a consumer that does not use the group management — so the 69 is only ever the answer of a frame
  that claims a membership of a group that does not exist.
* **The 113 belongs to the members of a KIP-848 group alone.** `ClassicGroup::validateOffsetCommit` @ 3.9.2
  compares the number with its own generation and throws `IllegalGeneration`; `ConsumerGroup::validateOffsetCommit`
  compares it with the member epoch it holds and throws `StaleMemberEpoch` for **every** difference, an epoch
  above the current one included. A classic group therefore never answers 113, whatever version asks it.
* **A member of a KIP-848 group may not send a version below 9 at all**: the same
  `ConsumerGroup::validateOffsetCommit` refuses it with "OffsetCommit version 9 or above must be used by members
  using the modern group protocol", which reaches the client as a per-partition **35** `UnsupportedVersion` —
  a code that a served version of an api answers nowhere else on this line except the v0 of this very api.

`Client::commitGroupOffsets()` and with it `KafkaConsumer::commitSync()` send the version 9 with the generation
of the classic group they belong to; `OffsetCommitRequestV8`/`OffsetCommitResponseV8` keep the version below it
for a broker that does not serve 9. What a member epoch in that field does to a real KIP-848 consumer is the last
wave of this line: this client has no ConsumerGroupHeartbeat yet, and the frames above were produced by a
hand-built one.

## OffsetFetch API (key 9, v0 to v9)

**Kafka 4.0 removed the version 0** (KIP-896: `"validVersions": "1-9"` in `OffsetFetchRequest.json` @ 4.0.0): a
4.3.1 node closes the connection on it and answers the version 1 as before, measured
(`OffsetsCoordinatorTest::testTheVersionsKafkaFourRemovedCloseTheConnection`).

v0 and v1 are identical on the wire; v0 reads the offsets from ZooKeeper, v1 reads them from Kafka. **v2 (Kafka
0.10.2, KIP-88)** changes both halves of the exchange: the topic array of the request becomes nullable, and the
response gains a group-level error code after the topics.

```
OffsetFetchRequest (v0, v1) => ConsumerGroup [TopicName [Partition]]
  ConsumerGroup => string
  TopicName     => string
  Partition     => int32

OffsetFetchRequest (v2)     => ConsumerGroup [TopicName [Partition]]?   -- the topic array is NULLABLE
```

```
OffsetFetchResponse (v0, v1) => [TopicName [Partition Offset Metadata ErrorCode]]
  TopicName => string
  Partition => int32
  Offset    => int64
  Metadata  => string
  ErrorCode => int16

OffsetFetchResponse (v2)     => [TopicName [Partition Offset Metadata ErrorCode]] ErrorCode
  ErrorCode => int16   -- the error of the GROUP, after the topics

OffsetFetchRequest (v3)      => (the frame of v2, with the version field 3)
OffsetFetchRequest (v4)      => (the frame of v2, with the version field 4)
OffsetFetchRequest (v5)      => (the frame of v2, with the version field 5)
OffsetFetchRequest (v6)      => (the frame of v2 in the FLEXIBLE encoding of KIP-482)

OffsetFetchRequest (v7)      => ConsumerGroup [TopicName [Partition]]? RequireStable
  RequireStable => boolean   -- new in v7, behind the topic array

OffsetFetchResponse (v3, v4) => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicName [Partition Offset Metadata ErrorCode]] ErrorCode
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32   -- since version 3

OffsetFetchResponse (v5)     => ThrottleTimeMs
                                [TopicName [Partition Offset CommittedLeaderEpoch Metadata ErrorCode]] ErrorCode
  CommittedLeaderEpoch => int32   -- since version 5, -1 for an offset committed without one
```

Version 3 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) only added the leading throttle time — `OFFSET_FETCH_REQUEST_V3 =
OFFSET_FETCH_REQUEST_V2` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3 — which leaves the answer with a number at each of its ends:
the throttle time first, the topics, and then the group-level error code that version 2 appended.

**Version 4 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) changed neither half**: `OffsetFetchRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 adds nothing between the
nullable topic array of version 2 and the `require_stable` of version 7, and the partition of the answer only gains
its `committed_leader_epoch` at version 5 (KIP-320, Kafka 2.1). Sending version 4 is the promise that the client
honours the `throttle_time_ms` of the answer itself, because a throttled broker of 2.0 and above answers first and
mutes the channel afterwards. The frames are captured as `offsetfetch.request.v4` and `offsetfetch.response.v4`.

**Version 5 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-320) changed the ANSWER alone**: every partition entry gained a
`committed_leader_epoch` between the committed offset and the metadata, the epoch an OffsetCommit v6 stored with
that offset, or -1 for an offset that was committed without one — which is every offset written before Kafka 2.1.
The request is byte for byte the one of version 2, so `OffsetFetchRequestV4` and `OffsetFetchRequestV3` send the
same body one and two api versions lower and differ only in the answer class they read it with. Version 5 is the
highest non-flexible version; the one this client sends is the **v7** of KIP-447 (Kafka 2.5), see "Stable offsets
and the 88 of KIP-447 (Kafka 2.5)" below, and for the epoch itself "The leader epoch of a committed offset
(KIP-320)".

### The nullable topic array of v2: `null` is not `[]`

A **null** topic array — the four bytes `ff ff ff ff` — asks the coordinator for every topic-partition the group has
a committed offset for. It is the request an administrative tool needs, because a client cannot know what a group
committed before it has read it; `OffsetFetchRequest.forAllPartitions()` @ 0.10.2.2 builds exactly this frame, and
`kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` sends it. An **empty** array — `00 00 00 00` — is a *different* request that
names no topic at all and is answered with an empty topics array, even for a group that has committed offsets.
Verified on the 0.10.2.2 container, in that order, on one connection and one group: `null` answered the committed
`t6-vectors`-0, `[]` answered nothing at all (`offsetfetch.request.v2.all-topics` and
`offsetfetch.request.v2.no-topics`).

Only v2 has the nullable array. A version 1 or version 0 frame with `ff ff ff ff` in that position makes the broker
**close the connection** — it is a `SchemaException` like any other unparsable frame, see "An api the broker does
not serve closes the connection" — so a client that wants all topics has to send v2 or name the partitions itself.
`OffsetFetchRequest.Builder.build()` @ 0.10.2.2 refuses to build the lower versions with a null list for that
reason, and so does
[`Protocol\Kafka\Protocol\Request\OffsetFetchRequest`](../../src/Kafka/Protocol/Request/OffsetFetchRequest.php).

### The top-level error code of v2

The `ErrorCode` after the topics array reports what is wrong with the **group**, not with a partition: 15
(`GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable`), 16 (`NotCoordinatorForGroup`), 14 (`GroupLoadInProgress`) and 30
(`GroupAuthorizationFailed`) are what `GroupCoordinator.handleFetchOffsets` @ 0.10.2.2 can put there. An answer that
carries one of them has an **empty** topics array: `OffsetFetchRequest.getErrorResponse()` fills the per-partition
results only for the versions below 2, which had nowhere else to put a group error and therefore repeated it once
per requested partition. The per-partition codes did not change; a v2 answer can carry a group code of 0 and a
partition code of 3 at the same time.

A group that does not exist is **not** an error. Asking for all topics of a group that never committed anything
answers an empty topics array with the error code 0 — the coordinator "returns offsets blindly regardless the
current group state", `GroupCoordinator.handleFetchOffsets` — so a client cannot tell an unknown group from a group
without offsets through this api; DescribeGroups is where the state of a group lives.
