**The container of this branch never answers a group-level error at all.** It is the only broker of its cluster, so
it owns every partition of `__consumer_offsets` and is the coordinator of every group: `isCoordinatorForGroup` is
always true, the offsets are loaded long before a test runs, and there is no authorizer, which rules out 16, 14, 15
and 30 in turn. Verified: an unknown group, an empty group id and a 300-character group id all answered the error
code 0 with an empty topics array. The vector `offsetfetch.response.v2.group-error` is therefore the only
`constructed` response of this document — the frame that a broker which is not the coordinator sends — and the code
path it exercises is the one a real multi-broker cluster reaches after a coordinator move.

### A partition without a committed offset

When no offset has been committed for a topic-partition, v1 and v2 do not set an error code — they return offset
`-1`, empty metadata and the error code `0`. v0 reads a ZooKeeper node that does not exist and reports the same
offset `-1` with the error code `3`, `UnknownTopicOrPartition`; a client that fetches the starting position of a
group has to treat that code as "no offset yet", not as a failure.

**This is where 0.9 and later differ from 0.8.2.2.** A partition that the cluster does not host at all was answered
with the error code `3` by both versions on 0.8.2.2. From 0.9 on only v0 still does: `KafkaApis
.handleOffsetFetchRequest` hands the whole list to the group coordinator for v1 and above and notes that "we do not
need to filter the partitions in the metadata cache as the topic partitions will be filtered in coordinator's offset
manager through the offset cache" - and a partition that the offset cache does not know is just an uncommitted one.
Asking v1 or v2 for the partition 4242 of a topic with three partitions therefore answers offset `-1`, empty
metadata and the error code `0`, exactly like an existing partition without a committed offset. A client cannot use
OffsetFetch v1/v2 to find out whether a partition exists; Metadata is the api for that.

**The metadata of a committed offset comes back as an empty string, never as null.** A `null` metadata in an
OffsetCommit is stored as `OffsetMetadata.NoMetadata`, which is `""`, so the OffsetFetch answer carries `00 00` and
not `ff ff` — observed on the 0.10.2.2 container for both v1 and v2, where the 0.8.2.2 capture of
`offsetfetch.response.v1` still shows `ff ff`. The field stays a `NULLABLE_STRING` on the wire, so a client has to
handle both.

### Stable offsets and the 88 of KIP-447 (Kafka 2.5)

A transactional producer commits the offsets of the consumer it feeds *inside* its transaction, with TxnOffsetCommit
("TxnOffsetCommit API (key 28, v0 to v5)" below): the coordinator holds such an offset in
`GroupMetadata.pendingTransactionalOffsetCommits` and moves it into the committed offsets only when the transaction
commits. Until then the group has two answers to "where does this partition stand" — the last stable offset and the
one the open transaction wrote — and every version below 7 answers the first one without saying that the second
exists. A consumer that starts from it may read records the transaction is about to abort, or re-read records it is
about to commit.

**Version 7 lets the client ask for the stable answer only.** The boolean `require_stable` behind the topic array
makes the coordinator answer a partition whose last commit is still pending with the **retriable** error code
**88** (`UnstableOffsetCommit`) instead of an offset; `GroupMetadataManager.getOffsets` @ 2.8.2 is the one line
that decides it:

```
if (requireStable && group.hasPendingOffsetCommitsForTopicPartition(topicPartition))
  new PartitionData(INVALID_OFFSET, Optional.empty(), "", Errors.UNSTABLE_OFFSET_COMMIT)
```

Measured on the container against one partition of one group, in this order — a plain commit of the offset 25, then
a transactional commit of 42 that is deliberately left open, then the end of that transaction:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| v7 with `require_stable = false`, nothing pending | offset **25**, error code 0 |
| v7 with `require_stable = true`, nothing pending | offset **25**, error code 0 — byte for byte the same answer |
| v7 with `require_stable = true`, a pending transactional commit of 42 | offset **-1**, empty metadata, error code **88**; the group-level error code stays **0** |
| v7 with `require_stable = false`, the same pending commit | offset **25**, error code 0 — the *last stable* offset, not the pending 42 |
| v7 with `require_stable = true`, after the transaction committed | offset **42**, error code 0 |

So the flag never invents an offset and never reports the pending one: it is a choice between "the last stable
offset" and "tell me that you cannot answer yet". The 88 is retriable — `UnstableOffsetCommitException` here, a
`RetriableException` in the Java client — and the only cure is to ask again once the transaction has ended, which
is bounded by the producer's `transaction.timeout.ms` and not by a request timeout.

**This client asks for stable offsets exactly when it reads committed data.**
[`KafkaConsumer`](../../src/Kafka/Consumer/KafkaConsumer.php) sets `require_stable` when `isolation.level` is
`read_committed`, for both the positions it resolves after a rebalance and the `committed()` of the application,
and waits an 88 out with `retry.backoff.ms`. The Java consumer of 2.8 sets the flag on **every** fetch of committed
offsets and uses an internal option to decide whether an old broker is an error or a silent downgrade
(`ConsumerCoordinator.fetchCommittedOffsets`, `internal.throw.on.fetch.stable.offset.unsupported`); a
read-uncommitted consumer of this client sends `false` instead, because an offset that a transaction may still roll
back is exactly what such a consumer is allowed to see.

### The batched request of v8 (Kafka 3.0)

**Version 8 asks for the committed offsets of several groups at once.** `OffsetFetchRequest.json` @ 3.0.2 —
*"Version 8 is adding support for fetching offsets for multiple groups at a time"* — ends `GroupId` and `Topics`
at the version 7 and puts an array of groups in their place, each with a group id and a nullable topic array of
its own, while the single `require_stable` of KIP-447 stays behind the array and holds for the whole batch. The
answer moves its topics and its group-level error code into the same shape and has **no top-level error code any
more**:

```
OffsetFetch Request (Version: 8) => [groups] require_stable
  groups => group_id [topics]
    group_id => COMPACT_STRING
    topics   => name [partition_indexes]     -- NULLABLE, as the top-level array of v2 is
  require_stable => BOOLEAN

OffsetFetch Response (Version: 8) => throttle_time_ms [groups]
  throttle_time_ms => INT32
  groups => group_id [topics] error_code
    group_id   => COMPACT_STRING
    topics     => (the topic entry of version 7, `committed_leader_epoch` included)
    error_code => INT16       -- the group-level code, per group
```

Nothing inside a topic or a partition changed: the entries of a version 8 answer are the ones of version 7 byte
for byte, which is why this client keeps decoding them with the same `OffsetFetchResponseTopic` and
`OffsetFetchResponsePartition`. What moved is the *frame around them*, and with it two rules of the versions
below:

* **The nullable topic array is now per group.** A `null` — the compact `00` — asks for every topic-partition
  that group has a committed offset for, an empty array names no topic at all, and the two can be mixed inside
  one batch (`offsetfetch.request.v8.all-topics`, `offsetfetch.request.v8.batch`).
* **The group-level error code is per group.** A batch of three groups reports three codes, and the answer has no
  place left for a fourth one: a client that read `error_code` at the top level of a version 7 answer reads
  `groups[<id>].error_code` here. A group the coordinator does not know is still **not** an error — it answers an
  empty topic array with the code 0, or the offset -1 with the code 0 for a partition it was asked about by name,
  measured in `offsetfetch.response.v8.batch`.

The **88** of KIP-447 sits where it sat: `offsetfetch.request.v8.unstable` asks for the stable offsets of one
group while a transactional commit of its partition is open, and the answer carries the offset -1 and the
retriable code 88 in the *partition*, with the group-level code 0 (see "Stable offsets and the 88 of KIP-447
(Kafka 2.5)").

This client sends the batch for every fetch — at the version **9** since Kafka 3.7, whose entry is this one with
the two member fields of KIP-848 behind the group id: `Client::fetchGroupOffsets()` and
`AdminClient::listGroupOffsets()` keep naming one group and put it into a one-element batch,
`Client::fetchOffsetsOfGroups()` and `AdminClient::listConsumerGroupOffsets()` are the batched half — the latter
splits its groups by coordinator first, with one FindCoordinator v4 for all of them — and
`OffsetFetchResponse::groupOf($groupId)` reads one group out of either shape, building the entry from the
top-level topics and error code for a version below 8. `OffsetFetchRequestV7` is the keep-behind class of the
single-group frame and `OffsetFetchRequestV8` the one of this batch, see "The member id and epoch of KIP-848
(v9)".

**An empty batch is never sent.** A 3.9.2 node answers a `groups = []` frame with **nothing at all**: the handler
dies in `java.util.NoSuchElementException: key not found: null` (`docker logs` shows *"Unexpected error handling
request … OFFSET_FETCH … groups=[]"*), the connection stays open and is left owing an answer that never comes — so
the answer of the *next* request on that connection never arrives either, and only a new connection recovers.
`OffsetFetchRequest::forGroups()` therefore refuses an empty batch with an `InvalidRequestException` before a byte
leaves the client, and `AdminClient::listConsumerGroupOffsets([])` answers an empty array without sending
anything. The same node answers an empty `coordinator_keys` array of a FindCoordinator v4 quite normally, so this
is a property of the one handler and not of the batch shapes in general.

### The member id and epoch of KIP-848 (v9)

**Version 9 (Kafka 3.7) named the member inside every group entry.** `OffsetFetchRequest.json` @ 3.7.2 — *"Version
9 is the first version that can be used with the new consumer group protocol (KIP-848). It adds the MemberId and
MemberEpoch fields. Those are filled in and validated when the new consumer protocol is used."* — puts two fields
between the group id and the topic array of every entry of the batch, and touches nothing else of either half:

```
OffsetFetch Request (Version: 9) => [groups] require_stable
  groups => group_id member_id member_epoch [topics]
    group_id     => COMPACT_STRING
    member_id    => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING   -- new, default null
    member_epoch => INT32                     -- new, default -1
    topics       => (the topic entry of version 8, NULLABLE as there)
  require_stable => BOOLEAN                   -- still one flag for the whole batch

OffsetFetch Response (Version: 9) => (the answer of version 8, byte for byte)
```

The answer is the version 8 answer: *"the response is the same as version 8 but can return STALE_MEMBER_EPOCH and
UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID errors when the new consumer group protocol is used"* (`OffsetFetchResponse.json` @ 3.7.2). Both
of those codes stand in the **group-level** `error_code` of the entry they belong to, and the entry that carries
one names no topic at all — the same shape every other group-level error of this api has since version 2.

**Which code which kind of group answers**, measured on the node with one classic group (`t3-37-vectors-group`,
joined with JoinGroup/SyncGroup), one KIP-848 group (`t3-37-vectors-modern`, created with a hand-built
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat of key 68 — the api of the last wave of this line) and one group the coordinator has never
heard of (`t3-37-vectors-none`):

| The group entry | classic group | KIP-848 group | a group that does not exist |
|---|---|---|---|
| `member_id = null`, `member_epoch = -1` (the defaults) | **0**, the offsets | **0**, the offsets | **0**, the offset -1 per named partition |
| a member id the group does not hold, any epoch | **0**, ignored | **25** `UnknownMemberId` | **0** |
| the **empty** member id `""`, any epoch | **0**, ignored | **25** | **0** |
| the member's own id, its current epoch | **0**, ignored | **0**, the offsets | – |
| the member's own id, an epoch **below** the current one | **0**, ignored | **113** `StaleMemberEpoch` | – |
| the member's own id, an epoch **above** it | **0**, ignored | **113** | – |
| the member's own id with the epoch **-1** | **0**, ignored | **113** | – |
| `member_id = null` with an epoch **≥ 0** | **0**, ignored | **-1** `UnknownServerError` | **0** |
| version **8**, which has no member fields at all | **0** | **0**, the offsets | **0** |

Five of those rows are the whole of KIP-848 on this api:

* **A classic group ignores both fields.** `ClassicGroup::validateOffsetFetch` @ 3.9.2 takes the member id and the
  epoch and looks at neither — its whole body refuses a group in the state `Dead` with a `GroupIdNotFoundException`
  — so the 25 and the 113 can never come out of one, whatever a request claims
  (`offsetfetch.request.v9.classic-member` asks with a member id the group never had and is answered its offsets).
* **The 25 and the 113 belong to the KIP-848 groups alone.**
  `ConsumerGroup::validateOffsetFetch` @ 3.9.2 looks the member id up in the group and throws
  `UnknownMemberIdException` for an id it does not hold; for an id it holds it compares the epoch with
  `validateMemberEpoch` and throws `StaleMemberEpochException` for **every** difference, an epoch above the current
  one included — the same rule OffsetCommit v9 follows with its `generation_id_or_member_epoch`.
* **The defaults skip the member check entirely.** *"When the member id is null and the member epoch is -1, the
  request either comes from the admin client or from a client which does not provide them. In this case, the fetch
  request is accepted."* The early return needs **both** halves: a member id next to the epoch -1 is a member
  lookup with a stale epoch and is answered the 113, which is why an administrative reader has to leave the id
  `null` and not merely send a `-1`.
* **A null member id with an epoch that is not negative is answered `-1` `UnknownServerError`.** It is the one
  combination the early return lets through into the lookup, and the member table of the coordinator dereferences
  the key it is given (`BaseHashTable::findSlot` @ 3.9.2 calls `object.hashCode()`), so the handler dies in a
  `NullPointerException` that reaches the client as the group-level `ff ff`. Nothing is logged for it, the
  connection stays usable — the next request on it is answered normally — and it is a shape no client of the new
  protocol sends. `offsetfetch.response.v9.null-member-id` is that answer.
* **A member of a KIP-848 group may read its offsets with version 8** — and with the version 9 defaults. This is
  where OffsetFetch and OffsetCommit part: `ConsumerGroup::validateOffsetCommit` refuses a *commit* below version 9
  with the per-partition 35 `UnsupportedVersion`, while `validateOffsetFetch` has no version in its hands at all
  and only validates what the entry carries. Reading is open to everyone, writing is not.

**A group the coordinator does not know is still not an error**, and version 9 does not change that either: where
OffsetCommit v9 answers the **69** `GroupIdNotFound` that its release introduced, `OffsetMetadataManager::fetchOffsets`
@ 3.9.2 catches the `GroupIdNotFoundException` of the very same lookup, fails every named partition with the offset
-1 and the code 0, and answers an empty topic array for a `null` topic array — before a member field is ever looked
at (`offsetfetch.*.v9.unknown-group`).

`require_stable` and the member are independent: the flag makes the coordinator serve the read with a write
operation of its runtime instead of a read one, and the member is validated on both paths alike
(`offsetfetch.*.v9.stable` reads with the flag and the current epoch, and the same request with a stale epoch is
the 113). The validation is also **per entry** of a batch: `offsetfetch.*.v9.batch` asks for the classic group and
the stale KIP-848 member in one frame and is answered the offsets of the first and the 113 of the second.

This client sends version 9 for every fetch. `Client::fetchGroupOffsets()`, `Client::fetchOffsetsOfGroups()`,
`AdminClient::listGroupOffsets()` and `AdminClient::listConsumerGroupOffsets()` keep their signatures and leave the
two fields at `null` and `-1`; `Client::fetchGroupOffsetsAsMember()` and `OffsetFetchRequest::forMember()` fill
them, and `Protocol\Data\OffsetFetchRequestGroup` carries them per entry of a batch for the KIP-848 wave of this
line. `OffsetFetchRequestV8`/`OffsetFetchResponseV8` and `OffsetFetchRequestGroupV8` are the frames of a broker
below Kafka 3.7.

## ControlledShutdown API (key 7, v0 to v3)

This is the request that `kafka-server-stop.sh` triggers through `controlled.shutdown.enable`: the controller moves
every partition leader off the broker that is about to stop, so that no producer or consumer sees a leader election
timeout. It is a broker-to-controller request, not a client one, but nothing stops a client from sending it - and
version 0 of it is the one api of the protocol that a client cannot send with the common request header.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 3** (KIP-482), the same two integers in the flexible encoding. The answer of it is
the smallest frame of this document: **13 bytes** for the 8 of an unknown broker id, because the empty array of
remaining partitions is a single `01` and each of the two tag buffers a single `00`. `ControlledShutdownRequestV2`
and `ControlledShutdownResponseV2` are the frames of Kafka 2.2 and below.

```
ControlledShutdownRequest v0 and v1 => BrokerId
  BrokerId => int32
```

```
ControlledShutdownResponse v0 and v1 => ErrorCode [TopicName Partition]
  ErrorCode => int16
  TopicName => string
  Partition => int32
```

**The version 0 request has no `ClientId`.** The api version and the correlation id are followed by the broker id
directly; a client id string on the wire would be read as the broker id by version 0. Version 1, added by Kafka 0.9,
is the version that finally uses the common header, so `ControlledShutdownRequest` (v1) keeps the `clientId` of its
parent scheme and `ControlledShutdownRequestV0` drops it, which makes the version 0 frame a mere 12 bytes long.

**On this line that special case lives in a schema instead of in a Scala parser, and v0 is a served version again.**
Up to 0.11 the broker parsed key 7 with `ControlledShutdownRequest.readFrom()`, which read the client id only for
`versionId > 0` and validated nothing — so it answered *every* version, while ApiVersions reported the single
version 1. `RequestHeader` @ 1.1.1 has a `CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN_V0_SCHEMA` for that one frame and
`ControlledShutdownRequest.schemaVersions()` declares `{V0, V1}`, so a 1.1.1 broker announces `MinVersion = 0`,
answers both versions, and closes the connection on v2 like every other api — see "Every api of the table validates
its version".

The response has no version of its own: `ControlledShutdownResponse.schemaVersions()` @ 1.1.1 is the same frame for
both requests. The array of the response holds the topic-partitions that still have a leader or a replica on the
broker; an empty array with the error code 0 means the broker may be stopped. Unlike every other response, these are
flat pairs and not partitions grouped by their topic, so one topic may appear several times.

Only the active controller serves the request, and from Kafka 0.10.0 on a client no longer has to guess which
broker that is: the `ControllerId` of a Metadata v1/v2 answer names it, which is what
`Admin\AdminClient::findController()` reads. `AdminClient::controlledShutdown()` still asks the brokers in turn,
because a controlled shutdown is sent to a broker that is being stopped, not to the controller.

A broker id that the controller does not know is answered with the error code **8 (BrokerNotAvailable)** by a
1.1.1 broker, for both versions of the request: the controller's callback gets a `Failure` and
`controlledShutdownRequest.getErrorResponse(throwable)` maps the exception class. **This is a behaviour change
against 0.8.2.2**, which answered -1 (Unknown) in the very same situation, because that release mapped `e.getCause` -
null for a directly thrown exception - and `ErrorMapping.codeFor(null)` fell back to the Unknown code.

What did change against 0.11 is the **broker log**: a 0.10/0.11 broker printed

```
ERROR [KafkaApi-0] error when handling request Name: ControlledShutdownRequest; Version: 1; CorrelationId: 21; ClientId: Some(t2); BrokerId: 4242
kafka.common.BrokerNotAvailableException: Broker id 4242 does not exist.
```

for it, while `handleControlledShutdownRequest` @ 1.1.1 turns the `Failure` straight into a response and logs
**nothing at all**. The answer is the same; "look in the broker log" is no longer the way to find out why it is an 8.

An unknown broker id is therefore a harmless way to probe the api, which is what the integration test does - asking
for a real broker id would shut that broker down.

**Kafka 2.2 added the version 2** (KIP-380): the request gained a `broker_epoch int64` behind the broker id.

```
ControlledShutdownRequest (Version: 2) => BrokerId BrokerEpoch
  BrokerId    => int32
  BrokerEpoch => int64   -- since version 2, -1 when the sender does not know it
```

The epoch is the ZooKeeper registration epoch of the broker that wants to shut down, and it is what the controller
uses to recognise a **stale** request of a broker that has been restarted in the meantime: `doControlledShutdown`
@ 2.8.2 compares it with `controllerContext.liveBrokerIdAndEpochs(id)` and throws `StaleBrokerEpochException`
(**77**) when the request carries a lower one. The comparison is skipped entirely for the
`AbstractControlRequest.UNKNOWN_BROKER_EPOCH` **-1**: "broker epoch in the request is unknown if the controller
hasn't been upgraded to use KIP-380 so we will keep the previous behavior and don't reject the request".

**This repository never sends the real broker id.** A controlled shutdown of the broker of the container would
stop the container the whole suite runs against, so every vector and every test of this api names the broker id
**4242**, which no broker of the cluster has, and the answer is the **8** `BrokerNotAvailable` of
`if (!controllerContext.liveOrShuttingDownBrokerIds.contains(id))`. Measured on the container with the two epochs
a client can send:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| broker 4242, `broker_epoch = -1` | **8** `BrokerNotAvailable`, no remaining partitions — the epoch check is skipped, so the request reaches the "is that broker alive" test |
| broker 4242, `broker_epoch = 0` | **-1** `Unknown` — the epoch check comes **first** and looks the cached epoch of the broker up in a map that has no entry for 4242, so the controller dies on a `NoSuchElementException` that `Try{}` reports as an unknown error |

The second row is the one surprise of this api: with a broker epoch, an unknown broker id is an *unknown server
error* rather than the 8 of the version below, because the epoch check has no case for a broker the controller has
never seen. On the 2.8.2 ZooKeeper broker `AdminClient::controlledShutdown()` therefore defaulted to the -1 and took
the epoch as an optional argument.

**(3.x) No client listener of a KRaft node serves this api, and this line's admin client has no method for it any
more.** `ControlledShutdownRequest.json` @ 3.9.2 declares `"listeners": ["zkBroker", "controller"]`, so
`ApiVersionManager` leaves key 7 out of the ApiVersions answer of a `broker` listener, and every one of the four
versions is answered by closing the connection - `docker logs kafka-3-9-2` writes
`Received request api key CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN with version 0 which is not enabled` for it, the same line every
unserved key gets (`ApiVersionProbeTest::testControlledShutdownIsNotServedOnTheClientListenerInAnyVersion`).
A KRaft broker asks its controller to be shut down over the `BrokerRegistration`/`BrokerHeartbeat` apis (63, 62)
of the controller listener instead, which no client of this package sends. `AdminClient::controlledShutdown()` and
the three integration tests of `AdminApiTest` that exercised it are therefore **removed** on this line; the message
classes (`ControlledShutdownRequest`, `ControlledShutdownRequestV0`, `ControlledShutdownRequestV1`,
`ControlledShutdownRequestV2`, `ControlledShutdownResponse`, `ControlledShutdownResponseV2` and
`ControlledShutdownResponsePartition`) and every vector of this section stay - the api is still on the 3.9.2 wire,
on the controller listener, and the frames above are what it speaks there.

## Group membership protocol (keys 11 to 14)

Kafka 0.9 moved the coordination of a consumer group out of ZooKeeper and into the broker: the group coordinator
that already held the committed offsets ("GroupCoordinator API (key 10, v0 to v6)" above) now also runs the membership
protocol. Its four apis are generic - the broker never looks into the payloads a member sends - and the
`protocol_type` of the JoinGroup request names the meaning of those bytes; `consumer` is the one this client
implements, see "Consumer group protocol" below.

Every request of the four goes to the coordinator of the group and nowhere else; a request that reaches another
broker is answered with the error code 16 (`NotCoordinatorForGroup`).

The state machine of `kafka/coordinator/group/GroupMetadata.scala` @ 1.1.1 has **five** states - Kafka 0.10.1 added
`Empty` (`state: Byte = 5`) between "the last member left" and "the group is gone" - and each of them answers
differently. **Kafka 1.0 renamed one of the five**: the state between the last JoinGroup and the leader's SyncGroup
is `CompletingRebalance` here, where 0.9 to 0.11 called it `AwaitingSync`; nothing but the name changed, and the
name is what the coordinator puts on the wire in a DescribeGroups answer.

| State | Reached when | JoinGroup | SyncGroup | Heartbeat |
|-------|--------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| `PreparingRebalance` | A member joined, left or timed out | joins and waits for the other members | 27 `RebalanceInProgress` | 27 `RebalanceInProgress` |
| `CompletingRebalance` **(1.0)** | Every member has rejoined | answered right away for an unchanged member | held until the leader sends its assignment | 27 `RebalanceInProgress` |
| `Stable`        | The leader's assignment was stored | rebalances, unless a follower rejoins unchanged | returns the stored assignment | 0 |
| `Empty`         | **(0.10.1)** The last member left, the committed offsets are still there | registers the new member and rebalances | 25 `UnknownMemberId` | 25 `UnknownMemberId` |
| `Dead`          | The group was removed from this coordinator | 25 `UnknownMemberId` | 25 `UnknownMemberId` | 25 `UnknownMemberId` |

`Empty -> PreparingRebalance` is the only transition out of `Empty` (`GroupMetadata.validPreviousStates`), which is
what lets a restarted consumer of the same group take its committed offsets over; a 0.9.0.1 coordinator dropped the
group instead and answered `Dead` for it. See "DescribeGroups API (key 15, v0 to v6)".

The generation of a group starts at **1** and is incremented with every rebalance. A member id is assigned by the
coordinator as `<client id>-<random uuid>` (`GroupCoordinator.doJoinGroup` @ 1.1.1), e.g.
`t3-069f4b14-6878-407e-a708-a9288ca8b251` for the client id `t3`, so the client id of a member is visible in the
group forever; it is not otherwise interpreted.

The whole cycle of one generation, as the integration test
[`tests/Integration/GroupMembershipApiTest.php`](../../tests/Integration/GroupMembershipApiTest.php) drives it
against a real broker:

```
GroupCoordinator -> JoinGroup(member_id = "") -> 79 with the member id the coordinator assigned   (v4, KIP-394)
                 -> JoinGroup(member_id = that id) -> generation 1, the leader and the members
   leader:   SyncGroup(assignment of every member) -> its own assignment
   follower: SyncGroup([])                          -> its own assignment, once the leader has sent one
   both:     Heartbeat  ... every heartbeat.interval.ms, 0 while the group is stable
             Heartbeat  -> 27 as soon as another member joins or leaves: rejoin with JoinGroup
             LeaveGroup -> 0, the group rebalances right away instead of after the session timeout
```

### The member id of a first join (v4, KIP-394)

Up to JoinGroup v3 a client that had no member id sent the empty string and the coordinator added it to the group
right away, with the id it generated for it. That is cheap to abuse and expensive to survive: a client whose
JoinGroup times out - or one that simply retries - is added **again**, under a second id, and the group waits its
whole rebalance timeout for a member that will never come back. KIP-394 (Kafka 2.2) closed it by refusing the
first join:

| Version | `member_id = ""` |
|---|---|
| v0 to v3 | the member is added to the group and the join blocks until the rebalance is over |
| **v4 and above** | the join is answered **immediately** with the error code **79** (`MemberIdRequired`) and the member id the coordinator generated; nothing is added to the group |

The refusal is an ordinary error answer of the api - generation **-1**, empty group protocol, empty leader id, no
members - and its `member_id` is the whole point: the client sends the very same request again with that id and is
then added to the group like any rejoining member. Both frames are captured
(`joingroup.request.v4.empty-member-id` / `joingroup.response.v4.member-id-required` and `joingroup.request.v4` /
`joingroup.response.v4`).

Measured on the container, with `session.timeout.ms = 10000` and `rebalance_timeout = 20000`:

```
v3, member_id = ""                  -> error 0,  generation 1, member kafka-client-t3-394-c68bacf1-…   (2 ms)
v4, member_id = ""                  -> error 79, generation -1, member kafka-client-t3-394-972b483b-…  (0 ms)
v4, member_id = "…-972b483b-…"      -> error 0,  generation 1, leader = itself, 1 member              (0 ms)
```

**A client that never comes back with the id costs the group nothing.** `doUnknownJoinGroup` @ 2.8.2 puts the id
into `group.pendingMembers` and arms `addPendingMemberExpiration(group, id, sessionTimeoutMs)` for it, so the
entry is dropped after the session timeout of that request; the group itself is created and stays in the state
**`Empty` with 0 members** in the meantime — measured, both immediately after the 79 and twelve seconds later. A
pending member is not a member: it does not appear in DescribeGroups and does not hold a rebalance up. What does
end such a group is the coordinator's own reaper: `cleanupGroupMetadata` @ 2.8.2 runs every
`offsets.retention.check.interval.ms` (ten minutes by default) and **removes** an `Empty` group that holds no
offset, so a group that never got past the 79 is answered `Dead` from the next pass on — measured once on the
shared container, in the middle of an exchange that had been answered `Empty` a moment earlier.

`Consumer\Internals\ConsumerCoordinator` answers the 79 the way `AbstractCoordinator.handleJoinResponse` @ 2.8.2
does: it takes the id out of the answer and sends the join again **immediately** — no backoff, no rebalance in
between, and the attempt is not counted against its rebalance retries, because nothing failed. `Client::joinGroup()`
reports the code as a `MemberIdRequiredException` whose context carries the assigned id under `assignedMemberId`.

**The 81 `GroupMaxSizeReached` of the same release** is the other half of KIP-394: `group.max.size` bounds the
number of members of a group, and `acceptJoiningMember` @ 2.8.2 answers a join above it with the error code 81 and
the member id `""`, after removing the member from the group. It is **not producible on this container**:
`group.max.size` defaults to `2147483647` and is **not a dynamically updatable broker config** in Kafka 2.8, so it
cannot be lowered without restarting the broker, which a shared container does not allow. The code is implemented
(`GroupMaxSizeReachedException`) and documented from `GroupCoordinator.scala`, and it is not asserted against the
broker.

### Static membership (KIP-345)

A member of a group is normally **dynamic**: its identity is the member id the coordinator generates for it, so a
consumer that restarts is a new member, its partitions are taken away from it and given back by a rebalance, and
the group changes generation twice for nothing. KIP-345 (Kafka 2.3) gives a consumer a name of its own instead,
`group.instance.id`, which travels in the `group_instance_id` of **JoinGroup v5, SyncGroup v3, Heartbeat v3 and
OffsetCommit v7** - the four apis this client raised for it - and is a `NULLABLE_STRING` that a dynamic member
sends as `ff ff`.

What the coordinator does with it, measured on the container with the instance id `t3-345-one`:

| Situation | What the 2.8.2 coordinator answers |
|---|---|
| a static member joins a group that does not know its instance id, `member_id = ""` | it is **added right away**, with the member id `<group.instance.id>-<uuid>` - the 79 of KIP-394 is never sent, because `requireKnownMemberId` is `version >= 4 && groupInstanceId.isEmpty` in `KafkaApis.handleJoinGroupRequest` |
| the same instance id joins again with `member_id = ""` while the group is `Stable` | the **generation does not change** (1 → 1), the coordinator hands out a **new member id** and the answer arrives in 0 ms; the SyncGroup that follows returns the assignment the old member id had, so the consumer keeps its partitions **without a rebalance** |
| the older consumer keeps using its own member id afterwards | **82** (`FencedInstanceId`) on Heartbeat, on SyncGroup and per partition on OffsetCommit - it has been fenced for good |

The second row is the whole point of the KIP: `updateStaticMemberAndRebalance` @ 2.8.2 replaces the member id
behind the instance id, reschedules the heartbeat and, while the group is `Stable` and the selected protocol does
not change, only persists the group instead of rebalancing it. The third row is what makes the guarantee safe: the
identity belongs to exactly one live consumer, and the one that is fenced can not commit any more, so two
consumers can never write offsets for the same instance.

Two more observations of the container:

* the `leader_id` of the answer to the taking-over member is still the **old** member id up to JoinGroup **v8** -
  `leaderOrNull` is read before `replaceGroupInstance` swaps the ids - so a static member must not conclude from
  `leader_id != member_id` that it is a follower of somebody else; it syncs and receives its assignment either
  way. **Version 9 (KIP-814) answers the new member id there**, because the branch that carries the
  `skip_assignment` reads the leader after the swap, and that flag is what a leader of this version looks at
  instead of the comparison - see "The reason of KIP-800 and the skip_assignment of KIP-814 (v8 and v9)" below;
* a static member is expected **not to send LeaveGroup**: `Consumer\Internals\ConsumerCoordinator::leaveGroup()`
  does nothing for one, so the coordinator keeps its partitions for `session.timeout.ms` while it restarts. That is
  what turns a rolling restart into no rebalance at all. LeaveGroup itself gains no `group_instance_id` here - the
  batch of KIP-345 is **LeaveGroup v3**, Kafka 2.4, see "The batch leave of KIP-345 (v3)" below.

`ConsumerConfig::GROUP_INSTANCE_ID` is the option, and an empty string is treated as "not configured": the broker
answers an empty instance id with 42 (`InvalidRequest`).

## JoinGroup API (key 11, v0 to v9)

```
JoinGroupRequest (v0) => GroupId SessionTimeout MemberId ProtocolType [GroupProtocol]
  GroupId        => string
  SessionTimeout => int32
  MemberId       => string
  ProtocolType   => string
  GroupProtocol  => ProtocolName ProtocolMetadata
    ProtocolName     => string
    ProtocolMetadata => bytes

JoinGroupRequest (v1, v2, v3 and v4) => GroupId SessionTimeout RebalanceTimeout MemberId ProtocolType
                                        [GroupProtocol]
  RebalanceTimeout => int32   -- new in v1, right after SessionTimeout

JoinGroupRequest (v5) => GroupId SessionTimeout RebalanceTimeout MemberId GroupInstanceId ProtocolType
                         [GroupProtocol]
  GroupInstanceId => nullable_string   -- new in v5, right after MemberId

JoinGroupRequest (v6) => (the frame of v5 in the FLEXIBLE encoding of KIP-482)
JoinGroupRequest (v7) => (the frame of v6, with the version field 7)

JoinGroupRequest (v8 and v9) => GroupId SessionTimeout RebalanceTimeout MemberId GroupInstanceId ProtocolType
                                [GroupProtocol] Reason
  Reason => nullable_string   -- new in v8, BEHIND the protocol array, the last field of the body
```

```
JoinGroupResponse (v0 and v1) => ErrorCode GenerationId GroupProtocol LeaderId MemberId [Member]
  ErrorCode     => int16
  GenerationId  => int32
  GroupProtocol => string
  LeaderId      => string
  MemberId      => string
  Member        => MemberId MemberMetadata
    MemberId       => string
    MemberMetadata => bytes

JoinGroupResponse (v2, v3 and v4) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode GenerationId GroupProtocol LeaderId MemberId
                                     [Member]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32     -- since version 2

JoinGroupResponse (v5) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode GenerationId GroupProtocol LeaderId MemberId [Member]
  Member => MemberId GroupInstanceId MemberMetadata
    GroupInstanceId => nullable_string   -- new in v5, right after the member's MemberId

JoinGroupResponse (v6) => (the frame of v5 in the FLEXIBLE encoding of KIP-482)

JoinGroupResponse (v7 and v8) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode GenerationId ProtocolType GroupProtocol LeaderId
                                 MemberId [Member]
  ProtocolType  => nullable_string   -- new in v7, in front of the protocol name
  GroupProtocol => nullable_string   -- NULLABLE from v7 on, a plain string below it

JoinGroupResponse (v9) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode GenerationId ProtocolType GroupProtocol LeaderId
                          SkipAssignment MemberId [Member]
  SkipAssignment => boolean   -- new in v9, one byte BETWEEN the leader id and the member id
```

Version 2 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) is the throttle time and nothing else: `JOIN_GROUP_REQUEST_V2 =
JOIN_GROUP_REQUEST_V1` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3, so `JoinGroupRequestV1` and `JoinGroupRequestV2` send the same
body, and `JoinGroupResponseV1`/`JoinGroupResponseV0` decode the same answer without the leading field.

**Version 3 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) added nothing at all** — `JoinGroupRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 introduces no field
between the `rebalance_timeout` of version 1 and the `group_instance_id` of version 5 — and only moved the api into
the throttling contract of KIP-219, where a throttled broker answers first and mutes the channel afterwards.

**Version 4 (Kafka 2.2, KIP-394) added no field either** and changed what an **empty member id** means instead: it
is refused with the error code 79 and the id the coordinator assigned, see "The member id of a first join (v4,
KIP-394)" above. `JoinGroupRequestV4`/`JoinGroupResponseV4` are that frame, with `JoinGroupRequestV3` and
`JoinGroupRequestV2` below them.

**Version 5 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-345) added the `group_instance_id` to both halves**: to the request behind the member
id, and to every entry of the member array of the answer behind its member id, so that the leader of a generation
sees which of its members are static ones. `JoinGroupRequestV5` is that frame - the version this client sends is
the **v7** of KIP-559 (Kafka 2.5) - and a dynamic member writes `ff ff` for the field - see "Static membership
(KIP-345)" above for what the coordinator does with it. A join that carries an instance id is never answered 79.

**The error answer of a 2.x coordinator reports the generation `-1`**, the `UNKNOWN_GENERATION_ID` of the Java
client, where a 0.11 or 1.1 broker reported `0`; the group protocol, the leader id and the member array of such an
answer are still empty. Measured on the container with a session timeout below `group.min.session.timeout.ms`.

**Version 8 (Kafka 3.2, KIP-800) appended the `Reason` to the request and version 9 (KIP-814) put the
`SkipAssignment` into the answer**, the two fields of the section below; the version this client sends is the
**v9**, with `JoinGroupRequestV8`/`JoinGroupResponseV8` and `JoinGroupRequestV7`/`JoinGroupResponseV7` below it.

### The reason of KIP-800 and the skip_assignment of KIP-814 (v8 and v9)

Kafka 3.2 added one field to each half of this api, and neither of them changes what the coordinator *does*.

**`Reason` (v8, KIP-800)** is a nullable string at the very end of the request body, behind the protocol array:
"the reason why the member (re-)joins the group". The coordinator **logs** it and nothing else — every rebalance
line of a 3.9.2 node ends in `; client reason: <the text>`:

```
INFO [GroupCoordinator id=1 …] Preparing to rebalance group t3-32-vectors-group in state PreparingRebalance with
old generation 0 (reason: Adding new member kafka-client-t3-32-… with group instance id null; client reason: need
to re-join with the given member-id: kafka-client-t3-32-…).
```

A member that names none writes the compact null, one `00` byte. The Java client cuts the text at **255
characters** before it builds the request (`JoinGroupRequest.maybeTruncateReason` @ 3.2.3) and so does
`JoinGroupRequest::MAX_REASON_LENGTH` here — the field sits on the path of every rebalance of every member, and an
unbounded one is a way to fill the log of a broker. The reasons the Java consumer sends, which
`Consumer\Internals\ConsumerCoordinator` sends word for word, are the empty string for a first join,
`need to re-join with the given member-id: <id>` for the second join of the KIP-394 exchange and, for a
subscription that changed, a text of the caller; `AdminClient::removeMembersFromConsumerGroup()` sends
`member was removed by an admin`, the `DEFAULT_LEAVE_GROUP_REASON` of `KafkaAdminClient` @ 3.2.3.

**Measured on the node**: the reason of a join the coordinator refuses with the **79** of KIP-394 never reaches
the log at all — the line that answers it (`Dynamic member with unknown member id joins group … Created a new
member id …`) carries no `client reason` — and neither does the one of the static return below. Only a join that
really starts or ends a rebalance names its reason.

**`SkipAssignment` (v9, KIP-814)** is one byte of the answer, between the leader id and the member id: "True if
the leader must skip running the assignment". It reaches exactly one member in exactly one situation — a
**static** member that comes back with an empty member id under a `group.instance.id` the group still holds,
while the group is `Stable` and the protocol it would select does not change
(`GroupMetadataManager.updateStaticMemberAndRebalance` @ 3.9.2 answers with `skipAssignment = isLeader`). The
coordinator then does not rebalance the group at all: it replaces the member id of that instance, keeps the
generation and keeps the assignment, and the returning member is told not to compute a new one. Its SyncGroup
therefore carries an **empty** assignment array and is answered the share the generation already agreed on, which
is what `ConsumerCoordinator.onLeaderElected` @ 3.2.3 does and what this client does in
`Consumer\Internals\ConsumerCoordinator::rebalance()`.

Measured on the 3.9.2 node with one static member of `t3-32-vectors-static`, the topic `t3-32-vectors` and the
instance `t3-32-one`:

| The join | Answer |
|---|---|
| the **first** join of the instance (empty member id, fresh group) | after **3.00 s** — `group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms` — the generation 1, the member id `t3-32-one-<uuid>`, `skip_assignment` **false**: the group has no assignment yet |
| the **same instance again** with an empty member id, the group `Stable` | after **0.01 s**, the generation still **1**, a **new** member id `t3-32-one-<another uuid>`, the leader is that id and `skip_assignment` is **true** |
| that leader's SyncGroup with an **empty** assignment array | the error code 0 and the assignment of generation 1, unchanged |
| the same return at **version 8** | no such byte at all, so the leader computes the assignment as every client below 3.2 does |
| every **error** answer of version 9, the 79 of KIP-394 included | `skip_assignment` **false** |

**Version 9 answers another leader id than version 8 does, for the very same request.** The branch KIP-814 added
builds the answer with `.setLeader(group.leaderOrNull())`, which is read **after** `replaceStaticMember` swapped
the member id of the instance, so a version 9 return is told that the leader is its **own new** id; the branch
below it builds the answer with `.setLeader(currentLeader)`, a value read before the swap, so a version 8 return
is told that the leader is the id that has just been retired. Measured on the node with two live consumers under
one instance id (`StaticMembershipApiTest::testASecondMemberUnderTheSameInstanceIdFencesTheFirstOne`): the second
join is answered its own member id as the leader and `skip_assignment = true`, where the 2.x line measured the
member id of the consumer it had just fenced. A client that compares `member_id` with `leader_id` to find out
whether it has to assign therefore reaches the opposite conclusion on the two versions — which is why the flag
exists: it says what the leader is to do, and the comparison alone does not.

The node's log names the moment without naming the flag: `Static member with groupInstanceId=t3-32-one and
unknown member id joins group … in Stable state. Replacing previously mapped member … with this groupInstanceId.`
A **dynamic** member never sees `true`: a leader that rejoins a `Stable` group starts a rebalance
(`Leader … re-joining group during Stable`) and is answered `false` with a new generation.

### `RebalanceTimeout`, the wire half of `max.poll.interval.ms` (v1, Kafka 0.10.1, KIP-62)

Version 1 inserted one field, `RebalanceTimeout`, and changed nothing else — the answer is byte for byte the answer
of version 0 (`JOIN_GROUP_RESPONSE_V1 = JOIN_GROUP_RESPONSE_V0` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.10.2.2). The two timeouts of
the request answer two different questions:

* `SessionTimeout` is how long the coordinator keeps a member that sends no heartbeat, and it is the only one of the
  two that is **validated**: it has to lie between `group.min.session.timeout.ms` and `group.max.session.timeout.ms`
  of the broker, 6000 and 300000 by default, 1000 and 60000 on the container of this branch, and is answered with 26
  (`InvalidSessionTimeout`) otherwise.
* `RebalanceTimeout` is how long the coordinator waits for **each** member to rejoin once a rebalance has started,
  i.e. how long it holds every JoinGroup of that rebalance. `GroupMetadata.rebalanceTimeoutMs` @ 0.10.2.2 is the
  **largest** rebalance timeout of the members of the group, and the `DelayedJoin` of the rebalance is scheduled
  with it.

**The coordinator really waits the rebalance timeout, not the session timeout.** Observed on the 0.10.2.2 container
with two connections to one group: member A joined with `SessionTimeout = 30000` and `RebalanceTimeout = 4000`,
synced, and then went silent; member B joined the same group, which started a rebalance that A never rejoined, and
B's JoinGroup came back after **4.00 s** with the generation 2. The same experiment with version 0 requests and a
session timeout of 10000 answered after **10.00 s** — for a version 0 frame the broker uses the session timeout as
the rebalance timeout as well (`JoinGroupRequest.rebalanceTimeout` @ 0.10.2.2 falls back to `sessionTimeout` when
the struct has no such field), which is exactly what a Kafka 0.9 coordinator did.

**`RebalanceTimeout` is bounded by nothing.** `group.max.session.timeout.ms` only bounds the session timeout, and
`GroupCoordinator.handleJoinGroup` @ 0.10.2.2 validates nothing else: on the container, whose maximum session
timeout is 60000, a join with `SessionTimeout = 10000` and `RebalanceTimeout = 300000` was accepted with the error
code 0, while `SessionTimeout = 300000` with `RebalanceTimeout = 10000` was refused with 26. A `RebalanceTimeout` of
0 is accepted as well, and a rebalance then completes as soon as its `DelayedJoin` is checked.

Version 2 of this api is Kafka 0.11: a 0.10.2.2 broker **closes the connection** on a JoinGroup v2 frame, which is
what a client that guesses versions instead of asking ApiVersions finds out the hard way.

A client that has no member id yet sends an **empty** `MemberId` and receives the one the coordinator assigned to
it; a member that rejoins has to send the id of the previous generation, otherwise the coordinator answers 25
(`UnknownMemberId`) and the client has to join again with an empty id.

`GroupProtocol` lists the protocols the member supports, best first; the coordinator picks the first one that
*every* member of the group supports and reports it as the `GroupProtocol` of the answer. A member that offers none
of them, or another `ProtocolType` than the group has, is refused with 23 (`InconsistentGroupProtocol`).

The `Member` array of the answer is filled **only for the leader** - the member whose id equals `LeaderId` - and
carries the metadata every member sent for the selected protocol; every other member receives an empty array and
waits for its assignment. The leader is simply the first member of the group's internal map, and it changes with a
rebalance.

**This request blocks, and it is the only one of the protocol that does.** The coordinator answers it only once
every known member of the group has rejoined, i.e. when the rebalance is complete, or once the members that did not
show up have run out of their **rebalance** timeout (their session timeout, for a group whose members all joined
with version 0). A client therefore needs a socket read timeout - `request.timeout.ms` - larger than both its
`session.timeout.ms` and its `max.poll.interval.ms`, which is why the Java consumer of 0.10.1 and above defaults
that option to 305000 against a `max.poll.interval.ms` of 300000. Observed on the 0.10.2.2 container: the join of
the first member of a fresh group is answered immediately, the join of a second member is held until the first
member rejoins (it learns about the rebalance from the error code 27 of its next heartbeat) or its rebalance
timeout expires.

An error answer carries the generation **0** - not the `UNKNOWN_GENERATION_ID` of -1 that the Java client uses for
a member without a generation, `GroupCoordinator.joinError` @ 0.10.2.2 builds the answer with `generationId = 0` -
an empty `GroupProtocol`, an empty `LeaderId`, the `MemberId` that was sent and an empty member array.

The `Member` array comes out of the internal map of the coordinator and is **not** ordered by the moment the
members joined; a leader that needs a stable order - a range assignor does - has to sort it itself. Verified on the
0.9.0.1 container: after a rebalance the leader received the two members in the opposite order of their joins.

## SyncGroup API (key 14, v0 to v5)

```
SyncGroupRequest (v0, v1 and v2) => GroupId GenerationId MemberId [GroupAssignment]
  GroupId         => string
  GenerationId    => int32
  MemberId        => string
  GroupAssignment => MemberId MemberAssignment
    MemberId         => string
    MemberAssignment => bytes

SyncGroupRequest (v3) => GroupId GenerationId MemberId GroupInstanceId [GroupAssignment]
  GroupInstanceId => nullable_string   -- new in v3, right after MemberId

SyncGroupRequest (v4) => (the frame of v3 in the FLEXIBLE encoding of KIP-482)

SyncGroupRequest (v5) => GroupId GenerationId MemberId GroupInstanceId ProtocolType ProtocolName
                          [GroupAssignment]
  ProtocolType => nullable_string   -- new in v5, behind GroupInstanceId
  ProtocolName => nullable_string   -- new in v5, behind ProtocolType
```

```
SyncGroupResponse (v0) => ErrorCode MemberAssignment
  ErrorCode        => int16
  MemberAssignment => bytes

SyncGroupResponse (v1, v2 and v3) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode MemberAssignment
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32     -- since version 1

SyncGroupResponse (v4) => (the frame of v3 in the FLEXIBLE encoding of KIP-482)

SyncGroupResponse (v5) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ProtocolType ProtocolName MemberAssignment
  ProtocolType => nullable_string   -- new in v5, between the error code and the assignment
  ProtocolName => nullable_string   -- new in v5, behind ProtocolType
```

Version 1 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) added the leading `ThrottleTimeMs` to the answer and left the request alone
(`SYNC_GROUP_REQUEST_V1 = SYNC_GROUP_REQUEST_V0` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3), and version 2 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219)
changed neither half once more — `SyncGroupRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 has nothing between the member id of version 0 and
the `group_instance_id` of version 3 — so the three frames differ in their api version field alone.
**Version 3 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-345) is the first one that changed the frame**: the nullable `group_instance_id`
stands behind the member id of the request, and the answer is untouched once more. `SyncGroupRequestV3` and
`SyncGroupResponseV3` are that version - `SyncGroupRequest`/`SyncGroupResponse` are the **v5** of KIP-559 this
client sends - the versions below them keep their own `…V2`, `…V1` and `…V0` classes, and a
member whose instance id another consumer has taken over is answered **82** (`FencedInstanceId`) here as well.

**The rebalance timeout of the JoinGroup is also the deadline for this request.** From Kafka 2.5 on
(KAFKA-9752, the pending-sync expiration of KIP-345) `onCompleteJoin` schedules a `DelayedSync` with
`group.rebalanceTimeoutMs` and `onExpirePendingSync` removes every member of the fresh generation that has not sent
its SyncGroup by then, which starts another rebalance. A member that takes longer than its own
`max.poll.interval.ms` between the JoinGroup answer and the SyncGroup is therefore dropped; with a rebalance
timeout of `0` the expiry fires the moment the generation is formed and the member is gone before it can use the
answer at all (measured, `GroupMembershipApiTest::testTheRebalanceTimeoutIsNotBoundedByTheBrokerButIsAlsoTheSyncDeadline`).

Every member sends SyncGroup right after its JoinGroup answer, but only the leader fills `GroupAssignment`: it
computes the assignment of the whole generation out of the members it received and hands the coordinator one byte
array per member. The coordinator stores them and answers every member with its own share; the answers of the
members that synced before the leader are held until the leader's request arrives. A member the leader did not
mention receives an **empty** assignment (`GroupCoordinator.doSyncGroup` @ 0.10.2.2 fills the missing members in),
which is how a consumer learns that it got no partitions.

A generation that is not the current one is answered with 22 (`IllegalGeneration`), a member id the group does not
have with 25 (`UnknownMemberId`), and a group that started to rebalance in the meantime with 27
(`RebalanceInProgress`). Every error answer carries an empty `MemberAssignment`.

### The protocol type and name of KIP-559 (Kafka 2.5)

Up to Kafka 2.4 a member learned the protocol of its generation from the JoinGroup answer and told the coordinator
nothing about it afterwards: the coordinator knew what the group ran on, the member knew what it had asked for, and
nothing on the wire connected the two. **KIP-559 made both halves explicit** and raised two apis by one version for
it — JoinGroup **v7** and SyncGroup **v5** — while the third api of the pair, the JoinGroup *request*, did not
change at all.

| Frame | What Kafka 2.5 added |
|---|---|
| JoinGroup request v7 | nothing — "Version 7 is the same as version 6" |
| JoinGroup response v7 | a nullable `protocol_type` in front of `protocol_name`, and `protocol_name` itself became **nullable** |
| SyncGroup request v5 | a nullable `protocol_type` and `protocol_name` behind `group_instance_id` |
| SyncGroup response v5 | the same pair between the error code and the assignment |

**The two fields of a SyncGroup v5 are nullable on the wire and mandatory in the broker.**
`KafkaApis.handleSyncGroupRequest` @ 2.8.2 asks `syncGroupRequest.areMandatoryProtocolTypeAndNamePresent()` before
the authorizer and before the coordinator, and answers **23** (`InconsistentGroupProtocol`) when either of them is
null in a version 5 — the check is skipped for every version below, which has nowhere to put them.
`GroupCoordinator.handleSyncGroup` then compares them with what the group settled on and answers the very same 23
when they differ. Measured on the container, all three on one member of a settled generation:

| SyncGroup v5 of a member of generation 1 | Answer |
|---|---|
| `protocol_type = null`, `protocol_name = null` | **23**, a null type, a null name and an empty assignment — and the membership untouched: the next request of the member is answered normally |
| `protocol_type = "consumer"`, `protocol_name = "roundrobin"` (the group runs `range`) | **23** as well, one check later |
| `protocol_type = "consumer"`, `protocol_name = "range"` | **0**, the assignment, and the same pair echoed back |

A member therefore sends what it knows: the `protocol_type` it joined with and the `protocol_name` of the JoinGroup
answer of that generation, which is exactly what `AbstractCoordinator` @ 2.8.2 does and what
[`ConsumerCoordinator`](../../src/Kafka/Consumer/Internals/ConsumerCoordinator.php) passes to
`Client::syncGroup()`. A caller of that method which names **neither** field is sent as a **version 4** instead of
being refused: the frame of Kafka 2.4 has no such field, a 2.8.2 broker serves it unchanged, and the alternative
would be a 23 for every caller written before this release.

**An error answer of a JoinGroup v7 carries two nulls where a v6 carries an empty string.** The protocol name of a
version below 7 is a plain string, so `KafkaApis` fills it with `GroupCoordinator.NoProtocol` — `""` — whenever the
join produced no protocol; from version 7 on it writes `joinResult.protocolName.orNull` instead, and the
`protocol_type` next to it is null for the same answers. Measured on the **79** of KIP-394, the refusal every first
join of a dynamic member gets: generation `-1`, an empty leader id, an empty member array, the assigned member id —
and `protocol_type = null`, `protocol_name = null`, the single byte `00` each in the flexible encoding
(`joingroup.response.v7.member-id-required`). An accepted join answers `consumer` and `range`.

## Heartbeat API (key 12, v0 to v4)

```
HeartbeatRequest (v0, v1 and v2) => GroupId GroupGenerationId MemberId
  GroupId           => string
  GroupGenerationId => int32
  MemberId          => string

HeartbeatRequest (v3) => GroupId GroupGenerationId MemberId GroupInstanceId
  GroupInstanceId => nullable_string   -- new in v3, it closes the frame
```

```
HeartbeatResponse (v0) => ErrorCode
  ErrorCode => int16

HeartbeatResponse (v1, v2 and v3) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32     -- since version 1
```

Version 1 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) added the leading throttle time and nothing else, so a v0 answer is a six-byte
frame where a v1 answer is a ten-byte one; the request is the same in both versions. Version 2 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219)
repeated that: the frame is untouched and only the throttling contract changed, so `HeartbeatRequest` (v2) and
`HeartbeatRequestV2` put the same bytes on the wire. **Version 3 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-345) appended the nullable
`group_instance_id`** to the request and left the answer alone; `HeartbeatRequestV3` is that frame, this client
sends the flexible **v4** of Kafka 2.4, and it is the heartbeat that tells a static member that another consumer
has taken its identity over - the answer is then **82** (`FencedInstanceId`), which is fatal (captured as
`heartbeat.request.v3.fenced-instance-id` / `heartbeat.response.v3.fenced-instance-id`).

The error code is the whole answer, and it is how the coordinator drives the client: `0` means the member is alive
and its session timeout has been reset, 27 (`RebalanceInProgress`) that the group is rebalancing and the member has
to send JoinGroup again, 25 (`UnknownMemberId`) that the coordinator dropped it - after a missed session timeout,
for instance - and 22 (`IllegalGeneration`) that its generation is over. A heartbeat has to be sent within
`session.timeout.ms`; the Java client uses `heartbeat.interval.ms` (a third of it) and so does this one, from its
poll loop, because PHP has no background thread.

The order of the checks in `GroupCoordinator.handleHeartbeat` @ 0.10.2.2 is worth knowing: the state of the **group**
is checked before the member, so a heartbeat of an unknown member of a group that is rebalancing is answered 27 and
not 25. While the coordinator is still loading the group out of `__consumer_offsets` it answers `0` "blindly", so a
successful heartbeat is not a proof of membership either.

## LeaveGroup API (key 13, v0 to v5)

```
LeaveGroupRequest (v0, v1 and v2) => GroupId MemberId
  GroupId  => string
  MemberId => string

LeaveGroupRequest (v3 and v4) => GroupId [Members]
  GroupId => string
  Members => MemberId GroupInstanceId     -- the single MemberId is GONE
    MemberId        => string
    GroupInstanceId => nullable_string

LeaveGroupRequest (v5) => GroupId [Members]
  Members => MemberId GroupInstanceId Reason
    Reason => nullable_string   -- new in v5, per ENTRY, behind its instance id
```

```
LeaveGroupResponse (v0) => ErrorCode
  ErrorCode => int16

LeaveGroupResponse (v1 and v2) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32     -- since version 1

LeaveGroupResponse (v3, v4 and v5) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [Members]
  Members => MemberId GroupInstanceId ErrorCode    -- since version 3
    MemberId        => string
    GroupInstanceId => nullable_string
    ErrorCode       => int16
```

Version 1 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) added the leading throttle time and version 2 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) added nothing;
the request did not change in either, so `LeaveGroupRequestV2`, `LeaveGroupRequestV1` and `LeaveGroupRequestV0`
send the same body. **Version 3 (Kafka 2.4, KIP-345) replaced the single `MemberId` with a batch of member
identities** and gave the answer a matching member array - see "The batch leave of KIP-345 (v3)" below.
`LeaveGroupRequestV3` is that frame, this client sends the flexible **v4** of Kafka 2.4, and a member that removes
itself is that batch with exactly one entry.

Removing the member starts a rebalance right away, instead of after the session timeout of a member that simply
stopped answering; for a consumer that means that its partitions are reassigned to the other members within
milliseconds. This is what a consumer sends when it shuts down in an orderly way.

A member id the coordinator does not know - because the member already left, or because the group does not exist at
all - is answered with 25 (`UnknownMemberId`): in the top-level error code below version 3, and in the entry of
that member from version 3 on. Leaving the last member of a group leaves an empty group behind that `ListGroups`
still reports until its offsets expire.

### The batch leave of KIP-345 (v3)

Static membership is why this version exists. A **static** member does not leave its group when it shuts down -
that is what lets it keep its partitions across a restart - so an instance that is retired for good has to be
removed by hand, and it has to be removable **by its `group.instance.id`**, because its member id was generated by
the coordinator and is not something an operator knows. KIP-345 therefore replaced the single member id of the
request with a list of *member identities*, each of which names its member

* by its **`group.instance.id`**, with the member id left empty - what an administrator sends;
* by its **member id**, with a null instance id - what a dynamic member sends for itself;
* or by **both**, which is what a static member sends for itself: the coordinator then checks that the member id
  still belongs to that instance and answers 82 (`FencedInstanceId`) when another consumer has taken it over.

The answer has an entry per member, in the order of the request, and it **echoes the identity that was sent** -
`memberLeaveError(leavingMember, error)` @ 2.8.2 builds every entry out of the request entry, so an entry that was
named by its instance id comes back with an **empty member id**, not with the one the coordinator resolved.

**The top-level error code is about the request, not about its members.** `handleLeaveGroup` @ 2.8.2 answers 0
there for every batch it could read, whatever became of the members; the codes that do reach it are 30
(`GroupAuthorizationFailed`), 15 (`GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable`, for a group in the state `Dead`), 16
(`NotCoordinatorForGroup`) and 14 (`GroupLoadInProgress`). A client that only looks at it therefore sees success
where every single member was refused.

Measured on the container, with a group of two members - the static instance `t3-24a-one` and a dynamic member:

| The batch entry | Answer |
|---|---|
| the static member by its **instance id** (empty member id) | **0**, and the member is gone at once: the group does not wait out its session timeout |
| an **instance id the group does not have** | **25** `UnknownMemberId` |
| the dynamic member by its **member id** | **0** |
| the same member id a **second** time | **25** |
| a **pending** member - one that was refused with the 79 of KIP-394 and never came back - by the member id it was given | **0**: `removePendingMemberAndUpdateGroup` takes it out of the pending list |
| any member of a **group the coordinator has never heard of** | **25** per entry, with the top-level code **0** |
| an **empty batch** | top-level **0** and an empty member array, whether the group exists or not |

Removing both members of a group in one request left it in the state `Empty` with 0 members, i.e. the batch is
applied entry by entry and the group is rebalanced once at the end.

`Admin\AdminClient::removeMembersFromConsumerGroup()` is the api half of this: it takes `MemberToRemove` entries -
`byInstanceId()`, `byMemberId()` or `byBoth()`, and a plain string is an instance id, as in the Java admin client -
and answers with the error of every member, keyed by its identity, without throwing for a member that was refused.
`Client::leaveGroup()` sends the one-element batch of a member that removes itself and reports the error of that
entry as if it were the error code of the answer, which is what it was below version 3.

### The leave reason of KIP-800 (v5)

Version 5 (Kafka 3.2) appended a nullable `Reason` to **every entry** of the batch - "the reason why the member
left the group" - and left the answer alone ("Version 5 is the same as version 4" in `LeaveGroupResponse.json` @
3.2.3). The field is per member, not per request: a batch that removes three members can name a different reason
for each of them, and an entry that names none writes the compact null, one `00` byte. It is cut at the same
**255** characters as the join reason of the same KIP (`JoinGroupRequest::MAX_REASON_LENGTH`).

The node puts it into the line with which it removes the member, and this one is written whatever the reason says:

```
INFO [GroupCoordinator id=1 …] [Group t3-32-vectors-static] Member t3-32-one-… has left group through explicit
`LeaveGroup` request; client reason: the instance is retired
```

What this client sends is what the Java client sends: `KafkaConsumer::close()` names `the consumer is being
closed` and `KafkaConsumer::unsubscribe()` `the consumer unsubscribed from all topics`
(`ConsumerCoordinator::LEAVE_REASON_CLOSED` and `::LEAVE_REASON_UNSUBSCRIBED`, the texts of
`AbstractCoordinator` and `KafkaConsumer` @ 3.2.3), while
`Admin\AdminClient::removeMembersFromConsumerGroup()` writes `member was removed by an admin` into every entry it
did not get a reason for - `KafkaAdminClient.DEFAULT_LEAVE_GROUP_REASON` @ 3.2.3, which that client uses for an
empty option as well. `Client::leaveGroup()` takes the reason of the one member that removes itself.

The frame of the versions 3 and 4 has no such field, so `LeaveGroupRequestV4` builds its entries as
`Data\LeaveGroupRequestMemberV3` and a reason a caller names never reaches their wire.

## Consumer group protocol (protocol_type = consumer)

The group membership apis of 0.9 are deliberately generic: the coordinator knows a group by its `protocol_type` and
by the list of `protocol_name`s its members support, and it moves the `member_metadata` and `member_assignment`
byte arrays between the members without looking inside them. Everything a *consumer* group agrees on therefore
lives in the two structures below, which the broker never parses - `ConsumerProtocol` of the Java client of
0.10.2.2, `kafka.coordinator.GroupMetadata` treating both fields as opaque `bytes`.

A consumer group announces `protocol_type = "consumer"` in its JoinGroup request; a `protocol_name` is the name of
the partition assignor - `range` or `roundrobin` for the two built-in ones - and the coordinator picks a name that
every member of the group supports, answering with the error **23 (InconsistentGroupProtocol)** when there is none.

```
Subscription => Version [Topic] UserData
  Version  => int16
  Topic    => string
  UserData => bytes
```

```
MemberAssignment => Version [Topic [Partition]] UserData
  Version   => int16
  Topic     => string
  Partition => int32
  UserData  => bytes
```

A member packs a `Subscription` into the `member_metadata` of its JoinGroup request. The coordinator elects one
member as the leader and hands it every member's metadata in the `members` array of the JoinGroup response; the
leader runs the assignor on them and sends one `MemberAssignment` per member in its SyncGroup request, from which
every member gets its own back in the SyncGroup response.

Both structures start with a version, and Kafka 0.10.2.2 still only ever writes **0**: the consumer protocol is
one of the pieces the 0.10 line did not touch. The Java client parses a higher version with the layout of version 0
and ignores whatever follows the fields it knows, so a later version may only append fields - which is why this
line can pin the version to 0. This client
keeps the version it read, so a structure of an unknown version survives a decode and encode round trip.

`UserData` is the escape hatch of the protocol: a custom assignor can put anything into the `Subscription` it
builds - a rack id, the number of cpus of the machine, the assignment of the previous generation for a sticky
assignor - and reads it back in the assignment of the leader. The `bytes` primitive is nullable, but the Java
client of 0.9 defaults the field to an **empty byte array** (`00 00 00 00`, not `ff ff ff ff`) in both structures,
and so does this client; both accept the null form on the wire.

A member that the assignor left without partitions gets a complete structure with an **empty topic array**, not an
empty byte array: a Kafka 0.9.0.1 broker relayed `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` for the fourth member of a group
of four on a topic with three partitions.

### Assignors

| Name on the wire | Class | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `range` (default) | `Consumer\RangeAssignor` | Per topic: its members sorted lexicographically, its partitions in numeric order, `partitions / members` partitions each, the first `partitions % members` members get one more. |
| `roundrobin` | `Consumer\RoundRobinAssignor` | All partitions of all subscribed topics - topics lexicographically, partitions numerically - handed out one by one to the next member, in lexicographic order of the member ids, that subscribes to the topic of the partition. |

Both are the assignors of the Java client of 0.10.2.2 - the sticky assignor is Kafka 0.11 - with its ordering
rules, so a PHP member may lead a group of
Java members and the other way round: with two members on one topic with three partitions, `range` gives the
lexicographically first member the partitions 0 and 1 and the second one the partition 2, while `roundrobin` gives
the first one 0 and 2 and the second one 1. The difference shows on a group that consumes many topics with few
partitions each: `range` puts the first partition of every topic on the same member, `roundrobin` spreads them.

`partition.assignment.strategy` selects one of the two by its wire name, or names a class that implements
`Consumer\PartitionAssignorInterface`; `Consumer\AbstractPartitionAssignor::fromStrategy()` resolves the option.
The name an assignor announces is what the group agrees on, so every member of a group has to use the same one.

The vectors of this section were captured from the members of three groups of `kafka-console-consumer.sh
--new-consumer` processes (Kafka 0.9.0.1, one topic with three partitions), read back with a raw DescribeGroups v0
frame - the structures did not change in 0.10, so the same commands against the container of this branch
(`kafka-0-10-2-2`) produce the same bytes:

```bash
docker exec kafka-0-9-0-1 sh -c 'printf "group.id=g\n" > /tmp/c.properties'
docker exec -d kafka-0-9-0-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --new-consumer \
    --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic t6-consumer-protocol --consumer.config /tmp/c.properties
```

### Consumer group membership from `poll()`

PHP has no background thread, so everything the Java consumer does on its heartbeat thread happens inside
`KafkaConsumer::poll()` on this branch. What that means for an application, as
[`Consumer\Internals\ConsumerCoordinator`](../../src/Kafka/Consumer/Internals/ConsumerCoordinator.php) implements it
and `tests/Integration/ConsumerGroupTest.php` verifies against the broker:

* **The first `poll()` after `subscribe()` joins the group**: GroupCoordinator → JoinGroup → (the leader runs the
  assignor) → SyncGroup → the positions of the assigned partitions, from their committed offsets or from
  `auto.offset.reset`. Nothing is sent by `subscribe()` itself.
* **Every further `poll()` sends a heartbeat** once `heartbeat.interval.ms` has elapsed since the last one. A
  consumer that does not poll for longer than `session.timeout.ms` is dropped by the coordinator, its partitions are
  given to the other members, and its next heartbeat is answered 25 (`UnknownMemberId`) — it then rejoins with a
  **new member id**. Keep the processing of a batch well below the session timeout, or raise
  `session.timeout.ms` within the `group.min.session.timeout.ms`/`group.max.session.timeout.ms` of the broker.
* **`max.poll.interval.ms` is sent, but it does not police this consumer.** Its value goes out as the
  `RebalanceTimeout` of every JoinGroup v1, so it really is how long the coordinator waits for *this* member in a
  rebalance. What it does *not* do here is what it does in Java: a Java consumer whose application does not come
  back to `poll()` within the interval leaves the group by itself, which its heartbeat thread notices. **This
  consumer has no thread**, so an application that stops polling stops heartbeating as well, and it is the *session*
  timeout that ends the membership — the next `poll()` finds a 25 or a 27 on its heartbeat and joins again. The
  option therefore buys the group patience during a rebalance, and costs a `request.timeout.ms` above it.
* **The error codes drive the state machine**, as in `AbstractCoordinator`/`ConsumerCoordinator` @ 0.10.2.2: 27
  (`RebalanceInProgress`) and 22 (`IllegalGeneration`) rejoin with the member id of the previous generation, 25
  rejoins without one, 15 and 16 look the coordinator up again. A rebalance that another rebalance interrupts is
  simply repeated instead of being reported to the application.
* **The positions are committed before the partitions are given up** in a rebalance, and a 22/25/27 on that commit
  does not keep the member from rejoining. A `Consumer\ConsumerRebalanceListener` passed to `subscribe()` sees the
  same two moments (`onPartitionsRevoked()`, `onPartitionsAssigned()`), which is where a consumer with
  `enable.auto.commit` off commits what it has processed.
* **`request.timeout.ms` has to exceed both `session.timeout.ms` and `max.poll.interval.ms`** — the coordinator
  holds a JoinGroup until every known member has rejoined or has run out of its rebalance timeout, so the read
  timeout of the socket bounds the whole rebalance. `subscribe()` refuses a configuration that does not; the
  consumer defaults are 305000, 10000 and 300000, the defaults of the Java consumer of 0.10.1 and above, whose
  `request.timeout.ms` is documented as "chosen to be higher than the default of max.poll.interval.ms". An
  `assign()`ed consumer joins no group and is not affected.
* **`unsubscribe()` and `close()` send LeaveGroup**, so the group rebalances at once instead of after a session
  timeout; `close()` commits first when `enable.auto.commit` is on.
* Because a JoinGroup blocks its connection until the rebalance is over, **two members of one group cannot share a
  PHP process**: the second member's join can only be written while the first one is waiting for its own answer.
  The integration suite therefore runs the second member in a child process
  (`tests/Fixture/consumer-group-member.php`).
* **A rebalance is what a fetch session sees as `forgotten_topics_data`.** The partitions this member keeps stay in
  the session of their leader with the positions they had; the partitions that moved to another member are dropped
  from it in the first fetch after the rebalance, and the ones this member gained are added to it in the same
  request. Nothing of that is visible in `poll()`, and a session is never given up for a rebalance — it is the same
  session, one epoch further on. → "The consumer side of a fetch session".

## DescribeGroups API (key 15, v0 to v6)

Reports the state, the protocol and the members of the groups a broker coordinates. Together with
[ListGroups](#listgroups-api-key-16-v0-to-v2) this is what `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --new-consumer --describe` uses, and
what `Admin\AdminClient::describeGroup()` sends.

```
DescribeGroupsRequest (v0, v1 and v2) => [GroupId]
  GroupId => string

DescribeGroupsRequest (v3 to v6) => [GroupId] IncludeAuthorizedOperations
  IncludeAuthorizedOperations => boolean   -- new in v3, one byte at the end of the frame
```

```
DescribeGroupsResponse (v0) => [ErrorCode GroupId State ProtocolType Protocol [MemberId ClientId ClientHost MemberMetadata MemberAssignment]]
  ErrorCode        => int16
  GroupId          => string
  State            => string
  ProtocolType     => string
  Protocol         => string
  MemberId         => string
  ClientId         => string
  ClientHost       => string
  MemberMetadata   => bytes
  MemberAssignment => bytes

DescribeGroupsResponse (v1 and v2) => ThrottleTimeMs [ErrorCode GroupId State ProtocolType Protocol [Member]]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32     -- since version 1

DescribeGroupsResponse (v3) => ThrottleTimeMs [ErrorCode GroupId State ProtocolType Protocol [Member]
                                               AuthorizedOperations]
  AuthorizedOperations => int32   -- new in v3, it closes every group entry
```
