```
DescribeGroupsResponse (v4 and v5) => the same, every Member with a GroupInstanceId behind its MemberId (KIP-345);
                                      v5 is the flexible encoding of v4 (KIP-482)

DescribeGroupsResponse (v6) => ThrottleTimeMs [ErrorCode ErrorMessage GroupId State ProtocolType Protocol [Member]
                                               AuthorizedOperations]
  ErrorMessage => compact nullable string   -- new in v6 (KIP-1043), right behind the error code
```

Version 1 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) put the throttle time in front of the group array and left the entries alone —
`DESCRIBE_GROUPS_RESPONSE_V1` reuses `DESCRIBE_GROUPS_RESPONSE_GROUP_METADATA_V0` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3 —
and the request is the same in both versions. **Version 2 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) added nothing to either half**, so
the three frames differ in their api version field alone
(`DescribeGroupsRequestV2`, with `DescribeGroupsRequestV1` below it). **Version 3 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-430) is the
first one that changed either half** - see "The authorized operations of a group (v3, KIP-430)" below - and
`DescribeGroupsRequestV3` speaks it. The member entry gains a `group_instance_id` at version 4 (KIP-345, Kafka
2.4) and the flexible encoding at version 5 (`DescribeGroupsRequestV5`/`DescribeGroupsResponseV5`), and **version 6
(Kafka 4.0, KIP-1043)** is what `DescribeGroupsRequest`/`DescribeGroupsResponse` send: the request of version 5
again, and an answer whose group entries carry an `error_message` - see "The 69 of an unknown group (v6,
KIP-1043)" below.

### The authorized operations of a group (v3, KIP-430)

The boolean `include_authorized_operations` of the version 3 request asks the broker to report, per group, which
operations the **client that sends the request** may perform on it; the answer carries them as a 32-bit bit set at
the end of every group entry, where bit *n* stands for the operation whose code is *n* in
`org.apache.kafka.common.acl.AclOperation` @ 2.8.2:

| Code | Operation | Code | Operation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `UNKNOWN` | 7 | `ALTER` |
| 1 | `ANY` | 8 | `DESCRIBE` |
| 2 | `ALL` | 9 | `CLUSTER_ACTION` |
| 3 | `READ` | 10 | `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` |
| 4 | `WRITE` | 11 | `ALTER_CONFIGS` |
| 5 | `CREATE` | 12 | `IDEMPOTENT_WRITE` |
| 6 | `DELETE` | | |

Only the operations of the resource type can appear: `AclEntry.supportedOperations(GROUP)` @ 2.8.2 is
`{READ, DESCRIBE, DELETE}`, and `AuthHelper.authorizedOperations` answers **all** of them when the broker runs
without an authorizer, which is how the 2.8.2 container ran. Measured there: a request with the flag `true`
is answered **328** = `0b1_0100_1000`, the bits 3, 6 and 8. **Kafka 4.0 gave the group resource two more
operations**: `AclEntry.supportedOperations(GROUP)` @ 4.0.0 is `{READ, DESCRIBE, DELETE, DESCRIBE_CONFIGS,
ALTER_CONFIGS}` (3.9.2 still had the three), and the anonymous super user of the 4.3.1 node is answered **3400** =
`0b1101_0100_1000`, the bits 3, 6, 8, 10 and 11 (`describegroups.response.v6.stable`); a request with the flag `false` is answered
**-2147483648** (`Integer.MIN_VALUE`, `DescribeGroupResponseMetadata::OPERATIONS_NOT_REQUESTED`), the default of
`DescribeGroupsResponse.json` @ 2.8.2, which the broker leaves on the wire - "not asked for" is therefore *not* the
empty bit set `0`. A group entry that carries an error code keeps the default as well: `KafkaApis` fills the field
only `if (error == Errors.NONE && describeRequest.data.includeAuthorizedOperations)`.

`Admin\AdminClient::describeGroup()` and `describeGroups()` take the flag as their last argument and default it to
`false`. The same bit set of the same KIP reaches a client through the `topic_authorized_operations` and
`cluster_authorized_operations` of **Metadata v8** (Kafka 2.3), which is the other half of KIP-430.

The response has **no error code of its own**: every group carries one, and the groups come back in the order of the
request. An empty group array is legal and is answered with an empty group array.

A group has to be asked from **its own coordinator** ([GroupCoordinator](#groupcoordinator-api-key-10-v0-to-v2)); another
broker answers that group with the error code 16 (NotCoordinatorForGroup) and an otherwise empty description. The
other error codes a group entry can carry are 15 (GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable, the coordinator is shutting down),
14 (GroupLoadInProgress, it is still reading `__consumer_offsets`) and 30 (GroupAuthorizationFailed).

`State` is one of the **five** states of `kafka/coordinator/group/GroupMetadata.scala` @ 1.1.1 — Kafka 0.10.1 added
`Empty` to the four of 0.9, and Kafka 1.0 renamed `AwaitingSync` to **`CompletingRebalance`**. This is what a 1.1.1
broker really answered while a group was driven through the membership protocol:

| State                | When                                                              | ProtocolType | Protocol | Members |
|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|----------|---------|
| `PreparingRebalance` | a member joined or left and the coordinator waits for the others   | `consumer`   | `""`     | yes     |
| `CompletingRebalance` | every member has joined, the leader has not sent SyncGroup yet    | `consumer`   | `""`     | yes     |
| `Stable`             | the assignment is published, the members only send heartbeats      | `consumer`   | `range`  | yes     |
| `Empty`              | the last member has left, the committed offsets are still there    | `consumer`   | `""`     | no      |
| `Dead`               | the coordinator has never heard of the group, or has forgotten it  | `""`         | `""`     | no      |

`Protocol` is therefore only filled in while the group is `Stable`, exactly as `GroupMetadata.summary` says; every
other state answers `GroupCoordinator.NoProtocol`, the empty string.

**`Empty` is the state that Kafka 0.10.1 added, and it changes what "the group is gone" means.** A 0.9.0.1
coordinator dropped a group the moment its last member left: it disappeared from ListGroups and DescribeGroups
answered `Dead` for it, exactly as for a group that had never existed. From 0.10.1 on the group moves to `Empty`
instead and **lingers there with its committed offsets** until `offsets.retention.minutes` expires them; only the
periodic expiry task makes it `Dead` and removes it. In that state the coordinator

* still **lists** the group in ListGroups, with its protocol type,
* answers **JoinGroup normally**, so a new member simply takes the group over and rebalances it (`Empty` →
  `PreparingRebalance` is a legal transition, and it is the only one out of `Empty` that is not death),
* answers SyncGroup, Heartbeat, LeaveGroup and OffsetCommit with 25 (`UnknownMemberId`) — there is no member to
  speak for —
* and still answers **OffsetFetch**, which is what makes a restarted consumer of the same group resume where the
  group committed.

A group that only uses Kafka to store offsets and never joins is in `Empty` from the start, which is the second
reason the state exists.

A client can therefore tell "everybody left" (`Empty`) from "never existed" (`Dead`) on this line, which it could
not on 0.9.

**An unknown group is not an error - up to version 5.** A group the coordinator has never heard of is answered with
the error code 0, the state `Dead`, an empty protocol type, an empty protocol and no members -
`GroupCoordinator.handleDescribeGroup()` returns its `DeadGroup` summary for it. Version 6 turns that answer into
the 69, see the next section.

`ClientHost` is the address of the connection the member joined over, in the notation of Java's
`InetAddress.toString()`, i.e. with a leading slash: `/172.18.0.1`. `MemberMetadata` and `MemberAssignment` are the
opaque byte arrays of the protocol type: for `consumer` groups they hold the `Subscription` the member sent with its
JoinGroup request and the `MemberAssignment` the leader published with SyncGroup.

### The 69 of an unknown group (v6, KIP-1043)

*"Version 6 returns error code GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND if the group ID is not found (KIP-1043)"* stands over both halves
of the api @ 4.0.0, and the answer gains the one field that says why: a nullable `error_message` right behind the
`error_code` of every group entry. The request is the frame of version 5 with another version number.
`GroupMetadataManager.describeGroups` @ 4.3.1 decides on the version of the request alone:

```
} catch (GroupIdNotFoundException exception) {
    if (context.requestVersion() >= 6) {
        describedGroups.add(new DescribeGroupsResponseData.DescribedGroup()
            .setGroupId(groupId)
            .setGroupState(DEAD.toString())
            .setErrorCode(Errors.GROUP_ID_NOT_FOUND.code())
            .setErrorMessage(exception.getMessage())
        );
    } else { ... the state Dead and the code 0 ... }
```

and the exception is thrown for two different groups, which the message tells apart where the code does not.
Measured on the 4.3.1 node:

| Group | v5 answers | v6 answers |
|---|---|---|
| never heard of (`describegroups.*.v6.unknown-group`, `describegroups.*.v5.unknown-group`) | 0, `Dead` | **69**, `Dead`, "Group t3-40-vectors-none not found." |
| a live group of the consumer protocol of KIP-848 (`describegroups.*.v6.consumer-group`) | 0, `Dead` - and, asked with the flag, the authorized operations 3400 of a group that "does not exist" | **69**, `Dead`, "Group t3-40-vectors-group is not a classic group." |
| a stable classic group (`describegroups.*.v6.stable`) | 0, `Stable` | 0, `Stable`, the `00` of a null message |

The state stays `Dead` in a refused entry, the protocol type and the protocol stay empty and the authorized
operations stay at `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, because the handler fills them only for an entry without an error. The
second row is what version 6 is really for: up to version 5 the classic api described a KIP-848 group as a group that
was gone, and an admin client had to route by the `group_type` of a ListGroups v5 answer to learn otherwise.

`Admin\AdminClient::describeGroup()` and `describeGroups()` send version 6 and throw the 69 as a
`GroupIdNotFoundException` whose context carries the message of the node - which is what the Java admin client of
4.0 does with it (`DescribeConsumerGroupsHandler.handleError` @ 4.0.0: *"failed because the group does not
exist"*). A caller of the 3.x line that tested an unknown group for the state `Dead` catches the exception
instead; `DescribeGroupsRequestV5` still asks the old question and gets the old answer.

## ListGroups API (key 16, v0 to v5)

Lists the groups a broker is the coordinator of.

```
ListGroupsRequest (v0 to v3) =>

ListGroupsRequest (v4) => [StatesFilter]
  StatesFilter => string   -- new in v4, the states the answer is bounded to

ListGroupsRequest (v5) => [StatesFilter] [TypesFilter]
  TypesFilter  => string   -- new in v5, the types the answer is bounded to
```

```
ListGroupsResponse (v0) => ErrorCode [GroupId ProtocolType]
  ErrorCode    => int16
  GroupId      => string
  ProtocolType => string

ListGroupsResponse (v1, v2 and v3) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [GroupId ProtocolType]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32     -- since version 1

ListGroupsResponse (v4) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [GroupId ProtocolType GroupState]
  GroupState => string        -- new in v4, the state of that group

ListGroupsResponse (v5) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [GroupId ProtocolType GroupState GroupType]
  GroupType  => string        -- new in v5, the type of that group
```

The request had **no body at all** up to version 3, only the common request header - the frame is 12 bytes plus the
client id, and one byte more from version 3 on, whose flexible body is a single empty tag buffer. That is true of
version 1 (`LIST_GROUPS_REQUEST_V1 = LIST_GROUPS_REQUEST_V0` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3), which added the
throttle time to the answer alone, of version 2 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219), which added nothing at all, and of version 3
(Kafka 2.4, KIP-482), which only changed the encoding. Up to there **there is no way to ask for a subset of the
groups**: the answer is every group the broker coordinates, which on a container shared by several test runs is
every group of all of them — the captured `listgroups.response.v2` is exactly that, and the unfiltered version 4
answer of this line held **176** groups.

The error code belongs to the whole request: `GroupCoordinator.handleListGroups()` @ 0.10.2.2 answers 15
(GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable) while the coordinator is shutting down and 14 (GroupLoadInProgress) while it is still
reading the `__consumer_offsets` partitions it owns, both with an empty group array; the authorizer answers 31
(ClusterAuthorizationFailed).

Every broker only reports **the groups it coordinates itself**, and the groups of a cluster are spread over the
partitions of `__consumer_offsets`, so the list of the whole cluster is the union of the answers of every broker -
that is what `Admin\AdminClient::listAllGroups()` does. A group appears here as soon as it has a member and stays
until the coordinator forgets it, which on Kafka 0.10.1 and later is **not** the moment its last member leaves: the
group lingers in the state `Empty` with its committed offsets until `offsets.retention.minutes` expires them, and it
is listed all that time (a 0.9.0.1 broker dropped it at once - see the DescribeGroups section). Up to version 3 the
entry says nothing about the state of the group, DescribeGroups does; version 4 is where that changes.

### The group states of KIP-518 (Kafka 2.6)

Kafka 2.6 gave the api its **version 4**, and with it both halves of the same idea: the request may name the states
it is interested in, and every entry of the answer carries the state of that group.

```
ListGroupsRequest (v4)  => [StatesFilter]
ListGroupsResponse (v4) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [GroupId ProtocolType GroupState]
```

The names are those of `GroupState`, i.e. the very strings a DescribeGroups answer reports — `PreparingRebalance`,
`CompletingRebalance`, `Stable`, `Dead` and `Empty` — and the filter is a plain set membership test:
`GroupCoordinator.handleListGroups` @ 2.8.2 is

```
val groups = if (states.isEmpty) groupManager.currentGroups
             else groupManager.currentGroups.filter(g => states.contains(g.summary.state))
```

so three things follow, all of them measured on the container:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `states_filter = []` | every group of the coordinator — **176** of them on the shared container, each with its state |
| `states_filter = ["Stable"]` | exactly the stable ones: **1** group, the one the capture had just joined |
| `states_filter = ["stable"]` | the error code **0** and an **empty** array — the comparison is case sensitive, and a name that is not a state at all is simply no match rather than an error |
| `states_filter = ["Empty", "PreparingRebalance"]` | the other **175**, so the two filters partition the listing |
| `["Empty"]` after the member left | the group is there again, now `Empty` — the state follows the group through its life |

**A null filter is the empty one.** `KafkaApis.handleListGroupsRequest` @ 2.8.2 turns a null array into
`immutable.Set[String]()` with the comment "Handle a null array the same as empty", so a client that means "every
group" may send either; this package sends the empty array, which is the unsigned varint `01` of a compact array
with no entry.

[`Admin\AdminClient`](../../src/Kafka/Admin/AdminClient.php) takes the states as an optional argument of
`listGroups()` and `listAllGroups()`, and the new **`listConsumerGroups()`** — the name of the Java admin client —
lists the groups of the whole cluster whose protocol type is `consumer`, with the same filter. The state of each
group now comes with the listing, so finding the empty groups of a cluster no longer costs one DescribeGroups per
group.

### The group types of KIP-848 (Kafka 3.8)

Kafka 3.8 gave the api its **version 5**, and with it the same idea once more, on the other property of a group:
*"Version 5 adds the TypesFilter field (KIP-848)"* over the request, *"Version 5 adds the GroupType field
(KIP-848)"* over the answer (`ListGroupsRequest.json` / `ListGroupsResponse.json` @ 3.8.1).

```
ListGroupsRequest (v5)  => [StatesFilter] [TypesFilter]
ListGroupsResponse (v5) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [GroupId ProtocolType GroupState GroupType]
```

**The field exists because the `protocol_type` stopped saying what a group is.** A node that runs the new group
coordinator — `group.coordinator.rebalance.protocols=classic,consumer`, which is what the container of this line
sets — holds the groups of the classic membership protocol of Kafka 0.9 and the groups of the KIP-848 consumer
protocol side by side, and the `protocol_type` of **both** is the string `consumer`. Before this version a listing
could not tell them apart; `group_type` is the name of `Group.GroupType` @ 3.9.2:

| `group_type` | `Group.GroupType` | The group |
|---|---|---|
| `classic` | `CLASSIC` | joined with JoinGroup / SyncGroup / Heartbeat, whatever its protocol type is |
| `consumer` | `CONSUMER` | a member of the KIP-848 protocol created it with a ConsumerGroupHeartbeat (key 68) |
| `share` | `SHARE` | a share group of KIP-932, early access in Kafka 3.9 and out of this line by decision |
| `unknown` | `UNKNOWN` | what `parse()` answers for a name it does not know; no group ever *has* this type |

The names are lower case on the wire and are the `TYPE_*` constants of
[`Protocol\Data\ListGroupResponseProtocol`](../../src/Kafka/Protocol/Data/ListGroupResponseProtocol.php).

**The types filter is parsed, where the states filter is compared.** `GroupMetadataManager.listGroups` @ 3.9.2
builds the two filters differently:

```
Set<String> caseInsensitiveFilterSet = statesFilter.stream()
    .map(String::toLowerCase).map(String::trim).collect(Collectors.toSet());
Set<Group.GroupType> enumTypesFilter = typesFilter.stream()
    .map(Group.GroupType::parse).collect(Collectors.toSet());
Predicate<Group> combinedFilter = group -> {
    boolean stateCheck = statesFilter.isEmpty() || group.isInStates(caseInsensitiveFilterSet, committedOffset);
    boolean typeCheck  = enumTypesFilter.isEmpty() || enumTypesFilter.contains(group.type());
    return stateCheck && typeCheck;
};
```

so, all of it measured on the node with one classic group and one KIP-848 group in the state `Stable`:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `types_filter = []` | every type, exactly as every version below 5 asks implicitly — both groups, each with its `group_type` |
| `types_filter = ["consumer"]` | the KIP-848 group alone |
| `types_filter = ["classic"]` | the classic group alone |
| `types_filter = ["classic", "consumer"]` | both again: naming every type the node knows is the same question as naming none |
| `types_filter = ["CONSUMER"]` | the KIP-848 group — `GroupType.parse()` lower-cases the name, so the filter is **case insensitive** |
| `types_filter = ["streams"]` | the error code **0** and an **empty** array: the name parses to `UNKNOWN`, a type no group has |
| `types_filter = [""]`, `["share"]` | the same empty answer — an empty string, a misspelling and a type this node has no group of are one case |
| `types_filter = ["consumer", "nonsense"]` | the KIP-848 group: the unknown entry of a filter costs the known ones nothing |
| `states_filter = ["Stable"]` **and** `types_filter = ["classic"]` | the classic group alone — the two filters are combined with **and** |

Two things follow for a client. A types filter can no more be used to **validate** a type name than a states
filter can be used to validate a state name — both answer "no match" for a name that does not exist — and a client
that wants the groups of one protocol has to ask the *coordinator* for them, because the filter is applied there
and the answer of an unfiltered listing on a busy node is every group of every agent that shares it.

**The type belongs to the group, not to its membership.** Measured: after the one member of the KIP-848 group left
with the member epoch -1, the group stayed listed with its committed offsets, in the state `Empty` and with the
`group_type` **`consumer`** (`listgroups.response.v5.empty-group`) — the same rule the `Empty` classic groups of
this node follow, which stay `classic`.

[`Admin\AdminClient`](../../src/Kafka/Admin/AdminClient.php) takes the types as a second optional argument of
`listGroups()`, `listAllGroups()` and `listConsumerGroups()`, next to the states; that is the `withTypes()` of the
Java `ListGroupsOptions`. `listConsumerGroups()` still keeps the groups whose **protocol type** is `consumer` —
the two are different questions, and a client that wants the KIP-848 groups alone names the type.

## ConsumerGroupHeartbeat API (key 68, v0 and v1)

The whole membership protocol of a consumer in **one** api. New in Kafka **3.5** (KIP-848), **v0**, flexible from
that version, raised to **v1** by Kafka **4.0** (the regex subscription of KIP-848 and the member id of KIP-1082,
see the two sections below), served by any **broker** that runs the new group coordinator
(`group.coordinator.rebalance.protocols` has to name `consumer`, which the node of this line does). This client
sends version 1; `ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequestV0` is the frame of version 0. It replaces
**four** apis of the classic protocol at once - JoinGroup (11), SyncGroup (14), Heartbeat (12) and LeaveGroup
(13) - and it is what a Java consumer configured with `group.protocol=consumer` sends. This package sends it from
[`Consumer\Internals\ConsumerGroupHeartbeatCoordinator`](../../src/Kafka/Consumer/Internals/ConsumerGroupHeartbeatCoordinator.php),
through `Client::joinConsumerGroup()`, `Client::consumerGroupHeartbeat()` and `Client::leaveConsumerGroup()`.

```
ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest => GroupId MemberId MemberEpoch InstanceId RackId RebalanceTimeoutMs
                                 [SubscribedTopicNames] SubscribedTopicRegex ServerAssignor [TopicPartitions]
  GroupId              => compact string
  MemberId             => compact string           -- the uuid the MEMBER generated for itself; never empty in v1
  MemberEpoch          => int32                    -- 0 join, -1 leave, -2 static leave, else the current epoch
  InstanceId           => compact nullable string  -- null: not provided, or unchanged
  RackId               => compact nullable string  -- null: not provided, or unchanged
  RebalanceTimeoutMs   => int32                    -- -1: unchanged
  SubscribedTopicNames => compact array of compact string, NULLABLE   -- null: unchanged
  SubscribedTopicRegex => compact nullable string  -- v1 only; null: unchanged, "": dropped (RE2/J syntax)
  ServerAssignor       => compact nullable string  -- null: not used, or unchanged
  TopicPartitions      => compact array, NULLABLE  -- null: unchanged; EMPTY on a (re-)join
    TopicId    => uuid (16 raw bytes)
    Partitions => compact array of int32
```

```
ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage MemberId MemberEpoch
                                  HeartbeatIntervalMs Assignment
  ThrottleTimeMs      => int32
  ErrorCode           => int16
  ErrorMessage        => compact nullable string
  MemberId            => compact nullable string   -- the member's id; generated by the coordinator only for a
                                                   -- v0 join that named none
  MemberEpoch         => int32
  HeartbeatIntervalMs => int32                     -- group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms of the BROKER
  Assignment          => [TopicPartitions]         -- NULLABLE STRUCT: one int8, -1 = null, 1 = present
    TopicPartitions => TopicId [Partitions]
```

**The member epoch is the verb of the api.** `ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest.json` @ 3.9.2 says it in one line -
*"The current member epoch; 0 to join the group; -1 to leave the group; -2 to indicate that the static member will
rejoin"* - and there is nothing else that distinguishes a join from a heartbeat from a leave: the same frame does
all three.

**Everything else is a delta.** The five nullable fields and the `-1` of `rebalance_timeout_ms` mean *"unchanged
since the last heartbeat"*, so the steady state of a member is the group id, its member id, its epoch and five
nulls - 60-odd bytes, where a classic member sent a Heartbeat every `heartbeat.interval.ms` and a JoinGroup with
its packed subscription on every rebalance.

**The member id is the member's own.** A KIP-848 consumer generates a uuid for itself and keeps it for its whole
life; at version 0 the coordinator generates one for a request that names none, and the answer carries it back
because `MemberId` is *"only provided when the member joins with MemberEpoch == 0"* (@ 3.9.2). That is the opposite
of the classic protocol, where the id is handed out by the coordinator in the answer of a first JoinGroup (the
**79** of KIP-394). Version 1 made the rule absolute, see "The member id of the consumer (v1, KIP-1082)".

**A (re-)join must carry the EMPTY partition array.** This is the one shape rule of the api and the node enforces
it in `GroupMetadataManager.throwIfConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequestIsInvalid` @ 3.9.2. Measured on the node, both
frames below are the **42** `InvalidRequest` with the same message, *"TopicPartitions must be empty when
(re-)joining."*:

| `topic_partitions` of a frame with the epoch 0 | Answer |
|---|---|
| The **empty** array (`01` compact) | accepted |
| **null** (`00` compact), which is the default of the field | **42**, "TopicPartitions must be empty when (re-)joining." |
| One topic id with one partition | the same **42** |

### The reconciliation (v0, KIP-848)

The coordinator computes the assignment - no member is ever the leader of its group, and no
`PartitionAssignorInterface` of this package is on this path - and hands it over field by field:

* the `Assignment` of an answer is sent **only when it changed**. A `null` one means "nothing to do", which is
  what every steady-state answer carries, and an assignment with an **empty array** means "you own nothing at
  all". The two are different bytes (`ff` against `01 01`) and they are different instructions;
* a change is sent **once**. Measured: a member that was told to give two of its three partitions up and then
  heartbeated four times with a null `topic_partitions` was answered `null` every time - the coordinator does not
  repeat itself, so a client that drops an answer loses its assignment;
* a member **acknowledges** by echoing the partitions it owns now in the `topic_partitions` of its next
  heartbeat. Only then does the coordinator give what it released to somebody else, and only then does it bump
  the member's epoch to the group epoch.

The whole two-member reconciliation, as it was measured on the node against a topic of three partitions:

| Frame | Answer |
|---|---|
| A joins (epoch 0) | epoch **1**, assignment `[0,1,2]` - the group was created and reconciled in one frame |
| A acknowledges `[0,1,2]` | epoch 1, assignment **null** |
| B joins (epoch 0) | epoch **4**, assignment **`[]`** - the empty one: B owns nothing while A still holds everything |
| A heartbeats | assignment **`[2]`**: A is told to give two partitions up |
| A acknowledges `[2]` | epoch **4**, assignment null |
| B heartbeats | assignment **`[0,1]`**: now that A released them, B may have them |
| B acknowledges `[0,1]` | epoch 4, assignment null - the group is `Stable`, every epoch is 4 |

**That is the incremental rebalance of KIP-848**, and it is the one behaviour of this client an application can
feel: a classic member revokes its **whole** assignment before every JoinGroup and is given a whole new one
afterwards, so `ConsumerRebalanceListener::onPartitionsRevoked()` sees everything it owns on every rebalance,
while a KIP-848 member sees exactly the partitions that move. `ConsumerCoordinatorInterface::partitionsToRevoke()`
and `::partitionsToAssign()` are that difference in the client, and `KafkaConsumer` itself speaks neither
protocol.

**The interval is the coordinator's.** Every answer carries `heartbeat_interval_ms` -
`group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms` of the broker, **5000** on this node - and the `heartbeat.interval.ms` and
`session.timeout.ms` of the consumer are not sent anywhere in this protocol. A leave answers the interval **0**.

**A subscription that changed travels in an ordinary heartbeat**: there is nothing to re-join for. Measured: a
member that named a second topic in its `subscribed_topic_names` was answered a **new member epoch** (the group
epoch the change produced) and a null assignment, and it stayed the same member throughout.

**On a 4.3 node the target assignment is computed off the heartbeat path.** Kafka 4.3 added
`group.consumer.assignment.interval.ms` (1000 ms by default) and `group.consumer.assignor.offload.enable` (on by
default) to `GroupCoordinatorConfig` @ 4.3.0: the coordinator recomputes the target assignment of a group at most
once per interval, on a background thread, and the heartbeat that follows a join - or a change of subscription -
answers a null assignment while the group is `Assigning`. Measured on the 4.3.1 node: the second member of the
two-member reconciliation above is still answered the empty assignment at once, but the revoke of the first member
arrives a heartbeat or two later, not in the next frame, and a changed subscription earns its new epoch together
with its assignment rather than in the answer to the change. Nothing on the wire changed; a client that heartbeats
at the interval the coordinator dictates never notices, and the integration suite heartbeats until the assignment
arrives (`tests/Fixture/ConsumerGroupReconciliation.php`).

### The error codes of the api (v0, KIP-848)

Everything is reported in the **top-level** error code - there is no per-entry error anywhere in this frame - and
this is the one group api whose answer also carries an `error_message`, which the coordinator fills with the
sentence that says which rule was broken. Measured on the node:

| Code | Message | When |
|---|---|---|
| **110** `FencedMemberEpoch` | "The consumer group member has a greater member epoch (8) than the one known by the group coordinator (3). The member must abandon all its partitions and rejoin." | An epoch **above** the one the coordinator holds |
| **110** | the same sentence with "smaller (2) … (3)" | An epoch **below** it |
| **25** `UnknownMemberId` | "Member a-member-this-group-never-had is not a member of group t3-848-vectors-group." | A member id the group does not hold |
| **112** `UnsupportedAssignor` | "ServerAssignor sticky is not supported. Supported assignors: uniform, range." | A `server_assignor` the broker does not have |
| **111** `UnreleasedInstanceId` | "Static member … with instance id t3-848-one cannot join the group because the instance id is owned by … member." | A `group.instance.id` another member still holds |
| **42** `InvalidRequest` | "TopicPartitions must be empty when (re-)joining." | The shape rule above |
| **42** `InvalidRequest` | "MemberId can't be empty." | A **v1** frame without a member id (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.join-without-member-id`) |
| **128** `InvalidRegularExpression` | "SubscribedTopicRegex \`t3-40-(vec\` is not a valid regular expression: missing closing )." | A regex RE2/J cannot compile (v1, `consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.invalid-regex`) |
| **69** `GroupIdNotFound` | "Group t3-848-classic-group is not a consumer group." on 3.9.2; on 4.3.1 "Cannot upgrade classic group … to consumer group because the group does not use the consumer embedded protocol." | The group exists, speaks the **classic** protocol and cannot be upgraded, see "The mixed cluster (v0, KIP-848)" |
| **30** `GroupAuthorizationFailed` | null | The principal may not `READ` the group; measured with the SASL user `acltest` |

**The 110 and not the 113.** A stale member epoch is the **110** `FencedMemberEpoch` *on this api*, in both
directions, while the very same mismatch on an **OffsetCommit v9** or an **OffsetFetch v9** of the same member is
the **113** `StaleMemberEpoch` (see "The member epoch of KIP-848 (v9)"). The two codes divide the protocol rather
than the situation: the heartbeat api fences, the offset apis report a stale epoch and send the member back to its
heartbeat.

**Neither the 111 nor the 112 is retriable**: both are configuration errors and this client reports them to the
caller instead of joining again. The **110**, the **113** and the **25** are the three codes that mean "drop your
partitions, generate a new member id and join with the epoch 0".

**`group.consumer.max.size`** - the **81** `GroupMaxSizeReached` of this api - is the Java default
`Integer.MAX_VALUE` on this node and was therefore not reached: declared, not observed.

### The static member (v0, KIP-345 and KIP-848)

A static member fills `instance_id`, and the protocol gives it the one thing the classic one expressed by *not*
sending a LeaveGroup: the member epoch **-2**, *"the static member will rejoin"*. Measured end to end on the node:

* the leave with the epoch -2 is answered the epoch **-2** back, an interval of 0 and no assignment;
* a join under the same instance id afterwards gets a **new member id**, the epoch **1** and the **same
  assignment** the member had - and the **group epoch does not move**: a restart of a static member costs the
  group no rebalance, exactly as KIP-345 promised for the classic protocol;
* while the first member is still there, a second one under the same instance id is the **111**.

A dynamic member leaves with the epoch **-1**, which is what `KafkaConsumer::close()` and `::unsubscribe()` send;
there is no `reason` field in this api, so the KIP-800 texts of JoinGroup v8 and LeaveGroup v5 have nowhere to go
and are dropped.

### The mixed cluster (v0, KIP-848)

The node runs both protocols on **one** coordinator (`group.coordinator.rebalance.protocols=classic,consumer`),
and the two directions are **not** symmetric - which is the whole migration story of KIP-848, measured here:

* a ConsumerGroupHeartbeat that names a group the **classic** protocol created was the **69** `GroupIdNotFound`
  on the 3.9.2 node, with the message "Group … is not a consumer group.". **Kafka 4.0 turned that direction around**:
  `group.consumer.migration.policy` defaults to `bidirectional` since 4.0 (`disabled` @ 3.9.2), and
  `GroupMetadataManager.getOrMaybeCreateConsumerGroup` @ 4.3.1 converts a live classic group of the `consumer`
  protocol type into a consumer group on the first heartbeat that names it - measured: the heartbeat is accepted,
  ListGroups reports the type `consumer` from then on, and the classic member stays in the group as a member of the
  type 0 of KIP-1099 (see "The member type (v1, KIP-1099)"). The 69 is left for a classic group that cannot be
  upgraded - one of another protocol type (measured with `connect`: "Cannot upgrade classic group … to consumer group
  because the group does not use the consumer embedded protocol."), or a node whose policy says `disabled`;
* a classic **JoinGroup** for a group of the type `consumer` is **accepted**. Measured: the first join was
  answered the **79** of KIP-394 with a member id of the form `xyoWrOUISzCtz2LjtuVdFg` - a *base64* uuid, not the
  `<client.id>-<uuid>` a classic coordinator hands out - and the join that followed with that id was accepted
  with the generation **2** and an **empty leader id**, because there is no leader in this group: the coordinator
  assigns, and the "leader" of the JoinGroup answer has nobody to be.

That is the online upgrade path of KIP-848: a group is created by whoever creates it, a classic consumer may
still join a `consumer` group while the fleet is being upgraded, and the group type - which `ListGroups` **v5**
reports, see "ListGroups API (key 16, v0 to v5)" - never changes back.

### The member id of the consumer (v1, KIP-1082)

*"Version 1 … requires the consumer to generate their own Member ID (KIP-1082)"* (`ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest.json`
@ 4.0.0), and the field changed its description with it: *"The member id generated by the consumer. The member id
must be kept during the entire lifetime of the consumer process."* The coordinator enforces the first half:
`GroupCoordinatorService.throwIfConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequestIsInvalid` @ 4.0.0 refuses an empty member id in every
frame of version 1 - `apiVersion >= CONSUMER_GENERATED_MEMBER_ID_REQUIRED_VERSION` - and only in the frames of an
epoch above 0 or of the leave at version 0. Measured on the 4.3.1 node:

| Frame | Answer |
|---|---|
| v1 join with the id `E_JuXqDTTgSTgGbOnAbrFw` (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.join`) | accepted, the same id back |
| v1 join without an id (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.join-without-member-id`) | **42** "MemberId can't be empty." |
| v0 join without an id (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v0.join-without-member-id`) | accepted, and answered the id the coordinator generated: `ozp-jJINTL6Sra4OiHpnHw` |

The second half is the client's: `AbstractMembershipManager` @ 4.0.0 holds the id in a `final` field initialised
with `Uuid.randomUuid().toString()` - 16 random bytes of a version 4 uuid in the **URL-safe base64 without padding**
of Kafka's own `Uuid`, 22 characters, never starting with a `-` - and sends it with every heartbeat, every rejoin
after a fence and every rejoin after an unsubscribe. `Consumer\Internals\ConsumerGroupHeartbeatCoordinator` does
the same: `newMemberId()` draws that uuid once, a fenced member (110, 113, 25) joins again with the epoch 0 **under
the id it had**, and `KafkaConsumer` hands the id of its first membership to the next one. The ids the 3.x line
generated were the dashed hex of `java.util.UUID`, which a v0 coordinator accepted as well; the ids a coordinator
generates itself (the v0 join above, the member of a classic JoinGroup into a consumer group) have the base64 form.

### The regex subscription (v1, KIP-848)

`subscribed_topic_regex` is the other half of version 1: *"null if it didn't change since the last heartbeat; the
subscribed topic regex otherwise"*. The regex is matched by the **coordinator**, against every topic of the cluster
and every topic created later, in the RE2/J syntax of `com.google.re2j.Pattern` - `Utils.throwIfRegularExpressionIsInvalid`
@ 4.0.0 compiles it and answers one it cannot compile with the **128** `InvalidRegularExpression` of Kafka 4.0 and the
sentence of RE2/J. The member that subscribes by a regex names no topic: the Java consumer's join carries the
**empty** list of names next to the regex (`ConsumerHeartbeatRequestManager.HeartbeatState` @ 4.0.0), because a join
needs one of the two to be non-null - "Either SubscribedTopicNames or SubscribedTopicRegex must be non-null when
(re-)joining." - and a member that drops its regex sends the **empty string**, since the null says "unchanged".
Measured on the 4.3.1 node with the regex `t3-40-vec.*`, which matches the one topic `t3-40-vectors`:

| Frame | Answer |
|---|---|
| join, names `[]`, regex `t3-40-vec.*` (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.regex-join`) | epoch 1 and the **empty** assignment: the regex is resolved in the background |
| the next heartbeat, 1.5 s later (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.regex-assignment`) | epoch 2 and every partition of `t3-40-vectors` |
| a heartbeat that changes the regex to `t3-40-(vec` (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.invalid-regex`) | **128** "SubscribedTopicRegex \`t3-40-(vec\` is not a valid regular expression: missing closing )." |
| names `[t3-40-vectors]` and the regex `""` (`consumergroupheartbeat.*.v1.regex-dropped`) | accepted without a rejoin |

ConsumerGroupDescribe reports such a member with its regex in `subscribed_topic_regex` and the empty
`subscribed_topic_names`. `KafkaConsumer::subscribeByPattern()` takes a `Consumer\SubscriptionPattern`, the class the
Java client @ 4.0.0 calls the same, and is a subscription of `group.protocol=consumer` alone: the classic protocol has
no field for the regex, and the consumer refuses the call there with an `InvalidConfigurationException`, where the
Java `ClassicKafkaConsumer` throws an `UnsupportedOperationException`. The client evaluates nothing - RE2/J is not
PCRE - and `subscription()` stays empty; the topics are the ones the assignment names.

## ConsumerGroupDescribe API (key 69, v0 and v1)

The DescribeGroups of the new consumer protocol. New in Kafka **3.7** (KIP-848), **v0**, flexible from that
version, raised to **v1** by Kafka **4.0** (the member type of KIP-1099, see "The member type (v1, KIP-1099)"),
served by any **broker**, and it is what `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` sends for a group of the
type `consumer`. This client sends version 1; `ConsumerGroupDescribeRequestV0` is the frame of version 0. This package sends it from `Admin\AdminClient::describeConsumerGroups()` and
`::describeConsumerGroup()`, which answer an `Admin\ConsumerGroupDescription`; `describeGroups()` (key 15) stays
exactly what it was and describes the classic groups.

```
ConsumerGroupDescribeRequest => [GroupIds] IncludeAuthorizedOperations
  GroupIds                    => compact array of compact string
  IncludeAuthorizedOperations => boolean
```

```
ConsumerGroupDescribeResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Groups]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Groups => ErrorCode ErrorMessage GroupId GroupState GroupEpoch AssignmentEpoch AssignorName [Members]
            AuthorizedOperations
    ErrorCode       => int16
    ErrorMessage    => compact nullable string
    GroupId         => compact string
    GroupState      => compact string           -- Empty, Assigning, Reconciling, Stable, Dead
    GroupEpoch      => int32
    AssignmentEpoch => int32
    AssignorName    => compact string
    Members => MemberId InstanceId RackId MemberEpoch ClientId ClientHost [SubscribedTopicNames]
               SubscribedTopicRegex Assignment TargetAssignment
      MemberId             => compact string
      InstanceId           => compact nullable string
      RackId               => compact nullable string
      MemberEpoch          => int32
      ClientId             => compact string
      ClientHost           => compact string
      SubscribedTopicNames => compact array of compact string
      SubscribedTopicRegex => compact nullable string
      Assignment           => [TopicPartitions]
      TargetAssignment     => [TopicPartitions]
      MemberType           => int8                -- v1 only: -1 unknown, 0 classic, 1 consumer (KIP-1099)
        TopicPartitions => TopicId TopicName [Partitions]
          TopicId    => uuid (16 raw bytes)
          TopicName  => compact string
          Partitions => compact array of int32
    AuthorizedOperations => int32               -- -2147483648 when the request did not ask
```

**The `TopicPartitions` of this api is not the one of key 68**: it carries the **topic name** next to the id,
because this answer is read by a tool that has no metadata of its own, while a ConsumerGroupHeartbeat answer is
read by a consumer that has (`ConsumerGroupDescribeResponse.json` @ 3.9.2 declares its own `commonStructs`).

**There is no top-level error code.** Every group carries one of its own, as in a DescribeGroups answer, and the
frame itself stays error-free.

**The three epochs.** `group_epoch` is bumped whenever the *input* of the assignment changes - a member joins or
leaves, a subscription changes, a topic gains partitions - `assignment_epoch` is the group epoch the current
**target** assignment was computed for, and the `member_epoch` of every member is the epoch that member has
acknowledged. A settled group has all three equal, which the measured two-member group shows: `group_epoch` 4,
`assignment_epoch` 4, both members at the epoch 4, state `Stable`.

**Both assignments of every member** are in the answer - the partitions it owns and the partitions it is meant to
own - and their difference is a reconciliation in flight. That pair has no equivalent in the classic answer,
where a member carries the packed `assignment` byte array of the group protocol and nothing that says what it is
about to become.

**The states are the states of the new protocol**: `Empty`, `Assigning`, `Reconciling`, `Stable` and `Dead`
(`GroupState` @ 3.9.2). There is no `PreparingRebalance` and no `CompletingRebalance`, because nothing in this
protocol stops the world.

**The assignor of a group whose members name none is `uniform`**, the first of `group.consumer.assignors`
(`uniform,range` on this node); a group whose member asked for `range` in its `server_assignor` is reported with
`range`. It is a property of the **group**, not of a member.

### What the two describe apis answer for each other's groups (v0, KIP-848)

This is the measurement an admin client has to know, and the two answers are **not** symmetric:

| Question | Answer of the node |
|---|---|
| **ConsumerGroupDescribe (69)** of a group of the classic protocol | the **69** `GroupIdNotFound` in that entry and the empty `group_state`; the message was **null** on 3.9.2 and is "Group … is not a consumer group." on 4.3.1 |
| **ConsumerGroupDescribe (69)** of a group that does not exist at all | the same **69**; null on 3.9.2, "Group … not found." on 4.3.1 - the code does not distinguish "wrong protocol" from "no such group", the message of a 4.x node does |
| **DescribeGroups (15) v5** of a group of the new consumer protocol | the error code **0**, the state **`Dead`**, an empty protocol type and **no members** - exactly the answer a group that never existed gets |
| **DescribeGroups (15) v6** (Kafka 4.0) of the same group | the **69** with "Group … is not a classic group." (`describegroups.*.v6.consumer-group`) |

**Up to version 5 the classic api lies quietly**, and that is why an admin client of the 3.x line could not route by
trying: a KIP-848 group described with key 15 looked like a group that is gone. Version 6 of KIP-1043 made the two
apis symmetric - each refuses the other's groups with the 69 - and the `group_type` of a **ListGroups v5** answer,
which `Admin\AdminClient::listConsumerGroups($states, $types)` reports, is still the one question that names the
api to send without a refusal.

**The empty group id is the 24 on a 4.x node.** A ConsumerGroupDescribe whose `group_ids` holds the empty string
is answered a single entry with the **24** `InvalidGroupId`, the empty group id and a null message:
`GroupCoordinatorService.consumerGroupDescribe` @ 4.3.1 refuses it with `setGroupId("")` before any shard is asked.
The 3.9.2 node of the 3.x line crashed on the same frame - an entry with the error code **-1** and no group id, and a
`NullPointerException … because "this.groupId" is null` in `ConsumerGroupDescribeResponseData$DescribedGroup.addSize`
in its log (`KafkaApis.handleConsumerGroupDescribe` @ 3.9.2, line 3909), because the refusal entry was built without
the group id. This client never sends an empty group id.

### The authorized operations and the acl (v0, KIP-430)

`include_authorized_operations` is a field of the version 0 - the api was born long after KIP-430 - and it works
as everywhere else: **-2147483648** (`AclOperation::NOT_REQUESTED`) when the request did not ask, and the bit
field of the connection's principal when it did. Measured with the anonymous super user of the PLAINTEXT listener:
**328**, i.e. `DESCRIBE`, `READ` and `DELETE`, on the 3.9.2 node, and **3400** on the 4.3.1 node, which adds
`DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` and `ALTER_CONFIGS` - `AclEntry.supportedOperations(GROUP)` @ 4.0.0, see "The authorized
operations of a group (v3, KIP-430)".

The one principal outside `super.users`, the SASL user `acltest`, is refused **per entry**: the code **30**
`GroupAuthorizationFailed` with a **null** message, an empty state and the `authorized_operations` back at
-2147483648, while the frame itself is error-free. A ConsumerGroupHeartbeat of the same principal is refused with
the same code at the **top level**, because that api has no entries.

### What the answer says about a member

`client_host` is the address with the leading slash of the Java `InetAddress` - `/172.18.0.1` from inside the
container's network - exactly as a DescribeGroups answer reports it, and `client_id` is the `client.id` of the
consumer. `subscribed_topic_regex` is declared nullable with the default `null`, but the 3.9.2 and the 4.3.1 node
answer the **empty string** for a member that subscribed by name: a reader has to treat `""` and `null` alike
here; a member that subscribed by a regex (ConsumerGroupHeartbeat v1) is reported with its regex and the empty
`subscribed_topic_names`. `instance_id` is really null for a dynamic member, and the instance id for a static one.

### The member type (v1, KIP-1099)

*"Version 1 adds MemberType field (KIP-1099)"* stands over the answer @ 4.0.0, and *"For
ConsumerGroupDescribeRequest, version 1 is same as version 0"* over the request. The field is an **int8** behind the
`TargetAssignment` of every member - *"-1 for unknown. 0 for classic member. +1 for consumer member."*, default -1 -
and it exists because a group of the consumer protocol may hold members of the **classic** protocol: a classic
JoinGroup for a `consumer` group is accepted (the online upgrade of KIP-848, see "The mixed cluster (v0, KIP-848)"),
and on a 4.x node a heartbeat upgrades a live classic group the other way round. Measured on the 4.3.1 node with the
member of a regex subscription and a classic consumer that joined its group
(`consumergroupdescribe.*.v1.member-types`):

| Member | `subscribed_topic_names` | `subscribed_topic_regex` | `member_type` |
|---|---|---|---|
| the member of ConsumerGroupHeartbeat v1 | `[]` | `t3-40-vec.*` | **1** |
| the classic member, id `vPsuwwVLSuW9Rrbw6mhp2w` generated by the coordinator | `[t3-40-vectors]`, read out of the `Subscription` of its JoinGroup | `""` | **0** |

The same question at version 0 (`consumergroupdescribe.*.v0.member-types`) is the same answer without the two bytes,
and nothing in it tells the two members apart. The join of the classic member moved the group epoch to 3 while the
assignment epoch stayed at 2, so the group is `Assigning` in both answers. The Java admin client reports the type
as the `upgraded()` of a `MemberDescription` @ 4.0.0 - *empty* for -1, `true` for 1, `false` for 0 - and so does
`Admin\ConsumerGroupMemberDescription::upgraded()`, next to the raw `$memberType`.

## CreateTopics API (key 19, v0 to v7)

Creates topics through the protocol instead of writing to ZooKeeper. The api arrived with Kafka **0.10.1**;
the versions 0, 1 and 2 are the ones of the lines below, unchanged since 0.11.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 3** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`CREATE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V3 = CREATE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V2`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`createtopics.request.v3` / `createtopics.response.v3` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `CreateTopicsRequestV3` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.4.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 4** (KIP-464) and did not change a byte either - the layout of
`CreateTopicsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 is the same for the versions 1 to 4, and the answer gets its next field, the
`topic_configs` of KIP-525, only with the flexible version 5. What the version 4 buys is a **third way of
describing a topic**: `num_partitions` and `replication_factor` may BOTH be -1 while the assignment array is
**empty**, which asks the broker for its own `num.partitions` and `default.replication.factor`. Before KIP-464 the
-1 meant "the assignment below names the replicas" and nothing else, so a topic without an assignment had to carry
both numbers.

**The version check is in the CLIENT, not in the broker.** This was measured, and it is the one surprise of this
api: a 2.8.2 broker answers the -1/-1 of a **version 3** request with the error code 0 and creates the topic with
its defaults, exactly as it does for a version 4 request - `ZkAdminManager.createTopics` @ 2.8.2 resolves

```scala
val resolvedNumPartitions = if (topic.numPartitions == NO_NUM_PARTITIONS) defaultNumPartitions else topic.numPartitions
val resolvedReplicationFactor = if (topic.replicationFactor == NO_REPLICATION_FACTOR) defaultReplicationFactor else topic.replicationFactor
```

without looking at the api version at all. The fallback IS what KIP-464 added, so a broker of Kafka 2.3 or below
does not have it and answers such a topic with **37** `InvalidPartitions` or **38** `InvalidReplicationFactor`. The
guard therefore lives in `CreateTopicsRequest.Builder.build(version)` @ 2.8.2, which throws for it —

> Creating topics with default partitions/replication factor are only supported in CreateTopicRequest version 4+.
> The following topics need values for partitions and replicas: [...]

— and this client does the same in `CreateTopicsRequest::__construct()`, so that a caller who means the defaults
cannot silently send them to a broker that will refuse them. `NewTopic::withBrokerDefaults()` is the shape.

Measured on the container, whose `server.properties` carries `num.partitions=3` and no `default.replication.factor`
(so the Kafka default 1 applies): a version 4 request with -1/-1 and no assignment is answered **0**, and the
topic it creates has **3 partitions with 1 replica each**. The pair `createtopics.request.v4` /
`createtopics.response.v4` at the end of this document is that exchange.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 5** too, and it does two things at once. It is the **first flexible version** of the
api (KIP-482) - every string and array of the frame is compact, the request header carries a tag buffer and every
structure ends in one - and it answers KIP-525: the topic result carries the partition count, the replication
factor and the **whole configuration the new topic ended up with**.

```
CreateTopicsResponseTopic (Version: 5) => Topic ErrorCode ErrorMessage
                                          NumPartitions ReplicationFactor [Configs]
                                          <TAG_BUFFER: 0 => TopicConfigErrorCode>
  NumPartitions     => int32                    -- -1 when the broker does not know it
  ReplicationFactor => int16                    -- -1 when the broker does not know it
  Configs           => Name Value ReadOnly ConfigSource IsSensitive   -- NULLABLE array
```

The point of KIP-525 is the DescribeConfigs that a client used to send right after creating a topic: everything
that api would answer - the value, whether it is read-only, where it comes from and whether it is sensitive - is
already here, for every option of the topic and not only for the ones the request set. `num_partitions` and
`replication_factor` answer the other half of KIP-464: a client that asked for the broker defaults with -1/-1 is
told what it got.

The **`configs` array is nullable**, and the reason it is null is the **tagged** field 0 `topic_config_error_code`
of the same entry - the first tagged field this document meets that is not in the ApiVersions answer. It is absent
whenever the broker could read the configuration back, which is the rule of every tagged field: a value that
equals the default of the specification is not written.

Measured on the container, creating a one-partition topic with `retention.ms = 3600000`: the answer is **909
bytes**, it carries `num_partitions = 1`, `replication_factor = 1` and **26** configuration entries, and its
tagged section is empty. The sources of those 26 are the ones a DescribeConfigs would report - **1** with the
source 1 `DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG` (the `retention.ms` the request set), **2** with the source 4
`STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG` (`segment.bytes` and `message.format.version`, which this image sets in its
`server.properties`) and **23** with the source 5 `DEFAULT_CONFIG`.

`AdminClient::createTopicsWithResults()` is what hands that over: the same request as `createTopics()`, whose
result is the `error` of each of these entries, with the rest of the answer kept in a `CreatedTopic` -
`numPartitions`, `replicationFactor`, a `Config` and the `configErrorCode` of the tagged field.

```
CreateTopicsRequest => [CreateTopicRequest] Timeout [ValidateOnly]
  CreateTopicRequest => Topic NumPartitions ReplicationFactor [ReplicaAssignment] [Config]
    Topic             => string
    NumPartitions     => int32
    ReplicationFactor => int16
    ReplicaAssignment => PartitionId [Replica]
      PartitionId => int32
      Replica     => int32
    Config            => ConfigKey ConfigValue
      ConfigKey   => string
      ConfigValue => string
  Timeout      => int32
  ValidateOnly => boolean   # v1 only
```

```
CreateTopicsResponse (v0 and v1) => [TopicError]
  TopicError => Topic ErrorCode [ErrorMessage]
    Topic        => string
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string   # v1 and above

CreateTopicsResponse (v2) => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicError]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32             # since version 2
```

Version 1 adds exactly two fields (`CREATE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V1` / `CREATE_TOPICS_RESPONSE_V1` in `Protocol.java` @
0.11.0.3): the trailing `ValidateOnly` of the request - the first **boolean** of the protocol this client sees, a
single byte, `00` or `01` - and the `ErrorMessage` of every topic of the answer, which is the message of the
exception the controller caught. The topic entry of the request is byte for byte the one of version 0
(`SINGLE_CREATE_TOPIC_REQUEST_V1 = SINGLE_CREATE_TOPIC_REQUEST_V0`). Version 2 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) leaves the
request untouched again — `CREATE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V2 = CREATE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V1` — and only prefixes the answer with
the throttle time.

**`ConfigValue` is a `NULLABLE_STRING`, and it is one in every version.** `CONFIG_ENTRY` is a single shared schema
object in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3 — `config_name` STRING, `config_value` NULLABLE_STRING — and the topic entry
of the request is the same structure in v0, v1 and v2 (`SINGLE_CREATE_TOPIC_REQUEST_V1 =
SINGLE_CREATE_TOPIC_REQUEST_V0`, reused again by v2). Verified against the container by sending a `ff ff` value with
each of the three versions: all three **parse**, none of them closes the connection, and all three answer that topic
with the error code **-1** (`UNKNOWN`) without creating anything, because `AdminManager.createTopics` copies the
entries into a `java.util.Properties`, whose `setProperty` throws a `NullPointerException` on a null value:

```
ERROR [Admin Manager on Broker 0]: Error processing create topic request for topic t3-probe-null-config-v0 with
arguments (numPartitions=1, replicationFactor=1, replicasAssignments={}, configs={retention.ms=null})
java.lang.NullPointerException
	at java.util.Properties.setProperty(Properties.java:166)
	at kafka.server.AdminManager$$anonfun$2$$anonfun$apply$2.apply(AdminManager.scala:79)
```

`Data\CreateTopicsRequestConfig` therefore declares the field as `TYPE_NULLABLE_STRING` — the wire truth — while
this client never sends a null: a non-null value is byte for byte identical under either type, so no captured vector
changes.

**Only the active controller serves this api.** `KafkaApis.handleCreateTopicsRequest` @ 0.11.0.3 answers every topic
of the request with the error code 41 (NotController) when `controller.isActive` is false, before it looks at the
request at all. Metadata v0 does not name the controller; `ControllerId` of Metadata v1 does, which is what
`Admin\AdminClient::findController()` reads - see the "Metadata API" section above.

A topic is described in **one of two ways**, and mixing them is an error:

* `NumPartitions` and `ReplicationFactor` are set and the assignment array is **empty**: the controller places the
  replicas with `AdminUtils.assignReplicasToBrokers`;
* both are `-1` (`CreateTopicsRequest.NO_NUM_PARTITIONS` / `NO_REPLICATION_FACTOR`) and the assignment array names
  the broker ids of every partition, the preferred leader first.

Setting both is answered with **42 (InvalidRequest)** and the message *"Both numPartitions or replicationFactor and
replicasAssignments were set. Both cannot be used at the same time."*, which is the check at the top of
`AdminManager.createTopics`. The broker deliberately does **not** verify that an explicit assignment names brokers
that exist ("we don't check that replicaAssignment contains unknown brokers - unlike in add-partitions case, this
follows the existing logic in TopicCommand"): a topic assigned to a broker id that no broker has is written to
ZooKeeper, never gets a leader, and the request answers **7 (RequestTimedOut)** after `Timeout` - the topic then
exists in ZooKeeper but never appears in the metadata of the cluster, and DeleteTopics answers 3 for it.

`Timeout` is how long the **controller** waits for the topic to be created on it before it answers, not a socket
timeout. `Values <= 0 will trigger topic creation and return immediately`: the answer arrives at once and reports
**7 (RequestTimedOut)** for every topic that was accepted, although the creation is under way and finishes shortly
afterwards (observed: the topic is in the metadata of the broker ~50 ms later). The same is true for a timeout that
is simply too short. A successful answer means the topic exists **on the controller**; the other brokers learn about
it with the next metadata update, so a Metadata request may still answer 5 (LeaderNotAvailable) for a moment.

`ValidateOnly` runs the whole validation - the topic name, the replica placement, every topic-level option - and
answers without writing anything to ZooKeeper (`AdminUtils.validateCreateOrUpdateTopic` instead of
`createOrUpdateTopicPartitionAssignmentPathInZK`). A validated topic comes back with the error code **0** and does
not exist afterwards. Version 0 has no such flag, and the Java client refuses to even build a version 0 request with
it set.

Error codes observed on the container, with the `ErrorMessage` that the versions 1 and 2 carry. **Three of the
messages were rewritten by Kafka 1.0** — the codes did not change, only the text, and the 0.11 wording is in
parentheses behind each of them; a client that matches on the message rather than on the code notices the upgrade:

| Code | Name                     | Request that produces it                          | ErrorMessage                                                                 |
|------|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                     | The topic was created (or validated)              | `null`                                                                       |
| 7    | RequestTimedOut          | `Timeout` of 0, or an assignment to an unknown broker | `null`                                                                   |
| 17   | InvalidTopicException    | A topic name outside `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]`             | `Topic name "x" is illegal, it contains a character other than ASCII alphanumerics, '.', '_' and '-'` (0.11: `topic name ... is illegal, contains a character …`) |
| 36   | TopicAlreadyExists       | A topic of that name exists                       | `Topic 'x' already exists.`                                                  |
| 37   | InvalidPartitions        | `NumPartitions` = 0                               | `Number of partitions must be larger than 0.` (0.11: `number of partitions must be larger than 0`) |
| 38   | InvalidReplicationFactor | `ReplicationFactor` larger than the broker count  | `Replication factor: 2 larger than available brokers: 1.` (0.11: `replication factor: 2 larger than available brokers: 1`) |
| 40   | InvalidConfig            | An unknown topic-level option **name**            | `Unknown topic config name: nope.ms` (`Unknown Log configuration nope.ms.` on 0.10.2.2) |
| 41   | NotController            | Sent to a broker that is not the controller       | `null`                                                                       |
| 42   | InvalidRequest           | Partitions/factor **and** an explicit assignment; the same topic twice in one request | see above          |
| 44   | PolicyViolation          | A `create.topic.policy.class.name` refused it     | the message of the policy                                                    |

**Quirk: an unparsable option VALUE is not 40.** `LogConfig.validate` first calls `validateNames`, which throws
Kafka's own `InvalidConfigurationException` - an `ApiException`, mapped to 40 - for an unknown option name, and then
`configDef.parse`, which throws the plain `ConfigException` of the common config framework. That one is not an
`ApiException`, so `Errors.forException` falls through to **-1 (Unknown)**: `retention.ms=soon` is answered with the
code -1 and the message `Invalid value soon for configuration retention.ms: Not a number of type LONG`. Only the
name of an option is reported as 40.

**Quirk: duplicates are handled by the broker, not by the schema.** The wire format is an array, so the same topic
can appear twice in one request; `CreateTopicsRequest.duplicateTopics` collects those and `KafkaApis` answers each
of them with 42 (InvalidRequest) and a message that names them. This client keys its topic map by name and therefore
cannot produce such a frame.

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-599)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 6**, and `CreateTopicsRequest.json` @ 2.7.2 is explicit about it: "Version 6 is
identical to version 5 but may return a THROTTLING_QUOTA_EXCEEDED error". Not a byte of the request or of the
answer moves; what the version says is that this client understands the error code **89** and repeats a topic the
controller mutation quota refused, instead of having its request held back.
`CreateTopicsRequestV5`/`CreateTopicsResponseV5` keep the frame with its own version field, and the pair
`createtopics.request.v6` / `createtopics.response.v6` at the end of this document is the accepted exchange - the
KIP-525 answer unchanged, 26 configuration entries in 908 bytes.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-516)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 7**, whose request is the frame of the version 6 ("Version 7 is the same as version
6"): what it adds is in the **answer**, where every topic result carries the **`topic_id`** of the topic the
controller created - the 16 raw bytes of a UUID, between the name and the error code.

```
CreateTopicsResponseTopic (Version: 7) => Topic TopicId ErrorCode ErrorMessage
                                          NumPartitions ReplicationFactor [Configs]
                                          <TAG_BUFFER: 0 => TopicConfigErrorCode>
  TopicId => UUID   -- since version 7; sixteen zero bytes for a topic the broker refused
```

KIP-516 gave every topic an id that outlives its name: a topic that is deleted and created again under the same
name is a different topic, and the id is what says so. `uuid` is a fixed-width type of 16 bytes that no length
prefix precedes, so the compact encoding does not touch it; `CreateTopicsResponseTopic::NO_TOPIC_ID` is the
`Uuid.ZERO_UUID` of the specification, which a refused topic - and every version below 7, which has no such field
- carries. `Admin\CreatedTopic::$topicId` hands the id to the caller as those 16 raw bytes, and
`CreateTopicsResponseTopicV5` is the entry of the versions 5 and 6.

**A ZooKeeper-backed 2.8.2 controller fills the id, and only for a topic it really created.** Measured on the
container: `createtopics.response.v7` carries a random id for the new topic (`ZkAdminManager.createTopics` @
2.8.2 generates one per topic and writes it into `/brokers/topics/<name>`), while
`createtopics.response.v7.topic-exists` - the same request a second time, answered 36 `TopicExists` - carries the
**zero** id next to the error, because nothing was created to have one.

### KIP-599: the version that is answered instead of being held back

**Kafka 2.7 gave the three topic apis a version that changes no field** - CreateTopics **v6**, DeleteTopics **v5**
and CreatePartitions **v3** - and the JSON of each says the same thing: "Version N is identical to version N-1 but
may return a THROTTLING_QUOTA_EXCEEDED error" (DeleteTopics v5 also adds a field, see its section). What the
version really is, is a **promise of the client**.

KIP-599 put a quota on the *controller* - `controller_mutation_rate`, the number of partitions a client may create
or delete per second, per user and client id. Before Kafka 2.7 a client over that quota had its request **held
back**: the broker kept it in the quota queue and answered it when the debt was paid, which looks like a slow
controller and cannot be told apart from one. From these versions on the broker answers **at once**: the topics
the quota refused carry the error code **89** `ThrottlingQuotaExceeded`, the answer carries the
`throttle_time_ms` the client has to sit out, and the client repeats the request for those topics itself.

`Admin\AdminClient` does exactly that: `onController()` sends the request again while any topic of the answer
carries the 89, bounded by the `retries` of the configuration. The **waiting** is not its own - `Client` remembers
the moment the throttle of a broker ends and sleeps the rest of it before the next request goes there, which is
the promise this client made for KIP-219 in Kafka 2.0.

**The container cannot produce the 89**: a quota has to be configured for it (`kafka-configs.sh --alter
--add-config controller_mutation_rate=…`), and the broker of this line is shared by every suite, so nothing here
sets one. The retry is covered by the unit tests with a scripted controller
(`tests/Unit/Admin/AdminClientTest.php`), and the three version pairs at the end of this document are the accepted
exchanges.

## DeleteTopics API (key 20, v0 to v6)

Deletes topics through the protocol. The api arrived with Kafka **0.10.1** as version 0; Kafka 0.11 added the
version 1 with the leading `throttle_time_ms` of KIP-124.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 2** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`DELETE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V2 = DELETE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V1`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`deletetopics.request.v2` / `deletetopics.response.v2` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `DeleteTopicsRequestV2` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.1.

**Kafka 2.1 added the version 3**, again with the same frame (`DELETE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V3 = DELETE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V2`
in `Protocol.java` @ 2.1.1, whose comment reads "v3 request is the same that as v2. The response is different based
on the request version. In v3 version a TopicDeletionDisabledException is returned"), and it is the version this
client sent until Kafka 2.4. What it buys is an **error code**: a cluster whose `delete.topic.enable` is `false` accepts the
request and never carries the deletion out, and `KafkaApis.handleDeleteTopicsRequest` @ 2.8.2 says which code it
answers with —

```scala
} else if (!config.deleteTopicEnable) {
  val error = if (request.context.apiVersion < 3) Errors.INVALID_REQUEST else Errors.TOPIC_DELETION_DISABLED
**Kafka 2.4 added the version 4** (KIP-482) and changed no field at all: it is the **first flexible version** of
this api, so the topic names are a compact array of compact strings, the request header carries a tag buffer and
the body and every topic result end in one. `DeleteTopicsRequestV4` / `DeleteTopicsResponseV4` are
that flexible frame, which a broker below Kafka 2.7 gets, and `DeleteTopicsRequestV3` /
`DeleteTopicsResponseV3` the plain one of Kafka 2.1; what this client sends is the version **6** of Kafka 2.8
below.

```

— so a version 3 client is told what is really wrong (**73** `TopicDeletionDisabled`) where every lower version
gets the **42** `InvalidRequest` of the lines below. The option is **not** dynamically updatable and the container
of this line runs with `delete.topic.enable=true`, so the 73 is documented from the sources and not measured: it
is the one error code of this api that the vectors below cannot show. The check sits in front of the topic loop,
so it is answered for **every** topic of the request, and it comes before the `UnknownTopicOrPartition` of a topic
that does not exist.

```
DeleteTopicsRequest => [Topic] Timeout
  Topic   => string
  Timeout => int32
```

```
DeleteTopicsResponse (v0) => [TopicErrorCode]
  TopicErrorCode => Topic ErrorCode
    Topic     => string
    ErrorCode => int16

DeleteTopicsResponse (v1) => ThrottleTimeMs [TopicErrorCode]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32          # since version 1
```

The request is a plain array of topic **names**, not of structures, and the answer carries the bare
`TOPIC_ERROR_CODE` entries - there is no `ErrorMessage` in this api at all, the reason of a failure is only in the
log of the broker. Version 1 (Kafka 0.11, KIP-124) changed the request in no way
(`DELETE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V1 = DELETE_TOPICS_REQUEST_V0` in `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3) and prefixed the answer with
the throttle time.

**Only the active controller serves it**, exactly like CreateTopics: `KafkaApis.handleDeleteTopicsRequest` @
0.11.0.3 answers every topic of the request with 41 (NotController) when `controller.isActive` is false.

**Quirk: an empty topic array is answered by every broker with an empty array.** The handler builds the answer by
mapping over the topics of the **request** (`deleteTopicRequest.topics.asScala.map { topic => (topic,
Errors.NOT_CONTROLLER) }`), so a request without topics produces an answer without entries - on the controller and
on every follower alike. An empty DeleteTopics is therefore useless as a **controller probe**, which is how a
client of a line below 0.10 has to find the controller at all: it has to name **one topic whose name can never be
legal** (`#kafka-client-controller-probe#` - `Topic.validate` only allows `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]`), so that the controller
cannot find it in its metadata cache and answers 3 (UnknownTopicOrPartition) without touching ZooKeeper while every
other broker answers 41 for it, and nothing can ever be deleted by the probe. Verified against the container: the
empty request `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` comes back as `00 00 00 00`, the named one as one entry with the code 3.
From Kafka 0.10.0 on none of that is needed - `Admin\AdminClient::findController()` reads the `ControllerId` of a
Metadata answer instead.

**Deletion is asynchronous.** `AdminUtils.deleteTopic` only writes the topic into `/admin/delete_topics` in
ZooKeeper; the controller then stops the replicas and removes the partitions. `Timeout` is how long the controller
waits for that before it answers, and `Values <= 0 will trigger topic deletion and return immediately` - the answer
is then **7 (RequestTimedOut)** for every topic whose deletion was started. Measured on the single-broker container
with `delete.topic.enable=true`:

* `Timeout = 30000`: the controller answered **0** after ~60 ms, and the topic was gone from a Metadata answer ~50 ms
  after that;
* `Timeout = 0`: the answer came back at once with **7**, and the topic was gone from Metadata ~50 ms later.

So even a successful answer only says that the controller is done; a client that waits for the topic to disappear
has to poll the metadata. A cluster whose brokers run with `delete.topic.enable=false` - the **default** of Kafka
0.10 - accepts the request the same way and never carries the deletion out.

| Code | Name                     | Request that produces it                                            |
|------|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                     | The topic was deleted within `Timeout`                              |
| 3    | UnknownTopicOrPartition  | The metadata cache of the broker has no such topic - also the answer to deleting the same topic a second time, once the first deletion finished |
| 7    | RequestTimedOut          | `Timeout` of 0, or a deletion that was not finished in time         |
| 29   | TopicAuthorizationFailed | The client may describe the topic but not delete it                 |
| 41   | NotController            | Sent to a broker that is not the controller                         |

A topic that is **already marked** for deletion is accepted again without an error: `AdminManager.deleteTopics`
swallows the `TopicAlreadyMarkedForDeletionException` "and still track[s] deletion allowing multiple calls to wait
for deletion".

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-599 and the error message)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 5**, and it is the one version of the three that KIP-599 touched which really
changes the frame: every topic result gains an **`error_message`** - a compact nullable string - behind its error
code ("Version 5 adds ErrorMessage in the response and may return a THROTTLING_QUOTA_EXCEEDED error",
`DeleteTopicsResponse.json` @ 2.7.2).

```
DeleteTopicsResponseTopic (Version: 5) => Topic ErrorCode ErrorMessage
  ErrorMessage => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING   -- since version 5
```

**A 2.8.2 broker leaves it null even for an error.** Measured on the container: a topic the cluster does not have
is answered the error code 3 `UnknownTopicOrPartition` with the message `null`
(`deletetopics.response.v5.unknown-topic`), and so is a deleted topic - `ZkAdminManager.deleteTopics` @ 2.8.2
builds its results from the error code alone. The field is filled by the KRaft controller of the later releases;
`Client::deleteTopics()` reads it into the exception of the topic whenever the broker sends one, exactly as
CreateTopics has done since Kafka 0.11. `DeleteTopicsResponseTopicV0` is the result without the field, which every
version below 5 uses.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-516)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 6**, and it is the one version of this api that really rebuilds the request: the
flat `[]TopicNames` of every version below becomes a `[]DeleteTopicState`, a structure that names a topic by its
**name or by its id**.

```
DeleteTopicsRequest (Version: 6) => [Topics] TimeoutMs
  Topics => Name TopicId
    Name    => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING   -- null for a topic that is named by its id alone
    TopicId => UUID                      -- sixteen zero bytes for a topic that is named by its name

DeleteTopicsResponseTopic (Version: 6) => Name TopicId ErrorCode ErrorMessage
  Name    => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING   -- nullable since version 6
  TopicId => UUID                      -- since version 6
```

A topic that is named by its id survives a rename, and one that is named by its name is the topic of that name at
the moment the controller reads the request - which is what makes the two ways different rather than equivalent.
`Admin\AdminClient::deleteTopics()` takes names, so every entry it sends carries
`DeleteTopicsRequestTopic::NO_TOPIC_ID`, the sixteen zero bytes, and the answer is read back with the name it
sent; a caller that has an id - from `Admin\CreatedTopic::$topicId` - builds the entry itself and hands the
request a `DeleteTopicsRequestTopic(null, $id)`. `DeleteTopicsRequestV5`, `DeleteTopicsResponseV5` and
`DeleteTopicsResponseTopicV5` are the frames of the version 5.

**Four things measured on the container**, all in `deletetopics.*.v6` at the end of this document:

* a deletion **by name** is answered with the name and the **zero** id (`deletetopics.response.v6`).
