  `KafkaApis.handleDeleteTopicsRequest` @ 2.8.2 builds every result with `setTopicId(topic.topicId())`, the id of
  the **request**, and looks the *name* up for an id instead of the other way round - so an answer carries a real
  id only where the request did;
* a deletion **by id** is answered with the **name** the controller resolved
  (`controllerContext.topicName(topic.topicId)`) next to that id (`deletetopics.response.v6.by-id`), so a client
  learns which topic it just removed;
* an id no topic of the cluster carries is the error code **100** `UnknownTopicId` with a null name
  (`deletetopics.response.v6.unknown-topic-id`) - the handler calls an id it could not resolve an
  `unresolvedTopicId` and answers exactly that code, where a *name* the cluster does not have is still the 3
  `UnknownTopicOrPartition`;
* an entry that carries **both** a name and a non-zero id is answered **42** `InvalidRequest` with the name echoed
  back and a null error message: `if (topic.name() != null && topic.topicId() != Uuid.ZERO_UUID) throw new
  InvalidRequestException("Topic name and topic ID can not both be specified.")`. The exception fails the **whole
  request**, not the one entry - measured with a request of two topics, the malformed one and a topic that really
  existed: both entries came back with the 42 and the topic was still there afterwards.

Because the name of an answer may now be null, the decoder of an array that is keyed by a field - the topic
results are keyed by their name - appends an entry whose key is null instead of keying it by that null; this is
the only place of the protocol where that happens.

## OffsetForLeaderEpoch API (key 23, v0 to v4)

The api of **KIP-101**, "Alter Replication Protocol to use Leader Epoch rather than High Watermark for Truncation",
new in Kafka 0.11. It was a **broker-to-broker** request for two releases; since Kafka 2.1 (KIP-320) an ordinary
**consumer** sends it too, to validate its position after a leader change, which is what version 2 below is about.
This line implements **every version a 2.8.2 broker serves, v0 to v4**, the flexible v4 included.

```
OffsetForLeaderEpochRequest (v0 and v1) => [Topic [PartitionId LeaderEpoch]]
  Topic       => string
  PartitionId => int32
  LeaderEpoch => int32

OffsetForLeaderEpochRequest (v2) => [Topic [PartitionId CurrentLeaderEpoch LeaderEpoch]]
  CurrentLeaderEpoch => int32     # since version 2, IN FRONT of the epoch that is asked about

OffsetForLeaderEpochRequest (v3) => ReplicaId [Topic [PartitionId CurrentLeaderEpoch LeaderEpoch]]
  ReplicaId => int32              # since version 3, at the HEAD of the frame, default -2

OffsetForLeaderEpochRequest (v4) => ReplicaId
                                    [Topic [PartitionId CurrentLeaderEpoch LeaderEpoch TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                                    TAG_BUFFER
  Topic => compact string         # version 4 is the flexible version of KIP-482
```

```
OffsetForLeaderEpochResponse (v0) => [Topic [ErrorCode PartitionId EndOffset]]
  Topic       => string
  ErrorCode   => int16
  PartitionId => int32
  EndOffset   => int64

OffsetForLeaderEpochResponse (v1) => [Topic [ErrorCode PartitionId LeaderEpoch EndOffset]]
  LeaderEpoch => int32          # since version 1

OffsetForLeaderEpochResponse (v2) => ThrottleTimeMs [Topic [ErrorCode PartitionId LeaderEpoch EndOffset]]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32       # since version 2, at the HEAD of the frame

OffsetForLeaderEpochResponse (v4) => ThrottleTimeMs
                                     [Topic [ErrorCode PartitionId LeaderEpoch EndOffset TAG_BUFFER] TAG_BUFFER]
                                     TAG_BUFFER
```

**Version 4 (Kafka 2.8) is the flexible version of KIP-482 and changes no field at all**: both json files comment
"Version 4 enables flexible versions" and declare `"flexibleVersions": "4+"`. The request header **v2**, compact
strings and arrays, a tagged-field section behind every structure, the response header **v1** - and the same
`replica_id`, `current_leader_epoch` and `leader_epoch` as version 3. `OffsetForLeaderEpochRequestV3` and
`OffsetForLeaderEpochResponseV3` keep the plain frame; the pair
`offsetforleaderepoch.request.v4`/`offsetforleaderepoch.response.v4` below is the same exchange as the version 3
pair in 48 and 46 bytes instead of 51 and 49.

Note the order of a partition entry of the answer: the **error code comes first**, before the partition id, which no
other api of this protocol does.

**Version 1 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-279) inserted `leader_epoch` between the partition id and the end offset**, and left
the request untouched — `OffsetForLeaderEpochRequest.json` @ 2.8.2 says "Version 1 is the same as version 0". The
field is the epoch the answered `end_offset` really belongs to, which is **not** necessarily the epoch that was
asked for: `Log.endOffsetForEpoch` answers with the largest epoch that is smaller than or equal to the requested
one. Without it, a follower whose request crossed a leader change could truncate to an offset of an epoch it never
asked about, which is the divergence KIP-279 ("Fix log divergence between leader and follower after fast leader
fail over") closed. `OffsetForLeaderEpochResponsePartition::UNDEFINED_EPOCH` (`-1`) is what the leader answers when
it resolves nothing, and it is also what `OffsetForLeaderEpochResponsePartitionV0` leaves in the property, because
a version 0 answer does not carry the field at all.

The question it asks is *"you were the leader of the epoch `e` of this partition — which offset does that epoch end
at?"*. Until 0.11 a follower that came back after a leader change truncated its log to the high watermark it
remembered, which can diverge from the new leader in the two scenarios KIP-101 describes; from 0.11 on it asks the
new leader instead and truncates to the answer. The epoch a follower asks with is the `PartitionLeaderEpoch` that
the record batches on its disk carry, which is the other half of KIP-101 — see the "RecordBatch (message format v2)"
section.

`Log.endOffsetForEpoch` @ 2.8.2 answers the **start offset of the first epoch above the requested one**, and
`OffsetsForLeaderEpochResponse.UNDEFINED_EPOCH_OFFSET` (`-1`) when its epoch cache cannot answer at all — a log
written by a broker below 0.11, or an epoch it has never heard of. For the epoch the leader is **still** leading
the answer is the log end offset, which is what the vector `offsetforleaderepoch.response.v1` shows: partition 0 of
`t2-vectors` has only ever been led by broker 0, and the epoch 0 is answered with `leader_epoch = 0` and the end
offset of the log.

Re-measured on the 2.8.2 container, with both versions asked the same five questions:

| Partition                     | Requested epoch | v0 `end_offset` | v1 `leader_epoch` / `end_offset` | code |
|-------------------------------|-----------------|-----------------|----------------------------------|------|
| records, led by broker 0      | 0               | the log end offset | **0** / the log end offset    | 0    |
| records, led by broker 0      | 1 (never had)   | `-1`            | `-1` / `-1`                      | 0    |
| records, led by broker 0      | `-1`            | `-1`            | `-1` / `-1`                      | 0    |
| **empty**, led by broker 0    | 0               | **0**           | **0** / **0**                    | 0    |
| a topic that does not exist   | 0               | `-1`            | `-1` / `-1`                      | **3** |

**The fourth row is what changed with this line.** A **1.1.1** broker answered an empty partition with `-1` for the
epoch it was being led with, because the leader-epoch cache of a log was only written when the first record was
appended; a 2.8.2 broker answers the **log end offset**, i.e. `0`, for the epoch it currently leads, empty log or
not (KAFKA-7415, the `Log.endOffsetForEpoch` rewrite that KIP-320 needed). The code 0 with the offset `-1` still
means "I have no entry for that epoch", not a failure — but "I lead this epoch" is now always an offset.

There is **no throttle time and no top-level error code** in either frame: KIP-124 landed in the same release but
left this api alone, because a client quota does not apply to replication traffic. Every partition carries its own
code, and a 2.8.2 broker reports 0, 3 (`UnknownTopicOrPartition`, verified with the vector
`offsetforleaderepoch.response.v0.unknown-partition`, which answers the code 3 with the end offset `-1`), 6
(`NotLeaderForPartition`) and 31 (`ClusterAuthorizationFailed`).

**Version 2 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-320) is the version a consumer sends**, and it changes both halves of the frame:

* the request gains a **`current_leader_epoch`** in front of the epoch it asks about — "you are on epoch *c*;
  where did epoch *e* end?" — with the fencing rule of Fetch v9: `-1` skips the check, an epoch below the leader's
  is **74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH`, one above it **75** `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH`
  (`offsetforleaderepoch.response.v2.unknown-leader-epoch` is the 75, with the undefined epoch and offset `-1`);
* the answer gains a **`throttle_time_ms`** at the head of the frame. The api finally became one a client quota
  applies to, because from 2.1 on it is sent by ordinary consumers and not only by replicas — and it is a KIP-219
  answer from the start: the broker answers first and mutes the channel, so a client waits the value out itself,
  see "KIP-219" under "Quotas and throttle time".

`Client::offsetsForLeaderEpochs()` sends it — version 4 on this line, which is this frame in the flexible
encoding — and the consumer uses it for exactly one thing: the position validation of KIP-320, see "KIP-320 in
the consumer: leader epochs and truncation detection". The question it asks
there is the one this api was built for, only asked by a reader instead of by a replica — *"the position I hold was
taken in the epoch e; does the log you lead still have it?"* — and an `end_offset` below the position is the log
truncation the consumer reports. `OffsetForLeaderEpochRequestV1` and `OffsetForLeaderEpochResponseV1` keep the
version the Kafka 2.0 part of this line sent, which has neither field.

**Version 3 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-392) puts a `replica_id` at the head of the frame** and leaves the answer alone —
`OffsetForLeaderEpochResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 says "Version 3 is the same as version 2". The field says **who is
asking**: a follower sends its own broker id, an ordinary consumer `-1`
(`OffsetForLeaderEpochRequest::CONSUMER_REPLICA_ID`), and the **default of the field is `-2`**, the "debug"
client that may be served offsets beyond the high watermark — the json says so itself: "the default is -2 which
conventionally represents a *debug* consumer which is allowed to see offsets beyond the high watermark".

It arrived with the follower fetching of KIP-392, and for the same reason: from Kafka 2.3 a consumer may validate
its position against a **follower** instead of the leader, and a follower has to know whether it is talking to a
replica of the cluster or to a reader that must not see past its own high watermark. `offsetforleaderepoch.request.v3`
below is the frame with the consumer's `-1`; `OffsetForLeaderEpochRequestV2` keeps the version without the field,
which a broker serves as it serves a follower.

**A broker without an authorizer answers a plain client just as it answers a follower.**
`KafkaApis.handleOffsetForLeaderEpochRequest` @ 0.11.0.3 calls `authorizeClusterAction(request)`, which passes
unconditionally when no `authorizer.class.name` is configured, so the vectors above were captured from an ordinary
client connection on the container. On a secured cluster the same request is answered with the code 31.
## DeleteRecords API (key 21, v0 to v2)

Deletes the records **before an offset** of a partition. The api arrived with Kafka **0.11** (KIP-107) as
version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`DELETE_RECORDS_REQUEST_V1 = DELETE_RECORDS_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back. The pair `deleterecords.request.v1` / `deleterecords.response.v1` at the end of this
document was captured on the 2.8.2 container.

**Kafka 2.6 added the version 2, and it changes no field either: it is the first FLEXIBLE version of this api.**
`DeleteRecordsRequest.json` and `DeleteRecordsResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 both say "Version 2 is the first flexible
version" and declare `"flexibleVersions": "2+"`, so the version 0 question travels with the request header **v2**,
compact strings and arrays, and a tagged-field section at the end of the body, of every topic entry and of every
partition entry; the answer carries the response header **v1** and the same sections, see "Flexible versions in
the engine (KIP-482)". In this client that is two constants - `VERSION = 2` and `FLEXIBLE_VERSION = 2` on
`DeleteRecordsRequest` and `DeleteRecordsResponse` - and nothing else: the DTOs of the topic and of the partition
are the ones of version 0, because a scheme does not know the encoding it is written in.

**Version 2 is what this client sends**, and `DeleteRecordsRequestV1`/`DeleteRecordsResponseV1` keep the plain
frame of the versions 0 and 1 (their `VERSION` is below the inherited `FLEXIBLE_VERSION`, which is the whole of
the switch). `deleterecords.request.v2` and `deleterecords.response.v2` below are the pair, captured on the
container against the topic `t2-26-vectors`: they carry the same three questions and the same three answers as
the version 1 pair, in 48 and 42 bytes instead of 59 and 45 - a compact length is one byte where an `int32` array
header was four, and the six tagged-field sections cost one byte each.

```
DeleteRecordsRequest => [Topic] Timeout
  Topic => TopicName [Partition]
    TopicName => string
    Partition => PartitionId Offset
      PartitionId => int32
      Offset      => int64
  Timeout => int32
```

```
DeleteRecordsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Topic]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Topic => TopicName [Partition]
    TopicName => string
    Partition => PartitionId LowWatermark ErrorCode
      PartitionId  => int32
      LowWatermark => int64
      ErrorCode    => int16
```

Until Kafka 0.11 the only ways to get rid of records were the retention of the topic - by time or by size - and
deleting the topic itself. This api moves the **low watermark** of a partition (`logStartOffset` in the broker,
`log_start_offset` in a Fetch v5 answer) forward: everything **below** `Offset` becomes unreadable at once, the
record *at* `Offset` stays, and the segments that are then completely below the watermark are removed by the log
cleaner afterwards. `Offset = -1` (`DeleteRecordsRequest.HIGH_WATERMARK`) means "up to the high watermark", i.e.
everything that is fully replicated.

The answer reports the new low watermark of every partition, and it is the same number that three other places of
the protocol report: an Offsets request with `EARLIEST`, the `log_start_offset` of a Fetch v5 answer, and the
`LowWatermark` of the next DeleteRecords. Verified on the container with a partition holding five records, deleting
before the offset 2:

* `DeleteRecords(offset = 2)` → error 0, `LowWatermark = 2`;
* `Offsets(EARLIEST)` → 2, `Offsets(LATEST)` → 5, so nothing else moved;
* a raw **Fetch v5** at the offset 2 → `high_watermark = 5`, `log_start_offset = 2`, and the records come back;
* the same Fetch at the offset 0 or 1 → error **1 (OffsetOutOfRange)** with `high_watermark = -1` and
  `log_start_offset = -1`, which is what a consumer that was reading below the new watermark now sees.

**The leader of each partition serves it**, exactly like Produce and Fetch: `KafkaApis.handleDeleteRecordsRequest`
hands the partitions to `ReplicaManager.deleteRecords`, which works on the local `Partition` and answers
6 (NotLeaderForPartition) for a partition this broker does not lead. `Client::deleteRecords()` therefore splits the
request by leader like a produce, and `Admin\AdminClient::deleteRecords()` reports the new watermark per partition.

`Timeout` is how long the **leader** waits for the new watermark to be acknowledged by the followers of the ISR
(`DelayedDeleteRecords`) before it answers; the deletion itself is done on the leader before it waits, and nothing
is rolled back when the timeout expires - the partition is simply reported with 7 (RequestTimedOut). On the
one-broker container the ISR is the leader itself, so every answer is immediate.

Error codes observed on the 0.11.0.3 container:

| Code | Name                     | Request that produces it                                                     |
|------|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                     | The records below the offset are gone; `LowWatermark` is the new start offset |
| 1    | OffsetOutOfRange         | An offset **above the high watermark**, and every negative offset except -1   |
| 3    | UnknownTopicOrPartition  | A topic that is not in the metadata cache of the broker, or a partition the topic does not have |
| 6    | NotLeaderForPartition    | Sent to a broker that does not lead the partition                            |
| 7    | RequestTimedOut          | The new watermark was not acknowledged by the ISR within `Timeout`           |
| 29   | TopicAuthorizationFailed | The client may describe the topic but not delete from it                     |

A partition that failed carries the low watermark **-1** (`DeleteRecordsResponse.INVALID_LOW_WATERMARK`), never a
real offset.

**Quirk: deleting below the current watermark is not an error.** A request for an offset that is at or below the low
watermark the partition already has answers 0 and the *current* watermark, and changes nothing:
`Log.maybeIncrementLogStartOffset` only moves the value forward. Repeating the same request is therefore harmless,
which is what makes the api usable as "make sure everything before X is gone".

**Quirk: a negative offset other than -1 is 1, not 42.** `ReplicaManager.deleteRecordsOnLocalLog` resolves -1 to the
high watermark first and then checks `convertedOffset < 0`, throwing an `OffsetOutOfRangeException` for everything
else - so `-2`, which the Offsets api reads as "earliest", is answered with the error code **1** here.

**Quirk: an unknown topic is answered per partition, and it is not created.** The answer holds one entry per
partition of the *request*, so a topic the cluster does not have comes back with 3 for each of its requested
partitions - and unlike a Metadata request that names an unknown topic, this one does **not** create it while
`auto.create.topics.enable` is on: `KafkaApis` only asks `metadataCache.contains(topic)`. Internal topics are
refused as well, by `Topic.isInternal` inside `ReplicaManager.deleteRecordsOnLocalLog`.

## DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)

Reads the configuration of a topic or of a broker. The api arrived with Kafka **0.11** (KIP-133) and Kafka
**1.1** added the **version 1** of KIP-226, whose answer carries a config source and the synonyms of every
option.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 2** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`DESCRIBE_CONFIGS_REQUEST_V2 = DESCRIBE_CONFIGS_REQUEST_V1`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`describeconfigs.request.v2` / `describeconfigs.response.v2` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `DescribeConfigsRequestV2` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.6.

**Kafka 2.6 added the version 3** (KIP-569), and it is the first change to the frame of this api since KIP-226.
The request gains one more boolean behind `include_synonyms`:

```
DescribeConfigsRequest (Version: 3) => [resources] include_synonyms include_documentation
  include_documentation => BOOLEAN   -- since version 3
```

and every entry of the answer gains two fields **behind the synonyms**:

```
DescribeConfigsResponseConfigEntry (Version: 3) => config_name config_value read_only config_source
                                                    is_sensitive [config_synonyms] config_type documentation
  config_type   => INT8              -- since version 3
  documentation => NULLABLE_STRING   -- since version 3
```

`config_type` is the `ConfigDef.Type` of the option as the wire enum `DescribeConfigsResponse.ConfigType` @ 2.8.2
numbers it, which is the `ConfigEntry.ConfigType` of the Java admin client member for member
(`Protocol\Kafka\Admin\ConfigType`):

| Id | Name | What the value looks like |
|----|------|----------------------------|
| 0 | `UNKNOWN` | The broker has no `ConfigDef` entry for the name, or its type is none of the ones below |
| 1 | `BOOLEAN` | `true` or `false` |
| 2 | `STRING` | |
| 3 | `INT` | a 32-bit integer as text |
| 4 | `SHORT` | a 16-bit integer as text |
| 5 | `LONG` | a 64-bit integer as text |
| 6 | `DOUBLE` | |
| 7 | `LIST` | comma separated - the only type an IncrementalAlterConfigs APPEND or SUBTRACT accepts |
| 8 | `CLASS` | the fully qualified name of a Java class |
| 9 | `PASSWORD` | the value is **null** on the wire, in the entry and in every synonym |

**The type is filled whatever `include_documentation` says.** `ConfigHelper.createTopicConfigEntry` /
`createBrokerConfigEntry` @ 2.8.2 end in

```scala
.setDocumentation(configDocumentation).setConfigType(dataType.id)
```

where `configDocumentation` is `if (includeDocumentation) logConfig.documentationOf(name) else null` and
`dataType.id` is unconditional. Measured on the container: a version 3 answer to a request **without** the flag
carries the right type in every entry and the nullable string -1 for the documentation.

**Why a caller should name its `configuration_keys`.** The documentation strings are the ones of
`ConfigDef.define(...)`, i.e. whole paragraphs of prose, and a topic has around thirty options while a broker has
several hundred. An unrestricted `include_documentation` answer for the broker resource of this container is tens
of kilobytes; the vectors below therefore ask for **one** option, which is the shape a client that wants a type or
a help text should send anyway.

**Measured on the container**, all of it with the version 3:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `cleanup.policy` of a topic, `include_documentation = true` | `config_type` **7** `LIST`, a documentation of 329 characters, 403 bytes of frame |
| the same option, `include_documentation = false` | the same `config_type` **7**, `documentation` **null**, 74 bytes of frame |
| `retention.ms` / `preallocate` / `compression.type` / `min.insync.replicas` | **5** `LONG`, **1** `BOOLEAN`, **2** `STRING`, **3** `INT` |
| `ssl.key.password` of the broker resource, with synonyms and documentation | **9** `PASSWORD`, the value `null` as always for a sensitive option, and a documentation of 175 characters |
| **every** option of the topic with documentation | 26 entries, **9 284 bytes** |
| **every** option of the broker with documentation | 233 entries, **58 272 bytes** |
| the same option asked with the **version 2** | no type and no documentation at all: the entry ends after the synonyms, 71 bytes, and the client reads `ConfigType::UNKNOWN` and `null` |

```
DescribeConfigsRequest (Version: 0 and 1) => [Resource] IncludeSynonyms
  Resource => ResourceType ResourceName [ConfigName]
    ResourceType => int8
    ResourceName => string
    ConfigName   => nullable array of string
  IncludeSynonyms => boolean                                   -- since version 1
```

```
DescribeConfigsResponse (Version: 0 and 1) => ThrottleTimeMs [Resource]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Resource => ErrorCode ErrorMessage ResourceType ResourceName [ConfigEntry]
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string
    ResourceType => int8
    ResourceName => string
    ConfigEntry  => ConfigName ConfigValue ReadOnly (IsDefault | ConfigSource) IsSensitive [ConfigSynonym]
      ConfigName   => string
      ConfigValue  => nullable string
      ReadOnly     => boolean
      IsDefault    => boolean                                  -- version 0 only
      ConfigSource => int8                                     -- since version 1, in the place of IsDefault
      IsSensitive  => boolean
      ConfigSynonym => ConfigName ConfigValue ConfigSource     -- since version 1
        ConfigName   => string
        ConfigValue  => nullable string
        ConfigSource => int8
```

**Version 1 changed the config entry and nothing else.** The `is_default` boolean became a `config_source` int8 in
the very same place, the entry gained the array of its synonyms, and the request gained the trailing
`include_synonyms` boolean; the throttle time, the per-resource error and the resource entry itself are the frame of
version 0 (`DescribeConfigsResponse.java` @ 1.1.1). The classes follow that split:
`DescribeConfigsRequest`/`Response` are the version 1, `…RequestV0`/`…ResponseV0` the version 0, and the entry
classes `DescribeConfigsResponseConfigEntry` / `…ConfigEntryV0` are what the resource entry picks by its version.

`ResourceType` is the id of `org.apache.kafka.common.requests.ResourceType` @ 1.1.1 - `UNKNOWN(0)`, `ANY(1)`,
**`TOPIC(2)`**, `GROUP(3)`, **`BROKER(4)`** - and only the two bold ones are accepted by this api; anything else is
answered with 42 and `Unexpected resource type GROUP for resource …`. Those numbers are **not** the ones of the ACL
`ResourceType` of the same release, and they are not the ones of the `ConfigResource.Type` enum that Kafka 1.0
introduced. `ResourceName` is the topic name, the **broker id as a decimal string**, or - since KIP-226 - the
**empty string**, which addresses the cluster-wide dynamic default configuration (see below).

`ConfigName` is a NULLABLE array and the two empty cases mean different things: `null` (`ff ff ff ff`) asks for
**every** option of the resource, an **empty** array asks for none and answers with an empty entry list.

**A topic resource is answered by any broker, a broker resource only by that broker.**
`AdminManager.describeConfigs` @ 1.1.1 reads the entity config of a topic out of ZooKeeper and merges it with the
log defaults of the broker that answers, so every broker can serve it; a broker resource is the live `KafkaConfig`
of the process, and the manager compares the requested id with its own `config.brokerId` and throws for any other
one. `Admin\AdminClient::describeConfigs()` therefore splits a call by resource: the broker resources go to the
node they name, everything else to any broker.

### The config source (KIP-226)

`ConfigSource` is the enum `DescribeConfigsResponse.ConfigSource` @ 1.1.1, i.e. `Admin\ConfigSource` here, and it
is ordered by precedence - a value of a lower source wins over a value of a higher one:

| Id | Name in the wire enum           | Name in `ConfigEntry.ConfigSource` | What it says                                            |
|----|---------------------------------|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| 0  | `UNKNOWN_CONFIG`                | `UNKNOWN`                          | A source this client does not know                      |
| 1  | `TOPIC_CONFIG`                  | `DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG`             | The option stands in the ZooKeeper node of the topic    |
| 2  | `DYNAMIC_BROKER_CONFIG`         | `DYNAMIC_BROKER_CONFIG`            | KIP-226 set it on **this** broker at runtime            |
| 3  | `DYNAMIC_DEFAULT_BROKER_CONFIG` | `DYNAMIC_DEFAULT_BROKER_CONFIG`    | KIP-226 set it for **every** broker of the cluster      |
| 4  | `STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG`          | `STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG`             | It stands in the `server.properties` of the broker      |
| 5  | `DEFAULT_CONFIG`                | `DEFAULT_CONFIG`                   | Nobody configured it and this is the built-in default   |

The synonyms of an entry are exactly the places the broker looked for that value, **in that order**, and only the
ones it really found (`AdminManager.configSynonyms()`): the first entry of the array is the one that WON and carries
the value of the entry itself, everything behind it is shadowed. `AdminManager` computes the source as
`allSynonyms.head.source`, or `DEFAULT_CONFIG` when the list is empty, so the source and the first synonym always
agree. `include_synonyms = false` only decides whether the list is *sent* - the source is always there, and the
array is then empty (`00 00 00 00`).

A synonym is not necessarily named like the option: the synonyms of the *topic* option `segment.bytes` are its own
value and the *broker* option `log.segment.bytes`, once for the `server.properties` and once for the built-in
default, which is what `describeconfigs.response.v1.topic` shows.

`ReadOnly` changed its meaning with the same KIP. Up to 0.11 every entry of a broker resource was read-only,
because a broker could not change any of its own configuration at runtime;
`AdminManager.createBrokerConfigEntry()` @ 1.1.1 computes
`readOnly = !allNames.exists(DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs.contains)`, so an option that KIP-226 made
dynamic - directly or through one of its synonyms - is answered as **writable**. A topic entry is never read-only,
as before. `IsSensitive` is unchanged: it is true for every option whose `ConfigDef.Type` is `PASSWORD`, and the
value of such an entry is `null` on the wire - in the entry **and in every synonym of it**.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name                       | Request that produces it                                            | ErrorMessage                                          |
|------|----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                       | The configuration follows                                           | `null`                                                 |
| 17   | InvalidTopic               | A topic name outside `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]`                               | `Topic name "…" is illegal, it contains a character other than ASCII alphanumerics, '.', '_' and '-'` |
| 29   | TopicAuthorizationFailed   | The client may describe the topic but not its configuration         | `null`                                                 |
| 31   | ClusterAuthorizationFailed | The client may not read a broker resource                           | `null`                                                 |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A broker id that is not the one that answers                        | `Unexpected broker id, expected 0 or empty string, but received Resource(type=BROKER, name='7'}.name` |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A broker id that is not a number                                    | `Broker id must be an integer, but it is: nope`        |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A resource type other than 2 and 4                                  | `Unexpected resource type GROUP for resource t4-probe-group` |

**Quirk: the message of a wrong broker id quotes a Scala interpolation bug.** `AdminManager.describeConfigs` @ 1.1.1
writes `s"…but received $resource.name"`, which interpolates the *resource* and then appends the literal `.name`, so
the message ends with `Resource(type=BROKER, name='7'}.name` - including the `(`/`}` mismatch of
`Resource.toString()` that the AlterConfigs section describes. A 0.11.0.3 broker said
`Unexpected broker id, expected 0, but received 7`: the sentence changed twice, and a client must not parse it.

**Quirk: an option whose synonyms have another name reports `DEFAULT_CONFIG` and no synonyms at all.**
`configSynonyms()` ends with `allSynonyms.dropWhile(s => s.name != name)`, which is meant to drop the listener
overrides in front of a base config - and it drops the WHOLE list when nothing in it carries the requested name.
The container sets `log.retention.hours=168`, and the synonyms of the topic option `retention.ms` are looked up
under `log.retention.ms` (`LogConfig.TopicConfigSynonyms`), so the only synonym the broker finds is named
`log.retention.hours`, the `dropWhile` throws it away, and `retention.ms` comes back with the value `604800000`,
the source **5** and an empty synonym array. The same is true of the broker option `log.retention.ms` itself. The
source therefore says "nobody set it" for an option that the `server.properties` does set under another name.

**Quirk: a broker entry can be writable and still be refused by AlterConfigs.** `log.retention.hours` is answered
with `read_only = 00`, because its synonym `log.retention.ms` is one of the `AllDynamicConfigs`; altering it is
nevertheless answered with 42 and `Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(log.retention.hours)`, because
`DynamicBrokerConfig.validate()` looks at the name that was SENT. "Not read-only" means "one of its names is
dynamic", not "this name can be updated".

**Quirk: the version 0 answer of a 1.1 broker is not the version 0 answer of a 0.11 broker.**
`DescribeConfigsResponse` @ 1.1.1 writes `is_default = (source == DEFAULT_CONFIG)` into the old frame, where a
0.11.0.3 broker wrote `is_default = !topicProps.containsKey(name)`. On the container that flips exactly the options
whose broker synonym stands in the `server.properties`: `segment.bytes` of a fresh topic is `is_default = 00` here
and was `01` on the line below. `Admin\ConfigEntry::$isDefault` is derived from the source for both versions, and
`Admin\Config::ownValues()` - not `nonDefaultValues()` - is the set a read-modify-write has to send back.

**Quirk: the derivation of a source from a version 0 answer is lossy.** A client that reads the old frame -
`DescribeConfigsResponse(Struct)` @ 1.1.1 and `DescribeConfigsResponseConfigEntry::source()` here - turns
`is_default = 01` into `DEFAULT_CONFIG` and everything else into the "configured" source of the resource type,
`TOPIC_CONFIG` for a topic and `STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG` for a broker. That is exactly wrong for the option this
container has: `segment.bytes` of a topic really is a `STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG` and is derived as `TOPIC_CONFIG`. Only
version 1 says which of the two it is, which is why this client sends it.

**Quirk: a topic that does not exist is answered with the DEFAULTS, not with an error.**
`AdminUtils.fetchEntityConfig` returns empty properties for a topic that has no ZooKeeper node, and the broker
merges those with its own log defaults - so describing `t4-probe-absent` answers the error code **0** and the full
default configuration. The api says nothing about whether a topic exists; Metadata and CreatePartitions do. (It does
not create the topic either.)

**Quirk: an option name the broker does not know is silently dropped.** `createResponseConfig` filters the values it
*has* by the requested names, so a request for `no.such.option` answers the error code 0 and an **empty** entry
list - there is no "unknown config" error in this api, unlike in AlterConfigs.

**Quirk: the answer is not in the order of the request.** The broker walks a Scala `Map`, both over the resources
and over the entries of one resource, so the two options of `describeconfigs.request.v0.broker` come back in the
opposite order. A client matches an entry by name and a resource by type and name, never by position.

**The default broker resource** - resource type 4 with an **empty** name - is the cluster-wide dynamic
configuration of KIP-226, stored in ZooKeeper under `/config/brokers/<default>`. Describing it answers the dynamic
default configuration **alone**, one entry per option that was set that way (`describeconfigs.response.v1.broker-default`),
and not the ~190 options a broker resource carries; every entry of it has the source 3. Any broker answers it,
because it is not the configuration of one process.

**Three things a 2.8.2 broker answers differently from a 1.1.1 one**, all of them in
`core/src/main/scala/kafka/server/ConfigHelper.scala`, which is where the release moved the code of
`AdminManager`:

* **a topic that does not exist is refused with the error code 3.** `describeConfigs()` asks the metadata cache
  (`if (metadataCache.contains(topic)) … else UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION`) before it reads anything, where a 1.1.1
  broker read the - empty - entity config of the topic out of ZooKeeper and answered the log defaults of the broker
  with the error code 0. The api now says something about existence, and `AdminClient::describeConfigs()` raises
  the exception of that code;
* **`is_read_only` of a BROKER entry no longer looks at the synonyms of the option**:
  `readOnly = !DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs.contains(name)`, where 1.1.1 tested the option **and** its
  synonyms (`!allNames.exists(…)`). `log.retention.hours` is read-only here and was writable there, although
  `log.retention.ms` is a dynamic config in both; an option that is itself dynamic - `log.cleaner.backoff.ms` -
  is writable;
* **the `is_default` boolean of a version 0 answer is always `false`.** The answer is built from the generated
  `DescribeConfigsResponseData` and nothing calls `setIsDefault()` any more, so the field keeps the `false` of the
  generator for every entry - an option the topic set itself and an untouched default alike. The client-side
  derivation of a source out of that boolean (`ConfigEntry::$source`) therefore answers `DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG` for
  everything at version 0; the source is only reliable from version 1 on.

**The image of this line sets one broker option more than the 1.1.1 one**: `log.message.format.version=2.8-IV1`.
It is the broker synonym of the topic option `message.format.version`, so every topic of the container reports
that option with the source `STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG` next to `segment.bytes` - two options that are not defaults
although the topic itself sets nothing.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 4** and changed no field at all: it is the **first flexible version** of this api
(`"flexibleVersions": "4+"` in `DescribeConfigsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2). The resource names, the option names, the
values, the synonyms and the documentation strings of KIP-569 are written compactly, the request carries the
header v2 and the answer the header v1, and the body, every resource, every entry and every synonym end in a
tagged-field section. The pair `describeconfigs.request.v4` / `describeconfigs.response.v4` at the end of this
document is that exchange with both booleans set - 59 bytes of request and 363 of answer for the one option
`retention.ms` of a topic, with its one synonym and its documentation string; `DescribeConfigsRequestV3` is the
plain frame of Kafka 2.6, which is what a client sends to any broker below 2.8.

## AlterConfigs API (key 33, v0 to v2)

Replaces the configuration of a topic or of a broker. The api arrived with Kafka **0.11** (KIP-133) and had
**v0** alone in every release of the 1.x line; what Kafka 1.1 changed is the broker, not the frame.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`ALTER_CONFIGS_REQUEST_V1 = ALTER_CONFIGS_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`alterconfigs.request.v1` / `alterconfigs.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `AlterConfigsRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.8.

**Kafka 2.3 deprecated this api** (KIP-339) in favour of **IncrementalAlterConfigs** (key 44): a request of this one
carries the WHOLE configuration a resource should have afterwards, so a client that wants to change a single
option has to describe the resource first, send everything back, and silently reset whatever another client
changed in between. `Admin.alterConfigs()` @ 2.8.2 carries the javadoc "@deprecated Since 2.3. Use
{@link #incrementalAlterConfigs(Map)}." The broker keeps serving both, and this client keeps both: a broker
below 2.3 has nothing else. See "IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)".

```
AlterConfigsRequest => [Resource] ValidateOnly
  Resource => ResourceType ResourceName [ConfigEntry]
    ResourceType => int8
    ResourceName => string
    ConfigEntry  => ConfigName ConfigValue
      ConfigName  => string
      ConfigValue => nullable string
  ValidateOnly => boolean
```

```
AlterConfigsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Resource]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Resource => ErrorCode ErrorMessage ResourceType ResourceName
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string
    ResourceType => int8
    ResourceName => string
```

The counterpart of DescribeConfigs, and the api that replaces `kafka-configs.sh --alter`. The resource entry is the
one of DescribeConfigs with the configuration in place of the filter, the answer entry is the one of DescribeConfigs
without the configuration, and `ConfigEntry` is the shared `CONFIG_ENTRY` schema - the same two fields the `configs`
array of a CreateTopics request carries, except that the value is declared **nullable** here.

**Any broker serves it.** `KafkaApis.handleAlterConfigsRequest` has no controller check at all: it hands the
resources to `AdminManager.alterConfigs`, which writes the topic node in ZooKeeper, and the brokers pick the change
up from there. That is the difference to CreateTopics, DeleteTopics and CreatePartitions, which only the active
controller answers.

**The entries are the WHOLE configuration, not a patch.** `AdminManager.alterConfigs` builds a fresh `Properties`
from them and calls `AdminUtils.changeTopicConfig` (or `changeBrokerConfig`), which **replaces** the ZooKeeper node
of the resource. Verified on the container: after setting `retention.ms` and `cleanup.policy` in one request, a
second request that names only `retention.ms` left the topic with `retention.ms` alone and `cleanup.policy` back at
its default; a request with an **empty** entry array resets every option of the resource. A caller that wants to
change one option reads the current configuration with DescribeConfigs and sends it back with that option changed,
which is what `Admin\Config::ownValues()` exists for.

`ValidateOnly` runs the validation and writes nothing; a validated request answers 0 and leaves the resource
untouched - and it does not turn a refusal into an acceptance either, a static broker option is answered with 42
with the flag set or not.

### The dynamic broker configuration (KIP-226)

**A 1.1 broker alters a broker resource, where a 0.11 broker refused every one of them** with 42 and
`AlterConfigs is only supported for topics, but resource type is BROKER` (the vectors
`alterconfigs.request.v0.broker-resource` and its answer are that refusal, captured on the 0.11.0.3 container and
kept as history; the message of a 1.1.1 broker says `topics and brokers`, and no request of the container reaches
it any more). The frame did not change at all - the same bytes that were refused are accepted now. What a client
has to know about the new resource:

* the resource `broker:<id>` is the live configuration of THAT broker and is only served by it: another broker
  answers 42 with `Unexpected broker id, expected 0 or empty string, but received …`, exactly like DescribeConfigs;
* the resource `broker:` - the resource type 4 with an **empty** name - is the cluster-wide default, stored under
  `/config/brokers/<default>` in ZooKeeper, which every broker of the cluster picks up. A per-broker value wins over
  it, and DescribeConfigs shows both as synonyms of the entry (the sources 2 and 3);
* only the options of `DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs` can be changed at runtime: the log-cleaner options,
  the thread pools, the metric reporters, the listeners, the SSL keystores and everything
  `LogConfig.TopicConfigSynonyms` maps a topic option to (with `log.message.format.version` excluded). Anything else
  is answered with 42 and `Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(…)`, which names the offending options;
* the security options of `DynamicSecurityConfigs` are per-broker only: sending `ssl.keystore.location` to the
  DEFAULT resource is answered with 42 and `These security configs can be dynamically updated only per-listener
  using the listener prefix: Set(ssl.keystore.location)`;
* the validation is per RESOURCE, not per option: one option the broker cannot update refuses the whole resource,
  and none of its entries is applied.

An accepted change takes effect immediately - `alterconfigs.request.v0.broker-dynamic` sets
`log.cleaner.backoff.ms`, and the DescribeConfigs v1 of the same connection already reports the new value with the
source 2 - and it survives a restart, because it lives in ZooKeeper and not in the `server.properties`.

**What the 4.3.1 node answers differently** (measured by `ConfigsApiTest` and `IncrementalConfigsApiTest`):

* **The default resource `broker:` is not empty any more.** The node finalizes `eligible.leader.replicas.version` 1
  (KIP-966), and the controller writes a cluster-level `min.insync.replicas` - its own value, 1 - into the metadata
  log before it enables the eligible leader replicas (`ConfigurationControlManager.maybeGenerateElrSafetyRecords()`
  @ 4.3.1). DescribeConfigs reports it on `broker:` with the source **3** `DYNAMIC_DEFAULT_BROKER_CONFIG`, and every
  topic without an option of its own reports its `min.insync.replicas` as that source - not a default.
* **An AlterConfigs of `broker:` that leaves the option out is refused as a whole**: the api replaces the whole
  resource, and the controller answers **40** `InvalidConfig` with `Cluster-level min.insync.replicas cannot be
  removed while ELR is enabled.` (and `ConfigurationControlManager` @ 4.3.1 refuses a per-broker one with `Broker-level
  min.insync.replicas cannot be altered while ELR is enabled.`). An IncrementalAlterConfigs of one option is what
  changes the default resource without touching the rest of it.
* **The option names of a refusal are a Java list**: `Cannot update these configs dynamically: [log.retention.hours]`
  where the 2.8.2 and the 3.9.2 brokers wrote the Scala `Set(log.retention.hours)`.
* **DescribeConfigs v0 is gone** (KIP-896, `"validVersions": "1-4"` @ 4.0.0): the node closes the connection of a
  version 0 frame. The classes and the vectors of the version 0 stay.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Name                       | Request that produces it                    | ErrorMessage                                                     |
|------|----------------------------|---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                       | The configuration was replaced or validated | `null`                                                            |
| -1   | Unknown                    | A topic that does not exist                 | `Topic "t5-no-such-topic" does not exist.`                        |
| -1   | Unknown                    | A `null` config value, for a topic and for a broker | `null`                                                    |
| 29   | TopicAuthorizationFailed   | The client may describe but not alter it    | `null`                                                            |
| 31   | ClusterAuthorizationFailed | The client may not alter a broker resource  | `null`                                                            |
| 40   | InvalidConfig              | An unknown option **name** of a topic       | `Unknown topic config name: no.such.option`                       |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | An unparsable option **value**              | `Invalid config value for resource Resource(type=TOPIC, name='t5-vectors'}: Invalid value soon for configuration retention.ms: Not a number of type LONG` |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A broker option that is not dynamic         | `Invalid config value for resource Resource(type=BROKER, name='0'}: Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(log.retention.hours)` |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A per-broker option on the default resource | `Invalid config value for resource Resource(type=BROKER, name='}'}: These security configs can be dynamically updated only per-listener using the listener prefix: Set(ssl.keystore.location)` |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A broker id that is not the one that answers| `Unexpected broker id, expected 0, but received Resource(type=BROKER, name='7'}.name` |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A resource type other than 2 and 4          | `Unexpected resource type GROUP`                                  |

**Quirk: an unknown option NAME of a BROKER resource is accepted and stored.** A topic is validated against
`LogConfig` and an unknown name is the error code 40; a broker resource is validated by
`DynamicBrokerConfig.validate()`, which only checks the names it KNOWS - the intersection with the non-dynamic
options, the security prefixes and the types - so `no.such.broker.option` passes the validation, is written into
`/config/brokers/0` and is answered with **0**. It has no effect whatever; it stays in ZooKeeper until something
removes it. Measured on the container while this section was written, and cleaned up again.

**Quirk: and DescribeConfigs reports that unknown option back as a secret.** `createBrokerConfigEntry()` cannot
determine the `ConfigDef.Type` of a name it does not know and "treats it as a sensitive config to be safe", so the
entry comes back with `is_sensitive = 01`, a **null** value, `read_only = 01` (no name of it is in
`AllDynamicConfigs`) and the source **2** - a dynamic broker config the broker itself cannot use.

**Quirk: an unparsable VALUE is 42 here and -1 in CreateTopics.** Both apis end in the same `ConfigException` of the
common config framework, which is not an `ApiException`; `AdminManager.createTopics` lets it fall through to
`Errors.forException`, which answers **-1**, while `AdminManager.alterConfigs` catches it explicitly and re-throws
it as an `InvalidRequestException` - so the same wrong value is **42** through AlterConfigs and **-1** through
CreateTopics. The message of the 42 quotes `Resource.toString()`, which opens with `(` and closes with `}`.

**Quirk: an unknown option NAME of a topic is 40, and its message changed with 0.11.** `LogConfig.validateNames`
throws Kafka's own `InvalidConfigurationException`, which is an `ApiException` and maps to 40 - the same code
CreateTopics answers, but the message reads `Unknown topic config name: no.such.option` where a 0.10.2.2 broker
said `Unknown Log configuration no.such.option.`.

**Quirk: a `null` config value is an NPE, reported as -1 with a null message.** The schema declares the value
nullable, but `AdminManager.alterConfigs` copies every entry into a `java.util.Properties` with
`setProperty(name, value)`, which throws a `NullPointerException` on a null - for a topic and for a broker alike.
The resource comes back with the error code **-1** and no message at all. An option is reset to its default by
**leaving it out** of the request, never by sending a null.

**Quirk: altering a topic that does not exist is -1, not 3.** `AdminUtils.changeTopicConfig` checks the topic first
and throws an `AdminOperationException`, which is not an `ApiException` either: the resource is answered with **-1**
and the message `Topic "…" does not exist.`.

**Altering a topic that does not exist is the error code 3**, not the -1 of a 1.1.1 broker:
`ZkAdminManager.alterTopicConfigs()` @ 2.8.2 throws `UnknownTopicOrPartitionException("The topic '…' does not
exist.")` before it touches ZooKeeper, and `ApiError.fromThrowable` maps it to **3** with that message, where a
1.1.1 broker let the same exception escape from `changeTopicConfig` as an unexpected one and reported it as the
**-1** of an unknown error. The message is the same in both releases.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 2** and changed no field: it is the first flexible version of this api
(`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` in `AlterConfigsRequest.json` @ 2.8.2), so the resource names, the option names and
the values are compact, the `validate_only` boolean keeps its place at the end of the body, and the body, every
resource and every entry end in a tagged-field section. The pair `alterconfigs.request.v2` /
`alterconfigs.response.v2` at the end of this document is the replacement of one topic option in that encoding;
`AlterConfigsRequestV1` and `AlterConfigsResponseV1` are the plain frames of Kafka 2.0, which every broker below
2.8 gets. The **whole-configuration** semantics of this api are untouched by the version - what replaces single
options is still IncrementalAlterConfigs.

## ElectLeaders API (key 43, v0 to v2)

Asks the **controller** to elect the leader of partitions. New in Kafka **2.2** (KIP-183), where it was called
**ElectPreferredLeaders** and could ask for one kind of election only; Kafka 2.4 renamed it to ElectLeaders and
added the **version 1** of KIP-460, whose flexible twin - the version 2 below - is what this line sends.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 2 as well** (KIP-482), the same fields in the flexible encoding: a compact topic
array of compact strings, a tag buffer in the request header and one at the end of the body, of every topic and of
every partition result. It is the version this client sends; `ElectLeadersRequestV1` / `ElectLeadersResponseV1`
are the frame of KIP-460 without it, and `…V0` the one of KIP-183.

```
ElectLeadersRequest => ElectionType [TopicPartitions] TimeoutMs
  ElectionType    => int8                     -- since version 1: 0 preferred, 1 unclean
  TopicPartitions => Topic [PartitionId]      -- NULLABLE array: null means every partition of the cluster
    Topic       => string
    PartitionId => int32
  TimeoutMs => int32
```

```
ElectLeadersResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [ReplicaElectionResults]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16                     -- since version 1
  ReplicaElectionResults => Topic [PartitionResult]
    Topic => string
    PartitionResult => PartitionId ErrorCode ErrorMessage
      PartitionId  => int32
      ErrorCode    => int16
      ErrorMessage => NULLABLE_STRING
```

The `election_type` byte is the **first** field of a version 1 request, in front of the topic array, and the
top-level `error_code` sits between the throttle time and the results of a version 1 answer. Nothing else changed;
`ElectLeadersRequestV0` and `ElectLeadersResponseV0` are the two frames without those fields, and a version 0
request is read by the broker as `ElectionType.PREFERRED`.

Until Kafka 2.2 a **preferred replica election** — moving the leadership of a partition back to the first broker of
its replica assignment — was `kafka-preferred-replica-election.sh` writing the ZooKeeper node
`/admin/preferred_replica_election`, exactly as a topic was created by writing to ZooKeeper before KIP-4. KIP-183
made it an api, and `kafka-leader-election.sh` of Kafka 2.4 speaks it.

**The active controller alone serves it.** `KafkaApis.handleElectReplicaLeader` @ 2.8.2 needs the ZooKeeper support
of the broker and hands the partitions to `ReplicaManager.electLeaders`, which asks the controller; a broker that is
not the controller answers **41** `NotController` on every partition. The container of this line runs a single
broker, so it is always the controller, and `AdminClient::electLeaders()` looks the controller up in the metadata
exactly like `createTopics()` does and repeats the request once when a partition comes back with the 41.

The **`TopicPartitions` array is nullable**, and the two shapes are answered differently:

* a **named** array asks for those partitions alone, and every one of them gets an entry in the answer — including
  the ones that need no election at all;
* a **null** array asks the controller to look at `metadataCache.getAllPartitions()`, and the answer then holds
  only the partitions that were really elected or really failed: "When performing elections across all of the
  partitions we should only return partitions for which there was an eleciton or resulted in an error. In other
  words, partitions that didn't need election because they ready have the correct leader are not returned to the
  client" — the handler drops every `ELECTION_NOT_NEEDED` from such an answer. Measured on the container, where
  every partition is led by its only replica: a null request is answered with an **empty** result array, 16 bytes
  of frame. It is a request for the whole cluster and it is never sent by a test of this repository, because the
  container is shared with the other suites of this line.

**Version 0 has no top-level error code.** `ElectLeadersResponse(throttleTimeMs, errorCode, results, version)`
@ 2.8.2 writes it only `if (version >= 1)`, so the 31 `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` of a client that may not `Alter`
the cluster reaches a version 0 client as that code on every partition it named. Everything else is per partition
anyway; `KafkaController.processReplicaLeaderElection` @ 2.8.2 produces:

| Code | Name                        | Measured message / meaning                                                |
|------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                        | The partition has a new leader now                                        |
| 3    | UnknownTopicOrPartition     | `The partition does not exist.` — measured on the container               |
| 17   | InvalidTopic                | `The topic is being deleted`                                              |
| 80   | PreferredLeaderNotAvailable | A `StateChangeFailedException` of a preferred election: the preferred replica is not in the ISR (an unclean election answers 83 `EligibleLeadersNotAvailable` instead, which needs version 1) |
| 84   | ElectionNotNeeded           | `Leader election not needed for topic partition.` — measured on the container for a partition whose leader is already its preferred replica |

**(3.x) The KRaft controller words the two 3s itself.** `ReplicationControlManager.electLeader` @ 3.9.2 answers
`No such topic as <topic>` for a topic it does not know and `No such partition as <topic>-<partition>` for a
partition index the topic does not have, where the row above - measured on the 2.8.2 ZooKeeper broker - carried the
generic `The partition does not exist.` of the error code. The **84** keeps its `Leader election not needed for
topic partition.`, and the condition behind it is the same `partition.hasPreferredLeader()` for a preferred and
`partition.hasLeader()` for an unclean election. → the "(3.x)" block of "Broker quirks and observations".

The **84** is worth a second look: the error code was added in Kafka 2.4, but a 2.8.2 broker answers it to a
**version 0** client as well — the per-partition codes are not translated for the older version, only the
top-level one is left out. A client of this api therefore has to know the codes 80, 83 and 84 whatever version it
sends. Their neighbours in `Errors.java` @ 2.8.2 belong elsewhere: **81** `GroupMaxSizeReached`
("The consumer group has reached its max size.", `group.max.size` of KIP-389) and **82** `FencedInstanceId` (the
static membership of KIP-345) are answers of the group membership apis and never appear here.

`TimeoutMs` is how long the controller waits for the elections to finish before it answers (60 seconds in the Java
client, and the default of `ElectLeadersRequest`).

**The two election types of KIP-460** (`ElectionType` of the Java client, `Admin\ElectionType` here) are the whole
content of the byte:

| Byte | Type | What the controller does |
|------|------|--------------------------|
| 0 | `PREFERRED` | Moves the leadership to the **preferred replica** - the first broker of the assignment - when that replica is in the ISR. The election of `auto.leader.rebalance.enable` and of KIP-183 |
| 1 | `UNCLEAN` | Makes the first **live** replica the leader of a partition that has no leader at all, accepting the loss of every record the old leader had and the new one has not. The emergency button of `kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type unclean` |

`KafkaController.processReplicaLeaderElection` @ 2.8.2 decides per partition which ones are *electable* at all,
and the two types ask different questions:

```scala
case ElectionType.PREFERRED => currentLeader != preferredReplica
case ElectionType.UNCLEAN   => currentLeader == LeaderAndIsr.NoLeader || !liveBrokerIds.contains(currentLeader)
```

everything else lands in `alreadyValidLeader` and is answered **84** `ElectionNotNeeded`. **Measured on the
container**: an unclean election of a partition that still has a live leader is therefore the very same 84 as a
preferred one - the type does not make the controller elect where nothing has failed - and an unknown topic is the
same 3 in both. The **83** `EligibleLeadersNotAvailable` is what an unclean election gets when the controller does
try and the `StateChangeFailedException` comes back ("Eligible topic partition leaders are not available."), i.e.
when the partition has no live replica either; a one-broker container cannot produce it, because the one broker
that would have to be dead is the one answering the request. It is documented from
`KafkaController.processReplicaLeaderElection` @ 2.8.2, which picks the code from the election type:

```scala
val error = if (electionType == ElectionType.PREFERRED) Errors.PREFERRED_LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE
            else Errors.ELIGIBLE_LEADERS_NOT_AVAILABLE
```

**The top-level error code of version 1 is 0 for everything that reaches the controller.**
`handleElectReplicaLeader` @ 2.8.2 builds the answer with `sendResponseCallback(ApiError.NONE)` on the normal path
and with the 31 `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` only when the authorizer refuses the client `Alter` on the cluster -
the one case in which the controller is never asked. Every measured answer of this document carries the 0, and
`Client::electLeaders()` throws for anything else, because such an answer names no partition to attach an error to.

`AdminClient::electLeaders()` takes an `Admin\ElectionType` for the kind of election and refuses a value that is
neither of the two with an `UnsupportedVersionException`.

## IncrementalAlterConfigs API (key 44, v0 and v1)

Changes **single options** of a topic or a broker. New in Kafka **2.3** (KIP-339), and the api that repairs the one
real defect of the AlterConfigs above it: that request carries the whole configuration a resource should have
afterwards, so a client that wants to change one option has to read the current configuration first, send it all
back, and lose whatever another client changed in between. This one names an operation per option and leaves every
option it does not mention exactly as it is.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 1** (KIP-482): the same fields of KIP-339 in the flexible encoding, and nothing
else. It is the version this client sends; `IncrementalAlterConfigsRequestV0` / `…ResponseV0` are the frame Kafka
2.3 introduced.

```
IncrementalAlterConfigsRequest => [resources] validate_only
  resources => resource_type resource_name [configs]
    resource_type => INT8
    resource_name => STRING
    configs       => name config_operation value
      name             => STRING
      config_operation => INT8
      value            => NULLABLE_STRING
  validate_only => BOOLEAN
```

```
IncrementalAlterConfigsResponse => throttle_time_ms [responses]
  throttle_time_ms => INT32
  responses        => error_code error_message resource_type resource_name
    error_code    => INT16
    error_message => NULLABLE_STRING
    resource_type => INT8
    resource_name => STRING
```

The answer is byte for byte the one of AlterConfigs, under another name (`responses` instead of `resources`); the
request differs in the entry of an option alone, which gained the `config_operation` byte between the name and the
value.

**The four operations** are `AlterConfigOp.OpType` @ 2.8.2, and `ZkAdminManager.prepareIncrementalConfigs`
applies them to the `Properties` of the resource before it validates the result as a whole:

| Byte | Operation | What it does |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| 0 | `SET` | `properties.setProperty(name, value)` |
| 1 | `DELETE` | `properties.remove(name)` — the option falls back to the value it **inherits** (the broker setting behind it, which is not always the documented default), and it is the **only** operation whose value may be null |
| 2 | `APPEND` | Adds the comma separated values to a **list** option, starting from its current value or, when it has none, from its default |
| 3 | `SUBTRACT` | Removes them from that list. Removing a value the list does not have changes nothing, and removing every value leaves the **empty** list instead of restoring the default |

Everything else is unchanged from the AlterConfigs section: any broker serves a topic resource, a `broker:<id>`
resource is served by that broker alone, `broker:` (the empty name) is the cluster-wide default of KIP-226, and
`validate_only` runs the whole validation without writing anything.

**What the broker answers.** `ZkAdminManager.incrementalAlterConfigs` @ 2.8.2 validates the whole resource before
it writes anything, and reports one error code per resource with the message of the exception it caught. Measured
on the container, on a topic of one partition:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `SET retention.ms=3600000`, `APPEND cleanup.policy=compact`, `DELETE segment.bytes` | **0**, no message; `cleanup.policy` reads back `delete,compact` (the APPEND started from the default `delete`) and `retention.ms` `3600000`, both with the source `DYNAMIC_TOPIC_CONFIG` |
| `SUBTRACT cleanup.policy=compact` | **0**; the option reads back `delete` again |
| `APPEND retention.ms=1000` — an option that is not a list | **42** `InvalidRequest`, `Config value append is not allowed for config key: retention.ms` |
| The same option twice in one resource | **42**, `Error due to duplicate config keys : retention.ms` |
| `SET` with a **null** value | **42**, `Null value not supported for : SET:retention.ms` |
| `SET not.an.option=1` | **40** `InvalidConfig`, `Unknown topic config name: not.an.option` |
| `APPEND not.an.option=1` | **-1** `Unknown`, and **no message at all** — see below |
| `SET retention.ms=999000` with `validate_only` | **0**, and the option keeps the value it had |
| The default broker resource, the static option `log.dirs`, `validate_only` | **42**, `Invalid config value for resource ConfigResource(type=BROKER, name=''): Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(log.dirs)` |
| The default broker resource, the dynamic option `log.retention.ms`, `validate_only` | **0** |

**The -1 of an APPEND to an option that does not exist** is a defect of `prepareIncrementalConfigs` @ 2.8.2 worth
knowing about, because a client cannot tell it from a broker that broke. Its `listType()` reads

```scala
val configKey = configKeys(configName)
if (configKey == null)
  throw new InvalidConfigurationException(s"Unknown topic config name: $configName")
```

— and `configKeys` is an immutable Scala `Map`, whose `apply` throws `NoSuchElementException` for a key it does
not hold, so the null check below it is dead code. That exception is neither a `ConfigException` nor an
`IllegalArgumentException`, so the catch block hands it to `ApiError.fromThrowable` unchanged and the resource is
answered with the unknown server error and a null message. A `SET` of the same name reaches the validation of the
whole `Properties` instead and is the proper **40** with `Unknown topic config name: not.an.option`.

**Which broker serves it** is what the AlterConfigs section says: a topic resource goes to any broker, a
`broker:<id>` resource only to that broker, and `broker:` (the empty name) is the cluster-wide default of KIP-226.
Only the options of `DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs` can be changed at runtime, and a resource that names
one that cannot is refused **as a whole**. This repository never really alters the broker of the container - it is
shared with the other suites of this line - so both broker frames above were sent with `validate_only`.

`IncrementalAlterConfigs` also accepts a **`BROKER_LOGGER`** resource (type id 8, KIP-412), whose "options" are
log4j logger names and whose values are log levels. It is a per-broker, in-memory change that ZooKeeper never sees,
`SET` and `DELETE` are the only operations it allows, and this client does not model the resource type - the
`ConfigResource` of this package knows the types a config api of Kafka 0.11 to 2.8 stores.

## DescribeLogDirs API (key 35, v0 to v4)

Reports what each **log directory** of one broker holds. The api arrived with Kafka **1.0** (KIP-113) as
version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`DESCRIBE_LOG_DIRS_REQUEST_V1 = DESCRIBE_LOG_DIRS_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`describelogdirs.request.v1` / `describelogdirs.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `DescribeLogDirsRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.6.

**Kafka 2.6 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api (`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` of
`DescribeLogDirsRequest.json` and `DescribeLogDirsResponse.json` @ 2.8.2), and it adds no field: the same two
structures in the compact encoding, with the request header v2 and a tagged-field section at the end of the
header, of every topic entry, of every partition entry, of every log directory and of the body. The nullable
`Topic` array of the request is the compact nullable one, so the `ff ff ff ff` that asks for **every** replica of
every directory becomes the single byte `00` and the whole request is 15 bytes.
`DescribeLogDirsRequestV1`/`DescribeLogDirsResponseV1` keep the frame of the versions 0 and 1, whose
vectors are replayed through them.

**Kafka 3.2 added the version 3**, and it is the *answer* that changed: "Version 3 is the same as version 2 (new
field in response)" of `DescribeLogDirsRequest.json` @ 3.2.3 and "Version 3 adds the top-level ErrorCode field" of
`DescribeLogDirsResponse.json` of the same tag. The new field is an `int16` between `throttle_time_ms` and
`log_dirs`, `"ignorable": true`, and it carries the refusal of the **whole** request, next to the per-directory
error codes the version 0 already had. It is the version this client sends;
`DescribeLogDirsRequestV2`/`DescribeLogDirsResponseV2` keep the frame of the version 2, whose vectors are replayed
through them.

**Kafka 3.3 added the version 4**, and again only the answer changed: "Version 4 is the same as version 2 (new
fields in response)" of `DescribeLogDirsRequest.json` @ 3.3.2 and "Version 4 adds the TotalBytes and UsableBytes
fields" of `DescribeLogDirsResponse.json` of the same tag - the two `int64` of **KIP-827**, `"ignorable": true`
with the default `-1`, at the **end of every directory entry**, behind its topics. They describe the *volume* the
directory sits on and not the directory itself: `LogManager.describeLogDirs` @ 3.9.2 fills them with
`File.getTotalSpace` and `File.getUsableSpace` of the directory, which is what makes "will this disk still take
the partition" answerable without a shell on the broker. It is the version this client sends;
`DescribeLogDirsRequestV3`/`DescribeLogDirsResponseV3` keep the frame of the version 3, whose vectors are replayed
through them. **No release of the 3.x line changes the request at all** - the three versions 2, 3 and 4 of it are
the same bytes with a different version field.

```
DescribeLogDirsRequest => [Topic]
  Topic => TopicName [PartitionId]        -- the Topic array is NULLABLE
    TopicName   => string
    PartitionId => int32
```

```
DescribeLogDirsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [LogDir]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16                 -- since version 3
  LogDir => ErrorCode LogDirPath [Topic] TotalBytes UsableBytes
    ErrorCode   => int16
    LogDirPath  => string
    Topic => TopicName [Partition]
      TopicName => string
      Partition => PartitionId Size OffsetLag IsFuture
        PartitionId => int32
        Size        => int64
        OffsetLag   => int64
        IsFuture    => boolean
    TotalBytes  => int64                  -- since version 4
    UsableBytes => int64                  -- since version 4
```

A Kafka broker may be given more than one data directory - `log.dirs` is a list - and every replica lives in exactly
one of them. Before KIP-113 that was invisible from outside: a client could not tell which disk a partition was on,
and could not ask for it to be moved. This api answers the first question and
"AlterReplicaLogDirs API (key 34, v0 to v2)" the second. The container of this repository runs with **two** of them,
`log.dirs=/tmp/kafka-logs,/tmp/kafka-logs-2`, which is what every observation below was measured on.

**The api is broker-local.** `KafkaApis.handleDescribeLogDirsRequest` @ 1.1.1 hands the partitions to the local
`ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs`, so a broker only ever answers for its own disks; an administrator asks each broker
of the cluster separately, which is why `Admin\AdminClient::describeLogDirs()` takes a **list of broker ids** and
returns a map keyed by them. Sending the request to another broker is not an error - it answers about *itself*.

**The request array is nullable, and its two empty shapes are opposites.** `null`
(`DescribeLogDirsRequest.isAllTopicPartitions`) asks for **every** replica of every directory, which is what the
Java admin client and `kafka-log-dirs.sh --describe` always send; an **empty array** asks for no replica at all. On
the container the difference is dramatic and both answers are documented as vectors: the empty array answers 64
bytes - the two directories with an empty topic array each - while the null array answered **235 207 bytes** for
the several thousand replicas the shared container held when the vectors were captured. Name the partitions when
they are known.

**A 2.8.2 broker ignores the selection altogether**, and that is what the version 2 frames of this document
measured: `KafkaApis.handleDescribeLogDirsRequest` @ 2.8.2 builds the answer from
`replicaManager.describeLogDirs(partitions)` only to group *every* log of the directory around it, so a request
that names one partition, a request with an empty array and a request with the null one are answered with the
same frame - 16 391 bytes and 581 replicas when the version 2 pair was captured, against the 64 bytes a 1.1.1
broker answered an empty array with. That is why `describelogdirs.response.v1` and `describelogdirs.response.v2`
are the two **constructed** vectors of this api: the captured answers with the topics of the other suites removed.
An empty array is therefore no longer the cheap "which disks does this broker have" of the 1.x line; the frame it
saves is in the request alone (23 bytes against 15 for the null one).

The answer always lists **every** directory of `log.dirs`, whether or not it holds anything of the request, and
only the replicas that really live in it. On the container the entries arrive in the order of `log.dirs` -
`ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs` maps over `config.logDirs.toSet`, and a Scala set of two elements iterates in
insertion order - but `kafka-log-dirs.sh` prints them in the order of a Java `HashMap`, which is another one
entirely, so a client keys the answer by the path and never by position. Its three per-replica fields come from
`ReplicaManager.describeLogDirs` as `new ReplicaInfo(log.size, getLogEndOffsetLag(…), log.isFuture)`:

| Field       | What the broker puts in it                                                                     |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Size`      | `Log.size`, the bytes of the **log segments** of this replica in this directory; the indexes are not counted, so the number is much smaller than what `du` says about the directory |
| `OffsetLag` | For the **current** log `max(highWatermark - logEndOffset, 0)` - 0 on a healthy leader, and 0 for every replica of the one-broker container. For a **future** log `logEndOffset(current) - logEndOffset(future)`, i.e. the records the mover still has to copy. `-1` (`DescribeLogDirsResponse.INVALID_OFFSET_LAG`) when the broker has no replica object for the partition at all |
| `IsFuture`  | `true` for the log an AlterReplicaLogDirs created and that `ReplicaAlterLogDirsThread` is filling |

Error codes observed and documented on the 1.1.1 container:

| Code | Name              | Where it appears                                                                  |
|------|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None              | Per directory: the disk is online and `Topic` is what it holds of the request       |
| 56   | KafkaStorageError | Per directory: the directory is configured but **offline**, and its topic array is empty |
| -1   | Unknown           | Per directory: any other failure while it was read                                  |

Up to the version 2 there is **no top-level error code**: a failure is always a property of one directory. The one
whole-answer case is authorization - a client that may not `Describe` the cluster resource gets an empty `LogDir`
array, which the Java admin client turns back into 31 (ClusterAuthorizationFailed).

**That guess is what the version 3 of Kafka 3.2 replaced with a field.** `KafkaApis.handleDescribeLogDirsRequest`
@ 3.9.2 asks the authorizer for `DESCRIBE` on `CLUSTER` before it reads the topics of the request and answers
`(List.empty, Errors.CLUSTER_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED)` when the answer is no, so the same refusal is

| Version | What the node answers the SASL user `acltest`, the one principal outside `super.users` |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 4       | `throttle_time_ms = 0`, **`error_code = 31`**, an empty `log_dirs` - 17 bytes, the very frame of the version 3 (`describelogdirs.response.v4.unauthorized`) |
| 3       | `throttle_time_ms = 0`, **`error_code = 31`**, an empty `log_dirs` - 17 bytes (`describelogdirs.response.v3.unauthorized`) |
| 2       | `throttle_time_ms = 0`, the empty compact `log_dirs` - 15 bytes, no code anywhere (`describelogdirs.response.v2.unauthorized`) |
| 0, 1    | the same answer in the plain encoding: 16 bytes, the four zero bytes of an empty array |

and only the version 3 and above can be told apart from a broker that has no log directory at all. A refusal never
carries a volume size either, at any version: the two fields of KIP-827 live **inside** a directory entry, and a
refused request has no directory entry at all.
`Admin\AdminClient::describeLogDirs()` sends the version 4 and raises that code as the exception of the whole
