**The authorizer filters the list silently.** `KafkaApis.handleListTransactionsRequest` @ 3.9.2 removes every
entry whose transactional id the principal may not `Describe` after the coordinator has built the answer, so a
principal without rights is answered the error code 0 and an **empty** list, not the 53 that DescribeTransactions
gives it. Measured as the SASL user `acltest`, which is not one of the `super.users` of the node: 0 transactions,
where `ANONYMOUS` on the PLAINTEXT listener saw all of them.

### The duration filter of KIP-994 (v1)

**Version 1 (Kafka 3.8) appends one int64 to the request and changes the answer in nothing at all.** "Version 1:
adds DurationFilter to list transactions older than specified duration" stands above the `validVersions` of
`ListTransactionsRequest.json` @ 3.8.1, and "Version 1 is the same as version 0 (KIP-994)" above those of the
answer: the field changed what the coordinator *selects*, not what it reports, which is why
`ListTransactionsResponseV0` and `ListTransactionsResponse` declare the same fields on this line and a frame of
either version is the same bytes.

**The filter is an age in milliseconds, and it is measured from the start of the transaction.**
`TransactionStateManager.listTransactionStates` @ 3.9.2 drops an entry while
`now - txnMetadata.txnStartTimestamp <= filterDurationMs`, so the comparison is strict - a filter of **0** lists
every transaction that has started at all - and the clock it reads is `txnStartTimestamp`, the moment the *current*
transaction opened. That timestamp is never cleared (see "DescribeTransactions API (key 65, v0)"), so a
`CompleteCommit` id is still selected by the age of the transaction it committed, not by the age of the commit.
A negative filter, which is the `"default": -1` of the field, is "every transaction"; a version 0 frame is
answered as if it carried that default, because `ListTransactionsRequestData.durationFilter()` gives it to every
request that cannot carry the field.

**An id that never began a transaction passes every duration filter there is.** Its `txnStartTimestamp` is the -1
of "no transaction has ever started", `now - (-1)` is larger than any value a client can put into the field, and
the `Empty` entry is therefore listed by a filter of 60000 that drops a transaction which is seconds old - the one
answer of this api that looks backwards. Measured on the node with the transactional ids `t1-38-txn-open` and
`t1-38-txn-empty`: the filter 0 lists both, the filter 60000 lists only the id that never started.

The three filters are ANDed by the coordinator, and the duration is applied last, after the state names have been
resolved and the producer ids compared. `Admin\AdminClient::listTransactions()` takes it as its fourth argument,
in milliseconds, and sends the version 1 frame with the -1 when no caller names one.

Error codes observed on the node:

| Code | Request that produces it |
|------|---------------------------|
| 0    | Always on a broker that serves the api - an empty answer is a filter that matched nothing, not an error |
| 14   | *(`CoordinatorLoadInProgress`, while a `__transaction_state` partition is being read; not producible without restarting the shared node)* |
| 15   | *(`CoordinatorNotAvailable`, while the coordinator of the broker is shutting down)* |
| 128  | `InvalidRegularExpression` — **(4.1, KIP-1152)** a version 2 `transactional_id_pattern` that RE2/J cannot compile; observed on the node |

### The transactional id pattern of KIP-1152 (v2)

**Version 2 (Kafka 4.1) appends a nullable string to the request and changes the answer in nothing but one code.**
"Version 2: adds TransactionalIdPattern to list transactions with the same pattern(KIP-1152)" stands above the
`validVersions` of `ListTransactionsRequest.json` @ 4.1.0, and "This API can return InvalidRegularExpression
(KIP-1152)" above those of the answer. `ListTransactionsRequestV1` and `ListTransactionsResponseV1` keep the
frames below it; `Admin\AdminClient::listTransactions()` sends the version 2 and takes the pattern as its fifth
argument, the `ListTransactionsOptions.filterOnTransactionalIdPattern()` of the Java client.

**The pattern is RE2/J, and it has to match the whole id.** `TransactionStateManager.listTransactionStates` @ 4.1.0
compiles it with `com.google.re2j.Pattern` - the engine of the regex subscription of KIP-848, not
`java.util.regex` - and keeps a transaction while `pattern.matcher(transactionalId).matches()`: a prefix without a
wildcard matches nothing, and a construct RE2 does not have (a lookahead `(?=…)`) is as invalid as an unclosed
group. A null or empty pattern is not applied at all. The pattern is the fourth filter, ANDed with the other three,
and a pattern that does not compile is the top-level **128** (`InvalidRegularExpression`, Kafka 4.0) with an empty
list; the coordinator writes a message for it (`Transaction ID pattern … is not a valid regular expression: …`),
which the answer has no field for.

Measured on the node with the transactional ids `t1-41-vectors-a` and `t1-41-vectors-b`, each after one
`InitProducerId` (the state `Empty`):

| Pattern | Answer |
|---|---|
| `t1-41-vectors-.*` | both ids, code 0 |
| `t1-41-vectors` | no id, code 0 - the whole id has to match |
| `t1-41-(vectors` | no id, top-level **128** |
| null, and the producer id of `t1-41-vectors-a` | that one id |
| the same question at **version 1**, with a pattern the caller named | that one id: the version 1 frame has no field for the pattern |

## Client metrics (KIP-714) — wire only

Three api keys of Kafka **3.7** let a broker collect the metrics of its **clients**: 71
`GetTelemetrySubscriptions` asks what to measure, 72 `PushTelemetry` delivers it, and 74
`ListClientMetricsResources` names the subscriptions an operator has written. All three are flexible from v0, all
three are `"listeners": ["broker"]`, and all three exist in this package as **classes and vectors only** — there
is no client method, no telemetry emitter and no OpenTelemetry encoder, by decision of the owner. A PHP process
that lives for the length of one request has nothing to report over a 300-second push interval, and the payload
of the api is an OpenTelemetry `MetricsData` protobuf message, which is a dependency of its own. **(4.x)** The
key 74 is the exception since Kafka 4.1: its version 1 lists every configuration resource of the cluster, not only
the subscriptions, and `Admin\AdminClient::listConfigResources()` sends it (see "The config resources of KIP-1142
(v1)").

The subscription is a **configuration resource**: `kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092
--entity-type client-metrics --entity-name <name>` writes a `metrics` prefix list, an `interval.ms` between 100
and 3600000, and a `match` list of client properties (`client_id`, `client_instance_id`, `client_software_name`,
`client_software_version`, `client_source_address`, `client_source_port`). `ClientMetricsManager` @ 3.9.2 keeps
them in memory, matches every client instance against them and hands what it collects to a
`ClientMetricsReceiverPlugin`. **The node of this line has no such plugin**, which is why the rows of 71 and 72 are
missing from its ApiVersions answer (`ApiVersionManager` filters them while
`ClientMetricsManager.isTelemetryReceiverConfigured()` is false) — and why every frame below could still be
captured: the apis are *hidden*, not switched off, and 74 is not even hidden. A push is accepted and dropped.

The vectors of the three sections were captured with the client id `kafka-client-t1-37` and the `client-metrics`
resource `t1-37-metrics` (`metrics=org.apache.kafka.producer.`, `interval.ms=5000`,
`match=client_id=kafka-client-t1-37`), which was removed from the node again afterwards.

### GetTelemetrySubscriptions API (key 71, v0)

What the broker wants this client instance to measure. New in Kafka **3.7** (KIP-714), **v0**, flexible from that
version.

```
GetTelemetrySubscriptionsRequest => ClientInstanceId
  ClientInstanceId => uuid          (16 raw bytes; the ZERO uuid on the first request)
```

```
GetTelemetrySubscriptionsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ClientInstanceId SubscriptionId
                                     [AcceptedCompressionTypes] PushIntervalMs TelemetryMaxBytes
                                     DeltaTemporality [RequestedMetrics]
  ThrottleTimeMs           => int32
  ErrorCode                => int16
  ClientInstanceId         => uuid                     (the assigned id, or the zero uuid)
  SubscriptionId           => int32
  AcceptedCompressionTypes => compact array of int8    (the ids of `CompressionType`)
  PushIntervalMs           => int32
  TelemetryMaxBytes        => int32
  DeltaTemporality         => boolean
  RequestedMetrics         => compact array of compact string
```

**The whole request is one uuid**, and a client that has none sends the zero one — `"must be set to 0 on the first
request"`. The answer then carries the id the broker generated (`"Assigned client instance id if ClientInstanceId
was 0 in the request, else 0"`), and the client repeats it in every request from then on, this api's own included.
An instance lives in an LRU cache of 16384 entries for **60 seconds** without traffic.

Measured on the node, for an instance no `client-metrics` resource matches: the code **0**, a fresh uuid, a
**non-zero** `subscription_id` — it is the CRC-32C of the subscription xor the hash code of the instance id, so
"nothing subscribed" is a number like any other and never a sentinel — the four codecs `04 03 01 02` (zstd, lz4,
gzip, snappy, in the order `ClientMetricsManager.SUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPES` lists them), the **300000 ms** of
`ClientMetricsConfigs.DEFAULT_INTERVAL_MS`, the **1048576** bytes of `telemetry.max.bytes`, `delta_temporality`
**true** and an **empty** `requested_metrics`. The last one is the subscription itself: an empty array means *no
metric at all*, while an array holding a single empty string would mean *every* metric.

With the resource `t1-37-metrics` in place, the same first request is answered the **5000 ms** of its
`interval.ms` and the one prefix `org.apache.kafka.producer.`, and a client id its `match` does not cover is
answered the empty subscription again — the client id of the **request header** is what the broker matches, and
nothing of the body says who is asking.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Request that produces it                                                        |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Any first request, and any later one after the push interval has passed          |
| 89   | `ThrottlingQuotaExceeded` — a second request for the same instance **inside** the push interval. The refusal is built by `getErrorResponse`, so every other field is the default of its schema: the **zero** uuid, the subscription id 0, no codec, no interval, no limit, `delta_temporality = false`. **(4.x)** Only on the connection the instance was created on: see "The client instance lives on its connection (Kafka 4.0)" |

### PushTelemetry API (key 72, v0)

The metrics of one client instance. New in Kafka **3.7** (KIP-714), **v0**, flexible from that version.

```
PushTelemetryRequest => ClientInstanceId SubscriptionId Terminating CompressionType Metrics
  ClientInstanceId => uuid
  SubscriptionId   => int32
  Terminating      => boolean
  CompressionType  => int8            (the id of `CompressionType`, 0 = none)
  Metrics          => compact bytes   (OpenTelemetry `MetricsData` v1, protobuf)
```

```
PushTelemetryResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
```

**The answer is a throttle time, an error code and the two tag buffers**: twelve bytes behind the size field,
among the shortest this protocol has (a DescribeQuorum that names no topic is nine). The broker says nothing about what it did with the payload; everything a client
needs to do next is in the subscription it already has.

`ClientMetricsManager.validatePushRequest` @ 3.9.2 checks in this order, and the vectors follow it: the instance
must not have sent a `terminating` push before (**42**), the push must be outside the interval unless it is
terminating (**89**), the `subscription_id` must be the one of the instance (**117**), the codec must be one of
the four (**76**), and the blob must fit `telemetry.max.bytes` (**118**). The **zero** client instance id is
refused **42** before any of that, so a client that pushes before it has asked for an id gets no hint that it
should.

**A node without a receiver plugin answers 0.** The manager hands the blob to `receiverPlugin.exportMetrics` only
when it is non-empty, and an empty plugin list exports nothing, so both an empty push and a two-byte one are
accepted on this container. Nothing reads the payload on the way: the api never parses it, and the bytes of the
vector below are not valid `MetricsData` at all.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Request that produces it                                                        |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | A push of a known instance with its own subscription id — with or without a plugin behind it |
| 42   | `InvalidRequest` — the **zero** client instance id, or any push that follows a `terminating` one on the same instance (`Client [<uuid>] sent the previous request with state terminating to TRUE, can not accept any requests after that`); **(4.x)** the latter only on the connection of the instance |
| 76   | `UnsupportedCompressionType` — a `compression_type` that is no `CompressionType`; measured with the byte 7 |
| 89   | `ThrottlingQuotaExceeded` — a second push inside the push interval, unless it is `terminating` |
| 117  | `UnknownSubscriptionId` — **(3.7)** a `subscription_id` that is not the one of the instance. It is also how the broker says that the subscription has **changed**: the client asks key 71 again |
| 118  | `TelemetryTooLarge` — **(3.7)** a blob above `telemetry.max.bytes`. Observed on the node with 1048577 bytes, which is one byte over what its answer of key 71 promises; it is **not** stored as a vector, because the smallest frame that produces it is a megabyte |

### ListClientMetricsResources API (key 74, v0 and v1)

The names of the client-metrics subscriptions of the cluster. New in Kafka **3.7** (KIP-714), **v0**, flexible
from that version; its **v1** is Kafka **4.1** (KIP-1142), which made it `ListConfigResources` (see "The config
resources of KIP-1142 (v1)").

```
ListClientMetricsResourcesRequest => [ResourceTypes]
  ResourceTypes => int8        (since version 1; version 0 has no field at all)
```

```
ListClientMetricsResourcesResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [ClientMetricsResources]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ClientMetricsResources => Name ResourceType
    Name         => compact string
    ResourceType => int8       (since version 1, "default": 16)
```

**The request has no body at all**: `"fields": []` in the specification, so the frame is the request header v2
and the tag buffer of the body — the question is the api key itself. Two older apis have empty-bodied *versions*,
ApiVersions v0 to v2 and ListGroups v0 to v3, both below their first flexible version, and both grew fields
later; this is a flexible frame that carries nothing but its two tag buffers, one byte less than the single
boolean of DescribeCluster v0.

It answers **names only**, the entity names of the `client-metrics` configuration resources; what a subscription
contains is read with DescribeConfigs (32) on the resource type `CLIENT_METRICS`, which this client does not
speak. Unlike 71 and 72 the key **is** listed in the ApiVersions answer of the node, plugin or no plugin.

Error codes observed on the container:

| Code | Request that produces it                                                        |
|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Always, with an empty array while no `client-metrics` resource exists            |
| 31   | `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` — a principal without `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on the cluster; `KafkaApis.handleListClientMetricsResources` @ 3.9.2 checks that operation first. **(4.x)** Observed on the 4.3.1 node with the SASL user `acltest` (`listclientmetricsresources.response.v1.unauthorized`) |
| 35   | `UnsupportedVersion` — **(4.1, KIP-1142)** a version 1 `resource_types` with a type the broker does not support; observed with the bytes 0, 3 and 99 |

### The config resources of KIP-1142 (v1)

**Kafka 4.1 renamed the api and widened its question.** The specifications of the key 74 are
`ListConfigResourcesRequest.json` and `ListConfigResourcesResponse.json` @ 4.1.0: "Version 0 is used as
ListClientMetricsResourcesRequest which only lists client metrics resources. Version 1 adds ResourceTypes field
(KIP-1142). If there is no specified ResourceTypes, it should return all configuration resources." and "Version 1
adds ResourceType to ConfigResources (KIP-1142)". The version 1 names every resource a DescribeConfigs could be
asked about, with the byte of its `ConfigResource.Type` @ 4.1.0: **2** topic, **4** broker, **8** broker logger,
**16** client metrics and **32** group - not the ACL resource types, whose group is the 3. The published classes keep
their name (`ListClientMetricsResourcesRequest`/`Response`, with the constants `RESOURCE_TYPE_*`);
`ListClientMetricsResourcesRequestV0`/`ResponseV0` and `Data\ClientMetricsResourceV0` keep the version 0, and
`Admin\AdminClient::listConfigResources()` is `Admin.listConfigResources()` of the Java client @ 4.1.0.

**The answer of a version 1 request is a list, not a map.** `KafkaApis.handleListConfigResources` @ 4.3.1 appends
the groups with a configuration of their own, the client-metrics subscriptions, the broker loggers, the brokers and
the topics of the answering broker, in that order, for every type the request names - an empty type list is every
type of `ListConfigResourcesRequest.supportedResourceTypes()`, the five above at version 1 and `CLIENT_METRICS` alone
at version 0 - so the same broker id comes back once as a broker and once as a broker logger. A type outside that
set is refused as a whole with the **35** (`UnsupportedVersion`), and a principal without `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` on the
cluster with the 31, as at version 0.

Measured on the node, with the client-metrics resource `t1-41-metrics` and a configuration of the group
`t1-41-config-group` written for the capture and removed again afterwards:

| `resource_types` | Answer |
|---|---|
| none (empty) | the group, the subscription, the broker logger `1`, the broker `1` and every topic of the node |
| `2` | every topic of the node, the internal ones included (`__consumer_offsets`, `__transaction_state`, `__share_group_state`) |
| `4`, `8` | `1` as a broker logger and `1` as a broker |
| `16`, `32` | `t1-41-config-group` (32) and `t1-41-metrics` (16) |
| `0`, `3` or `99` | **35**, no resource |
| `16`, as the SASL user `acltest` | **31**, no resource |
| version 0 | `t1-41-metrics`, keyed by its name, without a type |

### The client instance lives on its connection (Kafka 4.0)

**A 4.x broker forgets a client instance when the connection it was created on closes.** `ClientMetricsManager` @
4.0.0 keeps a map from the connection id of the request that created an instance to the instance id, and its
`ClientConnectionDisconnectListener` removes the instance from the cache - and unregisters its metrics - when the
network layer reports that connection closed; `ClientMetricsManager` @ 3.9.2 had neither, and kept an instance for
its whole cache lifetime whatever happened to the connection. An instance id the manager does not hold is served
like a new instance: the manager creates it again under the id the request names.

Measured on the 4.3.1 node, each case with a fresh instance:

| Sequence | Answer on 4.3.1 | Answer on 3.9.2 |
|---|---|---|
| key 71, then key 71 with the id, on the **same** connection | **89** | 89 |
| key 71 on a connection, then key 71 with the id on a **second** connection while the first is open | **89** | 89 |
| key 71 on a connection, the connection closed, key 71 with the id on a new one | **0**, the same id and the same subscription id | 89 |
| key 71 and a `terminating` push on a connection, then a push on the **same** connection | **42** | 42 |
| key 71 and a `terminating` push on a connection, the connection closed, a push on a new one | **0** | 42 |

The close reaches the manager through the network thread of the broker a moment after the client closed its
socket, so a request on the new connection may still find the old instance for a few milliseconds. A Java client
keeps one connection per broker for its lifetime and never notices; a client that opens a connection per request -
which is what the `ClientMetricsApiTest` of the 3.x line did - sees the answers of the 3.9.2 column turn into
those of the 4.3.1 one, and every request of that class now travels over one connection per test.

## DescribeTopicPartitions API (key 75, v0)

The topics of a cluster, **page by page**, with the eligible leader replicas of KIP-966 next to every partition.
New in Kafka **3.8**, **v0**, flexible from that version, served by any **broker** (a KRaft controller does not
serve it). It is the api `kafka-topics.sh --describe` speaks since 3.8 and the one behind
`Admin.describeTopics(Collection<String>)` of the Java client; this package sends it from
`Admin\AdminClient::describeTopicPartitions()`.

```
DescribeTopicPartitionsRequest => [Topics] ResponsePartitionLimit Cursor
  Topics => Name
    Name => compact string
  ResponsePartitionLimit => int32                  -- default 2000
  Cursor => TopicName PartitionIndex               -- NULLABLE STRUCT: one int8, -1 = null, 1 = present
    TopicName      => compact string
    PartitionIndex => int32
```

```
DescribeTopicPartitionsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Topics] NextCursor
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Topics => ErrorCode Name TopicId IsInternal [Partitions] TopicAuthorizedOperations
    ErrorCode  => int16
    Name       => compact nullable string
    TopicId    => uuid (16 raw bytes)
    IsInternal => boolean
    Partitions => ErrorCode PartitionIndex LeaderId LeaderEpoch [ReplicaNodes] [IsrNodes]
                  [EligibleLeaderReplicas] [LastKnownElr] [OfflineReplicas]
      ErrorCode              => int16
      PartitionIndex         => int32
      LeaderId               => int32              -- -1 while the partition has no leader
      LeaderEpoch            => int32
      ReplicaNodes           => compact array of int32
      IsrNodes               => compact array of int32
      EligibleLeaderReplicas => compact array of int32, nullable
      LastKnownElr           => compact array of int32, nullable
      OfflineReplicas        => compact array of int32
    TopicAuthorizedOperations => int32
  NextCursor => TopicName PartitionIndex           -- NULLABLE STRUCT, as in the request
```

**The `cursor` is the first *nullable structure* of this protocol**, and it is encoded unlike every other nullable
field of it. A nullable string and a nullable array announce their absence in their own length - the compact `00`
of KIP-482, the int32 `-1` below it - but a structure has no length to borrow, so `MessageDataGenerator` @ 3.9.2
writes an **int8 in front of it**: `ff` (-1) for null, `01` for "a structure follows", and the structure that
follows still ends in its own tagged-field section. `Protocol\NullableStruct` is that marker in the schema engine
of this package, and the request of this api is the only place a client fills it.

**An empty topic array means every topic of the cluster**, the internal ones included - the opposite of what an
empty array means in nearly every other api of this protocol, and the same as the *null* topic array of Metadata.
`DescribeTopicPartitionsRequestHandler` @ 3.9.2 reads `fetchAllTopics` straight off `request.topics().isEmpty()`.

**The answer is sorted by topic name, and the order of the request is lost.** The handler sorts the names before it
asks the metadata cache, which is what makes the cursor a stable position at all: a page can only be resumed if
the sequence it walks does not move. A client that pages therefore has to merge the answers by name, and
`Admin\AdminClient::describeTopicPartitions()` does exactly that, indexing its result by the topic name.

**How the page ends.** `KRaftMetadataCache.getTopicMetadataForDescribeTopicResponse` @ 3.9.2 counts the partitions
it has written down and stops in one of two places:

* in the **middle of a topic** whose partitions did not fit, where the `next_cursor` names that topic and the
  **first partition that is missing**, never the last one that was delivered;
* in **front of a topic** that did not fit at all, where the cursor names that topic and the partition **0**.

A `next_cursor` of `null` is "the listing is complete", and the last page of a walk is byte for byte the shape of
an answer that never had to page. The `response_partition_limit` is clamped into
`[1, max.request.partition.size.limit]` (**2000** by default, which is also the default of the field itself), so
the limit **0** is a page of one partition and a limit of a million is a page of two thousand - a request can
neither ask for nothing nor for everything.

**Four shapes of a cursor, and what the node does with them.**

| Cursor | Answer |
|--------|--------|
| `null` | The listing starts at the first topic of the (sorted) request |
| A topic the request does not name (while it names any topic at all) | **42** `InvalidRequest` |
| A partition index below zero | **42** `InvalidRequest` |
| A partition index past the end of its topic | The code **0** with an **empty** partition array |

The 42 is not a top-level code - this api has none - but one entry **per requested topic**, with the zero topic
id, no partition and the `-2147483648` of "no acl bit field": `DescribeTopicPartitionsRequest.getErrorResponse`
@ 3.9.2 builds the error answer by naming every topic of the request with the code.

**`topic_authorized_operations` is reported without being asked.** The request has no
`include_topic_authorized_operations` flag as Metadata v8 has; the handler fills the bit field of KIP-430 for every
entry it answers, so the value is the one of the principal and never the `Integer.MIN_VALUE` of "you did not ask".
`ANONYMOUS` on the PLAINTEXT listener of this node is answered **3576**, and even the entry of a topic the cluster
does not host carries it. The entries that carry `-2147483648` are the *refused* ones - the 29 and the 42 - which
the handler builds without going near the authorizer a second time.

**The ELR fields of KIP-966 are the reason the api exists, and this node answers them empty.** Both are
`"nullableVersions": "0+"` with the default `null`, but the KRaft node writes `Replicas.toList(partition.elr)`,
which turns the empty replica array of the metadata image into an **empty list**: every partition of this node
carries the compact `01` of a zero-length array in `eligible_leader_replicas` and in `last_known_elr`, whatever
`eligible.leader.replicas.version` is. The two arrays are the set of replicas that were in the ISR when the
partition last lost its leader and may therefore be elected without losing an acknowledged write, and the set of
the election before it.

**The authorizer hides a topic in two different ways.** A topic that was **named** by a principal that may not
`Describe` it is answered **29** (`TopicAuthorizationFailed`) with the zero id, no partition and no bit field, and
the refused entries are appended **behind** the sorted ones, because the handler collects them in a set of their
own. A request with the **empty** topic array is answered the topics the principal may see and nothing about the
rest: the SASL user `acltest`, which may describe no topic of this node, is answered the twelve-byte frame of an
empty topic array and a null cursor, not a refusal - "we do not disclose the existence of topics unauthorized for
Describe", as the handler puts it.

**The empty topic name is the one frame of this api a 3.9.2 node cannot answer.** It is a legal frame and no legal
topic, and instead of the 17 that `Topic.validate` would give it the client is answered **-1**
(`UnknownServerError`): the handler compares the name with the empty default of the cursor topic name, finds them
equal, and dereferences the cursor that is `null`. The node logs the `NullPointerException` of
`DescribeTopicPartitionsRequestHandler.lambda$handleDescribeTopicPartitionsRequest$3`. A name that is merely
illegal - `t1 38 bad!` - is the **17** the code exists for.

Error codes observed on the node:

| Code | Where | Request that produces it |
|------|-------|---------------------------|
| 0    | per topic | The topic exists and the principal may describe it - an empty partition array is a cursor past the end, not an error |
| 3    | per topic | A topic the cluster does not host, named by the request |
| 17   | per topic | A name that is not a legal topic name (`Topic.validate` @ 3.9.2) |
| 29   | per topic | A topic the principal may not `Describe` - measured as the SASL user `acltest` |
| 42   | per topic, for every topic of the request | A cursor that names a topic the request does not, or a negative partition index |
| -1   | per topic, for every topic of the request | The topic whose name is the empty string, i.e. the `NullPointerException` above |

## DescribeShareGroupOffsets API (key 90, v0 and v1)

Reads the **share-partition start offsets** of share groups. New in Kafka **4.1** (KIP-932,
`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsRequest.json` @ 4.1.0, `"validVersions": "0"`), a `broker` listener api, **flexible from its
version 0**. **Kafka 4.2 added the version 1**, which puts the share-partition `lag` of KIP-1226 into the answer —
see "The share-partition lag of KIP-1226 (v1)" below; the grammar here is the version 0.

```
DescribeShareGroupOffsets Request (Version: 0) => [Groups] TAG_BUFFER
  Groups => GroupId [Topics] TAG_BUFFER
    GroupId => compact_string
    Topics  => compact_nullable_[ TopicName [Partitions] TAG_BUFFER ]   -- null: every partition of the group
      TopicName  => compact_string
      Partitions => compact_[int32]
```

```
DescribeShareGroupOffsets Response (Version: 0) => ThrottleTimeMs [Groups] TAG_BUFFER
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Groups => GroupId [Topics] ErrorCode ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER
    GroupId      => compact_string
    Topics       => compact_[ TopicName TopicId [Partitions] TAG_BUFFER ]
      TopicName  => compact_string
      TopicId    => uuid
      Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex StartOffset LeaderEpoch ErrorCode ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER ]
        PartitionIndex => int32
        StartOffset    => int64
        LeaderEpoch    => int32
        ErrorCode      => int16
        ErrorMessage   => compact_nullable_string
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => compact_nullable_string
```

A share group has no committed offset per member - its members acknowledge records one by one - so what describes
where the group stands in a partition is the **start offset**, the first offset the group is not done with, which
the share coordinator keeps in `__share_group_state`. The request goes to the **group coordinator** of every group
(FindCoordinator with the key type 0), which reads the state from the share coordinator with a
`ReadShareGroupStateSummary` (key 87) before it answers. There is **no top-level error code**: every group carries
its own **behind** its topics.

**What the node answers** (captured with the client id `kafka-client-t4-41`, the topic `t4-41-vectors` of two
partitions and the share group `t4-41-vectors-share`, whose start offsets an AlterShareGroupOffsets had set to 3 and 0):

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| the share group, a **null** topic array | every partition the group holds state for: **3** and **0**, the leader epoch 0, the code 0 — `describesharegroupoffsets.response.v0` |
| named partitions: one the group holds, one of a topic the node does not have, one of a group that does not exist | the start offset 3, and the **-1** "uninitialized offset" with the code 0 for the other two (the missing topic with the zero uuid) — `describesharegroupoffsets.response.v0.named` |
| a null topic array for a group that does not exist | an empty topic array and the code **0** — `describesharegroupoffsets.response.v0.no-state` |
| an empty topic array | an empty topic array and the code 0, answered by `KafkaApis` without asking the coordinator |
| a group of the **classic** protocol, null or named | the same empty array or -1, code 0 |

`GroupCoordinatorService.describeShareGroupOffsets()` @ 4.3.1 treats absent state as "absence of data, rather than
an error ... consistent with OffsetFetch", so the **69** `GroupIdNotFound` the specification lists is not what a
missing group gets from this api on the node. **Quirk: a partition beyond the partition count of a topic is not
refused, it is asked for** — the share coordinator retries the read of a state that cannot exist until its
retries are exhausted ("Exhausted max retries for read state summary RPC" in the log of the node), and the answer
arrives **31 seconds** later with the -1.

`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsRequest`/`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsResponse` with the `Data` classes
`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsRequestGroup`, `…RequestTopic`, `…ResponseGroup`, `…ResponseTopic` and
`…ResponsePartition` are wire classes of this line; the admin methods over them (`listShareGroupOffsets()`) belong
to the share-consumer wave.

### The share-partition lag of KIP-1226 (v1)

**Kafka 4.2 added the version 1**: *"Version 1 introduces Lag in the response (KIP-1226)"*
(`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsRequest.json` and the response file @ 4.2.0, `"validVersions": "0-1"`). The request does
not change; every partition of the answer gets one `int64` between the leader epoch and the error code:

```
DescribeShareGroupOffsets Response (Version: 1) => ThrottleTimeMs [Groups] TAG_BUFFER
  ...
      Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex StartOffset LeaderEpoch Lag ErrorCode ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER ]
        Lag => int64   -- "ignorable", default -1: the records of the partition the group has not finished with
```

The group coordinator computes it when it answers: it reads the start offset and the **delivery-complete count** of
the partition from the share coordinator (`ReadShareGroupStateSummary`, whose version 1 of the same release carries
that count), asks the leader for the end offset of the partition and answers `end offset - start offset -
delivery-complete count` (`GroupCoordinatorService.computeShareGroupLagAndBuildResponse()` @ 4.3.1). The count is
the number of records **past** the start offset that the group is done with — accepted, rejected, or archived after
too many deliveries — so the lag is what the group still has to deliver: the available, acquired and released
records from the start offset to the end. A partition whose read fails, whose start offset is not initialized or
whose count is not known gets the **-1** (`PartitionFactory.UNINITIALIZED_LAG`), and so does every partition of a
version 0 answer, which has no field for it.

**Measured with real share traffic** (the client id `kafka-client-t4-42`, the topic `t4-42-vectors` of one partition
with ten records, the share group `t4-42-vectors-share` with `share.auto.offset.reset=earliest`, one member that
acquired the ten records with `Client::shareFetch()` and acknowledged them with `Client::shareAcknowledge()`):

| State of the partition | Start offset | Lag |
|---|---|---|
| the ten records acquired, none acknowledged | -1 | **-1**: no start offset in the state the share coordinator returns yet |
| 0-3 and 6-7 accepted | 0 | **4**: 10 - 0 - 6; the start offset the coordinator keeps did not move yet |
| then 4, 5 and 9 released and 8 rejected | **4** | **3**: 10 - 4 - 3, the released 4, 5 and 9 — `describesharegroupoffsets.response.v1` |
| then two more records produced | 4 | **5**: the lag follows the end offset |
| the member closes its share session and leaves | 4 | 5: the state outlives the member |
| a group whose start offset only AlterShareGroupOffsets set, to 3 | 3 | **9**: 12 - 3, a count of 0 |
| a group that does not exist, a named partition | -1 | **-1**, code 0 — `describesharegroupoffsets.response.v1.named` |
| the same group asked with the version 0 | the same | not on the wire; `DescribeShareGroupOffsetsResponsePartition::$lag` stays -1 |

The start offset the share coordinator returns does not follow every acknowledgement: after the first one it still
said 0 - the ten records had been acquired as one batch - while the lag was already 4, and it moved to 4 with the
second. The lag is the same number either way, because the count of completed records is taken from that start
offset: what the start offset does not cover yet, the count does.

`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsRequest`/`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsResponse` are the version 1 and
`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsResponsePartition::$lag` carries the lag; `DescribeShareGroupOffsetsRequestV0`/
`DescribeShareGroupOffsetsResponseV0`, with the entries `DescribeShareGroupOffsetsResponseGroupV0`, `…TopicV0` and
`…PartitionV0`, keep the version 0 of Kafka 4.1 and its six vectors.

## AlterShareGroupOffsets API (key 91, v0)

Sets the share-partition start offsets of a share group. New in Kafka **4.1** (KIP-932,
`AlterShareGroupOffsetsRequest.json` @ 4.1.0, `"validVersions": "0"`), a `broker` listener api, flexible from its
version 0.

```
AlterShareGroupOffsets Request (Version: 0) => GroupId [Topics] TAG_BUFFER
  GroupId => compact_string
  Topics  => compact_[ TopicName [Partitions] TAG_BUFFER ]
    TopicName  => compact_string
    Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex StartOffset TAG_BUFFER ]
      PartitionIndex => int32
      StartOffset    => int64
```

```
AlterShareGroupOffsets Response (Version: 0) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Responses] TAG_BUFFER
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact_nullable_string
  Responses      => compact_[ TopicName TopicId [Partitions] TAG_BUFFER ]
    TopicName  => compact_string
    TopicId    => uuid
    Partitions => compact_[ PartitionIndex ErrorCode ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER ]
```

What `kafka-share-groups.sh --reset-offsets --execute` sends. The group coordinator writes the initializing state of
the partitions and hands the offsets to the share coordinator (`InitializeShareGroupState`, key 83) before it
answers. Measured on the node:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| a group that **does not exist**, two partitions of `t4-41-vectors`, a partition 2 the topic does not have and a topic the node does not have | top-level **0**: the group is **created** ("Get or create the share group", `GroupMetadataManager.alterShareGroupOffsets()` @ 4.3.1); the two partitions 0, the other two **3** `UnknownTopicOrPartition` with `This server does not host this topic-partition.` — `altersharegroupoffsets.response.v0` |
| a group of the **classic** protocol | top-level **69** `GroupIdNotFound` with `Group <id> is not a share group.` — `altersharegroupoffsets.response.v0.not-a-share-group` |
| a share group with a member (the `kafka-console-share-consumer.sh` of the image) | top-level **68** `NonEmptyGroup` with `The group is not empty.` — `altersharegroupoffsets.response.v0.non-empty` |
| an empty topic array, for a group that does not exist | top-level 0 and an empty result - and **no** group: a DeleteGroups of the id is answered the 69 afterwards, because the creation writes no record |

The node answers the topics of the result in the order of its own hash map, the missing topic of the first row
before the real one. `AlterShareGroupOffsetsRequest`/`AlterShareGroupOffsetsResponse` with the `Data` classes
`AlterShareGroupOffsetsRequestTopic`, `…RequestPartition`, `…ResponseTopic` and `…ResponsePartition` are wire
classes of this line.

## DeleteShareGroupOffsets API (key 92, v0)

Deletes the share-group state of whole topics. New in Kafka **4.1** (KIP-932, `DeleteShareGroupOffsetsRequest.json`
@ 4.1.0, `"validVersions": "0"`), a `broker` listener api, flexible from its version 0.

```
DeleteShareGroupOffsets Request (Version: 0) => GroupId [Topics] TAG_BUFFER
  GroupId => compact_string
  Topics  => compact_[ TopicName TAG_BUFFER ]
```

```
DeleteShareGroupOffsets Response (Version: 0) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Responses] TAG_BUFFER
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => compact_nullable_string
  Responses      => compact_[ TopicName TopicId ErrorCode ErrorMessage TAG_BUFFER ]
```

What `kafka-share-groups.sh --delete-offsets --topic …` sends: the group forgets where it stands in the named topics
- there is no partition list - and the share coordinator deletes the state (`DeleteShareGroupState`, key 86); a
later member starts those topics over at `share.auto.offset.reset`. Measured on the node:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| the share group, a topic it holds state for and a topic the node does not have | top-level 0, the topic **0** with its id, the missing one **3** with the zero uuid — `deletesharegroupoffsets.response.v0`; a describe afterwards answers the -1 for the deleted topic |
| a group that **does not exist** | top-level **69** with `Group <id> not found.` and an empty result — `deletesharegroupoffsets.response.v0.unknown-group`: unlike an alter, a delete does not create the group |
| a group of the classic protocol | top-level **69** with `Group <id> is not a share group.` |
| a share group with a member | top-level **68** `NonEmptyGroup` with `The group is not empty.` — `deletesharegroupoffsets.response.v0.non-empty` |

A share group itself is deleted with **DeleteGroups** (key 42), the api of every group type: the groups of these
measurements were removed that way. `DeleteShareGroupOffsetsRequest`/`DeleteShareGroupOffsetsResponse` with the
`Data` classes `DeleteShareGroupOffsetsRequestTopic` and `DeleteShareGroupOffsetsResponseTopic` are wire classes of
this line; `ShareGroupOffsetsApiTest` measures the three apis on the node.

## InitProducerId API (key 22, v0 to v5)

Hands out the **producer id** and the **epoch** that the record batches of an idempotent or transactional producer
carry. The api arrived with Kafka **0.11** (KIP-98) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 2**, which changes nothing either: it is the first **flexible** version of the api
(`"flexibleVersions": "2+"`), so the frame carries the request header v2, the transactional id is a compact string
and the header and the body each end in a tagged-field section. The same two fields, one byte shorter for a null
transactional id and two bytes longer for the answer, which has no string in it at all.

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 3** (KIP-360), the first version whose **request** changes since 0.11: the producer
names the id and the epoch it already holds, and the coordinator answers the same id with `epoch + 1` instead of a
fresh one.

```
InitProducerIdRequest (Version: 3) => TransactionalId TransactionTimeoutMs ProducerId ProducerEpoch
  ProducerId    => int64   -- since version 3; -1 asks for a NEW id, as every version below did
  ProducerEpoch => int16   -- since version 3; -1 with it
```

What the two meanings are, what the coordinator does with each of them and what a producer of this client does
with the bump is in "Bumping the epoch (KIP-360)" above. This client sends **v4**, the version of KIP-588, with
`InitProducerIdRequestV3`/`InitProducerIdResponseV3` for the same frame without the promise of the 90,
`InitProducerIdRequestV2`/`InitProducerIdResponseV2` for the flexible frame without the pair and
`InitProducerIdRequestV1`/`V0` below them. Measured on the container, with the transactional id
`t4-25-vectors-tx`: a request with -1/-1 is answered with the next epoch of the id (the `initproducerid.request.v3`
/ `.response.v3` pair), the same id and epoch sent back bump it by one (`…v3.bump`), a pair whose epoch the
coordinator has left behind is answered **47** `InvalidProducerEpoch` with the id -1 and the epoch -1
(`initproducerid.response.v3.fenced` - the 90 `ProducerFenced` the Java client expects there belongs to the
version 4 of Kafka 2.7), and a **null** transactional id with a real pair is answered 0 with a **brand-new** id and
the epoch 0: `handleInitProducerId` @ 2.8.2 returns on the null branch before it ever looks at the pair, so an
idempotent producer cannot bump anything and has to take a new id, which is what this client does for it.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`INIT_PRODUCER_ID_REQUEST_V1 = INIT_PRODUCER_ID_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`initproducerid.request.v1` / `initproducerid.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `InitProducerIdRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.4.

```
InitProducerIdRequest => TransactionalId TransactionTimeoutMs
  TransactionalId      => nullable_string
  TransactionTimeoutMs => int32
```

```
InitProducerIdResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ProducerId ProducerEpoch
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ProducerId     => int64
  ProducerEpoch  => int16
```

The api was born after KIP-124, so its answer starts with a `ThrottleTimeMs` like every other api of 0.11; there is
no version of it without one.

**`TransactionalId` decides everything about this request**, including which broker may answer it:

* **`null` — the idempotent producer.** `TransactionCoordinator.handleInitProducerId` @ 0.11.0.3 "blindly accepts"
  the request: it takes the next id out of the block the broker reserved in ZooKeeper (`ProducerIdManager`, blocks
  of 1000 ids, the next block written to `/latest_producer_id_block`) and answers it with the **epoch 0**. Nothing
  about that id is coordinated, so **any** broker of the cluster answers, and every call answers a *new* id — there
  is no way to ask for the id of a previous session again. On a **KRaft** node the block comes from the controller
  instead of from ZooKeeper — `AllocateProducerIds` (key 67, controller listener) and a `PRODUCER_IDS_RECORD` with
  `nextProducerId: 1000` in the metadata log — and nothing about the answer changes.
* **A non-empty id — the transactional producer.** The request has to reach the **transaction coordinator** of the
  id, the broker that leads the partition of `__transaction_state` the id hashes to, which the GroupCoordinator api
  with `CoordinatorType = 1` names. The answer is the producer id that `__transaction_state` holds for the id, with
  a **higher** epoch than the one the previous producer of that id had — the bump is what fences that producer.
  Verified: two requests for `t7-idempotent-txn` in a row answer the same producer id with the epochs 0 and 1, and a
  batch written with the epoch 0 afterwards is refused with 47. The step is `+1` for an id whose transaction is
  finished; an id with an **open** transaction is answered **51** while the coordinator rolls it back, and the epoch
  of the answer that follows has moved by **two** — see "Broker quirks and observations". A client reads the epoch
  it is given and never computes it.

`TransactionTimeoutMs` is how long the coordinator waits for a status update of an open transaction before it
aborts it. **It is only looked at for a non-null transactional id**: the null branch of `handleInitProducerId`
returns before the check, so a 0.11.0.3 broker answers a `transaction_timeout_ms` of 999999999 next to a null id
with a perfectly normal producer id, while the same value next to a transactional id is answered with **50**
(`InvalidTransactionTimeout`), because it is above the broker's `transaction.max.timeout.ms` (900000 by default).

The **empty string** is not a transactional id: it is answered with **42** (`InvalidRequest`), deliberately, "to
make TransactionCoordinator's behavior consistent with producer client", which refuses an empty
`transactional.id` in its configuration.

Error codes observed on the 0.11.0.3 container:

| Code | Name                         | Request that produces it                                                  |
|------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                         | A producer id and its epoch                                                |
| 15   | GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable | The very first lookup of a transactional id, while `__transaction_state` is being created |
| 16   | NotCoordinatorForGroup       | A transactional id sent to a broker that does not lead its `__transaction_state` partition — including **every** broker before the topic exists |
| 42   | InvalidRequest               | The empty string as a transactional id                                     |
| 50   | InvalidTransactionTimeout    | A `TransactionTimeoutMs` above `transaction.max.timeout.ms`, with a transactional id |
| 51   | ConcurrentTransactions       | The coordinator is fencing the previous epoch of the id; retry after a back-off |

An answer that carries an error carries **-1 as the producer id and -1 as the epoch**, the "no producer state" that
a record batch writes.

`Client::initProducerId(?string $transactionalId = null, int $transactionTimeoutMs = 60000)` sends the request to a
broker of the cluster for a null id and to `Client::getTransactionCoordinator()` for a real one, and answers with a
`Producer\Internals\ProducerIdAndEpoch`. What the client then does with the two values is in "The idempotent
producer" above.

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-588)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 4**, and it changes no field either: "Version 4 adds the support for new error code
PRODUCER_FENCED" (`InitProducerIdRequest.json` @ 2.7.2). What it changes is the **error code** a producer whose
epoch the coordinator has left behind is answered with - the **90** `ProducerFenced` instead of the 47
`InvalidProducerEpoch` - and the four transaction apis of KIP-588 (this one, AddPartitionsToTxn, AddOffsetsToTxn
and EndTxn) got that version together.

The point of the KIP is that the 47 meant two different things at once: "you were fenced, give up" and "your epoch
is one behind, ask for a bump" (the KIP-360 case of the version 3). The new code splits them: a version 4 request
is answered the **47 only where a retry can help** and the **90** where it cannot, which is what
`TransactionManager` here reacts to - a fatal state, exactly as for the 47.

**The identifiers keep the published names.** The code 47 is `ProducerFencedException` in this package, because
that is the name it has carried since Kafka 0.11 and a published name is never moved; the code 90 is
`TransactionalProducerFencedException`. The Java client renamed the 47 to `InvalidProducerEpochException` and gave
`ProducerFencedException` to the 90 - the two names are therefore swapped between the two clients, and this
document names the code, never the class, when it matters.

Measured on the container with the transactional id `t4-27-vectors-tx`: a version 4 request that names an epoch
the coordinator has really left behind (the epoch 0 of an id whose epoch is 5) is answered **90** with the id -1
and the epoch -1 (`initproducerid.response.v4.fenced`), while the pair one step behind the current epoch is still
taken as the **retry of a bump** and answered 0 with the current pair - `prepareInitProducerIdTransit` @ 2.8.2
treats `expectedEpoch == currentEpoch - 1` as one. `InitProducerIdRequestV3`/`InitProducerIdResponseV3` keep the
frame with the version field of Kafka 2.5.

### What Kafka 3.8 changed here (KIP-890): the version 5

**Kafka 3.8 added the version 5**, and the JSON spends one line on it, the typo included: *"Verison 5 adds support
for new error code TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE (KIP-890)."* (`InitProducerIdRequest.json` @ 3.8.1; the answer says the
same with the word spelled right). No field is declared for the version in either file, so the request is the four
fields of the version 3 and the answer the four values of the version 0, both in the flexible encoding of the
version 2 - `initproducerid.request.v5` / `initproducerid.response.v5` are the frames of the version 4 with a 5 in
the version field, 61 and 22 bytes of body. This is the version `Client::initProducerId()` sends;
`InitProducerIdRequestV4`/`InitProducerIdResponseV4` keep the frame of Kafka 2.7.

**What the node really answers.** The 120 is not one of the codes this api produces on a 3.9.2 node - see "The
transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 (Kafka 3.8), and what a client reaches on this node" under "Transactions": the
broker writes `TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE` in the `verify_only` path of AddPartitionsToTxn and nowhere else at that
tag. What a version 5 request is really refused with is the **90** of KIP-588, and the measurement of the 3.8 wave
sharpens the one of the 2.7 wave:

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `producer_id = -1`, `producer_epoch = -1` | the id of the transactional id and its **next** epoch, code 0 |
| the **current** pair of the id | the same id with `epoch + 1`, code 0 - the bump of KIP-360 |
| the **last** pair, i.e. the epoch before the current one | the current pair with the code **0**: `prepareInitProducerIdTransit` @ 3.9.2 reads it as a retry of a bump whose answer was lost, not as a fenced producer |
| an epoch below that | **90** `TransactionalProducerFenced`, with the id -1 and the epoch -1 |
| a producer id the coordinator does not hold for the id | **90** as well, not the 49 |

The third row is why the vector `initproducerid.request.v5.fenced` had to bump the epoch of
`t4-38-vectors-fenced-tx` **twice** before it could ask with the epoch 2 and be refused.

**Kafka 4.1 declared a version 6 (KIP-939, the two-phase commit: `enable_2pc` and `keep_prepared_txn`) and left it
`"latestVersionUnstable": true`, up to 4.3.1**: the node does not serve it and closes the connection of a version 6
frame with `InvalidRequestException: Received request for disabled api with key 22 (InitProducerId) and version 6`
- measured with a v5 body, the two booleans and a 6 in the header; `ApiVersionProbeTest` sends the same frame as the
"one above the table" of the key. This line has no class of it.

## AddPartitionsToTxn API (key 24, v0 to v5)

Enrols topic-partitions into the open transaction of a producer. Kafka **0.11** (KIP-98) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`ADD_PARTITIONS_TO_TXN_REQUEST_V1 = ADD_PARTITIONS_TO_TXN_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`addpartitionstotxn.request.v1` / `addpartitionstotxn.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `AddPartitionsToTxnRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.7.

```
AddPartitionsToTxnRequest => TransactionalId ProducerId ProducerEpoch [Topics]
  TransactionalId => string
  ProducerId      => int64
  ProducerEpoch   => int16
  Topics          => Topic [Partition]
    Topic     => string
    Partition => int32
```

```
AddPartitionsToTxnResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Errors]
  ThrottleTimeMs  => int32
  Errors          => Topic [PartitionErrors]
    Topic           => string
    PartitionErrors => Partition ErrorCode
      Partition => int32
      ErrorCode => int16
```

The request goes to the **transaction coordinator** of the transactional id and has to be answered **before the
first Produce request** that writes into one of the partitions it names: the list of partitions the coordinator
keeps is the one it walks when the transaction ends, to write a COMMIT or an ABORT marker into each of them, and a
partition that is missing from it would keep its records uncommitted for ever. The **first** call of a transaction
is also what starts it - `TransactionCoordinator.handleAddPartitionsToTransaction` moves the id into `Ongoing` and
stamps it with the start time that `transaction.timeout.ms` is counted from.

Adding a partition twice is not an error; the coordinator answers a partition it already holds with the code 0.

**There is no top-level error code.** Everything the coordinator has to say - including the errors that are about
the *transactional id* rather than about a partition - is repeated on **every** partition of the answer, because
`KafkaApis.handleAddPartitionToTxnRequest` maps the single error of the coordinator over the requested partitions.
The array is called `errors` and its inner one `partition_errors` although both also carry the partitions that
succeeded.

| Code | Name | Request that produces it |
|------|------|---------------------------|
| 0    | None                         | The partition is part of the transaction |
| 15   | GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable | The coordinator of the id is not available on this broker |
| 16   | NotCoordinatorForGroup       | Another broker coordinates this transactional id |
| 29   | TopicAuthorizationFailed     | The client may not `Write` the topic |
| 47   | InvalidProducerEpoch         | An epoch below the one `__transaction_state` holds - **verified**: a second `InitProducerId` for the id bumps the epoch, and the producer that kept the old one is answered 47 per partition |
| 48   | InvalidTxnState              | The id is in a state that may not add partitions |
| 49   | InvalidProducerIdMapping     | The producer id is not the one the coordinator holds for the id |
| 51   | ConcurrentTransactions       | The previous transaction of the id is still being completed; retry after a back-off |
| 55   | OperationNotAttempted        | Another partition of the same request was unauthorized, so this one was not even tried |

**55 is the code of this api and of no other.** `KafkaApis` answers a request in which any partition is
unauthorized with `OperationNotAttempted` for every partition it did not look at, so that a client cannot conclude
from a missing error that a partition was added.

`Client::addPartitionsToTxn(Node $coordinator, string $transactionalId, ProducerIdAndEpoch $idAndEpoch, array $topicPartitions)`
sends it and reports the first error code the answer carries;
`Producer\Internals\TransactionManager::maybeAddPartitionsToTransaction()` calls it once per flush, for the
partitions of the batch the coordinator does not hold yet.

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-588)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 2**: "Version 2 adds the support for new error code PRODUCER_FENCED"
(`AddPartitionsToTxnRequest.json` @ 2.7.2), and not a byte of the frame moves. A fenced producer is answered the
**90** `ProducerFenced` per partition where the versions 0 and 1 carry the 47 - see "What Kafka 2.7 changed here
(KIP-588)" in the InitProducerId section.

**The api is not flexible in this version.** `"flexibleVersions": "none"` at the 2.7.2 tag: the three transaction
apis of this group became flexible only with their version **3**, which Kafka 2.8 added.
`AddPartitionsToTxnRequestV1`/`AddPartitionsToTxnResponseV1` keep the frame with the version field of Kafka 2.0.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 3**, the **first flexible version** of this api (`"flexibleVersions": "3+"` in
`AddPartitionsToTxnRequest.json` @ 2.8.2), and it changes no field either: the transactional id and the topic
names are compact strings, the topics and their partitions compact arrays, and the body, every topic and - in the
answer - every partition result end in a tagged-field section. The pair `addpartitionstotxn.request.v3` /
`addpartitionstotxn.response.v3` at the end of this document is the frame this client sends from Kafka 2.8 on;
`AddPartitionsToTxnRequestV2` keeps the plain frame of Kafka 2.7, whose only news was the error code 90.

### What Kafka 3.5 changed here (KIP-890): the version 4 is a BROKER version

**Kafka 3.5 added the version 4**, and it is the first version of this api that a client does not send.
`AddPartitionsToTxnRequest.json` @ 3.5.2 says both halves of it in one comment: *"Version 4 adds VerifyOnly field
to check if partitions are already in transaction and adds support to batch multiple transactions. Versions 3 and
below will be exclusively used by clients and versions 4 and above will be used by brokers. The
AddPartitionsToTxnRequest version 4 API is added as part of KIP-890 and is still under developement. Hence, the
API is not exposed by default by brokers unless explicitely enabled."* - the version carried
`"latestVersionUnstable": true` at that tag and lost the flag with the version 5 of Kafka 3.8, which is why a
3.9.2 node announces the whole range **0 to 5** for the key 24 without `unstable.api.versions.enable`.

```
AddPartitionsToTxnRequest (Version: 4) => [Transactions]
  Transactions => TransactionalId ProducerId ProducerEpoch VerifyOnly [Topics]
    TransactionalId => compact_string
    ProducerId      => int64
    ProducerEpoch   => int16
    VerifyOnly      => bool
    Topics          => Name [Partitions]      # the structure of the versions 0 to 3, unchanged
```

```
AddPartitionsToTxnResponse (Version: 4) => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode [ResultsByTransaction]
  ThrottleTimeMs       => int32
  ErrorCode            => int16               # the first top-level error code this api ever had
  ResultsByTransaction => TransactionalId [TopicResults]
    TransactionalId => compact_string
    TopicResults    => Name [ResultsByPartition]    # the `errors` array of the versions 0 to 3
```

The four top-level fields of the request become one entry of a `transactions` array (the JSON renames them
`V3AndBelowTransactionalId`, `V3AndBelowProducerId`, `V3AndBelowProducerEpoch` and `V3AndBelowTopics` and ends them
at the version 3), the answer's `errors` array becomes `ResultsByTopicV3AndBelow` and a `results_by_transaction`
array takes its place, and every entry keeps the topic and partition structures it had. Nothing inside them moves.

**What the version is for.** `transaction.partition.verification.enable` is `true` by default from Kafka 3.6, so
the leader of a partition asks the transaction coordinator whether the partition really is part of the transaction
before it appends a transactional batch - the hole KIP-890 closed, see "A transactional batch for a partition the
transaction does not hold is refused" under "Broker quirks and observations". That question is this version:
`verify_only = true` changes nothing at all, and a broker that has the batches of many producers in flight asks it
for all of them in one frame, which is what the `transactions` array is for.

**Measured on the 3.9.2 node, and the reason this client keeps sending the version 3.**
`KafkaApis.handleAddPartitionsToTxnRequest` @ 3.9.2 authorizes the frame as a broker and not as a producer:

```scala
// Newer versions of the request should only come from other brokers.
if (version >= 4) authHelper.authorizeClusterOperation(request, CLUSTER_ACTION)
```

and skips both authorizations a client needs - `WRITE` on the `TRANSACTIONAL_ID` and `WRITE` on every topic of the
request are asked for `if (version < 4)` alone, while a version 4 takes `authorizedTopics =
partitionsToAdd.map(_.topic).toSet`. On this container `ANONYMOUS`, the principal of the PLAINTEXT listener, is in
`super.users`, so it passes `CLUSTER_ACTION` and the node answers the frame; the SASL user `acltest`, the one
principal of the node that is not a super user, is answered the **top-level 31**
(`ClusterAuthorizationFailed`) with an **empty** `results_by_transaction` - 13 bytes behind the size field, the
pair `addpartitionstotxn.request.v4.unauthorized` / `addpartitionstotxn.response.v4.unauthorized`. A cluster that
grants `CLUSTER_ACTION` to its brokers alone - which is every cluster with an authorizer - answers every client
that way, so **this client builds the version 4 and never sends it**:
`Client::addPartitionsToTxn()` keeps the `AddPartitionsToTxnRequestV3` frame of Kafka 2.8, and the classes
`AddPartitionsToTxnRequest`/`AddPartitionsToTxnResponse` of the version 4, the structures
`AddPartitionsToTxnTransaction` and `AddPartitionsToTxnResult` and the ten vectors below exist for the wire alone.
The **version 5** of Kafka 3.8 changes none of that: the authorization is `if (version >= 4)`, so the 3.8 wave
measured the same top-level 31 there, and the client stays at the version 3 for this whole line - see "What Kafka
3.8 changed here (KIP-890): the version 5 is a BROKER version too" below.

**The error codes of a version 4 are the ones a broker understands, not the ones a producer does.** Measured
against an open transaction of `t4-35-vectors-txn-3` on the node:

| Situation | Version 4 answers | What a client is told instead |
|------|------|------|
| The partition is in the transaction | 0 in that partition | the same |
| The partition is **not** in the transaction (`verify_only`) | **120** `TransactionAbortable` | 48 `InvalidTxnState` |
| The epoch is below the one `__transaction_state` holds | **90** `TransactionalProducerFenced` | 47 `InvalidProducerEpoch` |
| The topic does not exist | 3 `UnknownTopicOrPartition` in that partition | the same |
| The principal is not a broker | the **top-level 31** | 48 `InvalidTxnState` |

The third column is the frame the *producer* sees, because the broker that asked this question maps the codes
before it answers the Produce: `AddPartitionsToTxnManager` @ 3.9.2 turns a 90 into the 47 ("Producers expect to
handle INVALID_PRODUCER_EPOCH in this scenario"), a per-partition 120 into the 48 ("For backward compatibility
with clients") and even the top-level 31 into a 48 ("The client should not be exposed to
CLUSTER_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED so modify the error to signify the verification did not complete"). The **120** is
the code of `TransactionCoordinator.handleVerifyPartitionsInTransaction` @ 3.9.2 and not of the version: the
specification of the version 4 predates the code, and a 3.9.2 node answers it there all the same - an id that has
a producer id but no open transaction at all is answered the 120 on every partition it asks about, because its
`topicPartitions` set is empty.

**An empty `transactions` array is never answered.** `addResultAndMaybeSendResponse` sends the frame when every
transaction of the batch has a result, which zero transactions never reach, so the connection is left owing an
answer - the same trap as the empty `groups` array of an OffsetFetch v8/v9, measured at the version 4 as well as
at the version 5. `AddPartitionsToTxnRequest::forTransactions()` refuses an empty batch for that reason.

### What Kafka 3.8 changed here (KIP-890): the version 5 is a BROKER version too

**Kafka 3.8 added the version 5**, with the sentence every api of this group got - *"Version 5 adds support for new
error code TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE"* (`AddPartitionsToTxnRequest.json` @ 3.8.1, and the same in the response file) -
and with one thing more that is easy to miss: the **`"latestVersionUnstable": true` of the version 4 became
`false`**. That is why a 3.9.2 node announces the whole range **0 to 5** for the key 24 without
`unstable.api.versions.enable`, where the 3.5.2 sources hid the version 4 behind it. The sentence *"Versions 3 and
below will be exclusively used by clients and versions 4 and above will be used by brokers"* stayed where it was,
one line below.

**And the node keeps its word.** `KafkaApis.handleAddPartitionsToTxnRequest` @ 3.9.2 authorizes on `version >= 4`,
not on `version == 4`:

```scala
// Newer versions of the request should only come from other brokers.
if (version >= 4) authHelper.authorizeClusterOperation(request, CLUSTER_ACTION)
```

so the version 5 is the version 4 in every respect that matters to a client. Measured on the node as `acltest`,
the one principal that is not in `super.users`: `addpartitionstotxn.request.v5.unauthorized` is answered the
**top-level 31** `ClusterAuthorizationFailed` with an empty `results_by_transaction`, 13 bytes behind the size
field - the same 17-byte frame the version 4 is answered. **`Client::addPartitionsToTxn()` therefore stays at the
version 3** for this line, and `AddPartitionsToTxnRequest`/`AddPartitionsToTxnResponse` speak the version 5 for
the wire alone, with `AddPartitionsToTxnRequestV4`/`AddPartitionsToTxnResponseV4` keeping the frame of Kafka 3.5.

The frames are identical to the version 4's, field for field: `addpartitionstotxn.request.v5` is a `verify_only`
batch of one transaction asking about the partition 0 of `t4-38-vectors`, which the transaction of
`t4-38-vectors-tx` holds, and the partition 1, which it does not, and `addpartitionstotxn.response.v5` answers
**0** and **120**. That is the one place a 3.9.2 broker writes the code 120 at all
(`TransactionCoordinator.handleVerifyPartitionsInTransaction`), so the version that is named after the code
behaves exactly like the version that predates it - see "The transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 (Kafka 3.8), and
what a client reaches on this node" under "Transactions".

An empty `transactions` array is never answered at the version 5 either;
`AddPartitionsToTxnRequest::forTransactions()` refuses it for both versions.

## AddOffsetsToTxn API (key 25, v0 to v4)

Enrols the offsets of a consumer group into the open transaction. Kafka **0.11** (KIP-98) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`ADD_OFFSETS_TO_TXN_REQUEST_V1 = ADD_OFFSETS_TO_TXN_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`addoffsetstotxn.request.v1` / `addoffsetstotxn.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `AddOffsetsToTxnRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.7.

```
AddOffsetsToTxnRequest => TransactionalId ProducerId ProducerEpoch GroupId
  TransactionalId => string
  ProducerId      => int64
  ProducerEpoch   => int16
  GroupId         => string        # consumer_group_id
```

```
AddOffsetsToTxnResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
```

The first half of `sendOffsetsToTransaction()`. It goes to the **transaction coordinator**, and it is
`AddPartitionsToTxn` for exactly one partition: `TransactionCoordinator.handleAddPartitionsToTransaction` @
0.11.0.3 is literally the method that serves it, called with
`new TopicPartition(GROUP_METADATA_TOPIC_NAME, partitionFor(consumerGroupId))`. That is why it has **one**
error code and no array - there is nothing to report per partition.

The offsets are not in this request; they travel in the `TxnOffsetCommit` that follows it, to the **group**
coordinator. The split is what makes the commit atomic with the produced records: the group coordinator writes
them as transactional records, and only the COMMIT marker that this request put the partition on the list for
makes them visible.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|------|------|----------|
| 0    | None                               | `__consumer_offsets` of that group is part of the transaction |
| 15   | GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable       | The transaction coordinator is not available on this broker |
| 16   | NotCoordinatorForGroup             | Another broker coordinates this transactional id |
| 30   | GroupAuthorizationFailed           | The client may not `Read` the consumer group |
| 47   | InvalidProducerEpoch               | The epoch is below the one `__transaction_state` holds |
| 48   | InvalidTxnState                    | The id is in a state that may not add partitions |
| 49   | InvalidProducerIdMapping           | The producer id is not the one the coordinator holds for the id |
| 51   | ConcurrentTransactions             | The previous transaction of the id is still being completed |
| 53   | TransactionalIdAuthorizationFailed | The client may not `Write` the transactional id |

`Client::addOffsetsToTxn(Node $coordinator, string $transactionalId, ProducerIdAndEpoch $idAndEpoch, string $groupId)`.

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-588)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 2**, with the same words as for AddPartitionsToTxn: the frame is unchanged, the
version promises that the client understands the **90** `ProducerFenced`, and the api is **not** flexible in it
(`"flexibleVersions": "none"` @ 2.7.2; the flexible version 3 is Kafka 2.8).
`AddOffsetsToTxnRequestV1`/`AddOffsetsToTxnResponseV1` keep the frame below it.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 3**, the first flexible version of this api (`"flexibleVersions": "3+"` in
`AddOffsetsToTxnRequest.json` @ 2.8.2): the transactional id and the group id become compact strings and the body
of both frames ends in a tagged-field section - 73 bytes of request and 16 of answer, two bytes more than the 14
of every version below, because the tag buffer of the header and the one of the body cost a byte each and this
answer has nothing that a compact encoding could shorten. The pair `addoffsetstotxn.request.v3` / `addoffsetstotxn.response.v3` at the end of
this document is that exchange; `AddOffsetsToTxnRequestV2` is the plain frame of Kafka 2.7.

### What Kafka 3.8 changed here (KIP-890): the version 4

**Kafka 3.8 added the version 4**: *"Version 4 adds support for new error code TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE (KIP-890)"*
(`AddOffsetsToTxnRequest.json` @ 3.8.1 and the response file with it), no field, no encoding change. The request
is the four fields of the version 3 - 77 bytes of body with the transactional id `t4-38-vectors-tx` and the group
`t4-38-vectors-group` - and the answer the 12 bytes of a throttle time, one error code and two tag buffers:
`addoffsetstotxn.request.v4` / `addoffsetstotxn.response.v4`. `Client::addOffsetsToTxn()` sends it, and
`AddOffsetsToTxnRequestV3`/`AddOffsetsToTxnResponseV3` keep the frame of Kafka 2.8.

**The node answers the codes it always answered.** `addoffsetstotxn.request.v4.unknown-producer` names a producer
id the coordinator does not hold for the transactional id and is answered the **49** `InvalidProducerIdMapping`,
the code of the version 0. The 120 the version promises is written by a 3.9.2 broker in the `verify_only` path of
a partition **verification** and nowhere else, and this request *adds* the `__consumer_offsets` partition of the
group to the transaction instead of writing into it, so there is nothing to verify and the code never reaches this
api. The 120 of the offsets belongs to the TxnOffsetCommit that follows - see "The transaction protocol v2 of
KIP-890 (Kafka 3.8), and what a client reaches on this node" under "Transactions".

## EndTxn API (key 26, v0 to v5)

Commits or aborts the open transaction. Kafka **0.11** (KIP-98) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`END_TXN_REQUEST_V1 = END_TXN_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`endtxn.request.v1` / `endtxn.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `EndTxnRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.7.

```
EndTxnRequest => TransactionalId ProducerId ProducerEpoch TransactionResult
  TransactionalId   => string
  ProducerId        => int64
  ProducerEpoch     => int16
  TransactionResult => boolean      # 1 = COMMIT, 0 = ABORT
```

```
EndTxnResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
```

The last request of a transaction, sent to the **transaction coordinator**. A single boolean byte is the whole
difference between a commit and an abort.

**The answer does not mean that the transaction is visible.** The coordinator answers as soon as it has written
`PrepareCommit`/`PrepareAbort` into `__transaction_state`; what follows is broker business - a
`WriteTxnMarkers` request to the leader of every partition of the transaction, each of them appending the control
batch, and then the `CompleteCommit`/`CompleteAbort` entry. A `read_committed` consumer sees the records a moment
*after* this call returned, which is what moves the last stable offset of the partitions past them.

Two behaviours of a 0.11.0.3 coordinator that the state table of `TransactionCoordinator.handleEndTransaction`
explains and that were verified on the container:

* **A repeated commit is answered with 0.** An id in `CompleteCommit` that is asked to commit again is a no-op
  success, so a producer that lost the answer of its `EndTxn` may simply send it again.
* **An abort after a commit is 48.** The same id asked to *abort* while it is in `CompleteCommit` is an illegal
  state transition, `InvalidTxnState`.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|------|------|----------|
| 0    | None                               | The coordinator decided the outcome |
| 15   | GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable       | The transaction coordinator is not available on this broker |
| 16   | NotCoordinatorForGroup             | Another broker coordinates this transactional id |
| 47   | InvalidProducerEpoch               | The epoch is below the one `__transaction_state` holds - fenced |
| 48   | InvalidTxnState                    | There is no transaction in a state this result may be applied to |
| 49   | InvalidProducerIdMapping           | The producer id is not the one the coordinator holds for the id |
| 51   | ConcurrentTransactions             | The previous transaction of the id is still being completed |
| 53   | TransactionalIdAuthorizationFailed | The client may not `Write` the transactional id |

`Client::endTxn(Node $coordinator, string $transactionalId, ProducerIdAndEpoch $idAndEpoch, bool $transactionResult)`
with `EndTxnRequest::COMMIT` or `EndTxnRequest::ABORT`.

### What Kafka 2.7 changed here (KIP-588)

**Kafka 2.7 added the version 2** - the frame of the version 1, with the **90** `ProducerFenced` for a producer
that a later incarnation of the same transactional id has fenced, and without flexible versions
(`"flexibleVersions": "none"` @ 2.7.2). This is the one api of the four where the new code was **measured** on the
container: a producer of the transactional id `t4-27-vectors-tx` whose epoch a second `InitProducerId` had bumped
is answered **90** by its next EndTxn (`endtxn.response.v2.fenced`), where a version 1 request is answered the 47.
`EndTxnRequestV1`/`EndTxnResponseV1` keep the frame below it.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 3**, the first flexible version of this api (`"flexibleVersions": "3+"` in
`EndTxnRequest.json` @ 2.8.2). The transactional id is a compact string, the `committed` boolean keeps its place,
and both bodies end in a tagged-field section. The pair `endtxn.request.v3` / `endtxn.response.v3` at the end of
this document is the COMMIT of the transaction the AddPartitionsToTxn v3 above opened; `EndTxnRequestV2` is the
