plain frame of Kafka 2.7, which carries the 90 of KIP-588 just as well.

### What Kafka 3.8 changed here (KIP-890): the version 4

**Kafka 3.8 added the version 4** with the sentence of the whole group - *"Version 4 adds support for new error
code TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE (KIP-890)"* (`EndTxnRequest.json` @ 3.8.1) - and no field: the transactional id, the
producer id, the epoch and the single boolean of the result, in the flexible encoding of the version 3.
`endtxn.request.v4` / `endtxn.response.v4` are the COMMIT of the transaction the vectors of this wave opened, 58
and 12 bytes of body. `EndTxnRequestV4`/`EndTxnResponseV4` are its classes since Kafka 4.0 added the version 5,
and `Client::endTxn()` ends a transaction of the protocol v1 with them; `EndTxnRequestV3`/`EndTxnResponseV3` keep
the frame of Kafka 2.8.

**The state table is the one of Kafka 0.11.** `endtxn.request.v4.abort-after-commit` asks the same id, producer id
and epoch to ABORT once the commit above is through - the last byte of the body is a `00` where the commit has a
`01` - and is answered the **48** `InvalidTxnState`, exactly as on every line below, while a repeated *commit* of
the same id is a no-op success. The 120 is not among the codes a 3.9.2 coordinator writes here (see "The
transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 (Kafka 3.8), and what a client reaches on this node" under "Transactions"), and
the **90** of KIP-588 is still what a producer whose epoch was left behind is answered.

### What Kafka 4.0 changed here (KIP-890 part 2): the version 5

**Kafka 4.0 added the version 5** - *"Version 5 enables bumping epoch on every transaction (KIP-890 Part 2)"*
(`EndTxnRequest.json` @ 4.0.0) - and gave the **answer** two fields, *"so producer ID and epoch are included in
the response"* (`EndTxnResponse.json` @ 4.0.0):

```
EndTxnResponse (Version: 5) => throttle_time_ms error_code producer_id producer_epoch TAG_BUFFER
  producer_id    => int64    -- "ignorable", default -1
  producer_epoch => int16    -- "ignorable", default -1
```

The request is the frame of the version 4; its version is the switch. `KafkaApis.handleEndTxnRequest` @ 4.0.0
hands the coordinator `TransactionVersion.transactionVersionForEndTxn(request)`, and at the version 5 that is the
transaction protocol **v2**: the coordinator bumps the epoch of the producer as it prepares the commit or the abort
and answers the producer id and the epoch the **next** transaction runs under - a new producer id with the epoch 0
when the epoch is exhausted (`generateTxnTransitMetadataForTxnCompletion` @ 4.3.1). It is meant for a transaction
whose partitions a Produce v12 and a TxnOffsetCommit v5 enrolled, and the Java `EndTxnRequest.Builder` @ 4.0.0 caps
the version at `LAST_STABLE_VERSION_BEFORE_TRANSACTION_V2 = 4` unless the cluster finalizes `transaction.version`
2. Measured on the 4.3.1 node with the transactional id `t4-40-vectors-tx`, producer id 275 - the state table of
`TransactionCoordinator.endTransaction` @ 4.3.1 for the protocol v2, which reads the epoch differently from the
table above:

| Frames | What was sent | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `endtxn.request.v5` / `endtxn.response.v5` | COMMIT, epoch 0, of the transaction a TxnOffsetCommit v5 started | **0**, producer id 275, epoch **1** |
| `endtxn.request.v5.retry` / `endtxn.response.v5.retry` | the same commit again, epoch 0, once the markers are written | **0**, 275 and **1** again - an epoch one below the current one is `retryOnEpochBump` |
| `endtxn.request.v5.nothing-to-commit` / `endtxn.response.v5.nothing-to-commit` | COMMIT, epoch 1, nothing enrolled since | **48** `InvalidTxnState`, -1/-1 |
| `endtxn.request.v5.abort-of-nothing` / `endtxn.response.v5.abort-of-nothing` | ABORT, epoch 1, nothing enrolled since | **0**, 275 and epoch **2** - an abort of an empty transaction bumps the epoch too |
| `endtxn.request.v5.fenced` / `endtxn.response.v5.fenced` | ABORT, epoch 0, two below the current one | **90** `ProducerFenced`, -1/-1 |

A request that arrives while the markers of the previous end are still being written is answered the **51**
`ConcurrentTransactions` with -1/-1, and every error code carries the defaults -1/-1, so a producer takes the pair
over only when the producer id is not -1 (`EndTxnHandler` @ 4.0.0; `EndTxnResponse::hasProducerIdAndEpoch()`
here). **A retry is no longer answered by the result alone**: the "repeated commit is 0" of Kafka 0.11 above holds
at the version 5 for the epoch *below* the current one only - the same commit under the current epoch is the 48,
because under the protocol v2 the current epoch already names the next transaction.

`EndTxnRequest`/`EndTxnResponse` are the version 5 and `EndTxnRequestV4`/`EndTxnResponseV4` keep the frame of
Kafka 3.8. `Client::endTxnBumpingEpoch(Node $coordinator, string $transactionalId, ProducerIdAndEpoch
$idAndEpoch, bool $transactionResult): ProducerIdAndEpoch` sends the version 5 and answers the pair of the next
transaction (`ProducerIdAndEpoch::none()` for an answer that carries none); `Client::endTxn()` stays the version 4
of the protocol v1. See "The transaction protocol v2 on a node that finalizes it (Kafka 4.0)" under
"Transactions".

## WriteTxnMarkers API (key 27, v0 to v2)

Writes the control batches of a finished transaction into the partitions of it. Kafka **0.11** (KIP-98), **v0**
only, **broker to broker**.

```
WriteTxnMarkersRequest => [TransactionMarkers]
  TransactionMarkers => ProducerId ProducerEpoch TransactionResult [Topics] CoordinatorEpoch
    ProducerId        => int64
    ProducerEpoch     => int16
    TransactionResult => boolean
    Topics            => Topic [Partition]
      Topic     => string
      Partition => int32
    CoordinatorEpoch  => int32
```

```
WriteTxnMarkersResponse => [TransactionMarkers]
  TransactionMarkers => ProducerId [Topics]
    ProducerId => int64
    Topics     => Topic [Partitions]
      Topic      => string
      Partitions => Partition ErrorCode
        Partition => int32
        ErrorCode => int16
```

This is the request a **transaction coordinator** sends to the leader of every partition of a transaction after an
`EndTxn`, and it is what makes that leader append the control batch a `read_committed` consumer reads the outcome
from. `TransactionMarkerChannelManager` @ 0.11.0.3 groups the pending markers by destination broker - one entry per
producer, so one request may complete several transactions at once - and repeats them until every partition
answered without a retriable error; only then is `CompleteCommit`/`CompleteAbort` written.

**No client ever sends it**, and this line implements the classes for completeness of the api block, not for a
client method. Two peculiarities:

* **It is the only answer of Kafka 0.11 without a `throttle_time_ms`.** `WRITE_TXN_MARKERS_RESPONSE_V0` in
  `Protocol.java` starts with the array; the quotas of KIP-124 throttle clients, and this api has none.
* `CoordinatorEpoch` is the epoch of the `__transaction_state` partition the *sender* owns, not the epoch of the
  producer. A leader that has already seen a higher one refuses the marker with **52**
  (`TransactionCoordinatorFenced`), which is how a coordinator that lost its partition is kept from writing markers
  behind the back of the one that took it over.

`KafkaApis.handleWriteTxnMarkersRequest` requires `ClusterAction` on the cluster, which is only granted to the
broker principal on a *secured* cluster; the container of this branch runs without an authorizer, so it serves the
request for anybody - which is what makes a wire vector of it possible at all, and it really does append a COMMIT
control batch into the partition that the vector names.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|------|------|----------|
| 0    | None                         | The control batch was appended |
| 3    | UnknownTopicOrPartition      | The broker does not host that partition |
| 6    | NotLeaderForPartition        | The broker does not lead it any more |
| 31   | ClusterAuthorizationFailed   | The client may not perform a `ClusterAction` |
| 43   | UnsupportedForMessageFormat  | The `message.format.version` of the topic is below 0.11.0 and has no place for a control batch |
| 52   | TransactionCoordinatorFenced | The `CoordinatorEpoch` of the marker is below the one the leader saw |

An empty marker array is answered with an empty array, which is what the api probe of this branch sends to check
that the key is served at all.

### What Kafka 2.8 changed here (KIP-482)

**Kafka 2.8 added the version 1** and changed no field of this broker-to-broker api either
(`"flexibleVersions": "1+"` in `WriteTxnMarkersRequest.json` @ 2.8.2): the topic names are compact, the markers,
the topics and the partitions are compact arrays, and every marker, every topic and the body end in a
tagged-field section - the answer still begins with the marker array, because the api has no
`throttle_time_ms` to begin with. The pair `writetxnmarkers.request.v1` / `writetxnmarkers.response.v1` at the end
of this document was captured against the container, which runs without an authorizer and therefore serves the
`ClusterAction` of this api for anybody: the COMMIT marker of the producer of `t4-28-vectors-tx` was really
appended to `t4-28-vectors`-0 and answered with the error code 0. `WriteTxnMarkersRequestV0` and
`WriteTxnMarkersResponseV0` keep the plain frame of Kafka 0.11, which is the one every broker below 2.8 speaks.

### What Kafka 4.2 changed here (KIP-1228): the version 2

**Kafka 4.2 added the version 2**: *"Version 2 adds TransactionVersion field to the WritableTxnMarker (KIP-1228)"*
(`WriteTxnMarkersRequest.json` @ 4.2.0, `"validVersions": "1-2"`; the answer only *"matches WriteTxnMarkersRequest
version 2"*). Every marker ends with one more byte:

```
WriteTxnMarkers Request (Version: 2) => [Markers] TAG_BUFFER
  Markers => ProducerId ProducerEpoch TransactionResult [Topics] CoordinatorEpoch TransactionVersion TAG_BUFFER
    TransactionVersion => int8   -- "ignorable", default 0: 0/1 the legacy protocols, 2 the protocol v2 of KIP-890
```

The byte tells the leader of the partition **how to check the epoch of the marker**. A coordinator of the protocol
v2 bumps the producer epoch with every EndTxn, so the marker of a transaction v2 carries an epoch strictly **above**
the one its records were written with, and the leader refuses one that does not (`<=`); a legacy marker is only
refused below it (`<`), and a version 1 frame means the legacy check. The one exception is the idempotent retry of
KAFKA-19999: a v2 marker at the current epoch is let through when no transaction of the producer is open any more
(`ProducerAppendInfo.checkProducerEpoch()` @ 4.3.1). `KafkaApis.handleWriteTxnMarkersRequest()` hands the byte to
the append of the control batch and to the group coordinator for `__consumer_offsets`; it is not written into the
log.

**What the client listener of the node answers** — the api needs `ClusterAction`, which the PLAINTEXT listener's
`User:ANONYMOUS` has as a super user of the `StandardAuthorizer` (measured with the client id
`kafka-client-t4-42`, a transactional `KafkaProducer` of the protocol v2 holding a transaction open at its epoch 0 in
`t4-42-vectors-marker`-0, and DescribeProducers to watch that transaction):

| Frame | Answer |
|---|---|
| v2, no marker | an empty marker array, as v1 |
| v2, ABORT at the epoch of the open transaction, `TransactionVersion` 2 | **47** (`INVALID_PRODUCER_EPOCH`, this client's `ProducerFencedException`): `Epoch of producer 89 at offset 1 in t4-42-vectors-marker-0 is 0, which is <= the last seen epoch 0 (TV2)`; the transaction stays open — `writetxnmarkers.response.v2` |
| the same marker with `TransactionVersion` 0 | **0**: the control batch is written and the transaction is gone from DescribeProducers — `writetxnmarkers.response.v2.tv0` |
| the `TransactionVersion` 2 marker again, no transaction open | **0**: `Idempotent transaction marker retry detected for producer 89 epoch 0` — `writetxnmarkers.response.v2.retry` |
| v1 or v2, an epoch below the one the partition saw last (after the coordinator's own abort bumped it) | **47**, whatever the transaction version |
| v2, a partition the topic does not have | **3** |
| v1, the epoch **-1** | **-1** with no message: `IllegalArgumentException: Invalid negative producer epoch` escapes the handler ("Unexpected error handling request" in the log of the node) |

After the manual markers the producer's own `abortTransaction()` still succeeds: the coordinator bumps the epoch to 1
and its marker of the version 2 at the epoch 1 passes the strict check. `WriteTxnMarkersRequest`/
`WriteTxnMarkersResponse` are the version 2, `WriteTxnMarkersRequestMarker::$transactionVersion` the byte (a trailing
constructor parameter, default 0); `WriteTxnMarkersRequestV1`/`WriteTxnMarkersResponseV1` keep the version 1 and
encode their markers as `WriteTxnMarkersRequestMarkerV1`, without it. The api stays **without a client method**: it
is what a transaction coordinator sends, never a client.

## TxnOffsetCommit API (key 28, v0 to v5)

Commits consumer offsets inside a transaction. Kafka **0.11** (KIP-98) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`TXN_OFFSET_COMMIT_REQUEST_V1 = TXN_OFFSET_COMMIT_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`txnoffsetcommit.request.v1` / `txnoffsetcommit.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `TxnOffsetCommitRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.1.

**Kafka 2.1 added the version 2** (KIP-320), and it is the first version of this api whose **frame** really
changes: every partition entry carries a `committed_leader_epoch` between the offset and the metadata —

```
TxnOffsetCommitRequestPartition (Version: 2) => partition offset committed_leader_epoch metadata
  partition              => int32
  offset                 => int64
  committed_leader_epoch => int32              -- since version 2, -1 when the client does not know it
  metadata               => NULLABLE_STRING
```

— which is the epoch of the leader that produced the record the offset points behind. The coordinator stores it
next to the offset, so that a consumer which fetches the offset back can tell a log that was truncated under it
from a current one; `OffsetCommit` v6 carries the same field for a non-transactional commit. The default is the
**-1** of `TxnOffsetCommitRequest.json` @ 2.8.2, which every offset of this client carries until its consumer
tracks epochs: `OffsetAndMetadata::$leaderEpoch` is `null` for "not known" and the request writes
`OffsetAndMetadata::UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` for it — the offsets handed to
`KafkaProducer::sendOffsetsToTransaction()` may name one, and the value object is what carries it.

**The coordinator does not validate the epoch when it stores it.** Measured on the container: a commit of the
partition `t4-21-vectors-0`, whose leader epoch is 0, with `committed_leader_epoch = 4242` is answered with the
error code **0** — the epoch is data of the offset, and the codes 74 `FencedLeaderEpoch` and 75
`UnknownLeaderEpoch` belong to the apis that *use* it. The version 3 of KIP-447 is what this client sends; the answer carries the
fields of version 0 in every version of this api, in the flexible encoding from the version 3 on.

```
TxnOffsetCommitRequest => TransactionalId GroupId ProducerId ProducerEpoch [Topics]
  TransactionalId => string
  GroupId         => string        # consumer_group_id
  ProducerId      => int64
  ProducerEpoch   => int16
  Topics          => Topic [Partitions]
    Topic      => string
    Partitions => Partition Offset Metadata
      Partition => int32
      Offset    => int64
      Metadata  => nullable_string
```

```
TxnOffsetCommitResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Topics]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Topics         => Topic [Partitions]
    Topic      => string
    Partitions => Partition ErrorCode
      Partition => int32
      ErrorCode => int16
```

The second half of `sendOffsetsToTransaction()` and **the one request of the transaction protocol that goes to the
group coordinator**, because that is the broker which owns `__consumer_offsets`. It has to follow an
`AddOffsetsToTxn` for the same group; without it the group coordinator answers **48**, the code of a transactional
write into a partition that is not part of an open transaction.

What it writes is an ordinary offset commit **inside a transactional record batch** stamped with the producer id
and the epoch of this request. Those records are invisible to an OffsetFetch of the group until the transaction
coordinator has written the COMMIT marker into that partition; an aborted transaction leaves them in the log with
an ABORT marker behind them and the group keeps the offset it had before.

Compared with `OffsetCommit` the request has **no generation id, no member id and no retention time**: the
producer that commits the offsets is not a member of the group at all, and the fencing a generation would give is
done by the producer epoch instead.

As in `AddPartitionsToTxn` there is **no top-level error code**; the state of the group and of the transaction is
repeated on every partition of the answer.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|------|------|----------|
| 0    | None                         | The offset is in `__consumer_offsets`, invisible until the commit |
| 12   | OffsetMetadataTooLarge       | The metadata is above `offset.metadata.max.bytes` |
| 14   | GroupLoadInProgress          | The coordinator is still reading the group out of the log |
| 15   | GroupCoordinatorNotAvailable | The group coordinator is not available on this broker |
| 16   | NotCoordinatorForGroup       | Another broker coordinates this group |
| 30   | GroupAuthorizationFailed     | The client may not `Read` the group |
| 43   | UnsupportedForMessageFormat  | `__consumer_offsets` runs a `message.format.version` below 0.11.0 |
| 47   | InvalidProducerEpoch         | The epoch is below the one the log holds for the producer id |
| 48   | InvalidTxnState              | The offsets partition is not part of an open transaction of this producer |

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 3** (KIP-447), which is flexible (`"flexibleVersions": "3+"`) and, for the first
time, tells the coordinator **who the consumer is**: a `generation_id`, a `member_id` and a
`group_instance_id` behind the producer epoch. The paragraph above - "no generation id, no member id" - is true of
the versions 0 to 2 only.

```
TxnOffsetCommitRequest (Version: 3) => TransactionalId GroupId ProducerId ProducerEpoch
                                       GenerationId MemberId GroupInstanceId [Topics]
  GenerationId    => int32                     -- since version 3, -1 for "not a member"
  MemberId        => COMPACT_STRING            -- since version 3, the empty string with it
  GroupInstanceId => COMPACT_NULLABLE_STRING   -- since version 3, the `group.instance.id` of KIP-345
```

What the coordinator checks and the three codes it answers are in "The consumer group metadata of a transactional
commit (KIP-447)" above; measured on the container, the commit of the current generation is **0**, a generation
the group has left behind is **22** per partition, a member id the group does not have is **25**, and the -1 with
the empty member id is accepted exactly as every version below 3 was. `TxnOffsetCommitRequest`/`Response` are the
version 3 with `FLEXIBLE_VERSION = 3` and `TxnOffsetCommitRequestV2`/`ResponseV2` keep the frame of the version 2.

`Client::txnOffsetCommit(Node $groupCoordinator, string $transactionalId, string $groupId, ProducerIdAndEpoch $idAndEpoch, array $topicPartitionOffsets, ?ConsumerGroupMetadata $groupMetadata = null)`,
where the metadata is the `Consumer\ConsumerGroupMetadata` of the consumer whose offsets are committed and `null`
means the "not a member" commit.

### What Kafka 3.8 changed here (KIP-890): the version 4

**Kafka 3.8 added the version 4**: *"Version 4 adds support for new error code TRANSACTION_ABORTABLE (KIP-890)"*
(`TxnOffsetCommitRequest.json` @ 3.8.1 and the response file), and the frame of the version 3 stays as KIP-447
left it - the generation, the member id and the group instance id in front of the topics, every string compact,
every structure closed by a tag buffer. `txnoffsetcommit.request.v4` is the commit of a producer that is **not** a
member of the group (the generation -1 with an empty member id and a null instance id) for the offset 42 of
`t4-38-vectors-0`, and `txnoffsetcommit.response.v4` the per-partition 0 of the group coordinator.
`TxnOffsetCommitRequestV4`/`TxnOffsetCommitResponseV4` are its classes since Kafka 4.0 added the version 5, and
`Client::txnOffsetCommit()` sends it inside a transaction of the protocol v1;
`TxnOffsetCommitRequestV3`/`TxnOffsetCommitResponseV3` keep the frame of Kafka 2.5.

**The membership codes of KIP-447 are still the ones this api refuses with.**
`txnoffsetcommit.request.v4.unknown-member` fills the version 3 fields in with the generation 99 and the member id
`t4-38-no-such-member` and is answered the **25** `UnknownMemberId` per partition - `validateOffsetCommit` @ 3.9.2
checks the member id before the generation, so the 22 of an illegal generation needs a member the group really
holds, as the version 3 vectors of the 2.x line show.

**And this is the one client api of the five whose refusal the version really changes.** The group coordinator
does not write the offsets straight away: it first has the `__consumer_offsets` partition of the group **verified**
against the transaction coordinator, the partition verification of KIP-890 part 1 that
`transaction.partition.verification.enable` switches on, and `GroupCoordinator.handleTxnCommitOffsets` @ 3.9.2
chooses how the failure of that verification is reported by the version of the request:

```scala
val transactionSupportedOperation = if (apiVersion >= 4) genericError else defaultError
```

`AddPartitionsToTxnManager` @ 3.9.2 folds a per-partition 120 into a 48 unless the operation is `genericError`,
so the very same commit is answered two different codes at two neighbouring versions. Measured with a transaction
of `t4-38-vectors-abortable-tx` that holds a partition of `t4-38-vectors` and, because no AddOffsetsToTxn preceded
it, **not** the `__consumer_offsets` partition of `t4-38-vectors-group`:

| Version | Answer of the same commit |
|---|---|
| **v4** | **120** `TransactionAbortable` per partition — `txnoffsetcommit.response.v4.not-in-transaction` |
| v3 | **48** `InvalidTxnState` per partition — `txnoffsetcommit.response.v3.not-in-transaction` |

The difference matters to a producer: `TransactionManager` here treats the 48 as **fatal** (the producer is
finished) and the 120 as an **abortable** error, out of which `abortTransaction()` leads with the epoch bump of
KIP-360. Raising this api to the version 4 therefore turns a lost producer into a recoverable one, which is what
KIP-890 is for. See "The transaction protocol v2 of KIP-890 (Kafka 3.8), and what a client reaches on this node"
under "Transactions".

### What Kafka 4.0 changed here (KIP-890 part 2): the version 5

**Kafka 4.0 added the version 5** and no field on either side - *"Version 5 is the same as version 4 (KIP-890).
Note when TxnOffsetCommit requests are used in transaction, if transaction V2 (KIP_890 part 2) is enabled, the
TxnOffsetCommit request will also include the function for a AddOffsetsToTxn call. If V2 is disabled, the client
can't use TxnOffsetCommit request version higher than 4 within a transaction."* (`TxnOffsetCommitRequest.json` @
4.0.0; the answer says "the same with version 3"). The version is what the group coordinator acts on:

```scala
def txnOffsetCommitRequestVersionToTransactionSupportedOperation(version: Short) =
  if (version > 4) addPartition else if (version > 3) genericErrorSupported else defaultError
```

(`AddPartitionsToTxnManager` @ 4.0.0). `addPartition` sends the transaction coordinator an AddPartitionsToTxn
**without** `verify_only`, so the `__consumer_offsets` partition of the group is **enrolled** into the open
transaction - and the transaction started, if this is its first request - instead of merely verified. Measured on
the 4.3.1 node, which finalizes `transaction.version` 2, with the producer `t4-40-vectors-tx` right after its
InitProducerId and without any AddOffsetsToTxn:

| Version | Answer of the same commit |
|---|---|
| v4 | **120** `TransactionAbortable` per partition — `txnoffsetcommit.response.v4.not-enrolled`, the verification of KIP-890 part 1 as on the 3.9.2 node |
| **v5** | **0** — `txnoffsetcommit.response.v5`; the commit of the transaction it started is `endtxn.request.v5` |

`TxnOffsetCommitRequest`/`TxnOffsetCommitResponse` are the version 5 and
`TxnOffsetCommitRequestV4`/`TxnOffsetCommitResponseV4` keep the frame of Kafka 3.8. `Client::txnOffsetCommit()`
takes a last argument `bool $transactionV2 = false`: `true` sends the version 5 of the protocol v2, the default the
version 4 of the protocol v1, as the Java `TxnOffsetCommitRequest.Builder` @ 4.0.0 caps the version at 4 unless the
transaction protocol v2 is enabled.

## SaslHandshake API (key 17, v0 and v1)

The request that opens the authentication of a `SASL_PLAINTEXT` or `SASL_SSL` connection: it names the mechanism
the client wants, and it is - together with ApiVersions - one of the two requests a broker answers on such a
listener before the connection is authenticated.

```
SaslHandshake Request (Version: 0) => mechanism
SaslHandshake Request (Version: 1) => mechanism
  mechanism => STRING

SaslHandshake Response (Version: 0) => error_code [enabled_mechanisms]
SaslHandshake Response (Version: 1) => error_code [enabled_mechanisms]
  error_code         => INT16
  enabled_mechanisms => STRING
```

**The two versions are the same bytes.** `SaslHandshakeRequest.java` @ 1.1.1 declares
`SASL_HANDSHAKE_REQUEST_V1 = SASL_HANDSHAKE_REQUEST_V0` and the response does the same, so there is nothing to
decode differently; the api has no `throttle_time_ms` in either version, because it is answered before a quota can
apply (see "KIP-124: Kafka 0.11 gave the throttle time to almost every api").

What the version changes is **what the client promises about the frames that follow**, and the broker reads it as
such - `SaslServerAuthenticator.handleHandshakeRequest()` @ 1.1.1 is a single line:

```java
short version = context.header.apiVersion();
if (version >= 1)
    this.enableKafkaSaslAuthenticateHeaders(true);
```

| Version | Kafka | The tokens after the handshake | A refused credential |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0 | 0.10.0, KIP-43 | bare size-prefixed frames, no header at all | the connection is closed, no answer |
| v1 | 1.0, KIP-152 | `SaslAuthenticate` requests (key 36) | the error code **58** with a message |

The flag is per connection and it is not negotiable afterwards: a raw token after a v1 handshake and a
`SaslAuthenticate` after a v0 one are both read as garbage and cost the connection, see "SASL/PLAIN".

This client sends **v1** (`SaslHandshakeRequest`), and `SaslHandshakeRequestV0` is the class of the v0 frame - the
version every line up to `0.11.x` sends, and the one the vectors of those lines are replayed through. A 1.1.1
broker still serves v0 exactly as a 0.11.0.3 broker did, which is what
`SaslTransportTest::testTheRawTokenExchangeOfAVersionZeroHandshakeStillWorks` asserts.

**Error codes**, all three measured on `docker/kafka-1.1.1`:

| Code | When | `enabled_mechanisms` |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | the broker has the mechanism enabled | `sasl.enabled.mechanisms` of the broker, `["PLAIN"]` on the container |
| 33 `UnsupportedSaslMechanism` | it does not (`GSSAPI` against a `PLAIN`-only broker); the broker closes the connection right after the answer | the enabled ones, so the client can report what it could have asked for |
| 34 `IllegalSaslState` | the handshake did not reach the authenticator: a **second** handshake on the same connection (v1 only), or a handshake on a listener that does not authenticate at all | **empty** |

The empty list of the 34 is a **change of Kafka 1.1**: the answer is built by `getErrorResponse()` of the request
and by `KafkaApis.handleSaslHandshakeRequest`, and the latter still passed `config.saslEnabledMechanisms` in 1.0.2
while 1.1.1 passes `Collections.emptySet()`. A 0.10/0.11 broker therefore answered a handshake on the PLAINTEXT
listener with the mechanisms it had; a 1.1.1 broker answers `0000000a <corr> 0022 00000000` and nothing else -
the shortest SaslHandshake answer there is.

A **second handshake** shows the version difference plainly: after a v1 handshake the second frame is parsed as a
Kafka request, so the broker answers the 34 and *then* closes; after a v0 one the second frame is handed to the
mechanism as a token, and the connection is closed without a word. Neither leaves anything to recover.

## SaslAuthenticate API (key 36, v0 to v2)

Kafka 1.0 (KIP-152) gave the SASL tokens a request of their own, and with it the one thing the raw exchange never
had: an error code for a refused credential.

```
SaslAuthenticate Request (Version: 0) => sasl_auth_bytes
  sasl_auth_bytes => BYTES

SaslAuthenticate Response (Version: 0) => error_code error_message sasl_auth_bytes
  error_code      => INT16
  error_message   => NULLABLE_STRING
  sasl_auth_bytes => BYTES
```

The `sasl_auth_bytes` of the request are **byte for byte the payload** a v0 exchange writes on the socket raw - for
PLAIN the RFC 4616 message `authzid \0 authcid \0 passwd`. The length prefix of the `bytes` field is the same
`INT32` the bare token frame carries, so the only difference between the two exchanges is the request header in
front of it and the error code behind it.

Like SaslHandshake, the api carries **no `throttle_time_ms`**: it is answered by the authenticator, before the
connection has a principal a quota could be attached to.

**What a 1.1.1 broker answers** (measured on `docker/kafka-1.1.1`, both SASL listeners; the message is the whole
value of `error_message`, which is `null` only in the successful answer):

| Situation | `error_code` | `error_message` | `sasl_auth_bytes` |
|---|---|---|---|
| the token is accepted | 0 | `null` | the answer of the mechanism, empty for a completed PLAIN exchange |
| a wrong password | **58** `SaslAuthenticationFailed` | `Authentication failed: Invalid username or password` | empty |
| an unknown user | **58** | `Authentication failed: Invalid username or password` - the same words, on purpose | empty |
| a token the mechanism cannot even parse (no NUL separators, or the empty token) | **58** | `Authentication failed due to invalid credentials with SASL mechanism PLAIN` | empty |
| a second request after a successful authentication | **34** `IllegalSaslState` | `SaslAuthenticate request received after successful authentication` | empty |

The broker **closes the connection right after the 58**, so the answer is the last frame of that connection: the
error code buys a diagnosis, not a second attempt. The 34 is the opposite - it comes from `KafkaApis`, not from the
authenticator, and the connection stays open and usable for ordinary requests (verified by sending an ApiVersions
after it).

Three ways of getting it wrong cost the connection **without any answer**, and all three are visible in
`docker logs kafka-1-1-1`:

| Frame | What the broker does | The log line |
|---|---|---|
| a `SaslAuthenticate` as the **first** frame of a connection | closed; the authenticator only accepts ApiVersions and SaslHandshake in that state | `Unexpected Kafka request of type SASL_AUTHENTICATE during SASL handshake` (debug) |
| a `SaslAuthenticate` after a **v0** handshake | closed; the request bytes are handed to `PlainSaslServer.evaluateResponse()` as if they were the token | the `SaslException` of the mechanism |
| a `SaslAuthenticate` **v1** | closed; `handleSaslToken` throws before it can build an error response | `Invalid version for API key SASL_AUTHENTICATE: 1` |

The client sends exactly one of these requests per connection, from `IO\SocketStream::authenticate()`, and a
non-zero error code becomes a `SaslAuthenticationException` carrying the code, the message of the broker and the
matching `SaslAuthenticationFailedException` as its cause - never the password.

**Two things a 2.8.2 broker words differently.** A successful answer carries the **empty** error message instead
of a null one - the generated `SaslAuthenticateResponseData` initialises `ErrorMessage` with `""` and the
authenticator never sets it, so the frame ends with `00 00` where a 1.1.1 broker sent `ff ff` - and the **58** of a
token the mechanism cannot even parse carries the message of the mechanism itself, `Invalid SASL/PLAIN response:
expected 3 tokens, got 1`, where 1.1.1 answered the generic `Authentication failed due to invalid credentials with
SASL mechanism PLAIN` for a malformed token as well as for a wrong password. The message of a **wrong password** is
unchanged.

**Kafka 2.2 added the version 1** (KIP-368), and it changed the **answer** alone: a `session_lifetime_ms int64`
behind the `sasl_auth_bytes`.

```
SaslAuthenticateResponse (Version: 1) => ErrorCode ErrorMessage SaslAuthBytes SessionLifetimeMs
  SessionLifetimeMs => int64   -- since version 1
```

The field is the number of milliseconds after which the broker will no longer serve requests on this connection
unless the client has **re-authenticated** over it. `SaslServerAuthenticator.calcCompletionTimesAndReturnSession
LifetimeMs()` @ 2.8.2 computes it from two things and sends **0** — "no expiration" — when neither of them is set:

* `connections.max.reauth.ms`, a broker option that can be set per listener and per mechanism
  (`listener.name.sasl_plaintext.plain.connections.max.reauth.ms`), and
* the expiry of the credential itself, which only the mechanisms with an expiring credential have — a delegation
  token and OAUTHBEARER; SASL/PLAIN has none.

The container of this line sets neither, so **every answer of this document carries the lifetime 0**, which is what
`saslauthenticate.response.v1` shows. The option is listener-wide and the container is shared by the suites of this
line, so the suite does not set it.

**What a client does with a positive lifetime** (`SaslClientAuthenticator` @ 2.8.2, not implemented on this line —
the re-authentication belongs to the SaslAuthenticate v2 of Kafka 2.5): it picks a random **85 % to 95 %** of the
lifetime ("a random percentage … to avoid a reauthentication storm across many channels simultaneously") and, when
that much of the session is gone, sends a **SaslHandshake and a SaslAuthenticate again on the very same
connection**, in front of whatever request it wanted to send. The broker's `reauthenticate()` path expects exactly
that pair and refuses a principal that changed (`ensurePrincipalUnchanged`); a connection whose session expired
without a re-authentication is closed by the broker. Nothing else about the exchange changes, and a client that
ignores the field behaves exactly as it did before KIP-368 — which is what this client does today, with the
lifetime available as `SaslAuthenticateResponse::$sessionLifetimeMs` and as
`SocketStream::getSaslSessionLifetimeMs()` for the line that implements the re-authentication.

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api (`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` of
`SaslAuthenticateRequest.json` @ 2.8.2): the token is a compact `bytes` field, the error message a compact
nullable string, and the header of the request is the **v2** one with its tagged-field section. The frame around
the exchange is the only thing that changes; the token bytes are the same RFC 4616 message.

**The SaslHandshake in front of it stays the non-flexible v1**: key 17 is one of the two apis of Kafka 2.8 that
never became flexible at all (OffsetDelete is the other), so a SASL connection of this client opens with a v1
handshake in the old encoding and continues with a v2 authenticate in the new one - `IO\SocketStream` sends
exactly that pair. Measured over both SASL listeners of the container, SASL_PLAINTEXT 9094 and SASL_SSL 9095: the
answer is the error code 0, an empty compact error message, an empty token and the `session_lifetime_ms` 0, in
22 bytes (`saslauthenticate.request.v2` / `.response.v2`). `SaslAuthenticateRequestV1`/`ResponseV1` keep the frame
of the version 1 and `…V0` the one below it.

**The 3.9.2 KRaft node answers the same exchange, byte for byte**: `["PLAIN"]` as the enabled mechanisms, the
empty error message and the `session_lifetime_ms` 0 of a successful authentication, the 58 with
`Authentication failed: Invalid username or password` and with `Invalid SASL/PLAIN response: expected 3 tokens,
got 1`, and the 34 with `SaslAuthenticate request received after successful authentication`. What is new on that
node is what happens **after** the authentication: it runs the `StandardAuthorizer` with
`super.users=User:ANONYMOUS;User:admin;User:kafkatest` and `allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=false`, so the SASL
user `acltest` is authenticated exactly like the others and refused by every api afterwards — a principal is no
longer a formality of the connection. → "Broker quirks and observations", "API keys".

## Transport security (SSL)

Kafka 0.9.0.0 replaced the single `port` of a broker with a list of **listeners**, one per security protocol
(`listeners=PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092,SSL://0.0.0.0:9093`; the container of this branch adds
`SASL_PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9094,SASL_SSL://0.0.0.0:9095`). `SocketServer.scala` @ 0.10.2.2 opens one acceptor per
entry and remembers the listener of every connection; from there on the listeners are indistinguishable, they run
the same `KafkaApis` over the same request set - the two SASL ones only insert the authentication of the
"SASL/PLAIN" subsection before the first request. **No request or response changes a single byte because of the
transport**, which is why nothing above `IO\SocketStream` in this client knows that encryption exists.

A broker speaks TLS from the very first byte of a connection to its SSL listener: there is no in-protocol upgrade,
no `STARTTLS`-like request, and a plaintext request sent to 9093 is just an unparseable TLS record - the broker
drops the socket without an answer (verified: `tests/Integration/SslTransportTest.php`).

### Client configuration

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `security.protocol` | `PLAINTEXT` | `PLAINTEXT`, `SSL`, `SASL_PLAINTEXT`, `SASL_SSL`; the two SASL ones add the authentication of the "SASL/PLAIN" subsection below |
| `ssl.protocol` | `TLS` | `TLS`, `TLSv1_1`, `TLSv1_2`, `SSL`, `SSLv2`, `SSLv3` - the names of the Java client |
| `ssl.enabled.protocols` | - | list of the same values; when set it replaces `ssl.protocol` entirely |
| `ssl.ca.cert.location` | - | PEM bundle used as the trust anchor (`ssl.truststore.location` in Java) |
| `ssl.client.cert.location` | - | client certificate, only for `ssl.client.auth=required` brokers |
| `ssl.key.location` | - | private key of the client certificate |
| `ssl.key.password` | - | passphrase of that key |

`SocketStream` connects the TCP socket first and calls `stream_socket_enable_crypto()` on it afterwards, with the
crypto method that `ssl.enabled.protocols`/`ssl.protocol` map to. The stream context always carries
`verify_peer`, `verify_peer_name` and `peer_name`, so the certificate of the broker is verified and has to match
the host that was dialled; a failed handshake becomes a `NetworkException` carrying the OpenSSL message.

Two properties of PHP are worth recording, because neither is obvious:

* the handshake is bounded by the **connection timeout** the stream was created with, not by `request.timeout.ms` -
  the OpenSSL loop of PHP keeps the deadline the socket was opened with;
* `TLSv1_1` alone is refused by a current OpenSSL build (`no protocols available`) even though the broker offers
  it, because the default security level of OpenSSL 3 rejects TLS below 1.2. `TLS` (the default) and `TLSv1_2`
  negotiate TLSv1.2 against a default-configured 0.10.2.2 broker.

### Metadata answers with the endpoint of the listener it arrived on

Every version of the Metadata api - v0, v1 and v2 alike - carries exactly **one** `Host`/`Port` pair per broker, so
a single response cannot describe more than one listener. `KafkaApis.handleTopicMetadataRequest` @ 0.10.2.2 resolves
that with the listener the request came in on:

```scala
val responseBody = new MetadataResponse(
  brokers.map(_.getNode(request.listenerName)).asJava, clusterId, ..., requestVersion)
```

and `getTopicMetadata(authorizedTopics, request.listenerName, errorUnavailableEndpoints)` does the same for the
leader and replica endpoints. (The 0.9.0.1 broker of the line below did it with `request.securityProtocol`, which is
the same thing as long as a broker binds one listener per security protocol.)

Verified against the container of this branch, which advertises
`PLAINTEXT://127.0.0.1:9092,SSL://127.0.0.1:9093,SASL_PLAINTEXT://127.0.0.1:9094,SASL_SSL://127.0.0.1:9095`: the
identical Metadata request answers with broker `#0` at `127.0.0.1:9092` on the plaintext connection, at
`127.0.0.1:9093` on the encrypted one, and at `127.0.0.1:9094` / `127.0.0.1:9095` on the two authenticated ones.

The consequence for a client is that **the security protocol is a property of the whole client, not of a single
connection**: a client that bootstraps over TLS discovers TLS endpoints and keeps its configuration for every
connection it opens to them, and there is no way for it to fall back to plaintext by accident - the plaintext port
never appears in what it learned. This client gets that for free because the same configuration array reaches
`Cluster` -> `Node::getConnection()` -> `ConnectionFactory` -> `SocketStream`; the connection cache is keyed by the
security protocol as well, so a plaintext and an encrypted connection to one `host:port` can never be confused.

### SASL/PLAIN

Kafka 0.9 already shipped SASL, but only the GSSAPI (Kerberos) mechanism, and the exchange happened *outside* the
protocol: the broker expected the raw token exchange on a freshly opened connection, with nothing framing it and no
way to negotiate a mechanism. **Kafka 0.10.0 (KIP-43) put the negotiation inside the protocol** with the
`SaslHandshake` request (api key 17, v0) and added the PLAIN mechanism, which is what makes SASL implementable in
pure PHP: PLAIN is a single token carrying a user name and a password, no Kerberos ticket in sight. **Kafka 1.0
(KIP-152) put the tokens themselves inside the protocol** with the `SaslAuthenticate` request (api key 36) and
version 1 of the handshake, which is what finally gives a refused password an error code.

A `SASL_PLAINTEXT` or `SASL_SSL` connection therefore has three phases (`SaslServerAuthenticator.authenticate()` @
1.1.1, states `HANDSHAKE_OR_VERSIONS_REQUEST -> HANDSHAKE_REQUEST -> AUTHENTICATE -> COMPLETE`), and this client
walks them like this:

```
client                                     broker (SASL_PLAINTEXT://9094, SASL_SSL://9095)
  |                                                                 |
  |-- TCP connect ------------------------------------------------->|
  |-- TLS handshake (SASL_SSL only) ------------------------------->|
  |                                                                 |
  |-- Size ApiKey=17 ApiVersion=1 CorrelationId ClientId "PLAIN" -->|   an ordinary Kafka request
  |<-- Size CorrelationId ErrorCode=0 EnabledMechanisms=["PLAIN"] --|   an ordinary Kafka response
  |                                                                 |
  |-- Size ApiKey=36 ApiVersion=0 CorrelationId ClientId            |   another ordinary request:
  |        Bytes("\0<username>\0<password>") --------------------->|   the token has a header now
  |<-- Size CorrelationId ErrorCode=0 ErrorMessage=null Bytes("") --|   0 = authenticated
  |                                                                 |
  |-- Metadata, Produce, Fetch, ... ------------------------------->|   the connection is now ordinary
```

**The version of the handshake decides the framing of everything after it**, and nothing else does: `v1` makes the
broker read `SaslAuthenticate` requests, `v0` makes it read bare token frames. The v0 exchange is what every line
up to `0.11.x` speaks and a 1.1.1 broker still serves it unchanged:

```
  |-- Size ApiKey=17 ApiVersion=0 ... "PLAIN" --------------------->|
  |<-- Size CorrelationId ErrorCode=0 EnabledMechanisms=["PLAIN"] --|
  |-- Size "\0<username>\0<password>" ----------------------------->|   NOT a request: no header at all
  |<-- Size=0 ------------------------------------------------------|   the empty token, exchange complete
```

There the tokens are bare frames: an `INT32` length followed by that many bytes, which is precisely the `bytes`
primitive of the protocol - no api key, no api version, no correlation id, no client id. The broker reads them with
a plain `NetworkReceive` and hands the payload to `SaslServer.evaluateResponse()`. **The payload is the same in
both exchanges**; only the header in front of it and the error code behind it are new.

For PLAIN either exchange is one round trip. The client token is the RFC 4616 message `authzid \0 authcid \0
passwd`, which `PlainSaslServer.evaluateResponse()` splits on the NUL bytes into exactly three parts - this client
always sends an empty authorization id, as the Java `PlainLoginModule` does, and a broker accepts an authorization
id equal to the user name just as well - and the answer is `new byte[0]`, i.e. an empty token: the four bytes
`00 00 00 00` of an empty frame after v0, and an empty `sasl_auth_bytes` inside the response after v1. The
credentials travel in clear text inside the token, so `SASL_PLAINTEXT` is only sound on a trusted network;
`SASL_SSL` performs the identical exchange inside the TLS channel and is the same code path plus the `ssl.*`
options - both were measured, frame for frame, on 9094 and on 9095.

This client sends **v1** and has no option to make it send v0: there is nothing to gain from an exchange that
cannot report an error. The v0 path stays implemented (`SaslHandshakeRequestV0` and the raw token frames) because
it is the exchange of the four lines below and because a 1.1.1 broker still answers it; `SocketStream` selects it
through a single protected method, which is how the tests keep both paths covered.

#### Client configuration

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `security.protocol` | `PLAINTEXT` | `SASL_PLAINTEXT` and `SASL_SSL` authenticate; `SASL_SSL` also takes every `ssl.*` option |
| `sasl.mechanism` | `PLAIN` | the only implemented mechanism, see below |
| `sasl.username` | - | the `authcid` of the token, `user_<name>` in the JAAS file of the broker |
| `sasl.password` | - | sent in clear text inside the token |

The JAAS configuration of the Java client (`sasl.jaas.config`, or a `KafkaClient` login module named by
`java.security.auth.login.config`) is **not** reproduced: a login module is a Java class, and PHP has no JAAS. The
two options above are the whole equivalent of the `username`/`password` of `PlainLoginModule`. An empty or missing
one is refused before a socket is opened, because a broker would only answer it by dropping the connection.

Of the four mechanisms a 0.10.2.2 or 0.11.0.3 broker can enable, this client performs `PLAIN` only. `GSSAPI` needs a Kerberos
binding, which PHP has neither in core nor as a maintained extension that could produce tokens a broker accepts;
`SCRAM-SHA-256` and `SCRAM-SHA-512`, added by 0.10.2 (KIP-84), need the multi-round exchange of RFC 5802 with
SASLprep-normalized credentials, which is a mechanism of its own and is out of scope here. Both are refused with an
`InvalidConfigurationException` that names the reason rather than being sent to the broker.

#### What the broker does, observed on `docker/kafka-1.1.1`

Every one of these was measured with raw frames on the running container - both SASL listeners - and all of them
are asserted by `tests/Integration/SaslTransportTest.php`. The column that matters is the version of the handshake
the connection opened with:

| Situation | After a **v1** handshake | After a **v0** handshake |
|---|---|---|
| handshake with an enabled mechanism | `ErrorCode = 0`, `EnabledMechanisms = ["PLAIN"]` | the same frame |
| handshake with a mechanism it has not enabled | `ErrorCode = 33` (UnsupportedSaslMechanism) with the enabled ones, **then the connection is closed** | the same |
| token with a wrong password | `SaslAuthenticate` answer with `ErrorCode = 58` and `Authentication failed: Invalid username or password`, **then the connection is closed** | the connection is **closed during the token exchange**, without any answer (`SaslException` -> `IOException`) |
| token for an unknown user | the identical 58 answer - the two are deliberately indistinguishable | closed, as above |
| a token the mechanism cannot parse | `ErrorCode = 58`, `Authentication failed due to invalid credentials with SASL mechanism PLAIN` | closed |
| a `sasl_auth_bytes` of `-1` (null) | the connection is closed without an answer | (a null token frame is the same thing) |
| a second `SaslAuthenticate` after a successful one | `ErrorCode = 34` with `SaslAuthenticate request received after successful authentication`, and **the connection stays usable** | – |
| the wrong framing: a raw token after v1, a `SaslAuthenticate` after v0 | the connection is closed without an answer; the broker log shows `Error parsing request header. Our best guess of the apiKey is: 107` for the first case | the same, with the `SaslException` of the mechanism for the second |
| any other request as the first frame (Metadata, …) | the connection is closed without an answer - the broker parses the first frame as a handshake (or as a GSSAPI token, see below) and gives up | the same |
| a second `SaslHandshake` on the same connection | `ErrorCode = 34` with an **empty** mechanism list, then the connection is closed | closed without an answer: the second frame is read as a token |
| a version above the table (`SaslHandshake` v2, `SaslAuthenticate` v1) | the connection is closed without an answer, and `docker logs` says `Invalid version for API key …` | the same |
| `ApiVersions` (api key 18) before the handshake | **answered normally**, in v0 and v1 alike, with the full api-version list, and the handshake still works on that connection afterwards; a version above the table is answered with the error code 35 | the same |

The error code 58 is what Kafka 1.0 added to this picture, and it changes what a client can *say*: after a v1
handshake a wrong password is a fact the broker states, not a socket that went away. This client raises a
`SaslAuthenticationException` (client-side, deliberately not a `KafkaException`, so it leaves every retry loop) for
both shapes, carrying the code and the message of the broker when there is one and the closed connection when there
is not - retrying either is pointless.

The first frame of a connection is ambiguous on purpose: `SaslServerAuthenticator` @ 1.1.1 accepts a
`SaslHandshake` request, an `ApiVersions` request or a raw GSSAPI token there (the state `INITIAL_REQUEST`), so
that a 0.9 client, which knows nothing about the handshake, can still authenticate with Kerberos. That is why an
unparseable first frame is dropped silently rather than answered with an error: the broker cannot know whether it
was a malformed request or a token of a mechanism it does not have.

That the Java client of 1.1 sends **ApiVersions first** on a SASL connection (`SaslClientAuthenticator`, states
`SEND_APIVERSIONS_REQUEST -> RECEIVE_APIVERSIONS_RESPONSE -> SEND_HANDSHAKE_REQUEST`) is how it learns whether the
broker has key 36 at all before it promises the framed exchange. This client does not need the probe - it targets a
1.1.1 broker and sends v1 straight away - but the probe *works*: an ApiVersions before the handshake is answered
and costs the connection nothing, which is asserted over both listeners.

The endpoint property of the section above holds for the SASL listeners as well: the identical Metadata request
answers with `127.0.0.1:9094` on a `SASL_PLAINTEXT` connection and with `127.0.0.1:9095` on a `SASL_SSL` one, so a
client that bootstraps over SASL discovers the SASL endpoints of the cluster and keeps authenticating to every
broker it learns about. The connection cache is keyed by the security protocol **and** the user name, so two
clients with different credentials never share a connection.

## Delegation tokens (KIP-48)

Kafka **1.1** gave a cluster a second kind of credential. A **delegation token** is a short-lived secret that a
principal which has already authenticated asks the cluster for and then hands to somebody else — the worker
processes of a job, typically, which would otherwise all need the Kerberos keytab or the password of that
principal. The four apis of KIP-48 issue a token (**38**), move its expiry forward (**39**), shorten it or delete it
(**40**) and list the tokens the caller may see (**41**), all of them at version 0 and all of them new in 1.1.

A token has two halves, and they travel together in every answer:

* the **token id**, a 22-character base64 uuid (`CoreUtils.generateUuidAsBase64`), which identifies the token in
  ZooKeeper under `/delegation_token/<tokenId>`;
* the **HMAC**, the `HmacSHA512` of that id under the broker's `delegation.token.master.key`
  (`DelegationTokenManager.createHmac` @ 1.1.1), which is **64 bytes** on the wire and is the secret. Every later
  request names its token by those raw bytes and never by the id; the Kafka tools print and accept the base64 form
  of them.

Three things about the master key decide whether the apis do anything at all. It is not set by default, and a broker
without one answers **61** (`DelegationTokenAuthDisabled`); it has to be the same string on every broker of the
cluster, because the HMAC is derived from it and any broker has to be able to recompute it; and the container of
this repository sets it (`delegation.token.master.key=kafkatest-delegation-token-master-key`), which is why the four
apis can be exercised here at all.

**The owner of a token is never in a request.** It is `request.session.principal`, the principal of the connection,
which is why `KafkaApis.allowTokenRequests` @ 1.1.1 refuses all four apis with **64**
(`DelegationTokenRequestNotAllowed`) on three kinds of channel: a **PLAINTEXT** one, a one-way **SSL** one whose
principal is therefore `User:ANONYMOUS`, and a channel that itself authenticated **with a token** — a token may not
mint another token. On the container that leaves the two SASL listeners, 9094 and 9095, and the principal is the
SASL/PLAIN user: `User:kafkatest`.

**A token that this client issues cannot be used by this client.** Authenticating *with* a token is a SASL/SCRAM
login (`SCRAM-SHA-256` or `SCRAM-SHA-512`) whose user name is the token id, whose password is the base64 HMAC and
whose SASL extensions carry `tokenauth=true`; this package implements the mechanism **PLAIN** alone, so the four
apis are implemented and verified against a real broker while the login with their result is not. That is a
deliberate limitation of this line, see "What is not in Kafka 1.1.1".

The three timestamps every answer carries are absolute milliseconds of the **broker's** clock, and
`DelegationTokenManager.createToken` computes them like this, with the defaults of a broker that configures nothing
but the master key (`delegation.token.max.lifetime.ms` = 7 days, `delegation.token.expiry.time.ms` = 24 hours):

| Field             | Value                                                                            |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `issue_timestamp` | `time.milliseconds()` of the broker at the moment the token was created           |
| `max_timestamp`   | `issue + min(max_life_time, delegation.token.max.lifetime.ms)`, and a `max_life_time` of `-1` or of anything `<= 0` means the second term |
| `expiry_timestamp`| `min(max_timestamp, issue + delegation.token.expiry.time.ms)` — the earlier of the hard end and one default renewal period |

Measured on the container with `max_life_time = 3600000`: `max − issue = 3600000` and `expiry − issue = 3600000`,
i.e. the one-hour maximum is below the 24-hour default renewal period and therefore *is* the first expiry. With
`max_life_time = -1` both terms would be the defaults, 7 days and 24 hours.

`AdminClient::createDelegationToken()`, `renewDelegationToken()`, `expireDelegationToken()` and
`describeDelegationToken()` are the four methods of this client, and each of them goes to **any** broker of the
cluster (`sendAnyNode`, as the Scala `AdminClient.createToken` @ 1.1.1 does): the token lives in ZooKeeper and every
broker caches it, so there is no coordinator and no controller involved.

**(3.x) On a KRaft node the token lives in the metadata log, and three of the four apis are forwarded to the
controller.** KIP-900 (Kafka **3.6**) is what made delegation tokens work without ZooKeeper at all:
`DelegationTokenControlManager` writes a `DelegationTokenRecord` for a create and a renew and a
`RemoveDelegationTokenRecord` for an immediate expiry, and every token cache in the cluster - the controller's own
and the one of every broker - is filled by the `DelegationTokenPublisher` when that record is **replayed**. The
setting is `delegation.token.secret.key` now (`delegation.token.master.key` is its deprecated alias, and the image
of this line sets the new name); the id is still a base64 uuid and the hmac still the `HmacSHA512` of it, but there
is no `/delegation_token/<tokenId>` znode behind them any more. DescribeDelegationToken (41) stays a broker-local
read of that cache. What a client has to know is the **replay lag**: the answer of a create leaves the controller
before its own record has been replayed, so for a moment the token is not there yet - measured on the node of this
line, **about 66 ms** in which a renew or an expire of that very token is the **62** of an hmac that names no token,
and **about 77 ms** in which a describe does not list it. A client that creates a token and uses it in the next
statement has to wait for it (`DelegationTokenApiTest::awaitToken()`), and a 62 right after a create is not a lost
token. → the "(3.x)" block of "Broker quirks and observations".

## CreateDelegationToken API (key 38, v0 to v3)

Issues a delegation token. New in Kafka **1.1** (KIP-48) as version 0, for the principal of the connection alone;
since the version 3 of Kafka **3.3** (KIP-373) a caller may ask for a token of *another* principal.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`TOKEN_CREATE_REQUEST_V1 = TOKEN_CREATE_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back. The pair `createdelegationtoken.request.v1` / `createdelegationtoken.response.v1` at the end
of this document was captured on the 2.8.2 container.

**Kafka 2.4 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** one of this api (`"flexibleVersions": "2+"`), and it is
the version this client sends. No field is added: the renewer array and the two strings of every renewer are
compact, every structure ends in a tagged-field section, and **`throttle_time_ms` stays the LAST field of the
answer**, where KIP-124 put it for the four token apis. The **owner** of the answer is the one place where the
shape of this package and the shape of the specification differ: `PrincipalType` and `PrincipalName` are two
ordinary fields there, not a structure, so they carry **no** tag buffer of their own, and the scheme of the answer
declares the `KafkaPrincipal` of this package as an `InlineStruct` (see "Implementation model"). In the *request*
the very same class is a real structure - `[]CreatableRenewers` - and does carry one.

**Kafka 3.3 added the version 3, the owner principal of KIP-373**: "Version 3 adds owner principal" of
`CreateDelegationTokenRequest.json` @ 3.3.2 and "Version 3 adds token requester details" of the answer of the same
tag. Two nullable strings go **in front of** the renewer array - `owner_principal_type` and `owner_principal_name`
- and name the principal the token belongs to; both null is what every version below 3 sends, and the comment of
the specification says what that means: "If it's null it defaults to the token request principal". Two more
strings come back in the answer, behind the owner - `token_requester_principal_type` and
`token_requester_principal_name` - so that a token issued for somebody else says who asked for it. It is the
version this client sends; `CreateDelegationTokenRequestV2`/`CreateDelegationTokenResponseV2` keep the frame of
the version 2, whose vectors are replayed through them.

```
CreateDelegationTokenRequest => OwnerPrincipalType OwnerPrincipalName [Renewer] MaxLifeTime
  OwnerPrincipalType => nullable string   -- since version 3
  OwnerPrincipalName => nullable string   -- since version 3
  Renewer => PrincipalType Name
    PrincipalType => string
    Name          => string
  MaxLifeTime => int64
```

```
CreateDelegationTokenResponse => ErrorCode Owner TokenRequester IssueTimestamp ExpiryTimestamp MaxTimestamp
                                 TokenId Hmac ThrottleTimeMs
  ErrorCode => int16
  Owner => PrincipalType Name
    PrincipalType => string
    Name          => string
  TokenRequester => PrincipalType Name    -- since version 3
    PrincipalType => string
    Name          => string
  IssueTimestamp  => int64
  ExpiryTimestamp => int64
  MaxTimestamp    => int64
  TokenId         => string
  Hmac            => bytes
  ThrottleTimeMs  => int32
```

**`ThrottleTimeMs` is the last field of the answer, not the first one** — and the same is true of the other three
apis of KIP-48. KIP-124 put the field in front of every answer that Kafka 0.11 already had, but an api that was
*added* afterwards appends it instead: `CommonFields.THROTTLE_TIME_MS` stands at the end of the schema and is
written with `setIfExists` at the end of `toStruct` @ 1.1.1. The token apis are the exception of this line, not
the rule: SaslAuthenticate (36) carries no throttle time at all, and AlterReplicaLogDirs (34), DescribeLogDirs
(35), CreatePartitions (37) and DeleteGroups (42) put it first, like every api KIP-124 touched. Verified byte for
byte on the container, see the vectors below.

`Renewer` names the principals that may renew or expire the token besides its owner. Every one of them has to be of
the type **`User`** (`KafkaPrincipal.USER_TYPE`): `KafkaApis.handleCreateTokenRequest` checks the whole list before
it asks the token manager for anything and answers **67** (`InvalidPrincipalType`) for the first entry that is not,
without creating a token. An empty array is the normal case of a token nobody but its owner may touch.

`MaxLifeTime` is a **period in milliseconds**, not a timestamp, and it is capped at the broker's
`delegation.token.max.lifetime.ms`; `-1` — and any other value `<= 0` — asks for exactly that maximum.

The answer carries the whole token: the `Owner` the broker derived from the connection, the three timestamps, the
`TokenId` and the 64 bytes of the `Hmac`. It does **not** repeat the renewers of the request, which is why
`Admin\DelegationToken::fromCreateResponse()` takes them from the request the caller sent, as the Scala
`AdminClient.createToken` @ 1.1.1 does. An answer that carries an error carries the principal of the connection as
its owner and the "no token" values of `CreateDelegationTokenResponse(throttleTimeMs, error, owner)`: the three
timestamps are `-1`, the token id is the empty string and the hmac is an **empty** byte array — not a null one.

Error codes observed on the 1.1.1 container:

| Code | Name                             | Request that produces it                                                   |
|------|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                             | The token is in the answer                                                  |
| 61   | DelegationTokenAuthDisabled      | A broker without a `delegation.token.master.key` — **not** observable here, the container has one |
| 64   | DelegationTokenRequestNotAllowed | The same request on the PLAINTEXT listener, where the owner is `User:ANONYMOUS` |
| 67   | InvalidPrincipalType             | A renewer `Group:analytics` instead of a `User:` one                        |

**A token for another principal (version 3, KIP-373)**, measured on the 3.9.2 KRaft node over the SASL_PLAINTEXT
listener. `kafkatest` asking for a token of `User:acltest` is answered the code 0, the **owner** `User:acltest`
and the **requester** `User:kafkatest` (`createdelegationtoken.response.v3.other-owner`), while the ordinary
request of a token for the caller itself answers the same principal twice
(`createdelegationtoken.response.v3`). Who may ask for a token of somebody else is the second half of KIP-373:
the operation `CREATE_TOKENS` (13) on the `USER` resource (7) of that principal, both of them values the version
3 of the three ACL apis added in the same release - see "CreateAcls API (key 30, v0 to v3)". A super user needs no
acl for it; the SASL user `acltest` asking for a token of `User:admin` without one is answered **65**
(`DelegationTokenAuthorizationFailed`), *not* the 31 of the other apis of this line, with the owner it asked for,
itself as the requester and the "no token" values in the rest of the frame
(`createdelegationtoken.response.v3.unauthorized`).

**What the requester may do afterwards is not what it may see.** `TokenInformation.ownerOrRenewer` @ 3.9.2 counts
`owner || tokenRequester || renewers`, so the requester finds the token in a DescribeDelegationToken; the
controller of a KRaft cluster is narrower, `DelegationTokenControlManager.allowedToRenew` @ 3.9.2 being
`owner || renewers` **without** the requester. Measured on the node: `kafkatest`, which asked for the token of
`User:acltest`, sees it in its own describe and is answered **63** (`DelegationTokenOwnerMismatch`) by both
RenewDelegationToken and ExpireDelegationToken, while `acltest` renews and expires it with the code 0. A requester
that wants to keep the token alive has to name itself in the renewers of the request.

## RenewDelegationToken API (key 39, v0 to v2)

Moves the expiry of a token forward. New in Kafka **1.1** (KIP-48) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`TOKEN_RENEW_REQUEST_V1 = TOKEN_RENEW_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`renewdelegationtoken.request.v1` / `renewdelegationtoken.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `RenewDelegationTokenRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.5.

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api: the hmac becomes a compact `bytes`
field, the request carries the header v2, and the header and the body each end in a tagged-field section. The
`throttle_time_ms` stays **last** in the answer, where the three token apis have carried it since KIP-48 — the
flexible encoding moves no field. `RenewDelegationTokenRequest`/`Response` are the version 2 with
`FLEXIBLE_VERSION = 2` and `RenewDelegationTokenRequestV1`/`ResponseV1` keep the frame of the versions 0 and 1;
`renewdelegationtoken.request.v2` / `.response.v2` were measured over the SASL_PLAINTEXT listener.

```
RenewDelegationTokenRequest => Hmac RenewTimePeriod
  Hmac            => bytes
  RenewTimePeriod => int64
```

```
RenewDelegationTokenResponse => ErrorCode ExpiryTimestamp ThrottleTimeMs
  ErrorCode       => int16
  ExpiryTimestamp => int64
  ThrottleTimeMs  => int32
```

**A token is named by its HMAC, never by its id.** `DelegationTokenManager.getToken(hmac)` @ 1.1.1 looks the token
up by those bytes in the token cache, which is what makes the HMAC the secret half of a token: whoever has it can
renew the token, provided the principal of the connection is allowed to.

`RenewTimePeriod` is a **period counted from now**, and the new expiry is `min(maxTimestamp, now + period)`; a
negative period asks for the broker's `delegation.token.expiry.time.ms`. A renewal can therefore never move a token
past the maximum lifetime it was issued with — measured on the container with a token whose `MaxTimestamp` was one
hour away:

* `RenewTimePeriod = 600000` → `ExpiryTimestamp = now + 600000`, ten minutes away;
* `RenewTimePeriod = 604800000` (seven days) → `ExpiryTimestamp = MaxTimestamp` exactly, the cap;
* `RenewTimePeriod = -1` (the broker's 24 hours) → `ExpiryTimestamp = MaxTimestamp` as well, for the same reason.

**Only the owner and the renewers may renew.** `DelegationTokenManager.allowedToRenew` compares the principal of the
connection with the owner and with every entry of the token's renewer list, and answers **63**
(`DelegationTokenOwnerMismatch`) for anybody else. Both halves were measured: `User:admin` renewing a token of
`User:kafkatest` that names `User:admin` as a renewer succeeds, and the same principal renewing a token of
`User:kafkatest` with an empty renewer list is the 63.

Error codes observed on the 1.1.1 container:

| Code | Name                             | Request that produces it                                                   |
|------|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                             | The new expiry is in the answer                                             |
| 62   | DelegationTokenNotFound          | An HMAC no token of the cluster has, and an HMAC of a token that was deleted |
| 63   | DelegationTokenOwnerMismatch     | A principal that is neither the owner nor one of the renewers               |
| 64   | DelegationTokenRequestNotAllowed | The same request on the PLAINTEXT listener                                  |
| 66   | DelegationTokenExpired           | A token whose `ExpiryTimestamp` or `MaxTimestamp` is already in the past    |

Every error answers the timestamp **-1** (`DelegationTokenManager.ErrorTimestamp`), never a real one.

## ExpireDelegationToken API (key 40, v0 to v2)

Shortens the life of a token, or ends it now. New in Kafka **1.1** (KIP-48) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`TOKEN_EXPIRE_REQUEST_V1 = TOKEN_EXPIRE_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`expiredelegationtoken.request.v1` / `expiredelegationtoken.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `ExpireDelegationTokenRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.5.

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api, exactly as for RenewDelegationToken:
a compact hmac, the request header v2, two tagged-field sections, and the `throttle_time_ms` still last.
`ExpireDelegationTokenRequestV1`/`ResponseV1` keep the frame of the versions 0 and 1, and
`expiredelegationtoken.request.v2` / `.response.v2` are the deletion of the token of the vectors, measured over
the SASL_PLAINTEXT listener.

```
ExpireDelegationTokenRequest => Hmac ExpiryTimePeriod
  Hmac             => bytes
  ExpiryTimePeriod => int64
```

```
ExpireDelegationTokenResponse => ErrorCode ExpiryTimestamp ThrottleTimeMs
  ErrorCode       => int16
  ExpiryTimestamp => int64
  ThrottleTimeMs  => int32
```

The two frames are the ones of RenewDelegationToken, field for field — the schemas of the two answers are literally
identical in `*DelegationTokenResponse.java` @ 1.1.1 — and the same `allowedToRenew` check guards both. What differs
is the **sign** of the period, which chooses between two different operations in
`DelegationTokenManager.expireToken`:

* a **negative** `ExpiryTimePeriod` **deletes** the token: it is removed from ZooKeeper and from the token cache of
  every broker, and the answer carries the `now` of the broker as its `ExpiryTimestamp`. Measured: the timestamp
  lies inside the interval the client measured around the request;
* a **non-negative** one only moves the expiry, to `min(maxTimestamp, now + period)`, and the token stays. Measured
  with 120000: the answer and a DescribeDelegationToken afterwards both report `now + 120000`, and the token is
  still listed.

**A deleted token is 62, not 66.** Expiring the same token a second time answers `DelegationTokenNotFound`: for the
broker the token is not "expired", it is gone. Measured on the container.

**A token that is past its expiry can no longer be expired** — on the 2.8.2 ZooKeeper broker. The
`maxTimestamp < now || expiryTimestamp < now` check runs before the sign of the period is looked at there, so a
token that has run out answers **66** to an expire request just as it does to a renew one; only the broker's own
sweeper removes it, every `delegation.token.expiry.check.interval.ms` (one hour by default).

**(3.x) On a KRaft node it CAN be expired, because the checks are ordered the other way round.**
`DelegationTokenControlManager.expireDelegationToken` @ 3.9.2 looks the token up, checks `allowedToRenew` and then
handles `expiryTimePeriodMs < 0` **first**: an immediate expiry writes the `RemoveDelegationTokenRecord` and
answers **0** with the clock of the node, whatever the timestamps of the token say, and only the *non-negative*
branch below it tests `maxTimestamp < now || expiryTimestamp < now` and answers 66. A **renew** of such a token is
still 66 — there the expiry test comes before the ownership check, as it always did. Measured on the node with a
token created with `MaxLifeTime = 1`: renew → 66, expire → 0 and the token is gone, a second expire → 62. The
controller sweeps expired tokens as well (`sweepExpiredDelegationTokens`), so an application that leaks tokens
still does not leak them forever. → the "(3.x)" block of "Broker quirks and observations".

Error codes observed on the 1.1.1 container: the ones of RenewDelegationToken — 0, 62, 63, 64 and 66 — with the
same `-1` timestamp on every error.

## DescribeDelegationToken API (key 41, v0 to v3)

Lists the tokens the caller may see. New in Kafka **1.1** (KIP-48) as version 0.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1** and changed not one byte of the frame:
`TOKEN_DESCRIBE_REQUEST_V1 = TOKEN_DESCRIBE_REQUEST_V0`, and the same for the answer, in `Protocol.java` @ 2.0.1.
The higher version is the
client's promise of KIP-219 - that it honours `throttle_time_ms` itself instead of waiting for a broker that
holds the answer back - and a 2.8.2 broker still serves every version below it. The pair
`describedelegationtoken.request.v1` / `describedelegationtoken.response.v1` at the end of this document was captured on the 2.8.2
container; `DescribeDelegationTokenRequestV1` is what a client sends to a broker below Kafka 2.5.

**Kafka 2.5 added the version 2**, the first **flexible** version of the api, and it is the one token api whose
answer shows what a flexible frame does to a nested structure: every string of an owner and of a renewer becomes
compact, the hmac becomes a compact `bytes` field, and **every renewer entry ends in a tagged-field section**
while the `owner` does **not** - `DescribeDelegationTokenResponse.json` @ 2.8.2 declares the owner as two flat
fields of the token (`PrincipalType` and `PrincipalName`) that this client reads into one
`Common\Security\KafkaPrincipal`, and a field group of that kind is marked `Protocol\InlineStruct` so that the
engine writes no tag buffer behind it. `DescribeDelegationTokenRequestV1`/`ResponseV1` keep the frame of the
versions 0 and 1; `describedelegationtoken.request.v2` / `.response.v2` were measured over the SASL_PLAINTEXT
listener, with one token of `User:admin` that names `User:kafkatest` as its renewer.

**Kafka 3.3 added the version 3**, and it is the answer that changed: "Version 3 adds token requester details" of
`DescribeDelegationTokenResponse.json` @ 3.3.2 - two more flat strings inside every token, between its owner and
its timestamps, that name the principal which **asked** for it (KIP-373). The request did not change at all
("Version 3 adds token requester into the response" of the request json), so the version alone asks for them. It
is the version this client sends; `DescribeDelegationTokenRequestV2`/`DescribeDelegationTokenResponseV2` keep the
frame of the version 2, whose vectors are replayed through them, and the token entry of that frame is
`Protocol\Data\DescribeDelegationTokenResponseTokenV2`.

```
DescribeDelegationTokenRequest => [Owner]
  Owner => PrincipalType Name        (nullable array)
    PrincipalType => string
    Name          => string
```

```
DescribeDelegationTokenResponse => ErrorCode [TokenDetail] ThrottleTimeMs
  ErrorCode => int16
  TokenDetail => Owner TokenRequester IssueTimestamp ExpiryTimestamp MaxTimestamp TokenId Hmac [Renewer]
    Owner => PrincipalType Name
    TokenRequester => PrincipalType Name   -- since version 3
    IssueTimestamp  => int64
    ExpiryTimestamp => int64
    MaxTimestamp    => int64
    TokenId         => string
    Hmac            => bytes
    Renewer => PrincipalType Name
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
```

**The `Owner` array is nullable and its three shapes are three different questions**, which
`KafkaApis.handleDescribeTokensRequest` @ 1.1.1 tells apart before it filters anything:

* **null** asks for every token the caller may see;
* a **non-empty** array asks for the tokens that one of the named principals owns or may renew;
* an **empty** array asks for nothing at all and is answered with the error code 0 and an empty token array, without
  the token cache being read (`DescribeDelegationTokenRequest.ownersListEmpty()`). Measured: code 0, zero tokens.

An entry of the answer is a whole token, the **HMAC included** and with the renewers that the create request had
named and that the create answer had not repeated. Whoever may describe a token can therefore renew and expire it,
which is why the filter matters.

**Quirk: without an authorizer every authenticated principal describes every token.** `DelegationTokenManager.filterToken`
lets a token through when the requesting principal is its owner or one of its renewers **or** when
`authorize(session, Describe, DelegationToken(tokenId))` says yes — and `KafkaApis.authorize` is
`authorizer.forall(...)`, which is `true` when there is no authorizer at all. On the container, which runs without
one, `User:admin` asking with a null owner list gets the tokens of `User:kafkatest` back, HMACs and all. Measured.
That is not a hole a client can close; it is what "the ACL apis are not implemented on that line" cost, and it is
the same `forall` that makes the ACL apis themselves answer 54 there.
