**(3.x) With the `StandardAuthorizer` on, `super.users` decides it.** `DelegationTokenManager.filterToken` @ 3.9.2
asks `authorize(DESCRIBE_TOKENS, USER, <owner>)` first and falls back to "owner or renewer" only when that is
refused, so on the node of this line the super users `admin` and `kafkatest` still see every token with every hmac,
while `acltest` - the one SASL user that `super.users` does not list - sees the tokens it owns or may renew and
**nothing else**. Asking for a foreign owner is still the code 0 with an empty array there, never a 29 or a 63.
Measured on the node.

**(3.3) The requester of a token sees it without being named a renewer of it.**
`TokenInformation.ownerOrRenewer` @ 3.9.2 is `owner || tokenRequester || renewers`, and that is the question
`filterToken` asks: measured on the node, `kafkatest` - which asked for a token of `User:acltest` and is not a
renewer of it - finds that token in its own describe, with `User:acltest` as the owner and itself as the requester
(`describedelegationtoken.response.v3`), and finds it again when it names `User:acltest` as the owner it asks for
(`describedelegationtoken.response.v3.by-owner`). What it may **not** do is renew or expire it, see
"CreateDelegationToken API (key 38, v0 to v3)": the controller answers 63 there. A token of a KRaft node is a
controller write like every other one, so a describe that follows a create reads the image of the broker and may
need a second look - both tokens of the measurement were visible ~20 ms after their answers.

Naming an owner that has no token is not an error either: the answer is the code 0 with an empty array, the same
answer an owner whose tokens the caller may not see would produce.

Error codes observed on the 1.1.1 container:

| Code | Name                             | Request that produces it                                              |
|------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                             | Every visible token is in the answer, possibly none of them            |
| 61   | DelegationTokenAuthDisabled      | A broker without a master key — **not** observable here                |
| 64   | DelegationTokenRequestNotAllowed | The same request on the PLAINTEXT listener, with an empty token array  |

`Admin\AdminClient::describeDelegationToken()` returns the tokens indexed by their id, and
`Admin\DelegationToken::hmacAsBase64String()` is the form that `kafka-delegation-tokens.sh` prints, so the two can
be compared directly:

```
docker exec kafka-1-1-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-delegation-tokens.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9094 \
    --describe --command-config <a file with security.protocol=SASL_PLAINTEXT, sasl.mechanism=PLAIN and a PLAIN sasl.jaas.config>
```

## DescribeAcls API (key 29, v0 to v3)

Reads the acls of the cluster through a **filter**. New in Kafka **0.11** (KIP-140) as version 0, and implemented
on this line for the first time: the lines below left the three ACL apis out by decision, because a broker without
an `authorizer.class.name` answers every one of them with **54** (`SecurityDisabled`) and
`No Authorizer is configured on the broker`, and every wire vector of this repository comes from a real broker.
The node of this line runs `org.apache.kafka.metadata.authorizer.StandardAuthorizer` with
`super.users=User:ANONYMOUS;User:admin;User:kafkatest` and `allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=false`, so the SASL
user `acltest` is the one principal an acl can be written for and measured against.

**Kafka 2.0 added the version 1**, the `pattern_type_filter` of KIP-290: until then the resource of an acl was a
name, since then it is a **pattern** - a literal name or a prefix. **Kafka 2.4 added the version 2**, the first
**flexible** one (`"flexibleVersions": "2+"` of `DescribeAclsRequest.json` @ 3.3.2): the request header v2,
compact strings, a tagged-field section at the end of the header, of every acl, of every resource and of the body.
**Kafka 3.3 added the version 3**, which adds no field at all - "Version 3 adds user resource type" - and is the
promise that the client understands the `USER` resource type of KIP-373 in an answer. It is the version this
client sends, and the only one it has a class for: the api is new on this line, the node announces 0 to 3, and the
versions this client speaks are the ones that were captured on it.

```
DescribeAclsRequest => ResourceTypeFilter ResourceNameFilter PatternTypeFilter
                       PrincipalFilter HostFilter Operation PermissionType
  ResourceTypeFilter => int8
  ResourceNameFilter => nullable string
  PatternTypeFilter  => int8              -- since version 1
  PrincipalFilter    => nullable string
  HostFilter         => nullable string
  Operation          => int8
  PermissionType     => int8
```

```
DescribeAclsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs ErrorCode ErrorMessage [Resource]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  ErrorCode      => int16
  ErrorMessage   => nullable string
  Resource => ResourceType ResourceName PatternType [Acl]
    ResourceType => int8
    ResourceName => string
    PatternType  => int8                  -- since version 1
    Acl => Principal Host Operation PermissionType
      Principal      => string
      Host           => string
      Operation      => int8
      PermissionType => int8
```

**The request is one filter and the answer is grouped by pattern.** The seven fields of the request are the two
halves of an `AclBindingFilter` of the Java client - which resource patterns, and which of their acls - and this
package models them the same way, as a `Common\ResourcePatternFilter` and a `Common\AccessControlEntryFilter`
inside a `Common\AclBindingFilter`; neither half is a structure of the specification, so both are declared as an
`InlineStruct` and carry no tag buffer (see "Implementation model"). The answer names every matching **pattern**
once and puts its acls inside it, which is why `Admin\AdminClient::describeAcls()` flattens the groups back into
one `Common\AclBinding` per acl.

The codes are the ones of `org.apache.kafka.common.acl.AclOperation`, `AclPermissionType` and
`org.apache.kafka.common.resource.{ResourceType, PatternType}` @ 3.9.2, which this package publishes as
`Common\AclOperation`, `Common\AclPermissionType`, `Common\ResourceType` and `Common\PatternType`:

| Enumeration       | Values on the wire                                                                          |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ResourceType`    | `UNKNOWN` 0, `ANY` 1, `TOPIC` 2, `GROUP` 3, `CLUSTER` 4, `TRANSACTIONAL_ID` 5, `DELEGATION_TOKEN` 6, **`USER` 7 (Kafka 3.3, KIP-373)** |
| `PatternType`     | `UNKNOWN` 0, `ANY` 1, `MATCH` 2, `LITERAL` 3, `PREFIXED` 4 - only the last two are ever *stored* |
| `AclOperation`    | `UNKNOWN` 0, `ANY` 1, `ALL` 2, `READ` 3, `WRITE` 4, `CREATE` 5, `DELETE` 6, `ALTER` 7, `DESCRIBE` 8, `CLUSTER_ACTION` 9, `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS` 10, `ALTER_CONFIGS` 11, `IDEMPOTENT_WRITE` 12, **`CREATE_TOKENS` 13 and `DESCRIBE_TOKENS` 14 (Kafka 3.3, KIP-373)** |
| `AclPermissionType` | `UNKNOWN` 0, `ANY` 1, `DENY` 2, `ALLOW` 3                                                  |

**`ANY` and `MATCH` are filter values, and `MATCH` is the interesting one.** `ANY` (1) matches every value of its
field - a null name does the same for the three names - while the pattern type `MATCH` (2) asks a question no
other value asks: *which acls apply to this resource*. It answers the literal pattern of the given name, every
**prefixed** pattern the name starts with, and the wildcard `*`. Measured on the node with a prefixed acl on
`t4-33-acl-`: a `MATCH` filter for the group `t4-33-acl-group-one`, a group that does not even exist, answers that
acl (`describeacls.response.v3.match`), where a `LITERAL` or `ANY` filter for the same name answers nothing.

**The whole request is authorized before the filter is read.** `AclApis.handleDescribeAcls` @ 3.9.2 starts with
`authHelper.authorizeClusterOperation(request, DESCRIBE)`, so a principal that may not `Describe` the `CLUSTER`
resource is answered **31** (`ClusterAuthorizationFailed`) with no resource at all - it cannot even read the acls
that are written for itself. The `error_message` of that refusal is the whole request object of the broker,
because `AuthHelper.authorizeClusterOperation` builds the exception with `s"Request $request is not authorized."`:

```
Request Request(processor=8, connectionId=172.18.0.2:9094-172.18.0.1:44220-27,
session=org.apache.kafka.network.Session@2aa27ff7, listenerName=ListenerName(SASL_PLAINTEXT),
securityProtocol=SASL_PLAINTEXT, buffer=null, envelope=None) is not authorized.
```

A processor number, a connection id, the identity hash of a Java object and the listener of the connection: a
diagnosis for a log file and never a second source of truth. The code 31 is. **Kafka 4.1 names the missing
operation instead**: `AuthHelper.authorizeClusterOperation` @ 4.1.0 builds `s"Request $request needs $operation
permission."`, so the 4.3.1 node ends the same sentence with `needs DESCRIBE permission.` Kafka 4.0 removed the
version 0 of the three ACL apis (KIP-896); the node serves 1 to 3 and closes the connection of a version 0 frame.

**The `error_message` of a successful answer is the empty string, not null.** The generated
`DescribeAclsResponseData` @ 3.9.2 initialises the field with `""` and the handler sets the throttle time and the
resources and nothing else, so the field arrives as the compact `01` and never as the null `00` - the same is true
of DescribeQuorum and UnregisterBroker, and **not** of DescribeCluster, whose message really is null. → "Broker
quirks and observations".

What the node answers for the filter shapes this client sends, measured with two acls written by
`Admin\AdminClient::createAcls()` - a `LITERAL` `TOPIC` acl on `t4-33-acl-topic` and a `PREFIXED` `GROUP` acl on
`t4-33-acl-`, both `READ ALLOW` for `User:acltest` from every host:

| Filter                                                      | Answer                                              |
|-------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| everything (`AclBindingFilter::any()`)                       | both acls, as two resources with one acl each         |
| resource type `TOPIC`                                        | the literal `TOPIC` resource alone                    |
| principal `User:acltest`                                     | both acls - the principal filter is matched literally, as the whole `User:name` string |
| pattern type `MATCH` on a group name that starts with the prefix | the prefixed `GROUP` resource                     |
| resource type `TRANSACTIONAL_ID`, of which there is no acl   | the code 0 and an empty resource array - not an error |
| resource type `USER`                                         | the `USER` acl of KIP-373, resource type 7 with the operation 13 |
| any of them as `acltest`                                     | the code **31** and no resource                       |

Error codes of the api:

| Code | Name                       | Request that produces it                                                |
|------|----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | None                       | The filter was applied; `Resource` is what it matched, possibly nothing   |
| 31   | ClusterAuthorizationFailed | A principal that may not `Describe` the `CLUSTER` resource                |
| 42   | InvalidRequest             | A filter the authorizer cannot make sense of                              |
| 54   | SecurityDisabled           | A broker without an `authorizer.class.name` - every line below this one, and the 2.8.2 container of the line below |

`docker exec kafka-3-9-2 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list` sends exactly this
api with the filter that matches everything and prints its answer grouped by resource, which is the cross-check
for every measurement above - and the emptiness check every suite of this repository owes the shared node.

## CreateAcls API (key 30, v0 to v3)

Writes acls into the authorizer. New in Kafka **0.11** (KIP-140) as version 0; the versions 1, 2 and 3 are the
ones of DescribeAcls, added in the same releases and for the same reasons - the pattern type of KIP-290 (2.0), the
flexible encoding (2.4) and the `USER` resource type of KIP-373 (3.3), which adds no field.

```
CreateAclsRequest => [Creation]
  Creation => ResourceType ResourceName ResourcePatternType Principal Host Operation PermissionType
    ResourceType        => int8
    ResourceName        => string
    ResourcePatternType => int8           -- since version 1
    Principal           => string
    Host                => string
    Operation           => int8
    PermissionType      => int8
```

```
CreateAclsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [Result]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  Result => ErrorCode ErrorMessage
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string
```

**One request writes any number of acls, and every one of them is reported on its own.** The results come back in
the order of the creations and there is exactly one per creation - the api has **no top-level error code at all**,
which is why a request that is refused as a whole carries the same code in every entry. `Admin\AdminClient::createAcls()`
therefore throws nothing and returns the error of every acl of the call, like `alterConfigs()` does for a resource.

A creation is a concrete acl, not a filter: the pattern type is `LITERAL` or `PREFIXED`, the resource type, the
operation and the permission type are none of the `ANY`/`UNKNOWN` values, and the principal and the host are real
strings. The two checks `AclApis.handleCreateAcls` @ 3.9.2 makes itself are a `CLUSTER` resource whose name is not
`kafka-cluster` and an **empty** resource name, both of them `InvalidRequestException`:

| Creation                                     | What the node answers                                                    |
|----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| a valid acl                                  | the code 0 with the `error_message` **`""`**, the empty string of a bare `new AclCreationResult()` |
| the **same** acl a second time               | the code 0 again - the authorizer keeps a set, and writing an acl twice is not an error |
| an empty resource name                       | **42** (`InvalidRequest`) with `Invalid empty resource name` in the entry of that creation |
| a `CLUSTER` resource under another name      | 42 with `The only valid name for the CLUSTER resource is kafka-cluster`   |
| a pattern type `ANY` (1)                     | **-1** (`UnknownServerError`) with a **null** message, see below          |
| anything, sent by `acltest`                  | **31** (`ClusterAuthorizationFailed`) in every entry                      |

**The -1 is worth knowing about.** `CreateAclsRequest.aclBinding` @ 3.9.2 turns an entry of the request into a
`ResourcePattern` *before* any validation of the api runs, and that constructor throws the plain
`IllegalArgumentException("patternType must not be ANY")`, which `ApiError.fromThrowable` can only map to the
unknown error - the broker logs `Unexpected error handling request` with that stack trace and answers -1 with no
message at all (`createacls.response.v3.pattern-type-any`). A Java application never sees it, because its
`AclBinding` refuses to be built in the first place; a client that writes the bytes itself has to validate the
pattern type, which is what `Common\PatternType::isSpecific()` is for.

**A write of an acl is a controller write.** `CreateAcls` is one of the apis a KRaft broker forwards to the
controller in an **Envelope** (key 58), so the refusal of `acltest` is produced *there*: the `error_message` of
`createacls.response.v3.unauthorized` is a request object of the `CONTROLLER` listener with an
`envelope=Some(Request(...))` inside it, where the DescribeAcls refusal - which the broker answers itself - names
the SASL listener of the client. The acl is in the metadata log when the answer arrives, and the authorizer of a
broker applies it when it replays that record: a describe that follows a create needs a poll, which is what the
measurements of this section do (both acls were visible on the first retry, under 20 ms later).

**The `USER` resource of KIP-373 is why the version 3 exists.** `createacls.request.v3.user-resource` writes
`CREATE_TOKENS` (13) on the `USER` resource (7) named `acltest`, which is the acl that lets a principal ask for a
delegation token of that user - see "CreateDelegationToken API (key 38, v0 to v3)". The broker stores it like any
other acl and `kafka-acls.sh --list` prints it as
`ResourcePattern(resourceType=USER, name=acltest, patternType=LITERAL)`. Nothing in the answer of a *lower*
version hides such an acl, by the way: the version validation of `DescribeAclsResponse` @ 3.9.2 only refuses
non-literal pattern types to a version 0, so the "adds user resource type" of the three apis is a contract about
what a client understands, not a filter the broker applies.

## DeleteAcls API (key 31, v0 to v3)

Removes the acls that a filter matches. New in Kafka **0.11** (KIP-140) as version 0, with the same version
history as the two apis above.

```
DeleteAclsRequest => [Filter]
  Filter => ResourceTypeFilter ResourceNameFilter PatternTypeFilter
            PrincipalFilter HostFilter Operation PermissionType
```

```
DeleteAclsResponse => ThrottleTimeMs [FilterResult]
  ThrottleTimeMs => int32
  FilterResult => ErrorCode ErrorMessage [MatchingAcl]
    ErrorCode    => int16
    ErrorMessage => nullable string
    MatchingAcl => ErrorCode ErrorMessage ResourceType ResourceName PatternType
                   Principal Host Operation PermissionType
      ErrorCode    => int16
      ErrorMessage => nullable string
      ...          => the seven fields of the acl that was matched
```

**A delete never names an acl, it names a filter** - the very same `AclBindingFilter` a DescribeAcls request
carries, one or more of them in one frame - so the answer has to say what was removed: every acl a filter matched
is repeated **in full**, with an error code of its own, because the deletion of one acl can fail while the rest of
the same filter succeeds. `Common\AclBindingFilter::of()` builds the filter of one known acl, whose seven fields
are all concrete and which therefore matches at most one (`matchesAtMostOne()` of the Java client);
`Common\AclBindingFilter::any()` matches **every acl of the cluster** and is the delete that empties the
authorizer.

There is no top-level error code here either: one result per filter, in the order of the request.

| Filter of the request                        | Its result                                                              |
|----------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| a filter that matches acls                   | the code 0, a **null** `error_message`, and every matched acl in full with the code 0 of its own deletion |
| a filter that matches nothing                | the code 0 and an **empty** list - not an error, and what a delete of an acl that was never written looks like |
| any filter, sent by `acltest`                | **31** in every filter result, with no matching acl                       |

**The `error_message` of a successful filter is null, where the one of a successful creation is the empty
string.** The two handlers build their results differently: `AclApis.handleDeleteAcls` @ 3.9.2 goes through
`DeleteAclsResponse.filterResult(...)`, which sets the message of `ApiError.NONE` - a null - while
`handleCreateAcls` leaves the `""` that the generated data class starts with. Both were measured on the node
(`deleteacls.response.v3` against `createacls.response.v3`), and neither is worth reading: the code is.

Like a creation, a deletion is a **controller write** that a KRaft broker forwards in an Envelope, and the
authorizer of a broker forgets the acl when it replays the record - `deleteacls.response.v3.unauthorized` is
refused on the `CONTROLLER` listener for the same reason `createacls.response.v3.unauthorized` is.

## Cluster readiness

**This is one of the things Kafka 0.10 quietly fixed.** On the two lines below, a broker that had just started
answered a Metadata request with an **empty broker array** and kept doing so until some topic existed: the broker
list of a Metadata response comes from the metadata cache of the broker, that cache is only filled once the
controller has pushed an `UpdateMetadata` request to it, and on a cluster without a single topic that never
happened. Clients had to treat an empty broker array as "not ready, retry", never as "the cluster has no brokers".

A broker of **0.10.2.2 or 0.11.0.3** fills its cache with the live brokers as soon as the controller has elected
itself, with or without topics. `KafkaApis.handleTopicMetadataRequest` answers with `metadataCache.getAliveBrokers`,
and that is populated from the very first `UpdateMetadata` the controller sends on broker startup. Verified on a
throwaway container of the image of this branch, started empty and asked before anything else touched it:

```
Metadata v0, empty topic array:  brokers = 1, topics = 0
Metadata v1, null topic array:   brokers = 1, topics = 0
```

Two consequences, and neither of them makes the readiness probe obsolete:

* An empty broker array is **still** not "the cluster has no brokers" — it is "this broker has not caught up yet",
  and a broker that is still starting, or one whose controller connection has just been re-established, can answer
  it for a moment. `tests/Fixture/ClusterReadinessProbe.php` and `Cluster::bootstrap()` keep retrying it, and the
  probe costs nothing when the first answer is already complete. The probe asks with **version 0** on purpose: it
  is the first frame the suite sends to a broker that may still be booting, every release from 0.8 on serves that
  version, and nothing the later ones add is of any use before the cluster is up. `Cluster::bootstrap()` asks with
  version 2 instead — with the one topic it was given, or with a `null` topic array when it was given none.
* A **fresh topic** still answers 5 (`LeaderNotAvailable`) or 6 (`NotLeaderForPartition`) for a moment after it has
  been created, exactly as on 0.8 and 0.9, because the leader election is asynchronous. Every helper that creates a
  topic retries those two codes.
* **(3.x)** On a KRaft node the moment has two halves, and a Metadata answer only ends the first one. The broker
  publishes every metadata delta to its metadata cache first and to its replica manager after it, so a Metadata
  request that names the leader of a fresh partition is answered before a Produce, a Fetch or a ListOffsets to that
  very broker stops answering 6: the gap is the replay lag of the node, which was measured at tens of milliseconds
  on an idle node and at up to 2.4 seconds on a loaded CI runner (the run of `057ea5b`, where eleven tests of
  eight classes that had produced right after a complete Metadata answer were refused with 6, an acks=0 produce
  whose connection the broker closed, the 14 and 16 of a group coordinator that was still loading
  `__consumer_offsets`, and a client quota that was set but not yet applied). `tests/Fixture/TopicMetadataProbe.php`
  therefore returns only when the broker answers the latest offset of every partition with the code 0 (retrying
  3, 5, 6 and 9), `tests/Fixture/ClusterReadinessProbe.php` warms the group coordinator once per process (a
  FindCoordinator, then an OffsetFetch of a group that does not exist, until the answer is not 14, 15 or 16), and
  `tests/Fixture/ClientQuota.php` reads a quota back with DescribeClientQuotas until the broker reports it.

Note that readiness is not covered by a TCP health check either: the broker accepts connections on 9092 long before
it has registered itself with ZooKeeper.

## Broker quirks and observations

Everything a Kafka broker does that a client cannot read out of the protocol grammar, collected from the
integration suite of this branch and measured on the **2.8.2** ZooKeeper broker of the 2.x line; the last block,
"The 3.9.2 KRaft node of the 3.x line", holds what the node of this line does differently. The groups follow the apis, from
the framing through the record format, Produce/Fetch, the group apis and the admin apis to the transport and the
container; the section that describes each item in detail is named behind it. An item marked **(3.x)** is a change
this line measured against the 2.8.2 broker, one marked **(2.x)** a change the 2.x line measured against the 1.1.1 line, one marked **(1.1)** or **(1.0)** a change the 1.x line made against
0.11.0.3, one marked **(0.11)** or **(0.10)** a change an older line made that is still true; the older lists are
in `docs/protocol/2.8.md`, `docs/protocol/0.11.0.md`, `docs/protocol/0.10.2.md` and `docs/protocol/0.9.0.md` on their
branches.

**Framing and api surface**

* **(0.10) An api the broker cannot parse costs the connection.** The broker closes the socket - `docker logs
  kafka-1-1-1` shows `Closing socket for ... because of error` with the `InvalidRequestException` or
  `SchemaException` that caused it - where a 0.9.0.1 broker dropped the frame and kept the connection open, and a
  0.8.2.2 broker closed it. A **malformed body of a version the broker does serve** is punished the same way.
  → "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection".
* **(1.0) The version that costs the connection moved with the release, again.** A 0.11.0.3 broker hung up on
  Produce v4, Fetch v6, Metadata v5, SaslHandshake v1 and the api key 34; a 1.1.1 broker serves all of them and
  hangs up one version higher (Produce v6, Fetch v8, Metadata v6, SaslHandshake v2 …) and on the api key **43**.
  → "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection".
* **(1.0) The message the broker logs for it names the api and the connection.**
  `Error getting request for apiKey: OFFSET_COMMIT, apiVersion: 4, connectionId: …, listenerName:
  ListenerName(PLAINTEXT), principal: User:ANONYMOUS`, where 0.11 printed `apiKey: 8 and apiVersion: 4` and nothing
  else. An api key above the table is a one-line `InvalidRequestException: Unknown API key 43` without a cause.
  → "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection".
* **(1.0) ControlledShutdown (7) is no longer the exception to any of this.** Kafka 1.0 moved the api to the schemas
  of the Java client and gave `RequestHeader` a `CONTROLLED_SHUTDOWN_V0_SCHEMA` for the one frame whose header has
  no client id, so the ApiVersions answer reports **v0 and v1** where 0.11 reported v1 alone, and v2 closes the
  connection where a 0.11 broker answered it like v1. **ApiVersions (18) is now the only api that answers an unknown
  version.** → "Every api of the table validates its version".
* **(1.0) An unknown broker id in a ControlledShutdown is still answered with 8, and no longer logged.**
  `handleControlledShutdownRequest` @ 1.1.1 turns the controller's `Failure` straight into the response;
  the `ERROR [KafkaApi-0] error when handling request … BrokerNotAvailableException: Broker id 4242 does not exist.`
  that a 0.10/0.11 broker printed is gone. → "ControlledShutdown API (key 7, v0 to v3)".
* **(1.0) SaslAuthenticate (36) answers 34 with a message on a listener that did not authenticate with it.**
  `SaslAuthenticate request received after successful authentication` — on the PLAINTEXT listener, where there was
  no authentication at all, and on a SASL listener that finished its exchange. Like the handshake, the api never
  reaches `KafkaApis` while a SASL connection is being authenticated.
* **(1.1) The four delegation-token apis (38-41) answer 64 on a PLAINTEXT connection**, before they read their body.
  The container has a `delegation.token.master.key`, so the answer is not the 61 of a broker without one; a token is
  only issued over a channel that authenticated a real principal. → "API keys".
* **(1.1) DescribeLogDirs (35) with an *empty* topic array answers both log directories with no partition at all,
  and with a *null* one every partition of both.** The container runs `log.dirs=/tmp/kafka-logs,/tmp/kafka-logs-2`,
  so the empty-array answer is the 56-byte frame `error_code 0, /tmp/kafka-logs, [], error_code 0,
  /tmp/kafka-logs-2, []` — the cheapest way to ask a broker which log directories it has. → "API keys".
* **(0.10) ApiVersions (18) is the one api whose unknown version is answered**, with the error code 35, in the
  version 0 layout, on a connection that stays open. **(0.11)** That answer is still the *version 0* layout although
  the broker serves version 1, so it has no throttle time. **(2.4)** It is not empty any more either: KIP-511
  fills the array with the one row of ApiVersions itself (`18 0 3` on this container), so the 6-byte body of the
  lines below is 12 bytes here. → "ApiVersions API (key 18, v0 to v4)".
* **(2.4) The unknown version of ApiVersions still has to carry the request header its version prescribes.**
  `RequestHeader.parse` asks `ApiKeys.forId(18).requestHeaderVersion(apiVersion)` before anything validates the
  version, and that is the **header v2** from version 3 on, served or not: a v4 frame with the plain header of the
  versions 0 to 2 is `Error parsing request header. Our best guess of the apiKey is: 18` and a closed connection,
  the same frame with an empty tag buffer behind the client id is answered with the 35.
  → "An api the broker does not serve closes the connection".
* **(0.11) ApiVersions v1 appends its throttle time instead of prepending it.** Every other api KIP-124 touched puts
  `throttle_time_ms` first; this api puts it last, so that the leading `error_code` stays at the offset a version 0
  client reads it at. **(2.0)** The v2 of KIP-219 changes nothing about that - it is the v1 frame.
  → "ApiVersions API (key 18, v0 to v4)".
* **(0.11) The reported api set depends on `inter.broker.protocol.version`** —
  `ApiVersionsResponse.apiVersionsResponse()` filtered `ApiKeys.values()` by `minRequiredInterBrokerMagic <=
  minMagic` — and **(2.8) it depends on the listener** as well: `ApiVersionManager` @ 2.8.2 builds the answer from
  the apis of the `zkBroker`, `broker` or `controller` listener the request arrived on (KIP-500), which is why the
  56 keys of this container do not contain the KRaft apis 52-55, 58, 59 and 62-64 that `ApiKeys.java` @ 2.8.2 does
  contain, and why a frame of one of them is answered with a closed connection and
  `Received request api key VOTE which is not enabled`. → "API keys".
* **(0.11) The ACL apis 29, 30 and 31 are served but disabled.** Without an `authorizer.class.name` a 1.1.1
  broker answers all three with the error code **54** (`SecurityDisabled`) and the message
  `No Authorizer is configured on the broker` - with a trailing dot in the CreateAcls and DeleteAcls answer and
  without one in the DescribeAcls answer. → "API keys".
* **(0.11) `InitProducerId` (22) with a null `transactional_id` allocates a producer id and creates nothing else.**
  The broker answers error 0 with a fresh producer id and the epoch 0, straight out of the id block it reserved in
  ZooKeeper; no `__transaction_state` entry is written, which is what makes the api safe to probe. The
  `__transaction_state` topic is created by a `GroupCoordinator` (FindCoordinator) v1 request with
  `coordinator_type = 1`, not by this one.
* **(0.11) The reported api set depends on `inter.broker.protocol.version`** — see the bullet above; on this
  container it is `1.1-IV0`, which is why all 43 keys appear.
* **(0.10) SaslHandshake (17) on a non-SASL listener answers 34** (`IllegalSaslState`), whatever mechanism was
  asked for: on a SASL listener the request never reaches the api layer, so everything
  `KafkaApis.handleSaslHandshakeRequest` sees is a handshake at the wrong moment. **(1.1) That answer now carries
  an empty mechanism list**, where 0.10, 0.11 and 1.0.2 filled it with `config.saslEnabledMechanisms`; 1.1.1 passes
  `Collections.emptySet()`. The connection stays open on a PLAINTEXT listener, because the answer came from
  `KafkaApis` and not from the authenticator. → "SaslHandshake API (key 17, v0 and v1)".
* **(0.10) A broker without topics answers Metadata with its brokers**, where 0.8 and 0.9 answered zero brokers
  until a topic existed. An empty broker array is still "not ready, retry". → "Cluster readiness".
* **Metadata v0 answers with the endpoint of the listener the request arrived on**, one host/port per broker: a
  client that bootstraps over TLS learns the TLS endpoints of the whole cluster, one that bootstraps in plaintext
  learns the plaintext ones, and no request can ask one listener about the other.
  → "Metadata answers with the endpoint of the listener it arrived on".
* **An empty topic array means two different things.** In Metadata **v0** it asks for *every* topic of the cluster;
  in **v1** and above `[]` means "no topic at all" and `null` (`ff ff ff ff`) is what asks for every topic. A client
  that sends the v0 request unchanged as v1 gets an empty answer instead of the whole cluster.

**Message format and compression**

* **(0.10) The api version does not decide the format of the log, `message.format.version` of the topic does.** A
  magic 0 message set sent with Produce **v2** is accepted and stored as format v1 with the `Timestamp` -1, and a
  magic 1 set is accepted by a Produce v1 and even a Produce v0 request. The broker never checks one against the
  other. → "What the broker converts, and when".
* **(0.10) A Fetch below version 2 is answered down-converted to format v0**: the timestamps are stripped, the
  relative inner offsets of a compressed set are made absolute and the set is recompressed - an lz4 set then carries
  the *broken* frame checksum, because the result is a v0 set. Version 2 of the Fetch api is nothing but the
  statement "I understand message format v1". → "What the broker converts, and when".
* **(0.10) `message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime` rewrites only the wrapper of a compressed batch.** Its attributes
  announce the codec and the LogAppendTime bit and its timestamp is the append time; the inner messages keep the
  `CreateTime` values the producer sent, and a reader has to ignore them for the whole set.
  → "Timestamps inside a compressed message set".
* **(0.10) A compressed v1 set stores relative inner offsets**, 0, 1, 2 …, and the wrapper carries the absolute
  offset of the **last** inner message, so the reader computes `wrapperOffset - lastInnerOffset + innerOffset`. A v0
  set stores absolute ones. → "Offsets inside a compressed message set".
* **(0.10) The lz4 frame of a magic 0 message carries a broken descriptor checksum** (KAFKA-3160), the one of a
  magic 1 message the correct one; both the broker and this client write the one that belongs to the magic byte and
  accept either when reading. → "The lz4 codec and the KAFKA-3160 checksum".
* **(0.11) The on-disk bytes of a record batch are its wire bytes.** The log segment of a partition that a
  `docker cp` copies out of the container is byte for byte what a Fetch v4 answers for the same offsets, header
  fields and checksum included - which is what makes `DumpLogSegments` a second opinion on every capture.
  → "RecordBatch (message format v2)".
* **(0.11) A `LogAppendTime` batch keeps the timestamps of its producer.** Only `MaxTimestamp` is replaced with the
  append time and only bit 3 of the attributes is set; `FirstTimestamp` and every `TimestampDelta` stay as they were
  produced, and a reader has to answer `MaxTimestamp` for all of the records instead of adding the deltas.
  → "Offsets, timestamps and sequence numbers are deltas".
* **(0.11) The lz4 frame of a record batch always carries the correct descriptor checksum** `0x82`: KAFKA-3160 is
  bound to the message format v0, which a magic 2 batch can never be. → "Compression compresses the records, not a
  wrapper".
* **(0.11) The broker converts a produced batch down on write and the log down on read.** A record batch v2 sent to
  a topic with `message.format.version=0.9.0` is accepted by a Produce v3 and stored as format v0, and the log of a
  0.11 topic is answered as format v1 to a Fetch v2/v3 and as format v0 to a Fetch v0/v1, one message per record.
  → "What the broker stores, and what it answers".
* **(0.11) A record with headers can not be down-converted at all.** A Fetch below version 4 of a partition whose
  records carry headers answers that partition with the error code **-1** (`UnknownServerError`) and an empty
  record set, because the magic 1 builder of `MemoryRecordsBuilder.appendWithOffset` refuses them ("Magic v1 does
  not support record headers"). Headers therefore raise the minimum Fetch version of a topic, silently.
  → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(0.11) Time-based retention deletes a segment by the largest timestamp it holds, not by the time it was
  written.** A batch produced with a `CreateTime` of 1600000000000 (2020-09-13) into a container whose clock says
  2026 is deleted by the very next run of the retention check (`log.retention.check.interval.ms`, five minutes on
  this container) although it was appended seconds earlier: `log_start_offset` moves and the records are gone. That
  is why every capture and every integration test of this line stamps its records with the current clock, and why a
  capture has to be copied out of the container immediately. → "RecordBatch (message format v2)".

**Produce and Fetch**

* **(0.10) `LogAppendTime` of a Produce v2 answer is `-1` unless the topic asks for it**; on a
  `message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime` topic it is the clock of the broker, and it is then the timestamp every
  message of that batch is fetched back with. → "Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)".
* **(0.10) The request-level `MaxBytes` of Fetch v3 is spent in the order of the request.**
  `ReplicaManager.readFromLocalLog` subtracts what it has read from `limitBytes`, so a partition behind an exhausted
  budget comes back with an empty message set although its high water mark is above the fetch offset - and the same
  fetch with the partitions swapped serves the other one. An empty partition is therefore not proof that it is
  drained. → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(0.10) The first non-empty partition of a v3 fetch always makes progress.** `minOneMessage = !hardMaxBytesLimit`
  and `hardMaxBytesLimit` is `versionId <= 2`, so a 4 KiB message is returned whole even for `MaxBytes = 0`: an
  answer may be *larger* than the limit it asked for. The consequence is that the `RecordTooLargeException` of the
  lower versions cannot happen for a v3 client. → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(0.11) A Produce v3 answer is a Produce v2 answer.** `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V3` **is** `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V2` in
  `Protocol.java` @ 0.11.0.3: version 3 of the api changed the *request* only. The `log_start_offset` that a produce
  answer eventually got is Kafka 1.0 (Produce v5), so a client that reads a v3 answer with a partition entry of five
  fields runs past the end of the frame. Verified: the answer of `produce.request.v3` is 50 bytes and ends with its
  `ThrottleTime` right behind the `LogAppendTime`. → "Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)".
* **(0.11) A Produce v3 request with a message set closes the connection.** `ProduceRequest.parse` @ 0.11.0.3
  refuses a record set whose magic is below 2 for a version 3 request and the broker drops the socket instead of
  answering an error code (`InvalidRecordException: Produce requests with version 3 are only allowed to contain
  record batches with magic version 2`); the versions 0 to 2 accept every magic, the record batch v2 included. That
  is why `message.format.version` selects the api version here. → "Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)".
* **(0.11) A fetch is answered in whole batches, so it can carry records below the offset it asked for.** That was
  already true of a *compressed* message set, and the message format v2 makes it the normal case: every produce call
  writes one batch per topic-partition, and a fetch that starts inside one is answered with the whole batch. A
  partition whose records were deleted up to the offset 2 of a five-record batch therefore answers a fetch from the
  offset 2 with all five records; dropping the ones below the position is the job of the consumer
  (`KafkaConsumer::collectRecords()` does it, `Client::fetch()` reports what the broker sent).
  → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(0.11) `last_stable_offset` and `aborted_transactions` are the "not asked" answer of a `read_uncommitted`
  fetch, not a state of the partition.** A Fetch v4/v5 with `isolation_level = 0` is answered with
  `LastStableOffset = -1` and the element count **-1** of a null `AbortedTransactions` array, whatever the partition
  holds; with `isolation_level = 1` the same partition answers the real LSO - the high water mark when no
  transaction ever touched it - and an array that is present and *empty*. `log_start_offset` is reported for both
  levels, because it is a property of the log. → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(0.11) A fetch never crosses a segment boundary.** Observed while capturing the aborted transaction: when the
  abort marker of the coordinator landed in a segment of its own, a fetch from the offset 0 answered with the data
  batch alone although the last stable offset was two offsets further on, and the marker needed a second fetch.
  `Log.read` reads from a single segment, so an answer that stops below the high water mark says nothing about the
  log. → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(1.0) A record with headers is now readable by a client below Fetch v4 — without its headers.** A 1.1.1 broker
  converts such a batch down like any other and simply leaves the headers out ("Ignore headers when down-converting
  to V0 and V1 since they are not supported", `AbstractRecords.convertRecordBatch` @ 1.1.1): the partition is
  answered with the error code **0** and every one of its records, not with the error code **-1** and an empty
  record set that a 0.11.0.3 broker answered. Measured with a three-record batch whose middle record carries a
  header: a Fetch v3 answers magic 1 with all three records, their `CreateTime` and no headers, a Fetch v1 answers
  magic 0 with all three records and no timestamps, and `DumpLogSegments` still shows `headerKeys: [trace-id]` in
  the log. → "What the broker converts, and when", "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(1.0) A Produce v4 answer is a Produce v2 answer, and only v5 appends `log_start_offset`.**
  `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V4` **is** `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V3` **is** `PRODUCE_RESPONSE_V2` @ 1.1.1. What the versions 4 and
  6 of Produce and Fetch really state is which error code the client understands: a broker that would report **56**
  `KAFKA_STORAGE_ERROR` answers **6** `NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION` to a Produce v3 or a Fetch v5 instead. **The
  container cannot produce a storage error at all** - it has healthy log directories and no way to break one from
  the outside - so the translation is documented from `ProduceRequest.java`/`FetchRequest.java` @ 1.1.1 and from
  the api version, not from a measurement. → "Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)".
* **(1.0) `log_start_offset` of a Produce v5 answer is 0 for an untouched log, never -1.** It only moves when the
  retention of the topic or a `DeleteRecords` request removed something: a partition whose first two records were
  deleted answers 2 for every following append (`produce.response.v5`). → "Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)".
* **(1.1) A fetch session answers its errors with the session id 0, and the session survives them.** Both **70**
  `FETCH_SESSION_ID_NOT_FOUND` and **71** `INVALID_FETCH_SESSION_EPOCH` come back with an empty topics array and
  `session_id = 0` (`SessionErrorContext` @ 1.1.1 builds the answer with `INVALID_SESSION_ID`), so a client that
  copied the session id out of every answer would lose its own session on the first error. The session itself is
  untouched: the next request with the right epoch is served normally, and the way to start over is a full fetch
  with the same id and the epoch 0, which removes the old session and opens a new one with a **new** id.
  → "Fetch sessions (v7, KIP-227)".
* **(1.1) An incremental fetch answers a partition whose fetch offset did not move, again and again.** The session
  remembers the fetch offset of every partition, and a partition is included in the answer whenever its record set
  is non-empty - which it is as long as the client keeps asking from the same offset. "Only what changed" therefore
  means "only what changed *since the answer you were given*", and a client that does not send its new fetch
  offsets in the topics array of the next incremental request gets the same records over and over.
  → "Fetch sessions (v7, KIP-227)".
* **(1.1) An incremental fetch that forgets its last partition closes the session.** `FetchSession.update` removes
  the forgotten partitions and `newContext` falls back to a session-less answer when nothing is left
  (`session.isEmpty` ⇒ `SessionlessFetchContext`), so the answer carries `session_id = 0` and the id is gone: the
  next incremental request with it is answered with 70. → "Fetch sessions (v7, KIP-227)".
* **(1.1) A session-less Fetch v7 is served exactly like a Fetch v6.** `session_id = 0` with `epoch = -1` - the
  `LEGACY` metadata of the Java client - is answered with the whole requested set and `session_id = 0`, and the
  broker keeps no state for it. That is what `Client::fetchPartitions()` sends.
  → "Fetch sessions (v7, KIP-227)".
* **(1.1) A full session cache costs the *newcomer* its session, it does not evict anybody.** The cache holds
  `max.incremental.fetch.session.cache.slots` sessions, **1000** by default, and `FetchSessionCache.tryEvict`
  @ 1.1.1 may only evict an entry that is *stale* - unused for longer than the hard-coded
  `KafkaServer.MIN_INCREMENTAL_FETCH_SESSION_EVICTION_MS`, **two minutes** - or one that sits in `evictableByAll`,
  which `touch()` only fills for a session that is *older* than those two minutes. A young session is therefore not
  evictable at all: measured on the container, the 1000th `epoch = 0` request of a raw probe was answered with
  `error_code 0` and **`session_id = 0`**, i.e. "no session for you", while every session that already existed kept
  answering its incremental fetches normally. A client must read the id of its own answer and be able to live
  without one - which is the same state a broker below Kafka 1.1 leaves it in. The eviction that KIP-227 describes
  needs sessions older than two minutes, so a **70 is what a long-lived idle consumer sees**, never a fresh one.
  → "The consumer side of a fetch session".
* **(1.1) A fetch session outlives the connection it was opened on.** The session lives in the `FetchSessionCache`
  of the broker, keyed by its id alone: a client that drops its socket and reconnects continues the same session
  with the next epoch, and the records keep coming. What resets a session in a client is a request that *failed* -
  the client cannot know whether the broker processed it - not the reconnect itself.
  → "The consumer side of a fetch session".
* **(1.1) The epoch never becomes 0 or -1 by counting.** `FetchMetadata.nextEpoch` @ 1.1.1 answers
  `Integer.MAX_VALUE` with **1**, because 0 means "full fetch" and -1 means "no session"; a client that fetches
  often enough wraps around instead of accidentally closing its session. This one is read from the source, not
  measured: 2^31 incremental fetches take years. → "Fetch sessions (v7, KIP-227)".

* **(1.0) `offline_replicas` of a Metadata v5 answer is empty on a one-broker cluster, always.** The field is the
  set of replicas whose broker is down or whose log directory failed (KIP-112/113); the only broker of the
  container holds every replica and is up, so every partition of `metadata.response.v5` ends with `00 00 00 00`.
  An answer below version 5 does not carry the field at all, which is "the answer did not say", not "nothing is
  offline". → "Metadata API (key 3, v0 to v13)".
* **(2.0) A legacy message set in a Produce request of version 3 or higher is an error code, not a closed
  connection.** `ProduceRequest.validateRecords` @ 2.8.2 still refuses it - "Produce requests with version 3 or
  higher are only allowed to contain record batches with magic version 2" - but the offending **partition** is
  answered with **87** `INVALID_RECORD` and the connection stays open, where a 1.1.1 broker turned the same
  exception into an `InvalidRequestException` and hung up. Measured for every version 3 to 6 against all three
  magic bytes. → "Produce API (key 0, v0 to v13)".
* **(2.x) A read_uncommitted fetch is answered with the real `last_stable_offset`.** A 0.11.0.3 and a 1.1.1 broker
  answered -1 there - "you did not ask, so I did not compute it" - and this line's inherited vectors still carry
  that -1. A 2.8.2 broker fills the field in for both isolation levels; only `aborted_transactions` still
  distinguishes them (`null` for read_uncommitted, an array for read_committed). A client that used the -1 to tell
  the two answers apart has to look at the array instead. → "Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v18)".
* **(2.0) `message.downconversion.enable=false` answers 35, not 43.** A fetch that would need a down-conversion of
  such a topic is answered **35** `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` for that partition, with `high_watermark = -1` and an
  **empty** record set; the other partitions of the same request are served and the connection stays open. 43
  `UNSUPPORTED_FOR_MESSAGE_FORMAT` - the code of a timestamp lookup on a log below magic 1 - never appears here.
  A follower is exempt from the option altogether. → "KIP-283 (Kafka 2.0): lazy down-conversion, and the switch
  that refuses it".
* **(2.1) The `current_leader_epoch` of a Fetch v9 is checked in one direction on a one-broker container.** An
  epoch **above** the leader's is **75** `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH`, answered with `high_water_mark = -1` and an empty
  record set for that partition alone; `-1` skips the check entirely and is served like a version 8 fetch. The
  other direction, **74** `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH`, cannot be produced here: the single broker is never re-elected, so
  the epoch of every partition stays 0 and there is no smaller epoch to send. `Partition.checkCurrentLeaderEpoch`
  @ 2.8.2 is the rule, and both codes are retriable — a metadata refresh, never a move of the position.
  → "The leader epoch (KIP-320)".
* **(2.1) The zstd refusal of a fetch is decided by the TOPIC configuration, not by the records.**
  `KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest` @ 2.8.2 refuses a partition with **76** `UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE` when the
  request is below version 10 **and** the topic is configured `compression.type=zstd` — before it reads a byte of
  the log. A zstd batch that lies in a topic which is *not* configured that way, because a client compressed it
  itself, is served to a Fetch v9 as it lies, and only a refused *down-conversion* (35) stops it. Measured both
  ways on the container. → "Version 10 and the zstd codec (KIP-110)".
* **(2.1) A zstd record set below Produce v7 is an error code, not a closed connection.**
  `ProduceRequest.validateRecords` @ 2.8.2 refuses the codec while it parses the request — the broker parses with
  the very same class — and the partition comes back with **76**, `base_offset = -1`, `log_start_offset = -1`,
  while the connection stays open (`produce.response.v6.zstd`). The same batch sent with version 7 is appended
  with the error code 0. → "The zstd codec (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110)".
* **(2.4) A refused batch names its records by their batch index, and the good ones are not named.** A Produce
  **v8** of three records to a `cleanup.policy=compact` topic, the second and the third of them without a key,
  comes back with **87** `INVALID_RECORD`, `base_offset = -1`, a `record_errors` array of **two** entries -
  `batch_index` 1 and 2, each with "Compacted topic cannot accept message without key in topic partition …" -
  and the partition-wide `error_message` "One or more records have been rejected". The record with a key is not
  in the array: it holds the offenders, not the batch. The same request as a **version 7** one is answered the 87
  and the two `-1`s alone. → "The record errors of a refused batch (v8, KIP-467)".
* **(2.3) `preferred_read_replica` is always -1 without a `replica.selector.class`.** A Fetch v11 names the rack
  of the consumer and the **leader** answers which replica to read from; a broker with no selector configured -
  the default, and the container of this line - has nothing to ask and answers `-1`, "read from me", to every
  fetch whatever the rack. Measured with an empty rack and with `eu-1a`, which no broker of the container
  declares: the same answer, the same records, no error. → "Reading from a follower (v11, KIP-392)".
* **(2.3) A broker without an authorizer answers the authorized operations of KIP-430 as the SUPPORTED ones.**
  A Metadata v8 with both booleans on comes back with the cluster bitfield **8096** (`CREATE`, `ALTER`,
  `DESCRIBE`, `CLUSTER_ACTION`, `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS`, `ALTER_CONFIGS`, `IDEMPOTENT_WRITE`) and a topic bitfield
  **3576** (`READ`, `WRITE`, `CREATE`, `DELETE`, `ALTER`, `DESCRIBE`, `DESCRIBE_CONFIGS`, `ALTER_CONFIGS`) - the
  `AclEntry.supportedOperations` of the resource type, without `ALL` and `ANY`, because there is no authorizer to
  refuse anything. With the booleans off the same answer carries `80 00 00 00`, `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, in both
  fields: "you did not ask", which is **not** the empty set. → "The authorized operations (v8, KIP-430)".
* **(2.2) The error code 78 of a ListOffsets v5 replaces a 5, and only for a client.** A leader whose high
  watermark has not caught up with the start offset of the epoch it was just elected in can not say where the end
  of its log is; `Partition.fetchOffsetForTimestamp` @ 2.8.2 raises `OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE` for that state - for a
  **client** request only (`isolationLevel.isDefined`; a follower is exempt), and only for the latest offset or a
  timestamp beyond the last fetchable one - and `KafkaApis.handleListOffsetRequest` sends it **only to a version 5
  or higher** request, answering every lower one **5** `LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE` instead. A one-broker container
  never re-elects a leader, so this is the one rule of this line that is read from the source rather than
  measured. → "Offsets API (key 2, v0 to v11), a.k.a. ListOffset".
* **(2.1) The leader epoch of a fresh partition is 0, and every answer of the container reports it.** Metadata v7,
  ListOffsets v4 and OffsetForLeaderEpoch v2 all report `0` for a partition that has been led by the same broker
  since it was created, and `-1` (`UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH`) is what a client sends when it does not know one and what
  a leader answers when it resolves none. A vector captured on a one-broker container can therefore show the field
  but never its movement. → "KIP-320 in the consumer: leader epochs and truncation detection".

**Offsets**

* **(2.1) A commit that asks for the default retention no longer stores an expiry.** KIP-211 moved the expiry of
  the committed offsets of a group from "a fixed time after each commit" to "`offsets.retention.minutes` after the
  group became empty", and `GroupMetadataManager.offsetCommitValue` @ 2.8.2 writes the `__consumer_offsets` value
  schema **v3** (`offset leaderEpoch metadata commitTimestamp`, no expiry) for a `retention_time` of -1 and falls
  back to the schema **v1**, the only one that has an `expire_timestamp`, for a commit that brought a retention of
  its own. The field is still on the wire and still honoured up to version 4 of the api and is gone from version 5
  on. → "OffsetCommit API (key 8, v0 to v8)".
* **(2.x) A `null` OffsetFetch topic array answers the partitions in the order of the coordinator's map.** A
  2.8.2 coordinator walked the committed partitions 0 and 2 of one topic as `2, 0`; the 1.1.1 broker answered them
  in partition order. Nothing in the protocol promises an order, so a client that needs one sorts.
  → "OffsetFetch API (key 9, v0 to v9)".

* **OffsetFetch v1 no longer validates the partition**: a partition the cluster does not host is answered with the
  offset `-1` and the error code `0` ("nothing committed"), where 0.8.2.2 answered 3. Version 0, which reads
  ZooKeeper, still answers 3. → "OffsetFetch API (key 9, v0 to v9)".
* **An oversized offset metadata never reaches the coordinator cache.** A commit whose metadata exceeds
  `offset.metadata.max.bytes` is answered 12 (`OffsetMetadataTooLarge`) and the entry is filtered out before the
  append *and* before the cache is updated, so an immediate OffsetFetch reports "never committed". A 0.8.2.2 broker
  cached it. Verified with a 5000 character metadata. → "OffsetCommit API (key 8, v0 to v8)".
* **`RetentionTime` of OffsetCommit v2 counts from the commit.** `-1` asks for `offsets.retention.minutes` of the
  broker, any other value replaces it for that commit alone, and the expiry stored in `__consumer_offsets` is
  always `commitTimestamp + retention` with the commit timestamp being the receive time of the broker. Expired
  entries disappear at the next run of `offsets.retention.check.interval.ms`, not at the instant of the expiry.
  → "OffsetCommit API (key 8, v0 to v8)".
* **(0.10) "No message with that timestamp" is not an error.** Offsets **v1** answers a timestamp above the last
  message of the partition - and any timestamp on an empty log - with the error code **0**, the timestamp `-1` and
  the offset **-1**; only a topic whose `message.format.version` is 0.9.0 answers **43**
  (`UnsupportedForMessageFormat`), and `-1`/`-2` keep working even there. A lookup resolves to the **inner** record
  of a compressed batch, a `LogAppendTime` topic is searched by the append time the broker stamped, and the same
  partition twice in one request is answered 42 (`InvalidRequest`).
  → "What the broker answers (verified against the container)".
* **(0.10) The group-level error code of OffsetFetch v2 cannot be provoked on a one-broker cluster**, which
  coordinates every group itself: an unknown group id, an empty one and a 300-character one are all answered with
  the code 0 and an empty topic array, because `handleFetchOffsets` "returns offsets blindly regardless the current
  group state". → "The top-level error code of v2".
* **A null offset metadata comes back as an empty string**, not as `ff ff`: `OffsetMetadata.NoMetadata` is `""`, for
  v1 and v2 alike. The 0.8.2.2 capture of `offsetfetch.response.v1` still shows `ff ff`, so a client has to read
  both. → "A partition without a committed offset".

**Group membership**

* **JoinGroup blocks.** The coordinator answers a JoinGroup only once every known member has rejoined, so
  `request.timeout.ms` has to exceed `session.timeout.ms`, and two members of a group cannot be driven from one
  single-threaded process. → "Group membership protocol (keys 11 to 14)".
* **(2.x) An error answer of JoinGroup carries the generation `-1`**, the `UNKNOWN_GENERATION_ID` of the Java
  client, where a 0.11 or 1.1 coordinator answered `0` — `GroupCoordinator.joinError` built it with
  `generationId = 0` there. The group protocol, the leader id and the member array of an error answer are still
  empty. Measured with a session timeout below `group.min.session.timeout.ms`.
  → "JoinGroup API (key 11, v0 to v9)".
* **(2.3) A `consumer` group whose member metadata is not a `Subscription` never rebalances.** The member
  metadata is opaque to the four apis, but not to the coordinator any more: `GroupMetadata.computeSubscribedTopics()`
  (KIP-345, Kafka 2.3) parses the metadata of every member of a group whose `protocol_type` is **`consumer`** as a
  `ConsumerProtocolSubscription`, and `ConsumerProtocol.deserializeSubscription` throws a plain `RuntimeException`
  — not the `SchemaException` that `initNextGeneration` catches — for bytes whose topic array is nonsense. That
  exception escapes through `onCompleteJoin` into the **timer executor** of the rebalance purgatory, where
  `ExecutorService.submit()` swallows it into a `Future` nobody reads, so the group is left in
  `PreparingRebalance` **for good**: the JoinGroup is never answered, `kafka-consumer-groups.sh` reports
  `PreparingRebalance` for ever, and nothing but a broker restart clears the group. Measured on the container with
  a raw JoinGroup v1 to v4 carrying 22 arbitrary bytes; the same frame with a real `Subscription` is answered in
  2 ms, and the same arbitrary bytes under **any other protocol type** are answered in 4 ms, because
  `computeSubscribedTopics` matches `Some(ConsumerProtocol.PROTOCOL_TYPE)` alone. A client of a `consumer` group
  must therefore send a real `Subscription` as its member metadata; `GroupMembershipApiTest` uses the protocol
  type `t3-membership` for the tests whose payloads are arbitrary.
  → "Group membership protocol (keys 11 to 14)".
* **(2.2) A first join is refused once, and costs the group nothing.** From JoinGroup **v4** (KIP-394) a request
  with an empty member id is answered **immediately** with the error code **79** (`MemberIdRequired`) and the id
  the coordinator generated; the client sends the same request again with that id. Measured: the 79 comes back in
  0 ms, no rebalance is started, and a client that never comes back leaves the group in the state `Empty` with 0
  members until the pending entry expires after the session timeout of that request. A **v3** join with an empty
  member id is still added to the group at once. → "The member id of a first join (v4, KIP-394)".
* **(2.2) The 81 `GroupMaxSizeReached` cannot be produced on this container.** `group.max.size` (KIP-394) bounds
  the members of a group and defaults to `2147483647`; it is **not** a dynamically updatable broker config in
  Kafka 2.8, so it cannot be lowered without restarting the broker. The code and its exception exist and the
  behaviour is documented from `GroupCoordinator.acceptJoiningMember` @ 2.8.2 - a join above the bound is answered
  81 with an empty member id, after the member has been removed from the group - and it is not asserted here.
* **(2.3) A static member joins without the 79, and keeps its partitions across a restart.** A JoinGroup **v5**
  that carries a `group_instance_id` (KIP-345) is never refused with 79 - `requireKnownMemberId` is
  `version >= 4 && groupInstanceId.isEmpty` @ 2.8.2 - and the member id the coordinator generates for it is
  `<group.instance.id>-<uuid>`, not `<client.id>-<uuid>`. When the same instance id joins again with an empty
  member id while the group is `Stable`, the **generation does not change** and the SyncGroup that follows returns
  the assignment of the old member id: measured 1 → 1 with the three partitions back, answered in 0 ms.
  → "Static membership (KIP-345)".
* **(2.3) Taking an instance id over fences the older consumer for good.** The second consumer to join under a
  `group.instance.id` gets a new member id and the group keeps its generation; every request of the first one is
  answered **82** (`FencedInstanceId`) from then on - measured on Heartbeat v3 and per partition on OffsetCommit
  v7. The answer to the *taking-over* join still names the **old** member id in `leader_id`, because
  `leaderOrNull` is read before `replaceGroupInstance` swaps the ids. → "Static membership (KIP-345)".
* **(2.4) The top-level error code of a batch LeaveGroup says nothing about its members.** From version 3
  (KIP-345) `handleLeaveGroup` @ 2.8.2 answers **0** at the top for every batch it could read and puts the fate of
  each member into its own entry: 0 for a member that was removed, **25** for an instance id or member id the group
  does not have - which is also what *every* entry of a request against a group the coordinator has never heard of
  gets - and 82 for a member id that lost its instance. An empty batch is legal and is answered with 0 and an empty
  member array. The entries **echo the identity that was sent**, so one that named its member by the instance id
  comes back with an empty member id. → "The batch leave of KIP-345 (v3)".
* **(2.4) A pending member can remove itself.** A client that was refused with the 79 of KIP-394 and never came
  back is in `group.pendingMembers`, not in the group; a LeaveGroup that names the member id it was handed is
  answered **0** and takes it out of that list (`removePendingMemberAndUpdateGroup` @ 2.8.2) - measured.
  → "The batch leave of KIP-345 (v3)".
* **(2.3) "Not asked for" is not the empty bit set.** DescribeGroups **v3** (KIP-430) answers a group whose
  `include_authorized_operations` was `false` - and every group entry that carries an error code - with
  `authorized_operations = -2147483648` (`Integer.MIN_VALUE`), the default of `DescribeGroupsResponse.json`
  @ 2.8.2. With the flag `true` the container answers **328**, the bits 3, 6 and 8 (READ, DELETE, DESCRIBE):
  `AclEntry.supportedOperations(GROUP)` in full, because the broker runs without an authorizer.
  → "The authorized operations of a group (v3, KIP-430)".
* **(2.5) The rebalance timeout is also the SyncGroup deadline.** `onCompleteJoin` schedules a `DelayedSync` with
  `group.rebalanceTimeoutMs` (KAFKA-9752, the pending-sync expiration of KIP-345) and `onExpirePendingSync` removes
  every member of the fresh generation that has not sent its SyncGroup by then, which starts another rebalance. A
  member that joined with `rebalance_timeout = 0` is therefore gone before it can use the answer it just received:
  the LeaveGroup right after such a join is answered 25 (`UnknownMemberId`). → "SyncGroup API (key 14, v0 to v5)".
* **(2.x) A successful FindCoordinator answer carries the error message `"NONE"`.** Every answer of
  `KafkaApis.handleFindCoordinatorRequest` @ 2.8.2 is built with `Errors.message()`, and `Errors.NONE.message()`
  is the *name* of the constant, so the `NULLABLE_STRING` that version 1 added is `00 04 "NONE"` where a 0.11 or
  1.1 broker sent `ff ff`. A client still acts on the error code alone.
  → "GroupCoordinator API (key 10, v0 to v6)".
* **(2.x) An unknown `coordinator_type` is answered, not punished with a closed connection.** A 2.8.2 broker
  answers a FindCoordinator v1 or v2 whose type is neither 0 nor 1 with the error code **42** (`InvalidRequest`),
  the generic message of that code and the placeholder coordinator `-1:"":-1`, where a 0.11 or 1.1 broker let
  `CoordinatorType.forId` throw and closed the channel. Version 0 has no type byte and ignores the question.
  → "GroupCoordinator API (key 10, v0 to v6)".
* **The `members` array of a JoinGroup answer is filled only for the leader**, and its order is the order of the
  coordinator's internal map, not the order in which the members joined. An assignor must therefore sort what it
  gets — both assignors of this client do. → "JoinGroup API (key 11, v0 to v9)".
* **Heartbeat checks the group before the member**: an unknown member of a rebalancing group is answered 27
  (`RebalanceInProgress`), not 25 (`UnknownMemberId`), and while the coordinator is loading the group it answers 0
  to everything. → "Heartbeat API (key 12, v0 to v4)".
* **A member id is `<client id>-<uuid>`** and the first generation of a group is **1**.
  → "Group membership protocol (keys 11 to 14)".
* **(0.10) A group whose last member leaves survives as `Empty`.** It keeps its committed offsets until
  `offsets.retention.minutes` expires them, is still listed by ListGroups, is described as `Empty` with its
  protocol type and no members, and answers JoinGroup normally so that a new member can take it over. A 0.9.0.1
  coordinator dropped such a group at once and answered `Dead` for it, which made "everybody left" and "never
  existed" indistinguishable. DescribeGroups still answers `Dead` with the error code 0 for a group that really
  does not exist, and `ClientHost` still arrives in Java's `InetAddress` notation, with a leading slash
  (`/172.18.0.1`). → "DescribeGroups API (key 15, v0 to v6)".
* **An `Empty` group without committed offsets does not survive the next cleanup pass.** What keeps such a group
  alive is its offsets, not the retention: `GroupMetadataManager.cleanupGroupMetadata` — every
  `offsets.retention.check.interval.ms`, 600000 by default — transitions an `Empty` group whose `hasOffsets` is
  false to `Dead` and removes it immediately, so a test that leaves a group empty and then lists it races that
  pass unless the group committed something first. On this container the log says
  `Group … transitioned to Dead in generation 2` for a batch of them at once.
  → "DescribeGroups API (key 15, v0 to v6)".

* **(0.10) The coordinator waits the `RebalanceTimeout` of JoinGroup v1, not the session timeout.** A member that
  joined with `session = 30000, rebalance = 4000` and then went silent delayed the join of the next member by
  exactly 4.00 s; the same experiment with **v0** frames and `session = 10000` took 10.00 s, because
  `JoinGroupRequest.rebalanceTimeout` falls back to the session timeout for a v0 frame. The rebalance timeout is
  bounded by nothing - `group.max.session.timeout.ms` of the broker applies to the *session* timeout alone, so
  `rebalance = 300000` is accepted on a broker whose maximum is 60000, and `rebalance = 0` is accepted too (which
  on a 2.x broker costs the member its membership, see the pending-sync bullet above).
  → "`RebalanceTimeout`, the wire half of `max.poll.interval.ms` (v1, Kafka 0.10.1, KIP-62)".

**Topic administration (the controller apis)**

* **Only the controller can create or delete a topic**; every other broker answers 41 (`NotController`) for a topic
  it is asked about. The controller is the `ControllerId` of a Metadata v1/v2 answer, and a 41 means that id is
  stale. → "CreateTopics API (key 19, v0 to v7)".
* **An unparsable option *value* is answered -1, an unknown option *name* 40.** `LogConfig.validate` throws Kafka's
  own `InvalidConfigurationException` (an `ApiException`, code 40) for a name it does not know but the plain
  `ConfigException` for a value it cannot parse, and `Errors.forException` has no code for that one.
  **(0.11) The message text of the first case changed**: `LogConfig.validateNames()` @ 0.11.0.3 throws
  `Unknown topic config name: no.such.option`, where 0.10.2.2 let the generic `AbstractConfig` throw
  `Unknown Log configuration no.such.option.` — same code, same shape of answer, different `ErrorMessage`. A client
  that matched on the text broke; matching on the code did not.
  → "CreateTopics API (key 19, v0 to v7)".
* **`timeout = 0` answers 7 (`RequestTimedOut`) and does the work anyway**: the topic is in the metadata about 50 ms
  later, and a deletion finishes just as well. An assignment that names a broker id the cluster does not have is
  accepted and answered 7 as well - the topic is written to ZooKeeper and never gets a leader.
  → "CreateTopics API (key 19, v0 to v7)".
* **A DeleteTopics request with an empty topic array is answered with an empty array**, by the controller and by
  every follower alike: `KafkaApis.handleDeleteTopicsRequest` maps over the topics of the *request*. That is why the
  controller probe of `AdminClient::findController()` names one topic whose name can never be legal instead.
  Deleting a topic that does not exist answers 3 and creates nothing. → "DeleteTopics API (key 20, v0 to v6)".

**Records and configuration (the admin apis 21, 32 and 33)**

* **(0.11) DeleteRecords goes to the LEADER of a partition, not to the controller.** It is the only one of the five
  admin apis that is split per partition leader, like Produce and Fetch, and it reports the new low watermark of
  every partition - the same number that `Offsets(EARLIEST)` and the `log_start_offset` of a Fetch v5 answer carry.
  A consumer that was reading below the new watermark gets 1 (OffsetOutOfRange) on its next fetch.
  → "DeleteRecords API (key 21, v0 to v2)".
* **(0.11) An offset above the high watermark is 1, and so is every negative offset except -1.**
  `ReplicaManager.deleteRecordsOnLocalLog` resolves -1 to the high watermark and then rejects anything below zero
  with an `OffsetOutOfRangeException`, so `-2` - "earliest" in the Offsets api - is answered **1** and not 42.
  Deleting at or below the watermark the partition already has is **not** an error: it answers 0 and the current
  watermark, because `Log.maybeIncrementLogStartOffset` only moves it forward. → "DeleteRecords API (key 21, v0 to v2)".
* **(0.11) DeleteRecords does not create a topic that does not exist**, although the broker runs with
  `auto.create.topics.enable=true`: `KafkaApis` only asks `metadataCache.contains(topic)` and answers 3 for every
  requested partition of it. → "DeleteRecords API (key 21, v0 to v2)".
* **(0.11) DescribeConfigs answers a topic that does not exist with the DEFAULTS and the error code 0.**
  `AdminUtils.fetchEntityConfig` returns empty properties for a missing ZooKeeper node and the broker merges them
  with its own log defaults, so the api says nothing about whether a topic exists. An option name the broker does
  not know is dropped from the answer just as silently - the entry list simply comes back shorter, with the error
  code 0. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".
* **(0.11) A broker resource is answered by that broker alone**, with 42 everywhere else, and a broker id that is
  not a number with 42 and `Broker id must be an integer, but it is: nope`. The value of a `PASSWORD` option is
  always `null` on the wire - in the entry and in every synonym of it.
  **(1.1) The message of the wrong broker id and the meaning of `ReadOnly` both changed**: it now reads
  `Unexpected broker id, expected 0 or empty string, but received Resource(type=BROKER, name='7'}.name` (the
  literal `.name` is a Scala interpolation bug of `AdminManager.describeConfigs` @ 1.1.1, and the empty string is
  the cluster-wide default resource of KIP-226), where 0.11 said `Unexpected broker id, expected 0, but received
  7`; and an entry of a broker resource is read-only only when **no** name of it is in
  `DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs` — `broker.id` is read-only, `log.retention.hours` is not, although
  altering it is still refused. → "DescribeConfigs API (key 32, v0 to v4)".
* **(0.11) AlterConfigs REPLACES the configuration of a topic.** An option that was set and is not in the request is
  reset to its default, and an empty entry array resets all of them - the broker builds a fresh `Properties` and
  overwrites the ZooKeeper node. Any broker serves the request; the controller is not involved.
  → "AlterConfigs API (key 33, v0 to v2)".
* **(0.11) AlterConfigs answers a topic that does not exist and a `null` config value with -1**, because
  `AdminOperationException` and the `NullPointerException` of `Properties.setProperty` are not `ApiException`s. An
  unparsable option **value** is 42 here and -1 through CreateTopics, an unknown option **name** is 40 in both.
  → "AlterConfigs API (key 33, v0 to v2)".
* **(1.1) A broker resource is accepted now, and refused per option.** Where 0.11 answered every broker resource
  with 42 and `AlterConfigs is only supported for topics, but resource type is BROKER`, a 1.1 broker applies the
  options of `DynamicBrokerConfig.AllDynamicConfigs` at once and answers 42 with
  `Cannot update these configs dynamically: Set(log.retention.hours)` for anything else — refusing the **whole**
  resource, with `validate_only` or without it. The cluster-wide **default** resource is the resource type 4 with
  an *empty* name; a security option on it is refused with `These security configs can be dynamically updated only
  per-listener using the listener prefix: Set(ssl.keystore.location)`.
  → "The dynamic broker configuration (KIP-226)".
* **(1.1) An unknown option NAME of a broker resource is accepted, not answered 40.** The broker cannot type a name
  it does not know, so it stores the value in ZooKeeper and DescribeConfigs reports it back as a
  `DYNAMIC_BROKER_CONFIG` that is **sensitive**, with a `null` value. A topic answers 40 for the same mistake.
  → "The dynamic broker configuration (KIP-226)".
* **(1.1) Removing a dynamic broker option does not always restore the value the broker runs with.** The entry
  disappears from the config store while the live `KafkaConfig` keeps the last value it was given, so a test (or an
  operator) that wants the documented default back has to write it explicitly before it removes the entry.
  → "The dynamic broker configuration (KIP-226)".

**(1.1) Growing a topic and deleting a group (the admin apis 37 and 42)**

* **(1.1) CreatePartitions can only grow a topic, and it says so with 37.** A count below the current one is
  `Topic currently has 3 partitions, which is higher than the requested 2.` and a count equal to it
  `Topic already has 3 partitions.`, both **37** (`InvalidPartitions`). An unknown topic is **3** with
  `The topic '…' does not exist.` — the api does not create it, although the container runs with
  `auto.create.topics.enable=true` — and the same topic twice in one request is **42** with
  `Duplicate topic in request.`. A `timeout` of 0 answers **7** and adds the partitions anyway, exactly as
  CreateTopics does. → "CreatePartitions API (key 37, v0 to v3)".
* **(1.1) The assignment of CreatePartitions names the ADDED partitions only.** Its length has to be the number of
  new partitions and its width the replication factor: `Increasing the number of partitions by 2 but 1 assignments
  provided.` and `Unknown broker(s) in replica assignment: 7.` are both **39** (`InvalidReplicaAssignment`).
  → "CreatePartitions API (key 37, v0 to v3)".
* **(1.1) DeleteGroups is 68 for a group that has a member and 69 for one the coordinator does not know.** A group
  that is `Empty` is deleted with the code 0 — it disappears from ListGroups, its committed offsets are tombstoned
  and `describeGroup()` answers `Dead` — while a group with a live member is **68** (`NonEmptyGroup`) and an
  unknown group id, or one that was just deleted, is **69** (`GroupIdNotFound`). An **empty** group id is **24**
  (`InvalidGroupId`), and the same group twice in one request collapses, because the broker reads a `Set`.
  → "DeleteGroups API (key 42, v0 to v2)".
* **(1.1) An `Empty` group without a committed offset does not stay deletable.**
  `GroupMetadataManager.cleanupGroupMetadata()` drops such a group every `offsets.retention.check.interval.ms`
  (600 s on the container), so a group that is to be deleted through the protocol has to carry an offset.
  → "DeleteGroups API (key 42, v0 to v2)".

**(0.11, 1.0) The idempotent producer**

* **(0.11) A duplicate batch of a producer is answered with the error code 0 and the offset of the original
  append**, not with an error at all, and its `LogAppendTime` is the timestamp the log holds - which is how a
  `CreateTime` topic, whose real appends answer `-1`, gives a duplicate away. → "The idempotent producer".
* **(1.0) The broker remembers the last five batches of a producer id and partition**, not the single one 0.11
  kept (`ProducerStateEntry.NumBatchesToRetain = 5` @ 1.0.2 and 1.1.1). A duplicate of any of the five is answered
